full_text:
Quarterback Michael Penix Jr. was a full competitor at practice Monday for the first time since suffering a torn ACL last season. Dale Zanine / Imagn Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — The Atlanta Falcons’ quarterback competition can now begin! Or, it has already started. Or, it may never end.
It’s hard to keep up, but Monday was a significant step as Michael Penix Jr. returned to the field in full health for the first time since suffering a season-ending ACL tear in Week 11 last year.
“This is a big step for Mike, and he’s excited about it,” Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said.
What Stefanski didn’t say was whether Penix will play, alongside the rest of Atlanta’s starters, in Friday’s preseason finale against the Miami Dolphins. Or if it’s realistic to think Penix could overtake Tua Tagovailoa for the starting job by the regular-season opener, which is only 21 days away.
“I can’t speculate on those types of things,” Stefanski said. “I want to really stay in today with Mike and see how he does in practice. I really have to stay in the moment with this one. Let’s see how he feels after today.”
Penix was cleared last week by his surgeon to return to full 11-on-11 practice work . He has participated in team activities and seven-on-seven drills since the offseason, so Monday was only a small increase to his workload. But it was a significant one.
“It’s cool seeing him in 11-on-11 action,” wide receiver Jahan Dotson said. “It’s exciting for him. I know it’s been a tough journey for him. It’s good to see him on the opposite side of that. He had a little scramble today, which was cool to see.”
Penix was 4-for-8 passing Monday in 11-on-11 drills. He threw two passes noticeably short while under simulated pressure in the pocket (defenders aren’t allowed to touch quarterbacks in practice), but he also threw two on-target intermediate completions to Kyle Pitts and Drake London later in the practice. Penix has acknowledged that he has to overcome the mental hurdle of anticipating contact to his knee.
“There’s a way to play this game, and you have to play it free,” Stefanski said. “I think Mike takes great comfort in knowing he’s done everything he can to get his body ready. This is Day 1 of 11-on-11 for him. We will get through today, check in and have a plan for tomorrow.”
Tagovailoa took the first 11-on-11 reps of the day with the starters and in scout-team work but finished 0-for-3 passing. Penix did not speak to the media Monday. He is expected to talk Wednesday. There is still no timetable for naming a starter.
“Competition is near and dear to all of our hearts,” Stefanski said. “You are competing every single day. That alarm clock goes off, you’re competing. Everything we do in this building is about competing.”
Penix’s status is not the only quarterback question the Falcons have to answer. The competition for the No. 3 spot got very interesting Friday after undrafted free agent rookie Jack Strand went 12-of-17 for 212 yards and a touchdown against the Colts. The Division II product played well enough that a portion of the fan base is lobbying online for him to be elevated into the starting competition, but it doesn’t sound like that is in the Falcons’ plans.
“At this point, Jack is going to continue to work with the twos and threes, but we’re very excited about his development,” Stefanski said. “Player development is huge in what we do, and being intentional about how we bring players along is important to us.”
Strand is 18-of-29 passing for 262 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions in two preseason appearances. He is second in the NFL in yards per attempt (9.0) in preseason games.
“We want to make sure we put all our young guys, Jack included, through a process,” Stefanski said. “He’s doing everything we are asking him to do, but we are not going to put those types of conversations out there for our guys to worry about. He’s got to focus on the day-to-day.”
Strand’s family informed him after Friday’s game that he had briefly become an internet sensation, he said.
“They are kind of taking it in stride like I am,” he said. “They are happy for me that I have the opportunity to play football professionally, keep getting to play this game that I love. That’s kind of where I am at, too.”
NFL teams must trim their rosters to 53 players by Aug. 30 and can then begin filling their 16-man practice squads.
“I just want to be the best football player I can be, help the team in whatever way possible,” Strand said. “I’m not really focused on (cutdown day). I want to be where I’m at today. I was focused on practice today. I just want to be where my feet are.”

title: Rookie WR Ja'Kobi Lane has been the fun-filled star of Ravens training camp Lane's vibrant personality has brought energy and juice to Baltimore's locker room and allowed for an immediate kinship with Lamar Jackson. Jeff Zrebiec
summary:

OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Fans got off buses outside the Under Armour Performance Center and were serenaded by members of Baltimore’s Marching Ravens. Persistent cheers emanated from outside the locker room, where kids flanked the ramp to see the Ravens take the practice field. Quarterback Lamar Jackson’s arrival drew the biggest roar.
full_text:
Ja'Kobi Lane has been one of the more impressive players in Ravens camp, potentially earning himself a role in the offense as a rookie. Kara Durrette / Associated Press
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Fans got off buses outside the Under Armour Performance Center and were serenaded by members of Baltimore’s Marching Ravens. Persistent cheers emanated from outside the locker room, where kids flanked the ramp to see the Ravens take the practice field. Quarterback Lamar Jackson’s arrival drew the biggest roar.
Yet, there was one area where the noise rose above the typical buzz from the first practice of training camp. In the far bleachers, fans cheered and chanted.
The ringleader of it all was a 22-year-old rookie who hugged and high-fived his new fans and exhorted them to get louder. What? Did you expect Ja’Kobi Lane to be nervous ahead of his first practice?
“I think people sometimes feel that they have to be super serious to get to where they want to be,” Lane said. “Yes, you realize that hard work, dedication and being able to maintain a consistent level and lifestyle, that does matter. But there’s too much fun to be had in this world. I’m a very big testimony of that.”
Few Ravens have ever made as good a first impression. Lane’s acrobatic and seemingly effortless catches have enthralled a fan base obsessed with the idea of a dynamic homegrown receiving corps. His vibrant personality has brought energy and juice to the locker room and allowed for an immediate kinship with Jackson and the team’s offensive stars.
From his dancing into the building on report day to his rapping to Kodak Black at a team dinner to the live footage of him on a roller coaster last week at the Mall of America, Lane has been the star of the Ravens’ show this summer.
Drafted into an organization often derided as a wide receiver graveyard, the Arizona native and former USC standout says he couldn’t imagine being in a better place.
“My personality fits very well in the sense of being able to come to work and just be myself and not be worried about people trying to tell me what to do or trying to dictate how my day is going to go,” Lane said.
“It’s your option to do whatever you want, but you see guys like Derrick (Henry), Lamar, Mark (Andrews), they come in every day and work as hard as they can. The proof is in the pudding. It’s just crazy to think that now I’m in this position.”
For Lane, his impressive start with the Ravens is a continuation of what’s been true throughout his young life. When he’s comfortable, when he feels free to be himself, the results follow. So do the smiles.
The match was obvious. The Ravens have long coveted a big-bodied receiver who makes contested catches and plays “above the rim.” Lane, who’s 6-foot-4, 205 pounds, has 10.5-inch hands and a 40-inch vertical, fits the profile. There were legitimate questions about his high-end speed and ability to play through NFL physicality, but Lane got the ultimate stamp of Baltimore approval.
One of Lane’s coaches at Red Mountain High School in Mesa, Ariz., was longtime NFL tight end Todd Heap, who just happens to be in the Ravens’ Ring of Honor and is one of the most respected players in franchise history. General manager Eric DeCosta had a FaceTime call with Heap during Lane’s pre-draft visit.
“You don’t see a lot of kids with his talent, especially in high school,” Heap said. “Obviously, if you’re bigger, faster and stronger, you’re going to be a matchup problem. But I’ve been more impressed with how he moves his body and gets in and out of breaks. He’s really good for a guy his size in dropping his hips.”
Heap quickly became a mentor to Lane, and their relationship persisted through the wide receiver’s time at USC. Heap was hard on Lane because he saw the potential. He also recognized a kid who wanted to do the right things, but was learning to balance having fun with properly honoring and preparing for an enticing athletic future.
Displeased with Lane’s effort on a low throw during one practice, Heap followed the wide receiver back to the huddle and offered an ultimatum of sorts.
“Do you want me to tell you what you want to hear or do you want me to tell you what you need to improve on?” Heap asked Lane.
Lane’s response came quickly: “Can you keep lying to me a little bit longer?” he said.
Heap and everyone else on the field broke out in laughter. That was the essence of Lane. He loves football, always has. He knows when he’s erred. But he’s never going to take it too seriously where he can’t laugh at himself.
“I want him to stay young and fun-loving forever,” Heap said. “There are going to be ups and downs. It’s not going to go perfectly and smoothly. You have to be able to weather that storm. I want him to stay consistent and know that football is your livelihood and it’s extremely important, but it’s not the most important thing to who you are.”
Lane is a product of a one-parent household. He calls his mother, Megan, his rock and clings tightly to the lessons he learned from her. She always made it clear to her son that outsiders will have opinions, both good and bad, but he only needed to worry about being comfortable in his own skin and staying true to who he was.
That lesson has helped him navigate his first training camp and ignore the outside hype that surges with every catch made on the practice field.
She also taught him about the importance of acceptance. Megan opened her home to foster children and Lane grew close to several of them along the way. He credits those relationships with helping him learn to communicate better with people from different walks of life.
“I’ve been around kids with a lot of money, and I’ve also been around kids that are less fortunate,” Lane said. “I think it’s being able to see both sides of it and not see two different things. It’s how people live, and it’s not good, bad or indifferent. My mom never made it seem like it was a problem for everything. It was one of those things where people powered through their situation, and if you really wanted it, you would get it.”
Lane had other influences in his life, too. Leo Aviles was Lane’s youth football coach who opened a lot of doors for the youngster. He’s become Lane’s guardian. Another Mesa native, Terry Brennan, also became a major advocate and source of support. Lane had former NFL players, Heap and Chase Lucas, as role models, too.
“A lot of people behind the scenes,” Lane said. “The list goes on and on. It was more just being able to have people to lean on and not necessarily when things were going wrong, but also when things were going right and being able to maintain a level head.”
His athletic talent was obvious. Even in high school, Lane could effortlessly pluck a ball out of the air with either hand. He would watch Odell Beckham Jr. do it online and practice it himself. He once broke his hand while playing Pop Warner football, so he taught himself to catch with his healthy hand. He then broke that hand about a week later.
That’s not to say everything came easy for him, though. He didn’t become a regular contributor on the Red Mountain High football team until he was a junior. Lane’s acrobatic catches on the seven-on-seven circuit helped earn him the attention of recruiters and made him a YouTube sensation.
Even when he arrived at USC as a four-star recruit, Lane didn’t immediately contribute. He had to wait his turn, and some of the Trojans’ coaches were worried they could be losing him while he did.
“The notion of him not being engaged wasn’t really one of those issues,” said Dennis Simmons, Lane’s wide receiver coach at USC and also the Trojans’ assistant head coach and co-offensive coordinator. “It was just a matter of him just making the transition, relearning verbiage and being detailed on his alignments and his assignments. Once he got that down, and understood it like the back of his hand, he was obviously able to step in and let his talents be showcased.”
Lane’s first extensive run as a freshman for the Trojans…

full_text:
Aaron Rodgers led the Pittsburgh Steelers to 10 wins and an AFC North title in 2025. Mark Alberti / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
A quick glance at the AFC North oddsboard would suggest it’s either the Baltimore Ravens’ or Cincinnati Bengals’ to lose — but that’s also what the oddsboard indicated heading into last season, before the Pittsburgh Steelers emerged victorious.
Listed at +510 odds that give them around a 15 percent implied probability to win, major sportsbooks like DraftKings aren’t ruling the Steelers out, and neither is The Athletic’s predictive analyst Austin Mock. Let’s dive into how his model projects every AFC North team’s chances to win the division, make the playoffs and more.
It’s a long shot, but it’s entirely possible the Steelers could win the AFC North.
First, the roster is actually in pretty decent shape. It skews older, but there are still quality players on both sides of the ball. The offense has plenty of weapons with DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. at wide receiver, Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington at tight end, and Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle at running back. The offensive line is in pretty good shape as well. And while the linebacker group is average, the secondary has a good foundation and the defensive line has enough depth and potential to be awesome.
Of course, I left out a pretty important position. Aaron Rodgers’ prime is well behind him, but his reunion with Mike McCarthy could spark something. I wouldn’t say McCarthy is an elite offensive mind, but he has the ability to raise the offensive floor in Pittsburgh. And when you give him this much talent, there is a chance the Steelers could be around average (or slightly above). Would that good enough to win the division? I’m not sure. But paired with what should be a top-10 defense, they’re certainly good enough to challenge the Ravens and Bengals.
Another angle to factor in is that Baltimore and Cincinnati have pretty low floors.
Lamar Jackson was banged up last season and never quite seemed right. What if that spills into this season? Then you look at the Ravens’ offensive line and all of its question marks. The 32-year-old Derrick Henry has to eventually slow down. And the defense couldn’t generate pressure without blitzing last year. I’m bullish on coach Jesse Minter, and the addition of Trey Hendrickson should help, but that doesn’t guarantee a top-10 defense.
The team I’m most worried about is the Bengals. We know the offense is going to be really good if it’s healthy. And the Bengals finally added to a poor defense by trading for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence and adding pass rusher Boye Mafe in free agency. The Bengals were 14th in expected points added (EPA) per play on defense in the second half of last season, so I do believe they improve. But what if they don’t? And they’re still a well below average defense?
All of those possibilities are well within the range of outcomes, which gives me enough confidence to say the Steelers could defend their AFC North title. Is it likely? Probably not. But it’s possible.

full_text:
John Metchie III stood out against the Jaguars. Could he land one of the final WR spots for the Panthers? Melina Myers / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — About a half-hour after practice ended Monday, media members were still waiting for Chuba Hubbard.
As he does after every practice, the Carolina Panthers’ veteran running back was catching hundreds of balls shot at him out of a JUGS machine by a member of the equipment staff. It doesn’t matter that Hubbard hasn’t practiced in a couple of weeks because of a hamstring strain. His post-practice routine remains the same.
“It’s grown throughout the years,” Hubbard said. “I remember when we first started, it was probably, like, me, Tommy (Tremble), Terrace Marshall, maybe, like, one or two other people at times. … As time went on, more guys just want to get more work.”
Work has never been a problem for Hubbard, who is that rare player who tries to lead both vocally and by example. Hubbard doesn’t like to miss time. But after he returned too quickly from a calf injury last season, the Panthers are holding him back this summer.
“I feel pretty good. I think the coaches and training staff are just trying to take care of me,” he said. “Obviously, last year I kind of came back a little bit early, and it kind of lingered on for a little bit. So I think it’s just them protecting me from myself a little bit. I would have been out (practicing) the next day if I could’ve. But I feel good. I feel healthy. Just looking forward to Week 1.”
Getting a healthy Hubbard to the starting line is one of the most important issues facing the Panthers as they wrap up their preseason work with a joint practice with the Houston Texans on Wednesday before hosting the Texans two nights later in the exhibition finale. Provided Hubbard is good to go, Panthers coach Dave Canales said the plan is to have Hubbard and Jonathon Brooks share carries Week 1 against the Chicago Bears.
A look at four other items on the Panthers’ to-do list during the final week of training camp:
Xavier Legette still had a boot on his right foot Monday, five days after getting rolled up on during the practice with the Jacksonville Jaguars. Legette will get the boot off Thursday, but he will miss the Texans game with an eye on being 100 percent for the Sept. 13 opener.
As long as Legette doesn’t have any setbacks, the Panthers’ top three receivers are set with him, Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker. Brycen Tremayne is WR4 because of his blocking and special teams abilities. But there are still roster spots up for grabs beyond those first four.
Jimmy Horn Jr. and John Metchie III had big games against the Jaguars, and Ja’seem Reed caught touchdown passes in the first two preseason games. Casey Washington continues to make plays, as Canales noted. David Moore has been with Canales at all three of his NFL coaching stops, although Canales didn’t mention Moore on Monday when discussing the competition.
“It feels like we have about seven guys that I’d love to keep. I don’t know if we’re gonna be able to keep seven,” he said. “There’s been years where we were able to keep seven for a while. I don’t know if that’s possible. Those guys are competing. They’re pushing.”
The first-team offense looked better against Jacksonville than it did the previous week at Buffalo. That wasn’t a coincidence: Having guards Robert Hunt and Damien Lewis back in the lineup certainly helped.
Hunt (back) and Lewis (calf) were among several veterans who missed significant time during camp, along with Pro Bowl defensive tackle Derrick Brown (knee) and nose tackle Bobby Brown (hamstring). Canales indicated he would rest most starters Friday if they get enough work during Wednesday’s joint practice.
But he said it’s important the four aforementioned players keep building their stamina heading into the season. “Those are four guys that really need this week. They need Wednesday,” he said. “They need the following week and those couple of practices that we’ll get to get them up to speed from a conditioning standpoint.”
Waller put on pads Monday, a week after the 33-year-old tight end signed a one-year deal. Waller saw a few reps during team drills but wasn’t targeted. He’ll practice Wednesday, but he won’t play Friday as the team continues a slow ramp-up for a player who tore his quad at the Miami Dolphins’ camp in 2025 after ending a one-year retirement.
It was the first of three injuries last year for Waller, who caught 24 passes in nine games, including five in a Week 5 loss to Carolina. Canales said the Panthers will have to lean on Waller’s tape from last year in evaluating him.
“Hard to get an evaluation. We spent the first part of last week just running him and pushing him and making sure he was practice-ready,” Canales said. “We didn’t want to rush that part.”
Waller brings a size-speed element to a versatile tight end room. In our first roster projection that came out before the Jaguars exhibition game, we had Ja’Tavion Sanders missing the cut. But the fact that Sanders, the leading pass catcher among Carolina tight ends the past two seasons, was in sweats by the second half at Jacksonville seems like a good sign for the former Texas standout.
Because Waller is a vested veteran, he wouldn’t have to pass through waivers if the Panthers cut him. It’s possible they do that, then try to stash him on the practice squad until he is ready or they have a need at the position.
“It’s a good room. We love those guys and trust ’em. So (Waller) comes into a room to see if he can help us in some way,” Canales said. “But the guys are doing a great job of showing what they can do as well.”
There’s been a lot of talk this month about the inside linebacker battle between Trevin Wallace and Claudin Cherelus for the spot alongside Devin Lloyd. Given the amount of three-safety sets Ejiro Evero uses and Tre’von Moehrig’s prowess as an inside-the-box safety, the topic probably has gotten too much attention.
But no one has claimed the LB2 job yet, so Wallace and Cherelus will get a few more chances to separate from the other. Wallace, who started 20 games his first two seasons, is a better blitzer, but Cherelus is arguably stronger against the run. Both have had their struggles in coverage.
“We could use them both. And we’re gonna need them,” Canales said. “The nature of the position is a violent spot, and both of the guys can help us on special teams as well. So we’ll have to make that decision as we get closer.”

full_text:
Bears quarterback Caleb Williams' partnership with coach Ben Johnson continues to be a source of excitement in Chicago. Andy Lyons / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson seemed aggravated Saturday in Cincinnati, none too pleased with his team’s 27-9 preseason loss to the Bengals and more perturbed by all the clumsy stumbles that sent the Bears plummeting down that open manhole. The Bears committed 11 penalties, including a drive killer on the opening series, a hold by left tackle Braxton Jones that turned second-and-1 inside the red zone into first-and-20.
So much for the first-team offense — with quarterback Caleb Williams getting a brief cameo — delivering a feel-good touchdown drive to heighten the summer energy.
The defense, meanwhile, went without a sack and had just two tackles for loss across 58 plays. And the special teams miscues included a pushed 53-yard field goal attempt by Cairo Santos plus a shaky JP Richardson kickoff return that started with a muffed catch inside the end zone and included an illegal block by Qadir Ismail.
“It doesn’t matter if it’s preseason or not,” Johnson told reporters afterward. “It’s a bad feeling in that locker room after the game when you lose — particularly like that, when it’s by multiple scores. You don’t feel like you made it very close there at the end.”
Relatively speaking, in an August exhibition game with few significant stakes, Saturday’s loss feels easy to discard, particularly with the Bears quickly approaching the regular season and with their focus turning this week to a Thursday joint practice with the Titans in Nashville, Tenn.
But last weekend’s performance also likely gave Johnson and his staff plenty of video ammo to recapture their players’ attention. Thus, it’s vital that the Bears fashion a strong response.
In just two weeks, Johnson must have his group immersed in game-week preparation, locking in on a season-opening test at Carolina. The hope is, by then, that this group will be far more polished and effective than it was Saturday night and that Johnson will feel some wind at his back.
With that in mind, we’re offering this late-summer mood check from Halas Hall.
Goodness, does this offense have impressive weaponry for Johnson to play with. And it’s a big reason the hopes for a big developmental leap from Williams are realistic.
Running back D’Andre Swift? He’s had a terrific camp and could very easily emerge as the engine that gets the offense rolling in September.
Colston Loveland? He’s quickly put himself on track to become one of the most dangerous all-around tight ends in the league.
Wide receiver Rome Odunze? He’s been turning his coaches’ heads with consistent success on contested catches, which may increase his opportunities in the passing game.
Wide receiver Luther Burden III? Before a groin injury sidelined him this month, Burden was fast becoming a go-to target for Williams.
And Darnell Wright? Yes indeed, in Johnson’s eyes, an offensive tackle can count as a weapon when used properly.
Williams, meanwhile, continues to flash signs of growth. And Johnson, as one of the sport’s most respected offensive visionaries, brings a trust factor that generates significant excitement.
The unity between Johnson and Williams is as strong as ever, with the coach serving up an unlimited buffet of football knowledge and the quarterback constantly getting back in line for more.
What an incredible headspace that is for both men, particularly after the bumpy start they had in their first summer together. During training camp in 2025, Williams acknowledged he felt like he was drowning at times under Johnson’s demands and struggling to discern whether his coach even liked him. Johnson has revealed that, upon his arrival, he wasn’t fully certain Williams was coachable to the level he’d need to be to grow properly.
Now? The passion and intensity of Johnson and Williams are evident. But there’s minimal friction or anxiety in their day-to-day dealings.
Said Williams: “Everything he says to me, I’ll do it at 200 percent and won’t look back.”
Johnson’s review of his starting quarterback is truthful and to the point. He has no hesitation praising Williams for his elite arm talent, escape ability and playmaking prowess. “There are just so many layers to who he is as a player.”
But Johnson isn’t afraid to push — for better processing speed, for improved understanding of the game, for more steadiness.
“I think that word consistency comes up,” Johnson said. “Over the course of a 60-minute game or more, we need it to be where we’re playing high-level quarterback play all throughout that game. You see flashes and yet we’re trying to tap into that where we’re just consistently delivering the ball where it needs to go.”
And pleasantly so, by the depth and energy of the defensive tackle group. Justifiable outside concern has existed for months about whether the Bears have enough juice up front to cause consistent disruption. Yet on the interior, Dennis Allen’s defense seems to have so many hungry defensive tackles that final decisions on who makes the 53-man roster may prove difficult.
The defensive tackle room has established, intelligent veterans (Grady Jarrett, Neville Gallimore); eager rookies (Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving); and a starter in Gervon Dexter who’s in a contract year and feeling a confidence spike from the technical improvements the coaching staff has helped him make.
There is also Kentavius Street (an eighth-year vet on his fifth team) and James Lynch (now in his sixth season), both signed this spring as potential depth pieces.
“It’s one of the better defensive tackle groups I’ve been in,” Dexter said.
Added Gallimore: “The thing I love most about this group is everybody is just selfless. Everybody just comes to work every day and wants to compete, get better and do their job to the best of their abilities for whoever is to their left and right. I feel like that’s what you need.”
The Bears carried only four defensive tackles into last season’s season opener. So sorting through this competition and figuring out potential roles will be important this week.
The Bears’ signing of soon-to-be 30-year-old defensive end Marcus Davenport crossed the transaction wire Aug. 17. Yet Davenport, who has missed 37 games over the previous three seasons, is continuing a conditioning ramp-up phase and has yet to participate in practice.
It remains to be seen how quickly he might have an impact in the defensive line rotation — and how long he can stay on the field.
“Obviously the biggest thing for Marcus — and it’s been that way throughout his career — is his ability to be healthy and maintain his health,” Allen said last week. “But when he’s out there, he’s a disruptive force.”
Allen was the New Orleans Saints’ defensive coordinator when they drafted Davenport in the first round in 2018. Allen was still in that role in 2021 when Davenport delivered a career-high nine sacks in 11 games. So the defensive coordinator has credibility when he labels Davenport “a good fit” for what the Bears are building while lauding his mentality and ability to create opportunities for others.
“He has always been a disruptive player,” Allen said. “You can put on a lot of tape and see him in the backfield creating a lot of disruption.”
Davenport’s contract with the Bears includes a $1.3 million base salary. So his arrival offers a low-risk opportunity to enliven the pass rush. Said Johnson: “He’s going to add some competition for us on the edge. He’s still a very hungry and motivated individual. And we’ve got a plan for how we want him to come back and be able to help us out.”
Of the 46 players listed in the first two columns of the depth chart on offense or defense in last week’s game release, 17 have dealt with injury during camp. The current wait-and-see injury list includes receiver Burden (hamstring), running back Kyle Monangai (knee), cornerback Tyrique Stevenson (undisclosed) and backup…

full_text:
Javon Foster looks like the in-house frontrunner for the Bengals' swing tackle spot. Jay LaPrete / Associated Press
CINCINNATI — At the start of training camp, Cody Ford was the favorite to serve as the backup offensive tackle to starters Amarius Mims and Orlando Brown Jr.
Less than a month later, he was cut by the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday.
Brown endured rough moments in camp and the games, but the problems behind him have grown to the biggest concern on an otherwise stocked roster.
“This whole thing is not concluded yet,” head coach Zac Taylor said.
The question for Taylor on Monday was simple: Is this team’s Week 1 swing tackle currently on the roster?
“I think we’re always open to everything,” he said. “These guys are really competing. I feel like I’d like to see someone grab it and us be able to say that. But certainly with time still to practice, we got some stuff to sort out.”
Let’s dive into that stuff. Myriad options exist.
The Bengals land in a unique spot this year. They boast a desirable excess of talent at key positions (defensive line, receiver, tight end) and clear potential to add serviceable depth at swing tackle. That could mean an available veteran via trade or waiver wire cut.
The cutdown to 53 must be made by 6 p.m. ET Sunday. The situation offers options for a potential deal, but what would that trade look like? How likely are the Bengals to swing one? What impact will the current roster and Ford’s release have on the situation?
Here’s a look at the Bengals’ top trade candidates and the offensive tackle options that could be available via trade, waiver wire or in-house.
This list essentially serves as veterans on the current roster bubble, nearly all with rookies pushing them for a roster spot. The Bengals have not cut a draft pick after their first preseason since 2020.
DT Kris Jenkins. The 2024 second-round pick might stick on the roster, but the strong preseason from seventh-round rookie Landon Robinson makes his departure a possibility. Jenkins has never quite taken off in Cincinnati, but he’s still a second-round pick with potential. He also looked good in the preseason opener last year but could be the odd man out among a deep defensive line.
TE Tanner Hudson. A favorite of Joe Burrow (and every other quarterback to come through Cincinnati) with 77 receptions for 674 yards and four touchdowns over the last three seasons. But would the Bengals keep five tight ends again? Rookie Jack Endries has looked the part thus far. They still like Hudson, but could go young and get by without him if there’s a solid return.
WR/KR/PR Charlie Jones. He has returned a kick for a touchdown in three consecutive seasons, the only person who can make such a claim. His time at receiver has been limited behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins in Cincinnati and injuries have derailed too many seasons. If the Bengals go with Ke’Shawn Williams or Dohnte Meyers as the returner, the fourth-year pro could provide value to a WR-needy team.
WR Mitchell Tinsley. Somebody with quality NFL experience at receiver easily could be left off this roster. If it’s Tinsley, a team in need of a playmaker could find a match. His tape from last preseason and regular season, making acrobatic plays, would be tantalizing if Cincinnati opts to keep Meyers and Jones/Williams instead.
If looking for a list of veterans who could be acquired as teams enjoy enough depth at surrounding spots, it’s not particularly long or renowned, but full of players who could provide NFL starting experience and stability.
Fred Johnson, Philadelphia Eagles. Perhaps the best potential fit. The Eagles love what third-round pick Markel Bell showed this camp and appear poised to hand over the swing tackle role to the rookie. If they do, Johnson could have value. He has started 14 games over the last two seasons. He began his career with the Bengals in 2019 and played three seasons in Cincinnati. Would bring a proven veteran, a personality they know and experience. Also, was traded in August last year, so he’s familiar with starting over right before a season.
Trent Brown/Blake Fisher, Houston Texans. The Texans run four-deep at offensive tackle and are scary thin at receiver after the Jayden Higgins injury. Trading for New England Patriots’ Kayshon Boutte might have eased that pain, but general manager Nick Caserio has never been shy to deal. Brown was in Cincinnati just two years ago before suffering an injury. He obviously fits the tackle profile at 6-foot-8, 380 pounds, and the Bengals know what they’d be getting. Fisher is younger, but a second-round pick in his own right. He was selected 10 spots after Jenkins.
Matt Peart, Denver Broncos. Started 10 games in six seasons with the New York Giants and Broncos. Denver has the luxury of talent and depth at the position and could have interest in a pick or player. The 29-year-old would be an upgrade from the current options in camp, without question. Could probably be acquired for a late-round pick swap or player.
Looking for a young player showing promise elsewhere, who would be outside the roster bubble or available in a trade.
Christian Jones, Arizona Cardinals. He’s only played in four games with one start for the Cardinals since being selected in the fifth round in 2024. He’s looked improved this preseason, but it still might not be enough to crack the two-deep. He’s an intriguing option to pull off the waiver wire or offer a nominal trade to secure.
Albert Reese, Carolina Panthers. At 6-7, 330 pounds, he’s an undrafted rookie out of Mississippi State. He’s played great this preseason with the second-most snaps of any tackle and also the second-highest grade, according to PFF. He’s played solely at right tackle.
Chase Lundt, Buffalo Bills. There’s a roster crunch at tackle for the Bills, and Lundt finds himself on the bubble at the back of the rotation. Could be a waiver add or force the issue with a trade. He’s a sixth-round pick out of Connecticut in 2025.
The crop of available free agents is small, with many recently retiring, considering retirement or dealing with injuries. Former Bengals OL Jonah Williams is among that last group and not considered an option.
Cam Robinson. He has bounced around the league but made $74.8 million over the course of his career. He will turn 31 in October. He spent his first seven seasons with the Jacksonville Jaguars, but was involved in multiple trades, playing for four teams in the past two years (Jaguars, Cleveland Browns, Minnesota Vikings, Texans). He has 114 NFL starts.
Ford’s direct path to a roster spot closed once he failed to assume the swing tackle job and was moved back inside to guard. Despite three seasons where versatility provided value as a backup, the Bengals wanted to go young and liked the development from that group.
Jacob Bayer, Connor Lew and Brian Parker II all offered encouraging signs in recent weeks. Second-year pro Jalen Rivers still has a solid 2025 rookie season at guard on his resume.
The time was now to go young on the interior. The same youth movement could happen at tackle.
Rivers kicked outside to tackle over the last week but endured rough moments in the preseason game as he adjusts to being back at a spot he spent half his time at the University of Miami.
The leader in the clubhouse to hold the swing spot right now is Javon Foster. He was drafted by Jacksonville in the fourth round in 2024. The Jags cut him last year, and Cincinnati quickly scooped him up for the practice squad.
He’s shown improvement over time and specifically gained trust over the first two preseason games. He allowed just one pressure and no hits on the quarterbacks in 39 pass-blocking snaps on Saturday.
“Javon, big jump from Day 1 to now as he has taken to the coaching, he has done much better,” offensive line coach Scott Peters said. “If you are vying for that third tackle spot, you got to be consistent, reliable and be able to do it on both sides. I think Javon felt better at left in the past,…

full_text:
Aaron Rodgers led the Pittsburgh Steelers to 10 wins and an AFC North title in 2025. Mark Alberti / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
A quick glance at the AFC North oddsboard would suggest it’s either the Baltimore Ravens’ or Cincinnati Bengals’ to lose — but that’s also what the oddsboard indicated heading into last season, before the Pittsburgh Steelers emerged victorious.
Listed at +510 odds that give them around a 15 percent implied probability to win, major sportsbooks like DraftKings aren’t ruling the Steelers out, and neither is The Athletic’s predictive analyst Austin Mock. Let’s dive into how his model projects every AFC North team’s chances to win the division, make the playoffs and more.
It’s a long shot, but it’s entirely possible the Steelers could win the AFC North.
First, the roster is actually in pretty decent shape. It skews older, but there are still quality players on both sides of the ball. The offense has plenty of weapons with DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. at wide receiver, Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington at tight end, and Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle at running back. The offensive line is in pretty good shape as well. And while the linebacker group is average, the secondary has a good foundation and the defensive line has enough depth and potential to be awesome.
Of course, I left out a pretty important position. Aaron Rodgers’ prime is well behind him, but his reunion with Mike McCarthy could spark something. I wouldn’t say McCarthy is an elite offensive mind, but he has the ability to raise the offensive floor in Pittsburgh. And when you give him this much talent, there is a chance the Steelers could be around average (or slightly above). Would that good enough to win the division? I’m not sure. But paired with what should be a top-10 defense, they’re certainly good enough to challenge the Ravens and Bengals.
Another angle to factor in is that Baltimore and Cincinnati have pretty low floors.
Lamar Jackson was banged up last season and never quite seemed right. What if that spills into this season? Then you look at the Ravens’ offensive line and all of its question marks. The 32-year-old Derrick Henry has to eventually slow down. And the defense couldn’t generate pressure without blitzing last year. I’m bullish on coach Jesse Minter, and the addition of Trey Hendrickson should help, but that doesn’t guarantee a top-10 defense.
The team I’m most worried about is the Bengals. We know the offense is going to be really good if it’s healthy. And the Bengals finally added to a poor defense by trading for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence and adding pass rusher Boye Mafe in free agency. The Bengals were 14th in expected points added (EPA) per play on defense in the second half of last season, so I do believe they improve. But what if they don’t? And they’re still a well below average defense?
All of those possibilities are well within the range of outcomes, which gives me enough confidence to say the Steelers could defend their AFC North title. Is it likely? Probably not. But it’s possible.

full_text:
Cowboys VP of player personnel Will McClay touched on a lot of things from training camp and added that this year's team looks "like a more focused group." Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
Vice president of player personnel Will McClay is in his 25th season working in the Dallas Cowboys’ personnel department. He has been running the team’s drafts since 2014. He also plays a significant role in their free-agent and trade acquisitions. Near the end of training camp, we try to catch up with McClay to get his thoughts on several key topics. This year’s discussion touched on the team’s current positive vibes, the recent addition of Von Miller, their rookie class and other notable performers in camp.
You’ve had some really talented rosters over the years. Where do you think this one stacks up?
McClay: We’ll see when we start playing games and how it ends up, but I do think that we’ve added some quality depth players as well as starters. I think adding Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark, (Jalen Thompson), those vet guys, also gives us an opportunity to get some of that stuff on defense, too. You get some veteran leadership on defense, with a new defense. So, that’s real positive.
Does this season seem like there’s more positive momentum than others?
I think every year you come into it with expectations, and then you see how things unfold, and you begin to feel the temperature. We haven’t had to deal with a lot of things, either. So, you focus on football. I think that makes it even easier and better for the group. So it seems like a more focused group.
What do you think Von Miller can still contribute?
He can still get after the passer. When you have a bunch of rushers, the offense has to figure out what you’re doing, how you’re doing it. I think (new defensive coordinator Christian Parker) will use that very well. But also the leadership. We have young players that they’re learning from coaching, but they also learn better from guys that have done it at a high level. They’re probably more willing to listen to that. And he’s the right kind of guy to pour into a guy like Malachi (Lawrence) and some of the young guys we have. But he can still play. And he’ll contribute to the pass rush.
Where are you now on defense compared to last year when the season started?
You feel more of a connection within the group, like all of the pieces matching right now and everything, being more cohesive and together right now. It’s the communication, it’s all the things that they’re stressing defensively that’s important. Everybody’s doing it, so there’s a rhythm within the defense right now.
What’s it been like working with Christian Parker?
What you saw in the interview is real. And so many of these interviews, coaches come in with these books and (other things). One thing is to be a young man, as young as he is, and convince Jerry (Jones) and Stephen (Jones) that it’s the right thing to do, because he’s gone through all the steps with us. So then, you get on the field, and you realize that the way he puts things together, the process that he goes through, it’s everything that he does. It’s how he is, and so it makes a lot of sense. And it was unique in the box. Just being around him, and looking at him, he understands it, and has a plan, and he’s very confident. And the defense is confident in what he’s calling, because belief is a very big part of it, and they believe.
How has Parker been when it comes to adding a player like Miller or when you guys were looking at players in the draft?
He understands what players can and can’t do and how they fit and how he can use them. He’s very clear with the vision. He doesn’t have a strict prototype, but there are certain things you want. If you give him those things, he knows how to use them, how he’s going to put them in the defense. So that’s been really good for us, is that he’s very clear about the picture, how he’s going to use it, why certain things may match for something else, but not here. So it’s clear, and you can see how he wants to build it, so it does make it easier for us.
What has caught your eye in training camp with your three top picks on defense?
With Malachi, his speed is evident, but also being able to play the run and be physical like you have to in this defense, and (he’s) done it fairly quickly. And understanding that, I think the sky is the limit from a physical standpoint. And he’s getting the right coaching. Learning from somebody like Von to be able to use those tools. He’s got some juice off of the edge.
(Jaishawn) Barham is a grown man from a standpoint of, mentally, he’s shown that he can handle the different things that we’re doing with him. He’s very physical, very intentional, and dialed in. And with Caleb (Downs), those three guys, they almost seem like five-year vets the way they approach things.
Have you been around a rookie who carries himself like Downs?
I hate to compare, but very much like Dak (Prescott) in the way he carried himself when he came in, kind of the pied piper without being loud, just how he worked and how he did things. People follow that. And then backed it up by the way he played and the way he carries himself, on and off the field. Guys follow that.
Left tackle Tyler Guyton was one of the players that Brian Schottenheimer said exceeded his expectations during the first four weeks of training camp. What have you noticed from him?
He’s a young player that performed well when he was on the field, but it’s about the consistency of it. So he took the offseason challenge and everything we asked him to do. Offseason award winner, taking every rep. From the moment the season was over, it was important for him to get better and not let anybody down. And he’s really trying to do that every day. He’s always had the ability, now it’s the confidence. That’s very hard. He’s got to block all of the best (pass) rushers. His growth has been really, really good, and he’s confident in himself and the group’s confident in him.
What has stood out to you about Joe Milton in his second season in Dallas?
It’s growth. He’s becoming more comfortable in the system. I give (quarterbacks coach Steve Shimko) and the coaches credit for taking the time to help him figure it out and understand it in a way that he does, and then him taking it. And really, we brought in competition that pissed him off. And one of the things about competition is that it makes everybody better. It made Joe dial in.
What’s it been like to see everything start to come together for Shavon Revel?
It’s all about confidence. This is his first training camp, and there’s a lot of things that he didn’t go through, and he had to play. So this is really his rookie training camp with a new staff. And so we’re pouring into him, and it’s all the reps and the meetings, all those things that he missed the first year. He’s getting that now, and he’s healthy, and he’s really soaking it up. I think (defensive backs coach) Derrick Ansley and the staff are doing a great job with him, giving him that confidence. The tools are there. Now he’s starting to become confident in his abilities and what he’s doing.
I asked you a couple of years ago about your favorite and least favorite parts of your job. You said your least favorite was your lack of sleep. Is that the same? What is your favorite and least favorite part of the job now?
My favorite part of the job is I like being out (at training camp), being around it every day, seeing what we’re putting together and seeing it all come together. Every day you wake up excited because we have an opportunity to get better. We’re all working and doing the same thing, preparing to win.
The part that is not my favorite anymore, the older I get, all this damn technology. You got the analytics and the AI and all of these things. When you’re an old-school grinder and used to doing it, when somebody gives you a new way to do it, I’m becoming my dad because you become more stubborn and want to do stuff the old way. … We have a…

full_text:
Cam Achord's high-energy style has made an impression with players during his first training camp with the Packers. Tork Mason / Imagn Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Matt LaFleur is in his eighth season as Green Bay Packers head coach. He’s on his fourth special teams coordinator, though, after moving on from Shawn Mennenga and Maurice Drayton and having Rich Bisaccia step down this offseason.
Enter 39-year-old Cam Achord, formerly the New England Patriots’ special teams coordinator from 2020-2023 and the New York Giants’ assistant special teams coach the last two seasons.
Achord, the Mississippi native carrying a southern drawl, brings the juice. That’s normally a cliché, but Achord epitomizes it. He wears cleats to practice because former Patriots special teams ace Matthew Slater kept knocking him to the ground during gunner-release drills and Achord wanted better traction. They’ve played clips of Achord getting after it with Slater here in the Lambeau Field meeting rooms.
Achord also went viral recently for his lengthy demonstration during a news conference of how to properly hold for rookie kicker Trey Smack’s field-goal attempts depending on the wind.
“That was the first one I’ve seen in a long time,” LaFleur said of Achord’s coaching clinic for reporters. “He’s juiced up about football and brings great energy for our guys.”
First-year Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord was asked how Trey Smack likes his kicks to be held.
He then came off the podium and did this for almost two minutes.
Enjoy. pic.twitter.com/sD6yhBbZDB
— Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) August 5, 2026
To capture exactly what Achord brings to the Packers and how he goes about his day during practice as he tries to cure Green Bay’s chronic special teams illness, The Athletic watched Achord’s every move for almost two hours during Monday’s session. Here’s what I saw.
10:58 a.m.: Achord’s practice day begins with a sheet in hand, talking to longtime Packers trainer Bryan “Flea” Engel, now the vice president of player health and performance. They’re presumably going over which of his guys are dealing with aches and pains entering the final week of training camp and who he’ll have at his disposal. Achord meets with his two assistants, 36-year-old Corey Harkey, who played for the Rams from 2012-2016, and Jeff Koonz, who was a Packers defensive assistant last season and the West Virginia special teams coordinator before that.
Achord’s outfit for the day: black Nike cleats, low-cut black socks, green shorts, a white short-sleeve windbreaker-type top and a white visor with a green brim. Perfect attire for getting after it.
11:10: The horn sounds and Achord jumps into action. There are stretches throughout this two-hour practice in which he’s not doing much, but this isn’t one of them. It’s time for a punt drill and you can hear Achord’s voice over rap artist Quavo’s bars coming from the practice field speakers.
Achord gathers his primary punt coverage team, featuring the likes of linebacker Isaiah McDuffie, wide receiver Bo Melton, safety Kitan Oladapo and linebacker Nick Niemann. Achord is active throughout the drill, shouting instructions (we’re not allowed to directly quote people on the field), getting in an athletic stance like he’s about to return the punt and emphatically demonstrating how to approach certain blocks. Achord is in the huddle every play before retreating to the sideline. He then crouches down and, in sync with his return team, runs 30 yards from the 10- to the 40-yard line before coming to a balanced halt like he coaches his gunners to do.
“I was with Cam my rookie year when I was in New England, so Cam always brings juice,” running back and kick returner Pierre Strong Jr. said. “He gon’ make you work. He gon’ make you better, so I love Cam. He gon’ be hype every single day. It’s not fake energy. It’s him. That’s him. That’s who he been since I’ve known him.”
“He’s actually becoming one of my favorite coaches, just bringing that energy to the meeting room and to the field,” said wide receiver Skyy Moore, who’s likely to return kicks and punts come Week 1. “He’s just a ball of energy and the players feed off of that.”
11:22: Team drills start and Achord steps back from the action. He’s going over sheets, presumably littered with play calls for his units. He reconvenes with Harkey and Koonz, who bring over a turned-over yellow garbage can for a solid surface to write on. Nobody ever said being a special teams coach was glamorous. Achord squats slightly above the ground on this hot afternoon to give himself a rest while his specialists, punter Daniel Whelan, long snapper Cal Adomitis and Smack, work by themselves nearby.
11:42: Achord holds an iPad and general manager Brian Gutekunst joins him on the field. Gutekunst puts his arm around Achord’s far shoulder as they stand 50 yards behind the 11-on-11s taking place. He’s probably telling Achord to be thankful for the GM delivering him a seemingly competent kicker in Smack (at least that’s what it looks like so far after a couple of years of inconsistency at the position). Gutekunst and Achord will talk much more ahead of Sunday’s cutdown day, when some of those final spots will be determined by special teams ability. They talk for two minutes before Achord jogs to the other side of the field.
11:49: Standing behind the offense during a period in which Smack will kick live field goals, Achord drops a sheet of paper tucked into his shorts. He’s so locked into practice that it takes about 65 seconds to notice it’s gone. An equipment staff member picks it up, reads the sheet to see which coach it belongs to and returns it to Achord.
11:56: Smack drills a 60-yard field goal to finish one team period and LaFleur flashes a smile. Achord said Saturday that Smack, the sixth-rounder who’s gone 7-for-7 on field goals in two preseason games with makes from 51, 58 and 59 yards, only had two good games. He needs to stay consistent. Sure enough, Smack misses wide left from 40 while making two from 33 and 43. Achord stands behind Smack each time and, before one kick, rubs his belly with his other hand over his head as some sort of signal. I’ll try to figure out what that means.
11:58: Achord yells “KICKOFF RETURN” as his most animated period of practice begins. Last week, Achord sprinted almost the entire length of Melton’s kick return alongside one of the team’s fastest players. Achord said his own fastest 40-yard dash was 4.51 seconds going into his senior year at Belhaven College, a Division III school in Jackson, Miss.
“I told Bo I was gonna run about 22 (miles per hour) on that one,” Achord said. “Obviously, I didn’t get 22, but it’s good. I think for those guys, they like to compete, regardless if it’s me (or) another player.”
“I love Coach Cam,” Melton said. “He brings that juice every day and he told me right before that play, he said, ‘I’m running with your ass.’ So I was like, ‘Oh man!’ And he brings it every day … he going to get on your ass when you do great. He’s going to be happy as hell. He’s going to be jumping around when you do good and he going to rip your ass when you’re not doing so well, so he’s a through-and-through coach. He’s straightforward and he wants the best. That’s why I love him most.”
Watch Achord conduct a kickoff drill and it’s no surprise that former Patriots special teamer Justin Bethel once broke Achord’s nose in practice.
He gets into the mix. And Achord never walks. It’s more of an urgent pacing, a jog, a backpedal or a full-on run. Might as well make the most of those cleats.
He’s constantly moving between the sideline and the huddle, creeping up behind rookie edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton and whispering coaching points in his ear right before the snap like they’re sweet nothings. He dodges bodies when he insists on running into the chaos, which is probably why he broke his nose in New England. He compliments guys and pats them on the helmet when they do well and barks and shakes his…

full_text:
Chiefs rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods says, "I'm just the new guy around here. ... So I've always got something to prove." Denny Medley / Imagn Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — One of the biggest early stories in Kansas City Chiefs training camp was the emergence of first-round rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods, who flashed quick feet and active hands to dominate one-on-one drills .
Since then, though, Woods has mostly been a non-factor in two preseason games, logging 43 defensive snaps with no tackles and one QB pressure.
The logical answer is this: Woods hasn’t quite been himself after suffering a left ankle injury in practice on Aug. 12.
During a screen pass in 11-on-11 workouts, he landed awkwardly and immediately grabbed his lower left leg, though he stayed in drills then and hasn’t missed a practice since.
“Just a roll-up on my ankle. It’s fine now,” Woods said Monday. “Something that I decided to push through and work through. Nothing serious to be worried about.”
At least, not for the future. Woods did seem to lose some side-to-side burst the last two weeks while moving closer to full health.
What was most important, he said, was letting his new coaches and teammates know that small setbacks weren’t going to keep him off the field.
“I’m just the new guy around here,” Woods said. “Nobody really knows me yet. So I’ve always got something to prove. Send a message to my coaches and my teammates that I’m a fighter. (Staying in practice) was more about the message I’m sending my coaches, my teammates about my reliability and my dependability — and less about how I was feeling in the moment.”
The good news for the Chiefs? Woods said he felt plenty of progress in recent days after an early time when he was “telling myself to push through.” That included feeling more like himself during Saturday’s road preseason loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
“I feel like this weekend, I really got over that hump, like, ‘OK, I’m feeling good,'” Woods said. “So I’m ready to go. I’m excited.”
Woods — the 29th pick in April’s draft — says he is “100 percent” confident he’ll be back to full strength for the season opener against the Denver Broncos on Sept. 14.
Interestingly, fellow 2026 first-round pick Mansoor Delane said Monday that he too worked to remain on the field with a lingering training-camp injury to show his commitment. Delane, who’s been recovering from a shoulder ailment, only returned to full-team drills last week before getting into his first preseason game Saturday.
“I feel like I owe it to my brothers, owe it to this team, owe it to this organization,” Delane said of staying on the practice field as much as possible. “Like I said, I’m not here to just sit on that sideline, whatever it is. I’m here to contribute.”
Overall, Woods said he’d grown during the previous four weeks of training camp. Coach Andy Reid’s prep for the season in the Missouri heat and humidity is widely considered one of the NFL’s toughest preseason preps.
“It’s a grind. It’s where you go into that dark place. It’s just you and football, and it’s just testing your measure and how much you love it,” Woods said. “But I think it’s so necessary because we’re all going to face some type of adversity coming up in the season. So putting you in those adverse situations on purpose, intentionally, I think that’s important.”
Woods has also faced numerous double teams this preseason while playing alongside backups; he won’t get the benefit of multiple snaps next to starters Chris Jones and Khyiris Tonga until the regular season begins.
Still, Woods believes he’s learned something from his first two preseason games.
“It’s just been an exciting time for me, being out there, getting reps, learning different techniques that I can actually apply to a real-game scenario,” Woods said. “It’s just been a great experience.”

EAGAN, Minn. — This is crunch time for pro personnel employees throughout the NFL. They’re sifting through preseason tape, doing their darndest to uncover a gem that could fortify depth on the back end of the roster.

full_text:
Vikings rookie receiver Dillon Bell is one of the talented young players on the roster bubble entering the final preseason game. John Jones / Imagn Images
EAGAN, Minn. — This is crunch time for pro personnel employees throughout the NFL. They’re sifting through preseason tape, doing their darndest to uncover a gem that could fortify depth on the back end of the roster.
The Minnesota Vikings are no different. In fact, their relatively top-heavy talent is even more reason to stay in evaluation mode.
Coming off of the team’s second preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens, who is in line to make the 53? Where does the intrigue lie?
Here is an updated roster projection:
In: Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz, J.J. McCarthy
The backup quarterback conversation can misdirect from what’s actually most important. Can head coach Kevin O’Connell and Murray meld their preferences into a potent offensive vision?
Training camp has offered some clues. Expect the Vikings to play more from the shotgun in 2026. Furthermore, Minnesota’s staff plans to reconfigure the passing game around Murray’s strengths. These modifications matter in the bigger picture for a franchise that has not won a playoff game since 2019.
As for the backup situation, McCarthy took all of the No. 2 reps in last week’s joint practices. His performance was up and down. Another chaotic preseason outing for McCarthy — juxtaposed with Wentz’s professional-looking operation — could position the veteran as the most rational second option if Murray were to suffer an injury.
In: Aaron Jones, Jordan Mason, Demond Claiborne, Zavier Scott
Those associated with the rushing attack have spoken optimistically about what’s possible. The offensive line is flying off the line of scrimmage. Running backs have clear tracks with defined responsibilities to wheel around the edge or make sharp cuts. Jones’ reliability will earn him a hefty chunk of snaps. But Mason’s burst presents even more opportunity if he can improve in pass protection.
If the Vikings decide to keep an extra offensive lineman, or if they don’t think they can sneak a young defender onto the practice squad, they could further chisel down this room. But Claiborne’s explosiveness and Scott’s special teams impact should help both find their way to the 53.
Minnesota only used 21 personnel on 7.8 percent of its offensive snaps in 2025. As long as Bredeson stays healthy, that number will climb. He has been a fixture with the first-team offense during training camp.
Teammates rave about his aptitude. Learning O’Connell’s complex offense is one thing, but occupying a role that asks him to motion all over the formation is another. The way the Miami Dolphins deployed Alec Ingold is a perfect comparison for his projected usage.
In: Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, Myles Price, Tai Felton
Out: Dillon Bell, Jeshaun Jones, Dontae Fleming, Terrill Davis, Michael Briscoe, Trayvon Rudolph, Marcus Sanders Jr.
The top trio needs little introduction or explanation. It might be the most talented and potent starting group of wideouts in the NFL. Addison is quietly piecing together a phenomenal training camp, displaying an impressive rapport with Murray after the two spent significant time together this offseason in Dallas.
Perhaps the biggest issue here is depth. Price and Felton each took steps this offseason in their schematic understanding and trustworthiness as pass catchers. Both could have short-term roles. Bell, an undrafted signing from Georgia who excelled Saturday against the Ravens, isn’t going to be easy to slide to the practice squad. Lose him to another team, and the Vikings will have a pretty thin group of developmental receiver talent.
In: T.J. Hockenson, Josh Oliver, Ben Yurosek
Out: Gavin Bartholomew, Matt Lauter, Marshall Lang
A few years ago, O’Connell went so far as to call former Viking Johnny Mundt the best No. 3 tight end in the NFL. The franchise valued him as insurance. They’ve searched for a replacement since.
Yurosek’s blocking ability may give him the edge over Bartholomew, but Bartholomew might be more fluid as a receiver. This spot won’t receive much attention, but the Vikings offense needs to maintain its vision if Hockenson or Oliver misses time.
In: Christian Darrisaw, Donovan Jackson, Blake Brandel, Will Fries, Brian O’Neill, Ryan Van Demark, Caleb Tiernan, Michael Jurgens, Joe Huber
Out: Walter Rouse, Henry Byrd, Joshua Gray, Vershon Lee, Gavin Gerhardt, Tristan Leigh, Delby Lemieux, Tomas Rimac
All five starters are healthy. They’re also motivated and committed to a higher standard with coach Keith Carter at the helm. Brandel’s relative newness at center warrants observation once the season starts. Health for the three interior starters will also be integral, as none of the expected backups have fared particularly well during the preseason.
In: Jalen Redmond, Levi Drake Rodriguez, Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Caleb Banks, Domonique Orange, Elijah Williams
Out: Isaiahh Loudermilk, Jonathan Harris, Jahvaree Ritzie, Smith Vilbert
The youth of this defensive tackle group stands out. Redmond is the most senior of the bunch at 27. This places further responsibility on defensive line coaches Ryan Nielsen and Pat Hill.
Even though Brian Flores’ defensive system pulls levers to stop the run with its scheme, the pressure falls on these big men to hold up at the point of attack. The easier it becomes for opposing offenses to throw jabs, the more difficult it will be for the Vikings defense to create its patented chaos. Banks’ runway to play a major amount of snaps remains long. Orange could be more impactful early on, while Williams built off of his rookie season with some eyebrow-raising preseason tape.
In: Andrew Van Ginkel, Dallas Turner, Tyler Batty, Chaz Chambliss, Bo Richter
Out: Kenny Dyson, Cam’Ron Stewart
One of the more underdiscussed layers of the Jonathan Greenard-to-Turner transition was the added flexibility it offered Flores. Turner drops from the line of scrimmage with smoothness and awareness. This increases the deception for opposing offenses. Their protection schemes might expect edge rushers, but both Van Ginkel and Turner could drift backward, making the interior more susceptible.
Turner’s progression is one of the central pivot points for the Vikings in 2026. It’s also worth noting that Batty, Chambliss and Richter have all produced admirably throughout training camp.
Does this mean the Vikings won’t scour the free-agent market for reinforcements? The answer to that question should come in the next few weeks.
In: Blake Cashman, Eric Wilson, Jake Golday, Ivan Pace Jr.
Out: Jacob Roberts, Bangally Kamara, Josh Ross
Few, if any, positions improved from a depth perspective as much as linebacker. Golday continues to impress. Even offseason signings Roberts and Kamara made enough plays in the first two preseason games to capture some attention. Minnesota could keep five of them, but the floor of the first four may be high enough to supplement another position group.
It’s also easier to believe in the capability here when Cashman and Wilson are coming off the seasons they are. Few Vikings players have had better training camps than those two.
In: Byron Murphy Jr., Isaiah Rodgers, James Pierre, Charles Demmings
Out: Da’Veawn Armstead, Zemaiah Vaughn, Marcus Allen, Dwight McGlothern Jr., Jarod Washington, Bryce Phillips
The Vikings can get away with fewer cornerbacks because they utilize so many three-safety sets. Murphy, Rodgers, Pierre and Demmings are all locks. The only suspense is around a youngster like Armstead, who has had a good camp.
Pierre and Demmings both vied for the No. 3 role. But this also speaks to the growth at the back end of the room as compared to recent years.
In: Josh Metellus, Jay Ward, Theo Jackson, Jacob Thomas, Jakobe Thomas, Tavierre Thomas

title: Mike Vrabel is right about the Patriots' lack of depth. So how can they fix it? Vrabel was honest about New England's lack of depth at several positions. Is there a way to address it before the season kicks off? Chad Graff
summary:
Mike Vrabel was honest about the Patriots' lack of depth at several positions. Is there a way to address it before the season kicks off? Billie Weiss / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — When Jon Bon Jovi introduced the New England Patriots at the Super Bowl in February, the team ran out of the tunnel with a familiar starting lineup.
The five starting offensive linemen were the same as at the season opener five months earlier. Same quarterback, same running backs, same wide receivers. Same defensi
full_text:
Mike Vrabel was honest about the Patriots' lack of depth at several positions. Is there a way to address it before the season kicks off? Billie Weiss / Getty Images
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — When Jon Bon Jovi introduced the New England Patriots at the Super Bowl in February, the team ran out of the tunnel with a familiar starting lineup.
The five starting offensive linemen were the same as at the season opener five months earlier. Same quarterback, same running backs, same wide receivers. Same defensive line and same linebackers. Christian Gonzalez was out there after missing the start of the season, but beyond that, it was basically the same team.
Lost in all the success of the Patriots’ 2025 season is the reality that they stayed remarkably healthy. Viewed another way, their depth wasn’t really tested.
If that becomes the case again in 2026, another Super Bowl is certainly well within reach. But it also underscores another reality largely forgotten amid the team’s success, one coach Mike Vrabel put bluntly after the Patriots’ second preseason game on Saturday.
“I do not think we have a very deep team,” Vrabel said.
On Monday, Vrabel clarified what he meant. The direct assessment wasn’t a shot at the front office (especially considering Vrabel leads football operations).
Before 2025, several years of poor drafts had left the Patriots without much depth. Only Marcus Jones remains from the 10-man draft class of 2022. Of the seven players picked in the first five rounds of the 2023 draft, only Christian Gonzalez remains. Drake Maye will likely be the only player from the 2024 class to make the roster this season.
“I think that when you look at how you want to be constructed, we have to continue to draft very well,” Vrabel said during his WEEI radio appearance Monday.
The lack of depth contributes in two ways to the decisions the coaching staff has made this preseason. First, as Vrabel mentioned, it’s part of the reason he has been hesitant to play starters in the exhibition games. If depth is an issue, you need to do everything you can to keep the starters healthy. (Though it’s also worth mentioning that sitting your starters in the preseason is becoming more of a league-wide trend as teams place more value on joint practices, then sit their top players in the exhibition games that follow.)
Second, when depth is an issue, giving the backups and younger talent additional reps in games can only help. It can spur development and help identify which players have the most promise.
“I mean, depth has to be built,” Vrabel said. “That is something that has to be built through experience and making sure that the guys are in place to be the first backup in. Those are critical. Those are almost starters. We know how many people are going to have to play for you throughout the season and there cannot be a drop-off.”
Still, fixing that lack of depth isn’t going to be an easy task in the two weeks that remain before the regular-season opener. A year ago, as a byproduct of the previous season’s record, the Patriots had the fourth-highest priority on the waiver wire, offering them a chance to add players after roster cuts, which is how they landed Tommy DeVito, Charles Woods and Eric Gregory. This season, however, the Patriots enter with the 31st priority on the wire, so it could be difficult to find talent via waivers.
When it comes to improving the roster, two other options exist. The first is trades, an avenue the Patriots explored Monday when they sent Kayshon Boutte to the Houston Texans for safety depth in the form of Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round pick. But without another obvious trade candidate, the Patriots could go the more expensive route and try to add an established veteran.
Some big names who fit the Patriots’ needs are edge rushers Joey Bosa and Haason Reddick and linebacker Bobby Wagner. None of them would be long-term fixes to the team’s problems, but they could be enticed by a one-year deal to play for a team with Super Bowl aspirations. They’ve already gone down that road, albeit with a lesser name, signing veteran guard Greg Van Roten last week with the hope of using him as the first interior offensive lineman off the bench.
Running back and defensive line are other positions where the Patriots could look to improve their depth.
More clarity could arrive on Tuesday when front-office leaders Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden are scheduled to meet with the media. On Monday, Vrabel insisted his remark on the team’s depth wasn’t a shot at that group.
“We’re all on the same page,” Vrabel said. “There is no front office. There is no back office. There is the Patriots. There is me, there is Eliot, there is Ryan, there is (VP of football operations and strategy) Stretch (John Streicher). I told you those are the people that we rely on to make decisions. So, there is no message.”
