title: Falcons Provide Major Update on QB Michael Penix Jr.
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons ’ quarterback battle is finally about to become a true competition.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski announced after the preseason game that Michael Penix Jr. has been cleared to participate in 11-on-11 work, removing the biggest obstacle that has prevented Atlanta from fairly evaluating Penix and Tua Tagovailoa for the starting quarterback job.
Penix has spent much of training camp working his way back from a knee injury that ended his 2025 season. He has participated in individual drills and 7-on-7 periods, but he had not been cleared for full-team work. That changes now.
For much of camp, the Falcons haven't been able to make a true comparison between their two quarterbacks.
Tagovailoa has been participating in full-team periods, playing in preseason action and gaining valuable experience in Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees' offense. Penix, meanwhile, has been limited while completing his rehabilitation.
Now Penix can finally operate in the same environment as Tagovailoa.
That means working against a live pass rush, navigating protections, making decisions under pressure and operating the offense in 11-on-11 situations.
Those are critical parts of evaluating a quarterback that simply can't be replicated in 7-on-7 work.
The Falcons can finally begin making a more complete comparison.
Tagovailoa still has an advantage because of the experience he has gained in Atlanta's offense and his ability to participate fully throughout camp.
However, he hasn't completely eliminated the questions surrounding the position.
Tagovailoa's preseason debut against Denver was underwhelming, and his first joint practice against Indianapolis wasn't particularly strong either. He did show improvement during the second joint practice, but the overall evaluation remains incomplete.
That makes Penix's return even more significant.
If Tagovailoa had consistently dominated throughout camp, Penix's return might have been less threatening to his position.
Instead, there remains an opportunity for Penix to make this a legitimate competition.
Penix doesn't need to immediately win every practice. His first priority will be showing the Falcons that he is physically ready to handle full-team work.
Once that is established, the evaluation becomes about performance.
Can Penix consistently move the offense? Can he handle pressure? Can he make the downfield throws that made him such an intriguing prospect coming out of Washington?
Those answers could determine whether he has a legitimate chance to reclaim the starting job. The Falcons still have time before the regular season, but not much.
Penix's clearance means the QB1 competition is no longer hypothetical. For the first time this offseason, Atlanta can truly evaluate both quarterbacks side by side.
And now, the pressure is on both Tagovailoa and Penix to prove they should be the ones leading the Falcons into Week 1.

title: 7 Exciting Takeaways as Jack Strand, Atlanta Falcons Dominate Indianapolis Colts
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons spent most of the last week in Indiana, including a pair of joint practices against the Indianapolis Colts. After nearly a week, the Falcons looked right at home on Saturday afternoon in their 34-6 win in Lucas Oil Stadium.
While preseason games aren't a predictor of future success, the Falcons looked like a more inspired, deeper unit than the one that was dominated by the Denver Broncos last year. Every phase of the team clicked against the Colts, including their much-maligned special teams.
With several position battles on the line, there were some impressive performances by players trying to make the 53-man roster, and maybe even earn a starting job.
Here are seven takeaways from the Falcons convincing win over the Colts
Obviously, most of the attention has been on Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr., but with both of those players out on Saturday, it was an opportunity for Cooper Rush and undrafted rookie Jack Strand to shine.
Rush was an efficient 10/11 to start the game, and then Strand came in and continued his impressive training camp with a dominating performance on Saturday.
He started the game 8/8 for 155 yards and a touchdown, including dropping one in the bucket with a beautiful over-the-shoulder pass to Juice Wells for 36 yards. He took off for a 16-yard rushing touchdown on the next play to put the Falcons up 31-6.
"Spike it, Jack!" Matt Ryan on the call for the TD 😂 FOX | NFL+ pic.twitter.com/3KLcv5gxKJ
The Falcons only kept two quarterbacks on the initial 53-man roster last season . There’s just no way that can place Strand on waivers and hope to get him to the practice squad. The 6’5 and 240-pound Strand would be hoovered up by another team immediately.
Strand has played well enough that if Tagovailoa and/or Penix struggle early, fans will be calling for the rookie. Heck, they might be doing that already.
The Falcons had arguably the worst special teams unit in the entire NFL last year. They addressed every level of the special teams with a new punter, kicker, return man, and coordinator. Those changes showed in the first sequences of the game. Atlanta kicked off and got held. The Colts started their drive on the 18.
The defense held, and Zachariah Branch fielded a 48-yard punt and returned it five yards to the Falcons’ 38. After a kickoff and a Colts’ punt, the Falcons found themselves winning the early field position battle. They cashed in with a 51-yard field goal from new kicker Nick Folk.
Folk was signed as a free agent in the offseason after the Falcons struggled with place kicking the last two seasons. He's been the NFL's most accurate kicker for three consecutive years.  He hit another 50-yarder in the fourth quarter for good measure.
The ensuing kickoff looked like an instant replay. A Colts hold, and Indianapolis was on the wrong side of its 20-yard line.
Tyler Goodson took the Colts’ first kickoff at the four-yard line and returned it 37 yards to the 41. The Falcons were last in the NFL with 22.9 yards per return last season.
Atlanta didn’t punt until midway through the second quarter, but when they did, new punter Jake Bailey hit it 58 yards to the corner, and Darren Hall downed the ball on the Colts two.
The Falcons shined in every aspect of special teams after floundering last season.
A.J. Terrell, Avieon Terrell, and Mike Hughes may be the only cornerbacks guaranteed a spot on the roster. The battle for depth is tight, and Henderson had a good early showing after getting the start. He had tight coverage on the Colts’ first drive with a pass breakup on the left sideline, helping to force a punt.
On the Colts’ second drive, he made a quick open-field tackle on a third-and-five that forced a field goal instead of a first down.
With no Bijan or Brian Robinson, the Falcons aren’t exactly empty-handed at running back. Tyler Goodson and Nathan Carter are fighting for the No. 3 spot, and both have had moments in training camp.
Goodson has the marquee play so far with a 49-yard touchdown run in the first quarter. The left side of the line, led by tackle Michael Jerrell and guard Kyle Hinton, cleared the first line of defense, and Goodson did the rest. That entire drive was his, with a long kickoff return and touchdown run.
49 yards to the CRIB 😮‍💨 @tgood1110 FOX | NFL+ pic.twitter.com/g2qiwB6zTr
The Falcons have four wide receivers who are veritable locks to make the team: Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus, and Branch. They could keep as many as six, depending on special teams, but the fifth wide receiver has clearly been Chris Blair this preseason.
Blair has been head and shoulders above the others vying for a spot on the 53-man roster. He led the team in receiving last week against the Broncos, and he had another solid showing on Saturday against the Colts, including an 18-yard reception over the middle from Rush as the first quarter was closing.
He also drew a pass interference in the end zone on 4th and three from the Colts’ six that set up Atlanta’s second touchdown.
Pro Football Focus recently ranked the Falcons' defensive line as the worst in the NFL. There’s not a headliner on this team, although Brandon Dorlus led all defensive tackles in the NFC with 8.5 sacks last year. But this unit is deep.
With Zach Harrison returning, Da’Shawn Hand and newcomer Maason Smith give the Falcons a good rotation and depth on the defensive line.
That said, Carlos Allen Jr. was the star in Indianapolis. He made noise during joint practices, and he was a menace on Saturday afternoon when he got his chance. A product of Douglass High School in Atlanta, Allen is roughly 6’1 and 300 pounds, and he is forcing his way into the conversation on the defensive line.
Christian Harris was penciled in as a starter at linebacker next to Divine Deablo, but frankly, Kendal Daniels has looked more impressive. Daniels was limited during OTAs and minicamp, but he’s gotten a lot of work with the first team, and he started today over Harris. He's the biggest of the linebackers, and he has excellent instincts.
Incoming: @KendalDaniels__ 😤 FOX | NFL+ pic.twitter.com/gmRzRq71Xl
Edge rusher Azeez Ojulari seemed like a lock to make the 53, but Keshawn Banks has outplayed him across the duration of training camp and looked significantly more productive rushing the Colts’ quarterback than Ojulari.
Banks had five sacks for the UFL’s Orlando Storm last season.
The Falcons are on the road next week against the Miami Dolphins on Friday. Head coach Kevin Stefanski said the first and third games will include the starters. Expect to see several players from today's action working in the with the first team.
The 53-man roster must be set next Sunday, and there are plenty of jobs still up for grabs.

title: Inside Falcons RT Jawaan Taylor’s Return to Practice After Lengthy Absence
full_text:
Jawaan Taylor joined the Atlanta Falcons back in April on a one-year deal worth $5 million, however, his contract isn’t guaranteed.
However, throughout the offseason, questions persisted on when Taylor would join the team on the football field, as he missed June’s mandatory minicamp and was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list during the first two weeks of training camp.
The right tackle was reactivated and cleared to practice on Aug. 10 .
At joint practice with the Indianapolis Colts on Wednesday, Aug. 19, Taylor told reporters his absence from practice was due to recovering from a March “clean-up surgery” on his knee and subsequent rehabilitation for an on-field return.
He added that the season-ending triceps injury, which ended his 2025 NFL campaign and three-year tenure with the Kansas City Chiefs, was at “100 percent” after a 12-week process.
“It’s always really tough seeing your brothers out there playing ball, and you’re just on the sideline rehabbing,” Taylor said in Indianapolis.
“Just kept coming in, keeping my head down, working every day. Had a great team, great group around me, so it just kept me motivated and I’m just glad to be back out there.”
Taylor has been a full participant in Atlanta’s joint practices at the Colts’ Grand Park Sports Campus .
The 6-foot-5, 313-pound Super Bowl champion has been inserted with the starters in team drills, as expected when he first signed with the Falcons.
“Good to get Jawaan going,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said. “There were some really good moments out there, and also some moments where you can see he’s still working through the time off. Pleased where he is. He’s a guy that I’ve witnessed putting in so much work to get back out here.”
The eighth-year veteran enters his first season in Atlanta in a very important role after stints with the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Chiefs.
At right tackle, he’s responsible for protecting the blindside of whoever wins the Falcons quarterback battle, Michael Penix Jr. or Tua Tagovailoa, both left-handers . Taylor, the NFL’s most penalized player, must also be clean in his protection to increase his staying power in
Atlanta after his one-year contract expires following the 2026 NFL season.
“At the end of the day, it’s just ball,” Taylor said. “I just got to go out there and do my job, and help the team in every way I can.”
The Falcons and Colts will follow two days of joint practices with an NFL preseason Week 2 game on Saturday, Aug. 22, at Lucas Oil Stadium. Kickoff is at 1 p.m. EST and will be televised locally on FOX 5 Atlanta.
Taylor and the starters likely won’t play as Stefanski plans to rest them.

title: Marlon Humphrey Is The Ravens Cornerback Who Should Be Dealt. ASAP
full_text:
The best time to trade Marlon Humphrey is right now.
I mean, don’t get me wrong, it’s far from perfect timing given the recent film and the age and the contract. But it also is unlikely to get any better and they have defensive backs to spare, and he’s always been the one who should go if possible . And with so many youngsters making the case this summer, it’s more obvious now than ever.
The Ravens have a glut of corners. They especially have some emerging and interesting body types to man the slot with real upside at a cheap cost with years of control, and Humphrey should be headed to the slot. It won’t be easy, and they might have to move some more salary to make it work, but if we’re being serious about the situation in the secondary and who should be the odd-man out, and who could fetch the most in return … it’s Humphrey.
Oh, it would be difficult for general manager Eric DeCosta, so sentimental about certain players he is willing to overpay for too long, but it should happen. Mark Andrews is another one of his favorites in this category whose contract threatens to work against them. Knowing when it’s time to move on is a vital trait of a sports executive; it hasn’t been a strength of this franchise under DeCosta (long list of overpays on old guys or guys he kept too long – OBJ, Justin Houston, Kyle Van Noy, etc).
They already ate $4M on Humphrey’s roster bonus, he is an older corner with an injury history coming off a terrible season, they are going to be playing a ton of zone and one of Jesse Minter’s superpowers is finding long and rangy boundary corners on the cheap who fit his system expertly and allow the team to allocate funds elsewhere.
So tying up this much money in Humphrey is silly and already $355M into the payroll, with an older roster and the quarterback only really under contract for one more year, you might as well be willing to eat more here to get more back in return.
Longtime NFL personnel exec Pat Kirwan, a friend of mine for over 15 years, and someone who negotiated contracts and ran the cap and understands present value and future value, told me he would he marketing the heck out of Humphrey over the younger roster-bubble type corners most assume the Ravens would deal. Kirwan and I dissect the Ravens roster in depth on “The Daily Flock Show” episode coming out Tuesday, and he made it clear he would be going to owner Steve Bisciotti and explaining why absorbing more of Humphrey’s contract to make a deal is in the franchise’s best interest.
“You might trade one or two of them to someone who is short a corner and has the cap space to take on Marlon or even (Chidobe) Awuzie,” Kirwan said. “Someone who loses their starring corner who thinks, ‘Hey were on the edge of this thing.’ … How many times have you and I watched someone trade some guy and pay half money to get rid of him?”
Touche my friend. I’d have done it months ago. This guy as the tenth highest-paid corner in the NFL? Not on my watch.
Could they land a pass catcher with some upside and a late-round pick for him? Is it addition by subtraction getting someone like Keyon Martin into the slot and fully vested in this defense from Week 1 with Minter in charge? What I do know is having a $19M corner, who has been a face of the franchise and voice of the defense, on the bench, ain’t gonna work.
Humphrey didn’t seem to be joking when he spoke about Minter referring to his “trash” play at times this summer , and this has always been a contract either begging to be cut or begging to be moved somewhere for a fresh start. Out of qualified corners a year ago, he was 70th or worse in far too many metrics, no one fears throwing on him, and while this should be a corner friendly system, isn’t that all the more reason to lean into some who are younger and cheaper with more upside?
Even if they save $8M cash, that’s money that could be put to use at another position before the midseason trade deadline. Forget trying to trade the seventh-or-eighth corner for anything at all – rather than just lose him on waivers – and make room for youth by fully incentivizing another team to take a chance that Humphrey can return to form with them, for about $10M total.
He’s the one who should go. The sooner the better.

title: Ravens Trying To Restore Order To The Middle Of The Field On Defense
full_text:
A year ago, the spine of the Ravens defense was compromised and vulnerable.
The unit was bad all around, but suffered extensively right in the middle, through all three levels, which is impossible to overcome. Some of it was injury. Some of it was a suspect roster. Some of it was, perhaps, highly-paid veterans hitting the wall after thousands of snaps playing this incredibly violent game.
And it much be a point of significant gain and recovery and rebirth for rookie head coach Jesse Minter as he operates that side of the ball and oversees the defense through the week and on game day. Getting All Pro defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike back fully from neck surgery and back to himself would be massive. Getting middle linebacker Roquan Smith back to being anything close to a $20M player would be massive, and not having to rely on guys like Alohi Gilman in centerfield in the secondary should be a significant boost, too.
The roster looks better and deeper and more formidable in that regard, now about three weeks from the start of the regular season, than at any point sine Madubuike went down in September. But there are also serious questions lingering about the spine, as well, from a health and productivity standpoint, starting with Madubuike, whose 2023 season was as close to Aaron Donald-esque as we’re going to see.
Madubuike remains the key to everything, on a very incremental schedule as he adds to his workload, but still just working on an individual basis. He has added a blocking sled to his duties, starting to test the head and neck area in new ways, yet with there always inherent caveats about such a progression and what could happen when games are played.
“it’s all part of the process with him,” Minter said after practice Monday. “We think he’s in a great place and it’s a progression week-to-week, seeing him hit the sled and do things like that.”
The Ravens remain very cautious about any timeline and remain hopeful he can participate and be impactful early in the season, but time will tell.
Teams didn’t both trying to run inside a ton last year even without Madubuike, and John Jenkins and Broderick Washington are big bodies and Travis Jones does well against the run, too. The Ravens had no pass rush whatsoever, and so even without their All Pro tackle, only six teams faced fewer inside runs than the Ravens last season.
Opponents were too busy lighting them up passing there. The Ravens ranked 21st in the NFL in opposing passer rating throwing between the hashes last season (109.4). Smith has been a liability in coverage for a few years now and he spoke candidly about his decline early in the spring , and defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver vowed a return to top form for the former All Pro as well.
Inside linebackers coach Tyler Santucci was a bit more circumspect discussing Smith, 29, after Monday’s practice, with one of the holdovers from head coach John Harbaugh’s former staff acknowledging work needs to be done.
Santucci mentioned how he had to “earn some trust, being able to have the talks that we need to have,” and he praised Smith’s response to them. He believes they can overcome that adversity together and explained that Smith has been “chasing the best version of himself over the past several months.”
Whether includes the veteran on the field for every snap or making getting a rest in some dime packages remains to be seen. Teddye Buchanan was stout in coverage with athleticism and good instincts before his rookie season was cut short by an ACL tear and he was recently activated from the Physically Unable to Perform list ahead of schedule from that surgery but still, like Madubuike, working through his recovery.
“I’ve seen a lot of patience with him, combined with urgency,” Santucci said.
What that means for Week 1 remains to be seen, and we continue to hear the Ravens are keeping close tabs on several middle linebackers with ties to this scheme and NFL playing experience, knowing that while undrafted rookie linebackers like Ethan Burke and Dominic DeLuca have done some nice things in preseason games , things are very different come September.
And while Trenton Simpson continues to earn rave reviews, we suspect he is out in space more and on the edge, where his speed is most impactful. Santucci termed his progress “a tremendous jump,” with him not dressing for exhibition games speaking to that.
The Ravens are looking for much more playmaking from their safeties on the back end, especially in the middle of the field.
Kyle Hamilton is freed up to menace offenses around the line of scrimmage with a deep compliment of others to hold up downfield. Second-year pro Malaki Starks seemed primed for a breakthrough – especially if the Ravens are able to pressure the quarterback this season – while Gilman was a target back there, missing tackles and struggling mightily in coverage (opponents completed eight of their final 10 attempts on him last year for 134 yards, and that wasn’t an anomaly).
The Ravens need a combination of health, scheme and luck to restore order in the middle of the field. Smith playing behind two stout tackles, taken out of some challenging coverage assignments and with play makers behind him, would go a long way to sorting it out and letting him run around and thump and disrupt.

title: Updated Ravens 53-Man Roster After Second Preseason Game
full_text:
A few more practices. One more preseason game.
That’s it until we have a 53-man roster for real. It’s almost here.
Of course, that first 53-man that formulates next weekend doesn’t amount to much as the Ravens will be adding players from other rosters and trying to make various moves. And then we get the 53 that starts practicing and moving to Week 1. (And, yes, we already have some practice squad projections, too).
We have a few shakeups in this projection; more than most other recent iterations. All of the mystery really remains on one side of the ball. And than will continue into the season, with so much new and uncertain and unproven with Declan Doyle’s offense, while Jesse Minter's defense best be ready to perform in midseason form a few weeks from now.
Don't expect many players truly on the roster bubble, let alone on the roster, to do much of anything Friday night against the Commanders and that's mostly practice squad spots at stake.
All of a sudden things got complicated for this group. The trip to Minnesota resulted in some minor injuries and their first major injury with Danny Pinter’s patella tendon, and also the first dark cloud of legal matters with Rashod Bateman, whose always seemed like damaged goods to me, having his arrest from June come to light.
QB (2) – Lamar Jackson, Snoop Huntley: Joe Fagnone did it again. Pretty amazing stuff from an undrafted kid from UCONN.
RB (4) – Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Adam Randall, Rasheen Ali: Both Randall and Ali banged up isn’t great. Jonathan Ward probably isn’t a great fit but he might have a chance here pending these medicals. Regardless, I think they are going to need some numbers here and I’m no longer going with a three-man projection.
TE (4) – Mark Andrews, Durham Smythe, Matthew Hibner, Josh Cuevas: I think they’ll regret not signing Darren Waller and going so inexperienced here.
WR (6) - Zay Flowers, WAIVER CLAIM/signing/trade, Ja’Kobi Lane, Elijah Sarratt, Devontez Walker, LaJohntay Wester: The allegations around Rashod Bateman’s arrest for family violence are ugly. The NFL created the Commissioner’s Exempt List with these types of situations in mind. Maybe they trade a corner for a depth receiver or sign someone cut elsewhere.
OL (9) - Ronnie Stanley, Vega Ioane, John Simpson, Roger Rosengarten, Ehtan Pocic, Jovaughn Gwyn, Carson Vinson, Emery Jones, Andrew Vorhees: I was skeptical about Gwyn being more than a practice squad guy before Pinter suffered a season-ending injury. Pocic was always going to be the starting center.
There just doesn't seem to be too much to wring your hands over on this side fo the ball. They have more corners than they know what to do with. They have a lot of deep depth at some other spots but those decisions will be more about whether to cut them or put them on the practice squad, not so much for the 53-man itself.
DL (7) – Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, Broderick Washington, John Jenkins, Rayshaun Benny, Adisa Isaac: Does Aeneas Peebles having a four-pressure game change the math? I’m still slotting him to the practice squad but many that is Isaac.
LB (7) – Trey Hendrickson, Roquan Smith, Teddye Buchanan, Zion Young, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Trenton Simpson: Wonder if Buchanan needs a few weeks inactive until he is good to go with so much time he missed.
CB (6) – Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, Marlon Humphrey, Chandler Rivers, TJ Tampa, Keyon Martin: Somebody is getting dealt and maybe it’s someone listed above, and maybe not. Hope Amani Oruwariye makes it to the practice squad .
S (5) – Kyle Hamilton, Malaki Starks, Jaylinn Hawkins, K’Von Wallace, Keondre Jackson: Said it before and will say it again - it’s a loaded group. Going to see some interesting blitzes from this group and not just Hamilton.
K – Tyler Loop – Would like to see him try some from 50 plus on Friday.
P – Ryan Eckley – Monster game from him Saturday. Love to see it.
LS – Nick Moore – Steady Eady. Er, Steady Nick.

title: 4 Biggest Takeaways From Ravens Preseason Week 2 Victory
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens grinded to the second win of the Jesse Minter era as head coach in dominant defensive fashion with a decisive 13-3 win over the hosting Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on Saturday afternoon.
This exhibition bout followed two days of highly productive joint practices between the two teams, and it followed the same theme as those practices. Defense led the way for both teams, but in the end, it was the visiting Ravens who managed to do just enough on offense to emerge victorious.
"I'm proud of our guys [for] the way they played in that game," Minter said. "I thought we, especially in the second half, were able to kind of play the game the way we wanted to play a little bit more [and] control the ball a little bit more. [We] did a nice job on defense [in the] red zone [and] got a couple turnovers which we wanted to get"
Here are four of the biggest takeaways from the Ravens' preseason win over the Vikings:
Last week in the opener, it was the Ravens' second-stringers on defense who led the charge for their domination of the Philadelphia Eagles. This time around, it was players who didn't appear in that game until the fourth quarter or were just penciled in at third and fourth on the depth chart who stepped up and made pivotal splash plays.
Up front, they got 1.5 sacks, a tackle for loss and several run-stuffs from rotational interior defensive linemen C.J. Okoye, Rayshaun Benny and David Olajiga. On the edge, Kaimon Rucker had some nice pressures and a quarterback hit, while undrafted rookie Ethan Burke had the game of his life as a pro with three solo tackles, a sack, a tackle for loss, two quarterback hits, two batted passes and a forced fumble.
Ravens undrafted rookie OLB Ethan Burke: 34 snaps 2 tackles 2 pressures 1 sack 1 forced fumble 1 PBU pic.twitter.com/nJhwNUIjjy
At the second level, Jay Higgins IV made his return from a concussion, started the game, wore the green dot for the whole game, and recorded four total tackles, including three solos. Starting and playing next to him for all but nine snaps was undrafted rookie Dominic DeLuca, who also recorded four tackles, including one for a loss early in the game.
In the secondary, the three brightest standouts were second-year safety Keondre Jackson, fifth-round nickel Chandler Rivers and undrafted safety Silas Walters. The latter two didn't see any playing time until the fourth quarter last week but were on the field early and often in this game. Each of them recorded a pass breakup, five-plus tackles and a splash play, with Rivers' being a splitting a sack with Olajiga and Walters making up for an earlier blunder with a late interception to ice the game and secure a double-digit margin of victory. Jackson was all over the field on defense and special teams, finishing with a game-high eight total tackles, including two for a loss, a sack and a quarterback hit.
"We preach not having a drop-off on our backend, and on the defense," Jackson said. "So, the 'ones' hold us accountable; they go out there and play great. The 'twos' and 'threes,' we want to follow suit because you're just as good as your weakest link. Not saying that we have a weak link, but [we want] no drop-offs with that."
Coming out of the preseason opener, a dark horse emerged as a deserving candidate to start receiving first-team reps: Jovaughn Gwyn. Even before Danny Pinter went down with a season-ending injury on the first day of joint practices against the Vikings, the fourth-year pro was receiving a groundswell of support amongst the film-watchers for the impressive tape he put together against the Eagles in live action and against Minnesota's starters.
Unfortunately for Gwyn, he didn't carry over that momentum into the second preseason game despite getting the starting nod. This left the door open for 10th-year veteran Ethan Pocic to reemerge as the favorite to replace three-time Pro Bowler Tyler Linderbaum, as was widely expected following his signing at the onset of training camp.
The team has been gradually increasing Pocic's involvement in practices and games, given that he suffered a torn Achilles late last season, and he performed quite well in relief duty, starting in the second quarter this time around after not checking in until the fourth in the opener. With one preseason game left, Pocic will likely get to make his first start as a Raven and will likely get to play most of the first half, during which he can cement himself as the victor of the team's most anticipated and closely contested position battle.
Pocic's anchor looks as advertised. Hell of a drop against Big Citrus. #RavensFlock pic.twitter.com/OO3j4xKfcA
Even though he's not projected to be a full-time starter heading into his second season in the league, expectations for the 2025 second-rounder are sky-high given his talent and improved environment from both schematic and player-personnel aspects. Against the Vikings, he showed some proof of concept to support the hype he's been getting all summer with his performance in the first half.
Green completely derailed Minnesota's offensive possession of the game when he recorded a sack on second down for a loss of six yards and followed it up by drawing a holding penalty on third down that negated a 19-yard gain that would've gone for a first down. Both rushes came off the left side of the line and saw him show great bend and explosion around the edge on the sack and a nice inside move on the second play that likely would've led to a second straight sack had he not gotten held.
Practice paying off for Mike Green! For more highlights, visit https://t.co/ciLFizvHBw . pic.twitter.com/CN9q1kfB7P
"Regardless [of] what game it is, it is still a confidence boost, and it shows you that the work that you put in [and] the moves that I have been practicing [have been] paying off," Green said. "[I'm] trying to work on [my] craft in practice, [so] being able to go out there in the game and be successful with it, it means a lot."
For the second week in a row, arguably the brightest standout on offense for the Ravens was undrafted rookie signal caller Joe Fagnano. Once again, he led multiple scoring drives, was highly efficient, completing 15-of-20 attempts and produced a pass rating of over 90 with a game-high 106.9. His 123 passing yards were the most of any quarterback who touched the field in his game, and he was the only one to throw for a touchdown.
"[The Vikings] got [to] me a couple of times [and] showed a couple of different looks," Fagnano said. "It's kind of what their defense is known for, and they play really sound, really good defense. They try to confuse you and make you speed up your feet, and that's kind of the big emphasis for me is just playing my game, taking it one play at a time and taking what they gave me."
Joe Fagnano links up with Devontez Walker to get the @Ravens in the redzone Steam on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Ju3bX0SkZW
The most impressive aspect of Fagnano's performance was how calm and poised he stayed under pressure, not letting himself get rattled or caught off guard. He didn't put the ball in harm's way and continues to show a high-level ability as a processor. Even though he's an older rookie at 25 years old, he's still just a first-year pro and is already showing the maturity and other alluring traits of a veteran reserve.
"I thought Joe [Fagnano] came in again — [the] second week in a row — and just kind of managed the offense really well," Minter said. "[He] got us down there a few times, made some really key plays throwing the ball, [and] guys made some nice catches for him."
It's been half a decade since the Ravens opened a season with three quarterbacks on their roster, and after being viewed as an afterthought when he was initially brought in as a rookie minicamp tryout, Fagnano is playing himself into no worse than a prime practice squad candidate, if not an initial 53-man roster consideration.

title: Stop Me If You've Heard This Before, But The Ravens Might Have A Receiver Problem
full_text:
The Ravens have always looked like a team at least one playmaker short on offense.
It appeared that way in March after some quality tight ends left the building in free agency. It seemed that way in April when they decided to stick with mercurial and pouty and largely ineffective Rashod Bateman as a potential starter rather than trade him. It looked that way in May, even after throwing a bunch of day two-and-three draft capital at potential pass catchers.
It looked that way a few weeks into training camp when even the Ravens coaches couldn’t really muster talking up any of these project tight ends as being close to ready to do actual assignments asked of real NFL tight ends ( the ability to block matters ), and if Mark Andrrews is anything close to as cooked as I believe he is, it’s going to be even more heightened in September, too.
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter is being uber conservative about how he approached the preseason, so his real offense and real offensive players did absolutely nothing in these games. And now that Bateman is facing three family violence charges in Georgia with word leaking out last week of his arrest, they probably need to get real about what this means for their football team.
Not sure Minter is going to be able to “no comment” his way through this situation, try as he might.
The allegations and details within the police report are disturbing. The NFL is looking into the matter and the NFL might decide that it’s in the league’s best interest to have a quasi-effective NFL player removed from the team and n longer representing that team and this league in its workplace and on its sidelines, by putting him on the Commissioner’s Exempt List.
Legal matters such as this can take quite some time to resolve, and as we know the NFL can take discipline even when the law does not. Bateman is a player I am on record that I would have traded for whatever you can get y ears ago and called it addition by subtraction. I’d have walked from him, and have urged the team to do in this space and others multiple times.
They’ve always been fooling themselves about this guy.
He doesn’t exude winning traits. He has only stuck around here this long because the general manager hates being ripped for years for failing with wide receivers and he’s a former first-round pick and he works cheap. He works cheap because of a shortsighted holdout a few years back, against the counsel he was receiving, which cost him service time.
He’s clashed with the team over his medicals and he’s felt aggrieved by coaches repeatedly, and seems to be forever basking in that next last chance. Again, he’s off my team years ago. I wouldn’t have had him on the plane back to Baltimore. I’d call the league and beg them to put him on that list ASAP. Pay him to stay away. It’s Roger’s way.
Bateman’s never clicked with a two-time MVP quarterback, Lamar Jackson, for any long period of time. His health tends to be iffy. Wouldn’t want him in my receiver room for a multitude of reasons. They got over on him with the contract, and seem to think that will motivate him to become something he never will be. Certainly not in Baltimore.
(When someone is the subject of this many trade rumors, it's for good reasons).
Instead, they built a roster in which he’s kinda got be a thing for this to work. Devontez Walker might be better than him, but we won’t know until he gets a real run in games that count, and he can’t stay healthy to this point. Ja’Kobi Lane looks like the real deal, but the learning curve tends to be steep, and consistency is usually elusive at first. Preseason can be a fickle indicator.
Zay Flowers is heck of a football player, but he’s not getting any taller.
Last week in Minnesota - losing the second-best center on the roster for the season and then with Bateman’s arrest coming to light - could prove to be significant for this offense months to come. A forward-thinking operation would have a plan to address the public’s concerns about a situation involving a three-month old child ready to roll out, as well as some options for finding capable replacements at receiver.

title: 13 Winners and  4 Losers From Ravens Preseason Win Over Vikings
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens played their second preseason game on Saturday and notched the first road win of the Jesse Minter era in a 13-3 triumph over the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium.
Once again, neither team played their star players, and with hardly any starters coming off an invaluable and fruitful two days of joint practices. The depth of the Ravens' defense at all three levels shone brightly and was the main catalyst that propelled them to the low-scoring victory.
Here are several Ravens players who showed out and a few who still have work to do after the second preseason game.
No player on either side of the ball or in any of the three phases of the game did more to help themselves and raise their respective stock than the undrafted rookie edge defender. All three of Burke's tackles were solos, including one for a loss, and he recorded a sack, two quarterback hits, two batted passes and generated the Ravens' first turnover of the preseason on a forced fumble to open the fourth quarter.
After watching his fellow rookie at the same position, Matthew Hibner , spark the offense with a big 20-plus-yard play last week, he got a chance to do the same against the Vikings. His 23-yard reception early in the second quarter jump-started the Ravens' first scoring drive of the game, and he finished with three catches for a team-leading 46 receiving yards.
If each half could have a Defensive Player of the Game, the second-year pro would be deserving of the first-half honors, based on a two-play sequence where he pretty much single-handedly torpedoed a promising Vikings drive. Late in the first quarter, he showed great bend and flexibility around the edge to sack J.J. McCarthy for a loss of six yards, and on the next play, he drew a holding penalty that backed them up even more after he beat the left tackle with an inside move.
The second-year pro didn't record a sack, quarterback hit or tackle for loss, but was a noticeably disruptive force when he was on the field, getting penetration into the backfield on run downs and generating pressure.
The undrafted rookie had another impressively solid and efficient outing, showing the most poise under pressure of the three Ravens signal callers who took the field in this game. He went 15-of-20 for 123 passing yards and a touchdown, with no turnovers and a passer rating of 106.9.
The sixth-round rookie made Ravens fans say, 'Jordan Stout, who?' during and after his masterful performance against the Vikings. Eckley was plenty busy in this game amid the lack of consistent offense from both squads, and he was a field-flipping weapon, averaging 55.3 yards per punt with a long of 60 and pinning Minnesota inside its own 10-yard line twice.
The second-year pro earned himself some much-needed redemption and good faith after going 2-for-2 on his field goal attempts. While his second was a chip shot, his first was from 49 yards out, the same distance he missed wide left from in the opener- but he drilled it down the middle this time. He also continues to appear to have solved his struggles with getting kickoffs in the landing zone after leading the league in infractions as a rookie.
The undrafted rookie had an up-and-down game, allowing the 36-yard completion that set up the Vikings' only points of the game in the first half on a pass he could've intercepted had he not tripped over his own feet. He made up for it by thwarting Minnesota's final scoring attempt when he recorded his first career interception in the fourth quarter and finished with six total tackles and a pass defense.
The fifth-round rookie saw a lot more playing time this time around compared to last week, when he didn't check into the game until the fourth quarter. He was on defense and making plays in the first half and finished with five total tackles, a pass breakup, a quarterback hit and half a sack.
The second-year pro flashed his all-purpose playmaking on offense by finishing as the team's leader in targets and receptions, hauling in 5-of-7 for 24 receiving yards and the only touchdown of the game. He was fearless going over the middle and held onto the ball despite being on the receiving end of some big hits. On special teams, he returned a kickoff for 29 yards and a pair of punts for 31 yards, with a long of 19.
The second-year pro was flying around all over the field on defense and special teams, playing downhill and with tremendous physicality. Jackson finished with sa game-high eight total tackles, including six solos and two for a loss, a quarterback hit and a drive-ending sack on a blitz.
The 10th-year veteran might've just played his way into the pole position to become the Ravens' next starting center in the wake of the season-ending injury suffered by Danny Pinter. Even though he didn't start for the second week in a row, he checked into the game much sooner than the final 14 plays, as he did in the opener, and this time around, he played the best of the three centers who took the field.
The seventh-round rookie flashed once again as an interior pass rusher, recording his first sack, a quarterback hit and a solo tackle for loss.
While Burke had a great bounce-back performance, the third-year pro continued to fade into obscurity and likely out of favor with the front office and coaches with another unimpactful outing. Isaac was the only edge defender who suited up for this game who didn't make their presence felt in a tangible way or even record so much as a tackle. At this point, the 2024 third-rounder will need one hell of a preseason finale to keep himself off either the trading or chopping block.
The fourth-year pro got to make his first start after impressing in relief duty in the opener, but he wasn't able to build on that performance and was in the middle of the blocking unit that struggled out of the gate. Instead of further proving that he should be the frontrunner to win the starting center job, he left the door open for Pocic to leapfrog him with a lackluster performance against the Vikings' second-team defensive line.
After only playing a handful of snaps on the first two drives in the opener, the first-round pick and starting right guard played the whole first quarter and then some, and wasn't nearly as impressive as he was in his debut, getting called for his first holding penalty as a pro on the Ravens' opening drive.
The second-year pro made his second straight at right tackle and played the bulk of offensive snaps, but unlike the opener, he was far from disciplined in his technique and execution. He led the team with three holding penalties, two of which came on the same drive on the Ravens' second-to-last possession. Lichtenhan will need a strong bounce-back performance in the finale to make a push for a roster spot.

title: Key Players The Ravens Want To Stash On Their Practice Squad
full_text:
The practice squad isn’t the sexiest aspect of summer in the NFL by far.
But proper construction of the unit is paramount, a lot of these guys are a single injury away from the active roster and with eligibility for this unit expanded in recent years the competition to land the best and deepest squad is quite intense. For tanking/rebuilding teams, the squad is about stashing as many potential future NFL bodies as possible, and while that goal remain for teams in Super Bowl mode like the Ravens, they also need to have a strong veteran presence at vital positions as well, who already have NFL experience for if/when they make the 53-man active unit.
This is the first time rookie head coach Jesse Minter and 30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle have been in these roles, and the reality is the Ravens personnel department has as much jam as ever in all matters of rosters and cuts and contracts. The coaches have enough going on just figuring out how to do their jobs, which was a core element in why team president Sashi Brown and general manager Eric DeCosta were always going to hire first-time guys. This is their building in ways it never could have been with a coach like John Harbaugh still around.
Despite having a large draft class -11 players – the Ravens continue to have undrafted rookies and players who were on the practice squad last year without seeing real NFL action making a case for staying in Owings Mills in some capacity. How many do, and how many perhaps see a path to quickly playing time on someone else’s practice squad, or even their active roster, is a challenging calculus that will make next weekend an absolute whirlwind.
We continue to anticipate the Ravens making at least one trade given their glut of interesting and capable cornerbacks , and they will look to upgrade on some youngsters who would be pegged for the PS today if they had to make cuts right now.
These are some interesting cases of youngsters I believe they will want to keep on the PS:
It’s been a minute since the Ravens have had a guy stashed on their practice squad come through and flash even a little bit as a situational pass rusher. And for as many resources as they have invested in EDGE this offseason, Trey Hendrickson’s age and health must be monitored and Zion Young, second-round pick or not, is going to need time to develop.
This roster is just too deep and too healthy on the defensive side for him to crack it.
Would seem a little redundant for both of them to end up sticking here. DeLuca is a undrafted kid out of Penn State, who was a former walk-on, and has ended up playing 74 snaps thus far, more than anyone on defense. Doesn’t mean much in the end and sometimes the guys who play the most are the ones most likely gone.
Burke, undrafted from Texas, was all over the place Saturday and had the kind of motor they love. These are both the kind of stories they love. Friday night against the Commanders I figure is a huge night for them. The Ravens are on the prowl for veteran understudies to Roquan Smith on other rosters.
The Ravens depth corners have made a steady buzz all summer. This name hasn’t really been mentioned anywhere. The front office probably loves it that way. Everything about his frame and body screams out a DB who could excel in quarters coverage and the things Minter loves to do.
I don’t really care about him scooping up a fumble Saturday. Him getting on the field after being banged up earlier is big. He has legit NFL experience and size and length you don’t find everywhere.
The fact I can now spell his name correctly the first time I go to type it tells you quite a bit. Did not expect to be watching him this much and writing about him this much. But they clearly view him as a developmental tackle, and you have to be constantly churning for them, and the way they looked at a Carson Vinson in the past might be a portal into what they think they can do with this undrafted kid out of Oregon State.
I’d make the case that OT is an area they should be looking to scoop up a veteran, bigtime, when roster cuts start flying around the league. But giving Lichtenhan 121 reps through two games – he’s played 23 more snaps than anyone  else on the roster, and all but like six of their overall snaps on offense – isn’t a fluke.
Did I mention this kid is 6-foot-8, 330 pounds? We know Ronnie Stanley has been an injury risk for years and Roger Rosengarten might be another guy who the market wants to reward in ways the Ravens just won’t meet (we’ve seen this with offensive linemen here over and over with Tyler Linderbaum the latest example ).
They should be hording raw tackles with upside if possible.
With so many veteran QBs about to be cut, it would be pretty surprising if the Ravens weren’t able to usher him right back to their practice squad. But you never totally know, and I wonder if they opt to play him a ton Friday or, just give that game to Austin Reed thinking no reason to put any more quality film from Fagnano out there to whet someone’s whistle.

title: These Critical Numbers Tell The Story Of The Ravens First Two Preseason Wins
full_text:
The numbers tend to tell a story, even in the preseason.
The Ravens won their second straight exhibition game under Jesse Minter in Minnesota, and it wasn’t nearly as easy as the first time around at home to the Eagles. Baltimore’s offense was particularly suspect in the first half and the defense have up more explosive plays than Minter would like and if Vikings quarterback JJ McCarthy was remotely accurate the would have given up more points.
Overall, no matter how you slice the numbers these preseason outings have gone better than anyone could have hoped for . The injuries have been at a minimum and the pre-snap issues have been at a minimum and the penalties have been at a minimum. This team needs its defense to lead the way right away and be infinitely better than it was under Zach Orr, and while it’s backups doing the work, the defense is getting pressure and stops.
These are key numbers that standout both Saturday and through two preseason games.
That’s what the offensive line allowed when Snoop Huntley was on the field Saturday. Vikings defensive coordinator blitzed a ton as we told you he would – 46% of the time on Huntley’s snaps – and the veteran QB was skittish and uncertain of his line.
The Ravens tried to lean into some heavy personnel and that didn’t really help, either. They ran nine plays out of 12 personnel in the first half, and averaged 2.2 yards per rush and 4.8 yards/play. The blitz and pressure overwhelmed them. These young tight ends can get pushed around .
Yeah it was a real struggle at the line of scrimmage for the Ravens on Saturday. We’ll see what the film tells the coaches, but that first offensive line group had their share of issues and they gave Jovaughn Gwyn a few series but they’ve always known who their starting center was going to be.
Not having rookie running back Adam Randall was significant and this would have been a great test for him in pass protection. Minter says he should be back soon and they should be careful with him. They haven’t offered much of an update on Rasheen Ali, and this is a position they may need to address in a more meaningful way soon.
The Ravens just added Jonathan Ward to the roster and he got 10 carries but it wasn’t pretty. They averaged 2.6 yards per rush as a team.
That’s what this defense has allowed on third down through two games. That’s pretty wild even for the preseason. Of course, it wasn’t perfect Saturday like it was last week, but holding tams to 5-for23 is pretty damn good. It’s a vital area they must improve in the regular season from a year ago.
It was ugly under Orr and the personnel wasn’t good enough and the scheme definitely wasn’t good enough. Minter exceled in this regard ( as we broke down in detail )
That’s what the Ravens QBs have done when throwing from under center in the preseason. Just a cool 18-for-22 for 209 yards. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano did throw a pick from under center in the back of the end zone in the preseason opener – not a horrible pass or decision – but otherwise it’s nearly perfect.
There is a lot of boot action being involved in these looks, often off play action. Loved the miss direction throw across the field to the running back for a nice first-down pick up Saturday. The young tight ends have shown up downfield in under center play action looks, helping them get open and stretch.
Sean Payton believes in it as much as anyone on the planet, as he explained it to us on “The Daily Flock,” and his is the voice in Declan Doyle’s head as the 30-year-old coordinator calls plays for the first time.
That’s what veteran center Ethan Pocic has played through two preseason games (28 of them came Saturday) and that should be enough. With Danny Pinter out for the season, and Pocic coming off an Achilles tear, Saturday should have been their opportunity to maximize his snaps because the final preseason game is no spot for a veteran as important as he is.
That’s usually a bleep show for the bottom of the roster. If they weren’t sure how far Pocic could do, this was probably the best chance to find out. Get him through practice and get him to Week 1. They need a savvy veteran there for his brain as much as his production.
That’s how many were generated on Saturday by the Ravens defensive linemen alone. Yeah. How about that? Feels like we could have gone a month last season and not approach that number.
Yes, they got to feast on some offensive linemen who will not be playing in the league. But Mike Green had dominant moments before he made way for others and seventh-round pick Rayshaun Benny flashed and Kaimon Rucker was moving people around and finding pass rush lanes.
Add in the fact how active and effective some of these defensive backs looked blitzing and it’s easy to get excited about what this defense could look like.
That’s how many flags have been thrown on Minter’s defense through two games. Yes, one penalty. Undrafted rookie linebacker Dominic DeLuca, who has looked better than anyone could have hoped for being asked to play as much as he has, picked up a pass interference call late in Saturday’s game.
Now on offense it was much more of what we warned you was coming given this game’s location and who was calling the defensive plays. They got flagged seven times and all the youth and inexperience of the players and the newness of the coordinator and the offense showed up. All of it was expected and part of the process.

title: Ravens Preseason Snap Counts: Who Played the Most?
full_text:
The Ravens did not lean nearly as heavily into their rookie class in the second preseason game as they did in the first.
Make of that what you will.
Perhaps, rookie head coach Jesse Minter just wanted to get a longer look at middling veterans. Maybe they liked so much of what they saw in the opener that they didn’t feel the need to duplicate that Saturday. Maybe the challenges brought by a unique defense gave then some pause. Maybe they had this plan all along.
Playing more doesn’t always indicate import – in fact a lot of times it’s just the opposite. We don’t have many repeat winners here in the snap count by position group, but on the offensive line and at quarterback the undrafted rookies continue to get the heaviest run. Here are your leaders from Saturday:
Okay, so he didn’t play every single snap at right tackle like he did in the opener. But he did play 45 snaps against the Vikings and at this point they see something they like in the undrafted rookie out of Oregon State (beyond just his size (6-foot-8, 330 pounds).
He played 10 more snaps than anyone else on the offensive line and will be in line for another big outing Friday. Would imagine they see practice squad potential here. The entire line has room for improvement after this outing but this is a body type that merits some work.
This kid continues to impress. Held up against the blitz. Didn’t play quite as much as in the opener as back-up Snoop Huntley got more of a run, so it was 28 snaps this time. He is definitely on the practice squad and there is some potential for him as a f uture backup if he keeps this up .
As noted, the rookies didn’t get as long a look at this spot. Ja’Kobi Lane (third round) played just 17 snaps and Elijah Sarratt (fourth round) logged just six snaps. Might this have something to do with the fact that starting wide receiver Rashod Bateman is facing three charges of family violence his time away from the team in June, with some ugly details from the police report coming from TMZ .
Either way, Walker played 30 snaps and he has the skillet to, frankly, phase out the brooding and oft-disgruntled Bateman, who this franchise should have moved on from and upgraded on in the past for pure football reasons.
He got more of a run than fellow rookie draft pick Matthew Hibner (27 snaps), on the field for 33 plays in leading this tepid offense with 46 receiving yards. Showed up for some under center play action shots early in the game. Has more of a chance to maybe, kinda hold up a little in a blocking role than Hibner. Maybe.
He just got signed and saw regular action in this game. Rasheen Ali and rookie Adam Randall were both out with injuries. Depth at this spot was always in question. Ward played 25 snaps. The line was not good and the run game was pretty ugly (2.6 yards/carry as a team).
Higgens led all Ravens, regardless of position, with 56 snaps played. Baltimore was on the field for 61 snaps on defense, so this was quite a run. He was knocked from the last game with an injury and he and rookie undrafted free agent Dominic DeLuca got active on some early blitzes and formed a nice tandem.
DeLuca led all Ravens linebackers in snaps last week and came in second on the team with 47 snaps played in this one. Undrafted linebacker Ethan Burke was all over the place in this game as well. We hear the Ravens are paying close attention to a former draft pick this summer , too looking for an understudy for Roquan Smith, with more knowledge and experience in this system.
They each played 36 snaps. Rivers, a late round pick with the body type to handle gadget guys in the slot, got active with the slot blitz. Walters had issues in coverage, getting tangled up and not able to high point some jumpballs, but finished strong with an interception. The Ravens didn’t even risk it much with another young slot corner as Keyon Martin, who is on this team, played just 17 snaps.
Keondre Jackson led the safeties in snaps with 35 and continues to shine when he blitzes from the slot or even takes off from the second level.
He flashed off the edge and showed some motor and bit of a pass rush plan. The UNC product spent last season on the practice squad and had a good week of practice against the Vikings and played 29 snaps Saturday. He produced two pressures and would seem like someone they want to stick around for depth again this season.

title: Ravens Rookie QB Joe Fagnano Playing Way Onto Practice Squad With Another Preseason Gem
full_text:
The boxscore from Joe Fagnano’s exhibition debut last week might pop a bit more than Saturday’s, perhaps. But this outing against the Minnesota Vikings, on the road, against a blitz-heavy defense, was probably more impressive.
The undrafted rookie out of UCONN had stellar film from thrashing the Eagles a week ago and coming out of nowhere to do so. Vikings aggressive defensive mastermind Brian Flores treats the preseason closer to the real thing than most who call plays on defense, and Fagnano entered this road game at a time when Baltimore’s offense was lifeless and suspect with No. 2 quarterback Snoop Huntley at the helm.
Once again Fagnano exceeded all reasonable hopes and expectations and he has absolutely played his way on to the roster as at least a practice squad signee. He was sharp in a 13-3 win at US Bank Stadium and he looks like a true developmental QB who should run their scout team and participate in their QB room getting trained and vested in this offense in case injuries really do strike. Preseason or not, his internal clock and decision making and poise look real, and he flashed some escapability as well away from home, and there is ample clay for Ravens rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle to mold here.
“Joe came in, second week in a row, and kind of managed the offense really well,” rookie head coach Jesse Minter said after the game Saturday. “He got us down there a few times, and he made some key plays throwing the ball. Guys made some nice catches for him. I just like the way we played in the second half.”
Fagnano could have felt the pressure, literally, in this one, getting blitzed 40 percent of the time, as Flores is apt to do.
With expectations peaked following a debut in which he led all NFL passers in completions and passing yardage, it would be natural if he took a step back. This was anything but, and he’s gone from a non-entity from a roster perspective to take better advantage of these opportunities than anyone could have imagined.
He finished 15/20 for 123 yards and a touchdown (106.5 rating) and after some early passes he’d want back Fagnano got into a lather and made things happen despite not having the run game and assistance he was getting from his novice teammates and line a week ago.
“Overall, just how I managed to operate the offense is something I really wanted to do,” Fagnano said in an interview with the Ravens broadcast team after the game. “That’s also a credit to the guys around me. I’m one of 11.”
Fagnano was a total surprise last Saturday , but the Ravens were already pushing the Eagles around when he entered that game and he got off to a great start. In Minnesota, the Ravens starters, including No. 2 QB Snoop Huntley, struggled mightily and the offensive line was shaky, and it wasn’t a situation where Baltimore’s rookie class of pass catchers was already taking a game over.
He entered late in the first half, didn’t have great field position (the 15), and rookie coordinator Declan Doyle eschewed a chance to go hurry up and lean into a two-minute opportunity. It seemed Doyle (who opted to call plays again from the pressbox) needed halftime as much as anyone, and his offense took major strides in the second half.
Fagnano led a TD drive in which he made a perfect pass to Devontez Walker in the middle of the field on third-and-11, he overcome an offensive pass interference penalty to keep the drive going and with the Ravens in the redzone for the first time in the game he found LaJohntay Wester open on the sidelines for score. His progressions were smooth and he didn't get jittery or sacrifice his footwork.
“I’m just blessed to be able to pay in a stadium like this,” he said looking around and taking it all in as he conducted the post-game chat. “Drafted or not drafted, I’m going to take my opportunities as they come.”
That pass to Walker was the first of nine straight completions for him. He was asked to operate under center – unusual to him from college – and he again excelled at that vital component of the Sean Payton offense that Doyle is running (as Payton explained to us) – going 8-for-10 for 66 yards and often incorporating boot action for misdirection and throwing back across the field.
The kid went 5-for-8 for 37 yards against the blitz, and he has dropped back 52 times through two games and taken just one sack.
“He’s a general out there,” rookie tight end Josh Cuevas, who led the team with 46 receiving yards, said of Fagnano after the game. “When he gets his chances he’s been great these first two outings ... I can’t say enough about that guy.”
Fagnano is taking everything in stride and continuing to open eyes. He doesn’t seem shocked by what he’s doing even if everyone else is. And it would stand to reason that he plays quite a bit in Friday’s preseason finale back in Baltimore.
“I’m just playing football,” Fagnano said. “It doesn’t matter how many people are in the stands or where we're playing … I’m taking it day by day and play by play, and seeing where this goes.”
It’s already been going far better, with much more upside, than anyone but Fagnano could have anticipated.

title: Bills Finally Receive Positive News on Injured Rookies Skyler Bell, Jalon Kilgore
full_text:
Fresh off an impressive 31-7 road victory over the Cleveland Browns during the team’s second preseason game, the Buffalo Bills returned to practice in Orchard Park on Monday morning as preparations for the regular season continue.
And, with Thursday night’s final preseason outing against the Pittsburgh Steelers just around the corner at the new Highmark Stadium prior to Sunday’s roster cut-down day, the Bills still have plenty of critical decisions left to make .
So far this summer Buffalo has been somewhat slammed by a lengthy injury report , particularly as of late , which has made the evaluation process a little harder for first-year head coach Joe Brady and general manager Brandon Beane.
Even still, the team has been impressive in its two exhibition matchups this month as the Bills have outscored their opponents 60-21.
We wrote about the 10 players who did not practice on Monday, including four new additions to the injury list .
But, be that as it may, on Monday there was actually also a bit of good news for Buffalo as rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell and rookie defensive back Jalon Kilgore returned to the practice field after a somewhat lengthy stay on the sidelines this month, especially for Bell, who hadn’t practiced since before the team’s “Return of the Blue and Red” scrimmage on Saturday, August 8. Fellow receiver Dante Pettis also returned to action after missing the preseason game against Cleveland .
Despite some important players still being out, it’s at least a good sign for Bell and Kilgore, two players who were once thought to possibly have fairly large roles during their rookie seasons in Western New York.
Not practicing today for the Bills: Sedrick Van Pran-Granger Connor McGovern Jude Bowry Ty Johnson Keon Coleman Khalil Shakir Ed Oliver Javon Solomon Terrel Bernard CJ Gardner-Johnson Returning: Jalon Kilgore, Dante Pettis, Skyler Bell
Kilgore will still presumably be stuck behind fellow safeties Cole Bishop and C.J. Gardner-Johnson for most of the season, but Bell has a chance to reclaim a top role this year that many thought was going to be his in Buffalo after he was drafted by the team earlier this spring.
Fellow wideouts Keon Coleman and Khalil Shakir remained out with injuries on Monday, which means the 2026 fourth-rounder out of University of Connecticut can make up some ground during the team’s final preseason game against Pittsburgh in just a few days.
The 5-foot-11, 192-pounder finished second in the entire FBS for receiving yardage during his senior collegiate season in 2025 for the Huskies by racking up 1,278 receiving yards and 13 receiving touchdowns on 101 receptions.
He has the talent: there’s a reason why the Bills selected him early on Day 3 of this April’s draft.
But, Bell was hampered by a hamstring injury during the spring, and the injury bug subsequently followed him into the summer as he’s been dealing with a separate groin issue lately.
However, the fact that he was able to finally return to action after more than two weeks away due to the ailment is definitely a sight for sore eyes amongst the coaches and the fanbase.
Now, it’s just a matter of Bell getting quickly back up to speed in order to contribute when the regular season rolls around.
The game against Houston will be here quicker than anyone realizes, so fans will have to keep a close eye on how things progress with the rookie moving forward.

title: Bills' History, Roster Underdog's Play Suggest Fullback Remains in Joe Brady's Plans
full_text:
They've been an endangered species in NFL circles for more than a decade now, but the Buffalo Bills have bucked the trend.
The Bills are one of the few teams who haven't, even partially, abandoned the fullback.
Whether it was former Pro Bowler Pat DiMarco for the first three years of general manager Brandon Beane's tenure or Reggie Gilliam for the next six seasons, the Bills have consistently kept a fullback in their arsenal. It's worth noting that Buffalo employed four different offensive coordinators over the aforementioned nine-year span, and the fullback position survived every change.
Needing to identify a replacement for Gilliam , who left in free agency, the Bills entered training camp with two fullbacks on the 90-man roster.
When they cut undrafted rookie Jackson Acker, leaving converted linebacker Ben VanSumeren as the only fullback on the 90-man roster, however, it raised the question of whether or not a fullback would be in the team's regular season plans .
"I would have loved to have kept two even through this point, but with some of the injury situations, some of the moves, it was unfortunate that we had to make a move," said rookie head coach Joe Brady. "We're still evaluating is it a position and a role that we'll be able to have on our football team."
During the 2025 season with Brady as the offensive coordinator, the Bills deployed Gilliam for 21 percent of the offense's snaps. Brady made it a point to highlight Gilliam's value on two separate occasions last summer with his comments suggesting an appreciation for the position.
The Bills took a hard look at VanSumeren during the August 22 preseason road game against the Cleveland Browns.
Buffalo used a fullback on 19 offensive snaps , equating to 32 percent of the time, and VanSumeren proved valuable in the run game.
"Ben has a great mentality of the way that he plays football, and he's still learning the position," said Brady. "The more opportunities he has at it, the more he has an opportunity to display if that can be a vision and a role for him."
If the Bills are to use a roster spot for a fullback, it will almost certainly come with the expectation of contributing to the kicking and return units. In a positive sign, VanSumeren logged a team-high 16 special teams reps against the Browns.
It's worth noting that Bills' new offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael kept a fullback in his arsenal when coaching quarterback Drew Brees and the New Orleans Saints.
The Saints gave Heath Evans a heavy volume of reps, especially in the run game, during the 2009 and 2010 seasons with Carmichael serving as offensive coordinator under Sean Payton.
Next, Jed Collins played more than 30 percent of snaps for the Saints from 2011 through 2013.
Add it all up, and VanSumeren is no longer a roster long shot.

title: Six Bills' Questions Still Lingering With Six Days Until Final Roster Cuts
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills had a busy few days last week— for many reasons —but in the midst of it all the team managed to come together for a 31-7 victory over the Cleveland Browns to move its preseason record to 2-0 under first-year head coach Joe Brady.
And, despite a bit of a slow start defensively , the Bills were quite dominant during their outing with the Browns at Huntington Bank Field on Saturday afternoon, which was clearly evidenced by the lopsided victory.
Even still, there are some things left unanswered from Brady’s squad as Buffalo prepares this week for its final preseason game with the Pittsburgh Steelers at the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday at 7 p.m. ET in Orchard Park, New York.
Final roster cuts must be made by August 30, so the matchup with Pittsburgh will loom large for a few of the veterans currently on the roster fringe.
Here are six questions that must be answered by the Bills before September rolls around in the coming days.
Like seemingly every summer, there have been more than a few surprise players thus far in training camp for the Bills that have made a positive impression.
Most of the time, however, those fan favorites tend to fade away come final roster cut-down day. Will that happen again this time around when the deadline approaches on August 30? Or will some of these stellar summer standouts hold onto a 53-man roster spot?
Bills Mafia will have to wait and find out after Buffalo’s upcoming game with Pittsburgh, but some names to monitor are rookie cornerback Kani Walker , former undrafted veteran linebackers Joe Andreessen and Keonta Jenkins, as well as receivers Mecole Hardman Jr., Dante Pettis, and Trent Sherfield Sr., who made his presence felt against the Browns in a major way by raking in a game-high four catches for 54 yards.
Veteran fullback Ben VanSumeren is also one player who fans should keep a close eye on over the next few days.
Honestly, for as much flak as these two players caught from fans and outside observers heading into training camp, both Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele have performed quite admirably for the majority of this summer.
The two backups had a slightly shaky start to camp at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford, New York, but both Allen and Buechele have done fairly well since being back at One Bills Drive.
They’ve also held up their end of the bargain in the two preseason games, as well, which is showcased by the team’s 60-21 scoring differential in the exhibition contests against the Carolina Panthers and Cleveland Browns.
And, their most recent performances against the Browns might’ve been the best either player has ever looked while wearing a Bills’ uniform.
Allen finished his day 10-of-12 for 128 yards and one touchdown, while Buechele went 5-for-10 for 111 yards and one passing touchdown in addition to tallying a rushing touchdown.
If Allen doesn’t play at all on Thursday against the Steelers, then it’s likely that the backup quarterback role on Buffalo’s roster is his for 2026.
However, if he sees the field, then it’ll mean it’s still a competition. And, if that’s the case, then who knows?
Maybe Buechele can surprise everyone and earn the Bills’ No. 2 spot seemingly out of nowhere.
Coming into Bills’ training camp, it was thought by many that 2025 second-round pick T.J. Sanders was going to assume the third starting defensive lineman role alongside fellow defenders Ed Oliver and Deone Walker this season in the team’s new 3-4 scheme under first-year NFL defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard .
However, it’s been a hot-and-cold summer so far from the former South Carolina Gamecock, and he hasn’t taken a firm grasp of the opportunity that was put before him by the Bills at the start of camp at St. John Fisher University .
Instead, somewhat shockingly, it’s been fellow second-year defensive lineman Landon Jackson who has seemingly stolen the spotlight away from Sanders through this portion of August.
It’s been a pleasant surprise from Jackson, to say the least, and it has put immense pressure on Sanders to step up in a big way over this final stretch before Week 1 rolls around on September 13.
It’ll be interesting to see if Jackson completes his hijacking of the vacant starting job, or if Sanders can reclaim relevancy on the roster for 2026.
Every offseason around this time, the thought comes around from fans that team president/ general manager Brandon Beane will be able to pull off some “ Beane After Dark ” magic and slyly trade away a few players to unsuspecting teams around the league in return for draft compensation instead of having to trim those same players from the final 53-man roster on cut-down day.
I mean, he’s done it before . . . remember former Bills’ offensive lineman Russell Bodine, anyone?
Anyway, be that as it may—while those types of moves are few and far between—the thought still remains the same this summer.
Some names to keep in mind are veteran interior offensive linemen Sedrick Van Pran-Granger and Chase Lundt, safeties Damar Hamlin and Geno Stone, as well as running back Ty Johnson, who has failed to practice since August 8 due to a soft-tissue injury, which has created quite the pathway for players like Frank Gore Jr. and Ian Wheeler to make some noise this preseason.
Let’s watch these possible developments closely, shall we?
Like with the backup quarterbacks that were previously mentioned, there are many other undecided roster battles ongoing in Western New York this month.
And, they’re at critical starting positions, nonetheless.
Starting spots at left guard , inside linebacker , and punter are all seemingly still without a winner, and the regular season starts in less than three weeks.
It’s getting time for head coach Joe Brady to start making some tough decisions.
This was a question that was also posed last week from us over here at Bills ON SI, but it’s still lingering: where are new defensive/offensive coordinators Jim Leonhard and Pete Carmichael Jr. going to be during the games this regular season?
Will they both be in the box? On the sideline beside head coach Joe Brady?
Well, so far the two coaches have split their time between the booth and the sideline during the first two preseason games, so it will be interesting to see which way they lean for the final exhibition game against the Steelers on Thursday.
Presumably, one would think that after doing one of each against Carolina and Cleveland, that the two coaches would choose their preferred destination for this third game in order to get one final true test run against Pittsburgh before the regular season starts in September.
