title: Browns Coach Todd Monken Shares When He Will Name His Starting QB
full_text:
Todd Monken is getting the full Cleveland Browns experience in his first season as head coach.
We are entering the final week of the preseason and he has still not named a starting quarterback. Deshaun Watson seemed to be the favorite over Shedeur Sanders throughout the summer, only to basically say he doesn't like Browns fans in Saturday's postgame press conference.
The situation is a bit of a mess but Monken still has to come to a decision. He spoke to the media Sunday and revealed when he will name his starter.
Monken opened his remarks with a declaration that he will make his announcement on Monday.
Browns HC Todd Monken told reporters today that he plans to announce his Week 1 starting quarterback on Monday.
Well, he said he "anticipates" naming his starter on Monday. Hopefully, that means he is in fact making Monday the deadline. That needs to happen so the starter, whether it's Watson or Sanders, can begin getting the full first-team reps in practice. Week 1 is only three weeks away.
Monken also let it be known he won't be playing Watson or Sanders in Thursday's preseason finale against the New England Patriots. Instead, fans will be seeing Dillon Gabriel and rookie Taylen Green at quarterback.
Thursday night will be Dillon Gabriel and Taylen Green at QB for the Browns, per Todd Monken. No more preseason game action for Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders.
Watson's postgame comments following an ugly performance on Saturday added a whole new layer to Monken's decision. The quarterback called out the fans for booing him and for cheering back in 2024 when he was carted off with a season-ending injury. That is a fair gripe, but does make it clear he is just not a good fit in 2026. It seems as if he hates the fans and the fans hate him. That is not a recipe for any type of success in the NFL.
Yet Monken's top goal is to win football games and he will go with Watson if he feels that gives the team the best chance at winning. That may just not be the case anymore after Saturday's performance both during and after the game.
The good news in all of this is that the debates can finally end and fans can start to focus on Week 1. Given recent history, it would not be surprising to see both quarterbacks make starts and do so early in the season. That is especially true if the team starts 0-2 before returning home in Week 1.
Fans may just mutiny if Watson starts the home opener in Week 3.

title: Deshaun Watson’s Meltdown Puts Browns QB Decision in Jimmy Haslam’s Hands
full_text:
When head coach Todd Monken revealed he would likely keep most of the Cleveland Browns' starters out of the Week 2 preseason game versus the Bills , it looked like we were headed towards an uneventful exhibition game with little relevance towards the team’s open quarterback competition.
Instead, we got an all-time post-game meltdown that might have decided it, once and for all.
Two days after twice stating he didn’t care about being booed, Deshaun Watson showed he actually did care -- a lot. He cared enough to expose a fractured psyche and a profound contempt for Cleveland that now takes the starting quarterback decision out of Monken’s hands and puts it squarely on Browns’ owner Jimmy Haslam’s shoulders.
And sure, there’s a good chance that the followup will be a statement trying to explain everything away, pointing to words taken out of context and being misconstrued -- because that’s all Watson seems to do these days, point his finger at everyone.
But make no mistake, Watson despises Cleveland to the point it’s evident he does not want to play for this team nor its fandom.
Perhaps the most damning part in Watson’s trainwreck of a presser came when he stated "I thought being away for two years and working myself back from two Achilles injuries and putting the time in and being around the facility, being around the city, doing charity work in the city, supporting the Cleveland Browns, hanging out with fans whenever I do see them, being honest, being the type of person that I know I am and the character would help. And I guess it hasn't.”
"Being honest, being the type of person I know I am and the character would help, but I guess it hasn't. That's why I say it's personal." #Browns Deshaun Watson on the negative reception he received from fans today at the preseason game: pic.twitter.com/rPMi2iaxVj
That paragraph illustrates that Watson has been carrying these feelings for some time, while also putting into question the motives behind what now appears to have been just a good guy act, instead of genuine engagement.
Watson’s biggest mistake is believing yesterday’s boos have nothing to do with performance. They have everything to do with performance. Because nowhere will Watson ever find a platform that will enable him to make amends with the character issues that led him to get booted out of Houston, than in sports, where winning cures everything.
Image rehabilitation through playing at a high level is not uncommon in the NFL, even in Cleveland. Just ask Kareem Hunt. And nobody has ever received a bigger second chance than Watson, to the tune of $230 million guaranteed over five years.
And every single fan in Cleveland knows that the returns on that investment, one that also cost the club six draft picks, including three-first rounders, have been underwhelming, including what he's shown at training camp and how he played yesterday during the third quarter at Huntington Bank Field.
By stating "I think the whole world knows it has nothing to do about the performance," Watson is attempting to shift responsibility for his sub-par showings, dating all the way back to before his first Achilles’ injury.
#Browns QB Deshaun Watson on being booed by fans today. "It has nothing to do about the performance. It's a little bit [more] personal than that. It's a disrespectful thing." "Last time I played on this field, I tore my Achilles. And that same fan base cheered when I got hurt." pic.twitter.com/yB1g0OznZf
Yes, Watson is entitled to feel disrespected for hearing cheers when he got injured . But he wasn’t injured yesterday.
Watson’s comments should take the final word on the quarterback competition away from Monken, because they are rooted in off-the-field issues, some of which could actually keep Watson from performing at all. And because it’s now a business decision, more than a purely sports competition.
“I don’t know. I don’t know,” said Watson when asked if he could overcome the boos. “It’s a mental battle every day.”
The Browns are currently slated to start selling Personal Seat Licenses for their new Brook Park Stadium in mid-September, and Watson’s meltdown couldn’t have come at a worse time from that perspective.
How likely is it that fans will flock to buy up PSLs with Watson as the team’s quarterback? And while there’s a very remote possibility that the quarterback that ends up playing for the Browns during their debut season at the new venue in 2029 is currently on the team’s roster, Cleveland still needs to drum up interest for the team ahead of the move.
Beyond all financial considerations, though, Haslam needs to look in the mirror and ask himself: Is this the guy I want leading my team? Because playing quarterback in the NFL is more than just slinging the ball. It’s about leadership, and accountability, and being the guy others can look up to in the locker room.
Watson exhibited none of the above yesterday.
Haslam’s hand could now be forced to impose a quarterback on his coaching staff. Watson, who was supposed to run away with the open competition, now looks like he’s ready to run away from the team that gave him every chance in the world.
And yes, performance was the biggest factor.

title: Cleveland Browns Add Veteran Defensive Lineman After Season-Ending Injury to Another
full_text:
The Cleveland Browns aren't done adding talent to the roster just yet.
After losing defensive lineman Alex Wright to a season-ending Achilles injury during a practice with the Buffalo Bills on Thursday, the Browns are officially adding a veteran from free agency to take his place.
On Sunday, August 23, it was announced that Derek Barnett would be signing a one-year deal worth $5.5 million to join the Browns for the 2026 campaign. The 30-year-old edge rusher last played with the Houston Texans, finishing the 2025 season with 21 tackles, eight for a loss, 10 quarterback hits and five sacks.
Just two days before it was announced, Browns OnSI shared that Barnett would be a good fit in Cleveland, especially on a short-term deal.
Immediately, Barnett will have a chance to get on the field with a relatively young and inexperienced group around him. Not only will this give him the best chance at showing the league he still has something in the tank, but he also has an opportunity to grow as a leader and increase his value in that regard.
Having won a Super Bowl with the Philadelphia Phillies just a few seasons ago, Barnett brings knowledge of the grandest stage of them all and experience in big-time moments.
Across nine years of ball at the highest level of the game, Barnett has totalled 216 tackles, 57 for a loss, 104 quarterback hits and 34 sacks. He has also jumped on top of five fumbles, forcing five himself.
While Barnett joining the Browns is a major positive, especially after Wright's announcement, he wasn't the organization's first choice.
The front office had been actively scouting the market for edge rushers, bringing in both Jadeveon Clowney and Za'Darius Smith for workouts over the last few weeks. Clowney ended up signing a deal with the Texans, where Barrett last played, while Smith joined his previous head coach, Kevin Stefanski, in Atlanta.
The Browns' top four edge rushers will likely now see a combination of Jared Verse, Isaiah McGuire, Mike Hall Jr. and Barrett getting a good chunk of time on the field.
Hall Jr. has spent much of the last few seasons playing defensive tackle, but did get the nod at defensive end this past Saturday in the Browns' preseason loss to the Buffalo Bills.
There is a chance that Barnett gets his first taste of action as a Brown on Thursday, August 27, when the Browns play host to the New England Patriots from Huntington Bank Field for the preseason finale. The two sides clash at 8:00 p.m. EST.

title: Dallas Cowboys Should Trade QB Joe Milton III Before It's Too Late
full_text:
Dallas Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton III is coming off of his best performances as an NFL player, even it was only a preseason game.
Milton shined in Dallas' 34-13 win over the Arizona Cardinals on Saturday, finishing 9 of 13 passing for 179 yards, two touchdowns and no picks along with one rushing score. All of this came in just one half of football, as Milton showed many why he might be the best choice over Sam Howell for the team's backup quarterback job.
However, we'd argue that the best course of action for Dallas is to seek out a trade for Milton before his value decreases in any fashion.
Teams will often pay up if it means acquiring a young quarterback with intriguing potential, and as things stand, that's the category Milton falls in to.
It's no secret that quarterback is the most valuable position in the NFL, and teams in need of one could fork over some notable assets in order to acquire one.
The Cleveland Browns immediately come to mind. Deshaun Watson was just announced as Cleveland's starting quarterback for the 2026 season, beating out Shedeur Sanders, but it's hard to imagine him having any sort of bounce-back success this fall.
Watson isn't the long-term answer in Cleveland. Sanders likely isn't either.
The Cowboys could give the Browns another future option to work with in Milton, who won't carry the negative publicity of Watson or the unmatched spotlight that's followed Sanders.
According to Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer, the backup quarterback battle remains close despite the fact Milton lit up the Arizona defense at State Farm Stadium.
This gives Dallas even more of a reason to seek out a trade. If Milton's performance against the Cardinals isn't enough to secure him the QB2 job, than what will? After all, Howell was "a little bit ahead" of Milton based on training camp, per Schottenheimer.
"I think quite honestly, if you would just take the training camp competition, it's probably neck and neck, and Sam may be a little bit ahead. That's why we actually started Sam in the first game," Schottenheimer said.
If there wasn't a legitimate third option at quarterback, the question of trading Milton would be off the table. But the Cowboys went and got Howell this offseason for an obvious reason: the jury was still out on Milton.
If the Cowboys truly thought that Milton was the next franchise quarterback in the post-Prescott era, they wouldn't have signed Howell earlier this offseason. Whoever will end up taking over for Prescott at some point simply isn't on the roster -- or maybe even in the league -- at this point.
When Dallas traded for Milton with the New England Patriots last offseason, the front office likely saw him as a potential candidate for that larger-than-life role, but it quickly became clear he was far too raw to
That's not to say Milton isn't a legit NFL talent, but a team like Dallas that has aspirations of ending a long Super Bowl drought can't afford to settle for anything less than Pro Bowl-level talent at quarterback.

title: Rookie Jaishawn Barham Could Be Cowboys Week 1 Starter At LB
full_text:
Entering the offseason, linebacker was one of the more pressing needs for the Dallas Cowboys, but they didn't make any major additions during free agency. While there were reports that they went after a few potential starters, Dallas didn't close the deal with any veterans.
Instead, they used draft capital to address the need. The Cowboys used the 92nd overall pick in Round 3 of the NFL draft on Michigan's Jaishawn Barham . They also brought in Dee Winters from the San Francisco 49ers, sending them a fifth-round pick for the Texas native.
When Winters was added, it was assumed that he would be the starter next to DeMarvion Overshown. Winters was coming off a breakout season, which saw him record 101 tackles, eight tackles for loss, and one interception. As we approach the end of the preseason, however, Winters' spot might be in question due to the ascension of Barham .
After making his preseason debut on Saturday, Barham has been earning plenty of praise, with the latest coming from Brian Schottenheimer. The head coach was impressed with Barham's physicality and hinted that he could be the Week 1 starter.
“The physical nature that he plays the game is real. You feel it. They felt it. We haven’t penciled in the starting lineup yet at really most spots and there’s still a lot of competition, but he’s the guy that maximizes opportunity. And he’s earned more opportunities. He plays the game the right way," Schottenheimer said via Jon Machota . “He was a guy that was trending up, and then he had the setback with the (groin) injury. I would say he’s trending up again.”
During his tenure at Michigan, Barham spent time at off-ball linebacker as well as on the edge. Once selected by the Cowboys, it was made clear that he would play inside linebacker in Christian Parker's scheme. Barham has been stellar in practice, but missed the preseason opener against the Seattle Seahawks. Against the Cardinals, he more than made up for the previous absence.
It was announced before the game that Barham would handle the green-dot duties , calling the plays for the defense. He handled this job well, with the entire defense operating on the same page. He was also a standout performer on his own, with five tackles and one tackle for loss. Barham was all over the field and could be the playmaker that this defense lacked in 2025.
The only question is whether he's ready for that role as a rookie. We'll soon find out, but Coach Schotty's comments suggest he might be.

title: Dallas Cowboys Rookie Drew Shelton Shows He Isn't Ready For Increased Role in OL
full_text:
When the Dallas Cowboys drafted offensive tackle Drew Shelton in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft, the hope was that he could seize the swing tackle role in Year 1.
However, through two preseason games, Shelton has shown he is far from being ready for role.
In preseason Week 1, Shelton surrendered three pressures and posted grades of 34.5 in pass-blocking and 65.2 in run-blocking, according to Pro Football Focus .
Just when we thought things couldn't get any worse for him in the second preseason game, they did. Shelton gave up four pressures and posted PFF grades of 47.9 and 3.0 in run-blocking and pass protection, respectively.
The glass-half-full look at those grades is that the pass pro grade has skyrocketed from the 0.0 PFF initially had it at.
#Cowboys LT Drew Shelton had a 0.0 pass-blocking grade in Week 2 of the preseason, according to @PFF . He allowed four pressures, three hurries, and one QB hit.
In all seriousness, it has been a dreadful start to Shelton's career in Dallas, as he's allowed seven pressures, three QB hits and has grades of 13.5 in pass-blocking and 53.9 in run-blocking over a pair of exhibition contests.
Not exactly what you want to see from a fourth-round pick and the numbers show the Cowboys cannot depend on him for any kind of a significant role, leaving Dallas one less option in the event Tyler Guyton struggles again in 2026.
On the bright side, this performance isn't totally shocking, as the overwhelming belief was that Shelton was going to need time before he could be relied upon.
As Lance Zierlein of NFL.com noted in his scouting report for the rookie, Shelton, who has great size at 6-foot-5 and 313 pounds, had strength and technique concerns going into the draft and figured to be a project at the next level.
The Cowboys may have also done Shelton a disservice by moving him around to different spots this offseason. Not only has Shelton gotten looks at both tackle spots , but he was also playing some guard earlier this offseason.
The best bet with a rookie who needs more development than most is to let him focus on one spot, which Dallas didn't do.
Shelton's struggles will also call into question the pick itself. There were no shortage of fans and analysts who doubted the pick to begin with, and their concerns have been validated thus far.
That said, there's still a ways to go before we can label Shelton a bust, so we can still hold out hope for the Penn State product at this early stage.

title: Brian Schottenheimer All But Confirms 53-Man Roster Decision on Safety & Special Teams Ace
full_text:
On Monday, Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer spoke at length about how important the ability to play on special teams is for the guys trying to grab the last nine or so spots on the 53-man roster.
And, in the process of talking about that, Schottenheimer all but confirmed that safety Markquese Bell is going to make the 53-man roster when cutdown day falls on Sunday, Aug. 30.
Schottenheimer revealed that he views Bell as one of the team's best special teams players and noted how that is going to help Bell's cause to make the cut.
"The easy answer is special teams," Schotty said when asked about how bubble players can stand out to make the roster. "When you get into roster spot 45 through 53, those are usually guys that are not starters or premium players that they play every snap or the majority of snaps, so you have to find guys that have the versatility to play special teams."
"I'll speak to this young, Markquese Bell," Schottenheimer added. "Markquese Bell is one of our most trusted leaders on the special teams. He's a really good football player. He's a good defensive player. I think he's a great special teams player."
The Cowboys have an added emphasis on special teams this year after they played poorly in that area last season.
We saw some major struggles on special teams for the Cowboys in the first preseason game, but things were better in preseason Week 2.
Despite Bell having played a good amount of snaps on defense and special teams over his career and being on the second year of a three-year contract , he wasn't exactly considered locked in, and for a few reasons.
For starters, the Cowboys overhauled their safeties room with the additions of Jalen Thompson, P.J. Locke and Caleb Downs, which made things tight for bubble players. And, we've also seen guys like Alijah Clark and Julius Wood play well in practice and in the preseason.
Another potential issue for Bell was his legal trouble.
Bell was arrested on drug charges back in April, including a felony count of possession of a controlled substance. However, it looks like, based on court records, that the case was closed shortly thereafter .
If Bell is indeed locked in, all spots at safety could be spoken for with Malik Hooker, Thompson, Locke and Downs set to make the cut.
That's terrible news for Clark and Wood, both of whom will now have to hope the Cowboys keep six. If not, at least one of them could land on the practice squad, assuming they clear waivers.

title: Dallas Cowboys Sign New Tight End Amid Micheal Trigg Injury Absence
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys are making an addition to their offense ahead of the team's final preseason game against the New Orleans Saints on Friday.
The Cowboys have signed former New England Patriots tight end Mitch Van Vooren, per reports from Nick Harris of the Fort Worth-Star Telegram.  In a corresponding move, Dallas released rookie defensive tackle Kelvin Gilliam.
Dallas undrafted rookie tight end Michael Trigg, who impressed in the preseason opener, didn't play against the Arizona Cardinals due to a toe injury. DJ Rogers also didn't play due to injury, leaving the Cowboys with just two healthy tight ends in Arizona with Luke Schoonmaker and Zack Kuntz.
Adding Van Vooren now gives Dallas another healthy body at the position. He will have a chance to impress the coaching staff this week in hopes of landing a spot on the practice squad.
The Van Vooren signing came shortly after Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer told the media that the team was looking at the possibility of adding a new tight end to the roster.
At 6-5, 255 pounds, the former Division III football player and former Marquette track star offers some intriuging upside as a depth piece. Other teams clearly recognized this, as Van Vooren also previously signed deals with the Seattle Seahawks and Cleveland Browns before ending up with New England.
"We're looking at that," Schottenheimer said. " ... I would expect us to add a tight end."
Schottenheimer added that he was impressed with what Kuntz brought to the table against Arizona. With Trigg sidelined and Schoonmaker potentially on the roster bubble, he could look to make some noise as the potential No. 3 tight end behind Jake Ferguson and Brevyn Spann-Ford.
"Talk about Zack Kuntz, I mean, he played really well," Schottenheimer said. "Was a little nervous getting in there at first. Got popped one time, and that kind of helped settle him down a little bit. He had the fourth-down drop, but he played really well. I think 40 something plays, and so I'm really pleased with him and proud of him. He deserves credit. Had a big explosive 25-yard play between him and Sam (Howell). But yeah, both those other tight ends are working back. Whether they make it back in time for the game, we'll see."
The Cowboys will begin their final preseason game against New Orleans at home on Friday at 7 p.m. CT.

title: Cowboys’ Sam Williams Named Among NFL’s Biggest Potential Roster Cuts
full_text:
Von Miller signing with the Dallas Cowboys has received much attention, and understandably so. Miller is one of the best pass-rushers the league has ever seen, and he happens to play a position of dire need in Dallas.
Beyond his individual performance, Miller will impact the franchise by helping teach the younger players on the team how to become more effective. One overlooked impact, however, from Miller’s addition is that it will ultimately come at someone’s expense.
To make room for the two-time Super Bowl champion, the Cowboys are going to have to release one of their promising young players who are currently on the bubble. One player who could end up being given the pink slip is former second-round pick Sam Williams.
Williams showed flashes early in his career with 8.5 sacks over the first two years, but hasn’t been as impactful since suffering a torn ACL ahead of the 2024 season. He was hoping to rebound in 2026, but Gary Davenport believes that Williams may need to look for a fresh start elsewhere as he named the Ole Miss product among the biggest names who could be released before the regular season.
“Williams may have to jump-start his career elsewhere. Rashan Gary, Donovan Ezeiruaku, rookie Malachi Lawrence and newly signed Von Miller appear to be locks for the 53-man roster. That could leave only one or two spots for Williams, Marist Liufau and James Houston, and Liufau is a core special teams contributor,” Davenport wrote.
“Williams would no doubt quickly get scooped up, but the truth is there may not be room for him in Dallas anymore.”
Marist Liufau is the main person Williams needs to beat to make the roster. Davenport also mentioned James Houston, but he had 5.5 sacks last season and deserves a spot as a rotational EDGE.
As for Williams and Liufau, either one will be buried on the depth chart but can make an impact on special teams. Liufau is a critical part of that unit, which will help him. That said, Williams has also been a special teams contributor and even possesses enough speed that he has lined up as a gunner on the punt team.
This won’t be an easy decision for the front office, but whoever is left without a spot is sure to be in-demand elsewhere.

title: One Trade Cowboys Should Make To Address Cornerback Concerns Before Preseason Ends
full_text:
The arrow is pointing up for the Dallas Cowboys at cornerback, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't still be exploring their options, both in the trade and free-agent markets.
Cobie Durant has been excellent in practice , but there's a reason why he only garnered a $4 million contract and it isn't because he's a top-flight starter.
Meanwhile, the jury is still out on both DaRon Bland, who has been injured and ineffective in recent years, and Shavon Revel, who had struggles during his rookie campaign but has come on strong this offseason .
If the Cowboys really want to shore up the cornerback position, there is one trade in particular they should be exploring.
The Cowboys need to put in a call to the Pittsburgh Steelers about cornerback Joey Porter Jr.
The 26-year-old, who is currently on the PUP list with a back injury, doesn't appear to be close to a new deal with Pittsburgh, Gerry Dulac of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reports.
“They saw nothing of this guy in the spring. They’re not gonna see anything of him in the preseason, so I don’t know what he’s going to do,” Dulac said on 102.5 WDVE. “That’s not to even mention his contract difficulties. They’re talking to him, but they’re nowhere near signing Joey Porter Jr."
"Is he going to go into the season without a contract? Which, you would think he would have been the first guy they would try to re-sign... To me, the biggest loser in training camp right now is that whole situation with JPJ,” Dulac concluded.
The cornerback market has exploded this offseason after multiple players at the position received huge extensions, so that is likely making things difficult for the Steelers.
Porter would be an ideal addition for the Cowboys, as he's more of a sure thing than anyone Dallas has at the cornerback position currently and is a legit CB1.
In 2025, the former second-round pick surrendered a completion rate of 48.5% and a passer rating of 57.2 when targeted. He also registered the 20th-best Pro Football Focus coverage grade among cornerbacks with a 74.1
Those numbers are all superior to those of what Revel, Bland and Durant posted last season, which means Porter would amount to an upgrade over all three and that's just what Dallas needs.
When it comes to a trade for Porter, not only do we have to bake in the cost of a deal with the Steelers, but a contract extension, also.
The Cowboys are probably looking at giving up a second-round pick for Porter, and Pittsburgh might want one of those three aforementioned cornerbacks in return, also, because trading Porter away would leave the Steelers with a gaping hole.
It's possible the draft pick compensation could be lower with Porter needing a new contract, and if the Cowboys throw in a cornerback to sweeten the pot.
The Cowboys have both their second- and third-round picks in each of the next two drafts.
As far as a new contract is concerned, Dallas is likely looking at a deal that pays Porter Jr. at least $30 million annually based on recent extensions at the position .
All of that is quite an expensive investment for the Cowboys, but with the way owner Jerry Jones has talked about urgency to win and being open to doing something "substantive" to add to the defense, we wouldn't rule out Dallas being game for it.

title: Dallas Cowboys' Answer For RB2 Couldn't Be Clearer Entering Preseason Finale
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys are firing on all cylinders through the first two weeks of the NFL preseason , jumping out to a 2-0 start with two convincing victories.
It is the first time since 2007 that the Cowboys have started the preseason with a 2-0 record, which has sparked plenty of hype and excitement around the team. While there is a lot of positive buzz around the team, there are still several questions ahead of the preseason finale.
A handful of positional battles still need to sort themselves out , and that will be done when the team returns to Frisco.
One of the most intriguing battles is in the offensive backfield, with no clear-cut backup running back behind 2025 breakout star Javonte Williams . Second-year running back Jaydon Blue and Malik Davis are the front-runners for the job, and there is one player who stands out as exactly what the offense needs.
Blue led the team in rushing yards with 75 against the Arizona Cardinals, but it was Davis who was the more efficient rusher.
Davis recorded 29 yards on just five carries, averaging 5.8 yards per run. He added an 8-yard touchdown catch. Davis is a player who always seems to make the right play for the team, while there have been concerns about Blue's consistency.
He also brings something that separates him from Blue: pass protection ; something Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram noted following the team's Week 2 preseason win.
"So, in 15 plays, we've seen Cowboys [running back] Malik Davis run for 29 yards on five carries, pick up a blitz in pass protection, and haul in an eight-yard TD reception on a third down in the red zone," he wrote. " Sounds like an RB2 to me ?"
Last season, Davis appeared in 10 games, carrying the ball 52 times for 250 yards and two touchdowns. He had a rushing success rate of 50 percent and averaged just under 4.8 yards per carry. Most importantly, he never fumbled the ball.
Blue, meanwhile, struggled to see action because of his inconsistency in practice and appeared in just five games. He recorded 129 yards on 38 carries and one touchdown, with a rush success rate of 36.8 percent. He also fumbled the ball once and has put the ball on the ground throughout training camp.
It's going to be interesting to see how the running back competition plays out over the next week, but if the offense values consistency, it should look no further than Davis to fill the role.

title: Dallas Cowboys 53-Man Roster Prediction Entering Preseason Week 3
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys defeated the Arizona Cardinals in the second week of the NFL preseason, 34-13. Now, the Cowboys head home for their preseason finale against the New Orleans Saints, the same franchise they couldn't stop fighting during their joint practice this past week.
This means the players on the bottom of the depth chart are running out of time to push for a spot on the 53-man roster. Shortly after this one concludes, those tough decisions will need to be made as the roster gets trimmed down from 90. While a few players could make a push in the finale, here's how the 53-man roster could look based on what we know through the first two weeks of the preseason.
Notable Cuts: Marquez Valdes-Scantling, Anthony Smith
Notable Cuts: Luke Schoonmaker
Notable cuts: Trevor Keegan
All three quarterbacks stay on the 53, but Joe Milton has done enough to take back the QB2 job. Phil Mafah had a late touchdown against the Cardinals, but it's not enough to leapfrog Jaydon Blue or Malik Davis. At wide receiver, Dallas goes six deep, which is what Cowboys On SI writer Mike Moraitis believes they need to do after the performances of Jonathan Mingo and Camden Brown.
At tight end, Luke Schoonmaker still has a chance to make the roster, especially with Michael Trigg's recent injury. For now, he's out, but that can change if Trigg misses the finale. Lastly, their offensive line won't be easy to figure out. Trevor Keegan and Nick Keverett have been solid, but Ajani Corenlius has been one of the top tackles in the preseason. Cornelius played some guard as well, which is why he makes it, but this is arguably the toughest to figure out right now.
Notable Cuts: Marist Liufau
Notable Cuts: Curtis Robinson, Langston Patterson, Justin Barron
Notable Cuts: Caelen Carson, Zion Childress
Notable Cuts: Alijah Clark
Oddly enough, it's the defensive side of the ball with the toughest cuts. That's a result of the added depth as they don't have room for nose tackle Jay Toia on the defensive line. At edge, Von Miller ends up pushing out Marist Liufau , which is unfortunate as he's been showing progress. Perhaps they decide to keep him over Sam Williams, but this final week will be huge in helping decide that battle.
At inside linebacker, the Cowboys go with just four players, although Justin Barron and Curtis Robinson both look the part. There are 11 players in the secondary, which is where they could decide to make a cut to keep someone on the bubble they don't want to risk. Julius Wood might be the one at risk, although his performance in the preseason will make it difficult to cut him.

title: Jaishawn Barham Flashed Elite Potential In Cowboys Debut & Numbers Back It Up
full_text:
Every year, we are warned not to overreact to the NFL preseason. Every year, we ignore that advice and fall into the same traps. For the Dallas Cowboys faithful, it usually involves falling in love with a training camp or preseason standout , and this year is no different.
When the Cowboys arrived in Oxnard for the start of training camp, there was immediately one name that continued to pop up: third-round pick Jaishawn Barham .
Barham wasted no time impressing the coaching staff, fans, and the team's beat writers, with rave reviews coming out every day for the former Michigan Wolverines star linebacker . Unfortunately, his momentum was slowed because of a minor groin injury that kept him out of practice.
This past week, Barham returned to practice, and on Saturday he made his preseason debut. He instantly lived up to the hype when he strapped on the pads , and he put on one heck of a show.
Here is every play from #Cowboys LB Jaishawn Barham in his NFL debut vs. ARZ: pic.twitter.com/6QVfKldC2Q
Barham was so impressive at the start of training camp that he was given the opportunity to wear the green dot and call plays on defense in his debut. He did not disappoint.
He finished the game with five tackles, three run stops, and one tackle for a loss. Most importantly, Barham was Dallas' highest-graded defender by PFF , recording an 89.9 grade in 22 snaps. In fact, he was the team's highest-graded player overall.
For the analytics lovers, Adam Carter on X put the numbers into perspective and highlighted just how elite Barham has been throughout his career.
Barham is just one of three FBS EDGE/Linebacker prospects in the past decade to post a pressure rate of greater than 25 percent, a win rate in true pass sets of greater than 27.5 percent, and a run stop rate of greater than 10 percent. The other two players to hit those marks? Micah Parsons and Abdul Carter.
Now, before everyone gets too excited, it is just one game, but the Cowboys fan base hasn't had much to be excited about on the defensive side of the ball in recent years, especially at the linebacker position.
Hopefully, Barham can continue to develop into a defensive stud, and prove to be the mid-round diamond in the rough that the franchise has been waiting for.

title: Jaylen Waddle Has Already Seen Enough to Know Bo Nix Is 'Different'
full_text:
Bo Nix returned to the football field over the weekend, starting the Denver Broncos' second preseason game vs. the Green Bay Packers.
Nix was given two series with the starters, and he put points on the board on both possessions. On the Broncos' first drive of the night, Nix led a six-play, 65-yard scoring drive that was capped off with a 21-yard touchdown pass to running back RJ Harvey.
But the play that set that Harvey wheel route up was Nix's 35-yard connection with wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, who made his Broncos debut on Friday night against Green Bay. Broncos Country is hoping that explosive Waddle play is but a small taste of Nix plans to cook up.
That speed after the catch is scary. Jaylen Waddle, it's gonna be a GREAT year! pic.twitter.com/T1btl9VaVJ
After the Packers game, Nix talked about how throwing the ball to Waddle is slightly different, just because of how fast he is and how quickly he gets in and out of his breaks. You could see Waddle slow down every so slightly to adjust to Nix's pass down the right seam.
On Monday, the Broncos were back at it, practicing in preparation for the preseason finale against the Minnesota Vikings on Friday night. After the session, Waddle was asked about what he's learned about Nix since teaming up with him in June.
“'B' is a baller. He has rare traits that only he can process and only he can do," Waddle said on Monday. "It’s just tremendous going out there. He’s so young, but he’s kind of so mature in the way he approaches the game. So yes, Bo’s different.”
The energy and boost Nix provided to his teammates was palpable on Friday night. The Mile High faithful could feel it, too. Nix is different, and in his first live-bullet action since fracturing his ankle in the playoffs last season, he appeared to pick up right where he left off.
Nix looked good. Poised. In control. Accurate. Mobile. Seeing him move around the pocket and evade pressure as if he didn't break his ankle and undergo two surgeries during the offseason was more than encouraging.
When it comes to throwing to a receiver like Waddle, Nix tried to put it into words after the Packers game. The truth is, it's going to take him a little time to get a feel for Waddle's unique skill set.
"You can’t really explain the type of player he is," Nix said of Waddle. "You just have to get out there and play, and when you throw him the ball, you understand that it’s a little bit different. He’s just a really great football player."
As much as Nix appreciates what Waddle does on the field as a playmaker, he's just as thankful for the receiver's intangible contributions. Waddle's infectious personality and positive mindset have already influenced the locker room.
"He adds a lot to our team, not only on the field, but like we just mentioned it, joking on the sideline, just him being on the sideline, his personality just gets everybody going," Nix said. "He’s very exciting. He has a great positive attitude. He’s going to be great for us.”
Waddle understands that it'll take a little time to get on the same page with Nix. They're off to a great start, to be sure, but between Waddle arriving via trade in the offseason, and missing about a week of training camp with a soft-tissue injury, and Nix's long recovery since January, the duo hasn't had as many reps together as they'd prefer in a perfect world.
But they're both such great pros that it's only a short matter of time before it happens. Waddle tried to explain why there's a slight acclimation period for a quarterback when it comes to throwing him the ball, but quickly segued to talking about the wealth of talent the Broncos have stockpiled at the skill positions.
"I just think the skill set," Waddle said. "Getting the ball in space is always something key, not just for me, but we have a lot of different playmakers. And we got a lot of versatility in the room. And, yeah, man, we can do a lot of great things with the ball in our hands. Not just me, man. We got a lot of playmakers on this team, and that’s the good thing. You want to play with a lot of dangerous players, and we got those."
One of those dangerous playmakers is Marvin Mims Jr., who hasn't played in the preseason yet because of a camp injury. He should be good to go by the regular-season opener, though.
Waddle has already expressed his admiration for Mims's dynamic skill set . Waddle's point on Monday, though, is a salient one: the nest the Broncos have built around Nix is evident, and all those moves and the development of each player are about to pay some dividends.
If Friday's performance against the Packers was any indication, Nix and the Broncos' offense are poised to take a big leap forward in 2026, just as new offensive coordinator Davis Webb began envisioning the second he saw Waddle on the practice field back in June.

title: How Broncos Are Handling Rib Injury to Starting CB Riley Moss
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are not pressing the panic button over the rib injury sustained by cornerback Riley Moss in last week's preseason loss to Green Bay.
Head coach Sean Payton told reporters Monday that Moss is "doing fine" and intimated he won't miss much, if any, time going forward.
"I would say it's nothing serious. We're being smart," Payton offered following training camp practice. "We'll see as the week progresses where he's at."
Moss started against the Packers and was injured after scooping up what was initially ruled a Patrick Surtain II forced fumble; he was promptly tackled by a host of players and landed with that weight and the football on his ribs area.
Moss exited the field in noticeable pain and was taken to the blue medical tent on the sideline before being escorted to the locker room for further evaluation. He finished the contest with one recorded pass deflection amid the 33-13 defeat .
"Good. We'll see," Payton said of Moss during his post-game press conference.
Among the biggest camp winners , Moss is one of several extension-eligible Broncos vying for a new deal from the organization. The fourth-year pro is currently scheduled to take home $3.674 million in base salary while counting a little under $4 million against the salary cap.
"It’s about taking things day by day, being where your feet are, competing, and improving at one thing every day," Moss said on Aug. 6 regarding his contractual status. "The rest will take care of itself. I trust that God has a plan for me. Whether I have a bad practice or a bad game, there’s always something to learn from it. I trust Him, and that’s how I approach it."
Denver has a final exhibition matchup this week, hosting the Minnesota Vikings on Friday evening, prior to its Week 1 regular-season tilt at Kansas City — exactly 21 days from the time of this writing.
Moss might not play versus Minnesota, but it appears he's in no real danger of missing the lid-lifter against the Chiefs, a matchup in which his services will be required.
In the interim, the Broncos could put a few additional reps on the respective plates of CBs Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine, both of whom have made plays this preseason. The club is also evaluating undrafted corners Sean Fresch Jr. and Brent Austin for potential placement on the practice squad.

title: Sean Payton Explains Why Broncos Really Signed Taylor Rapp
full_text:
Last week, the Denver Broncos signed veteran safety Taylor Rapp .
The signing came one day before the Broncos' second preseason game against the Green Bay Packers, so Rapp did not suit up. There wasn't even an opportunity for him to practice, let alone get familiar with the playbook.
However, cut to Monday, and the Broncos are back on the field to prepare for Friday's preseason finale against the Minnesota Vikings. We also learned from head coach Sean Payton why the Broncos signed the veteran safety.
"Veteran player we liked, and had good grades on," Payton said of Rapp. "And just more talent at that position."
Many, including yours truly, interpreted the Rapp move as a sign that Denver wasn't fully convinced in its safety depth. With P.J. Locke departing to Dallas this past offseason, the Broncos have a big hole to fill at the No. 3 safety spot, and the play of the depth players behind starters Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones hasn't inspired much confidence from the outside looking in.
However, Payton seemed aware of the potential implications the Rapp signing could have on the Broncos' competition at safety, and how it could be interpreted, and got ahead of the issue.
"It wasn't, like, us pounding the table, 'We need a safety,'" Payton said. "It was, 'Hey, this player's available and let's work him out and sign him if possible,' so I'm glad he's here."
Rapp's arrival could push Devon Key down a spot on the depth chart. Key had been the leader in the clubhouse to take Locke's former spot as the No. 3 safety, but he's yet to fully lay claim to it with his play on the field, although, as a first-team All-Pro special teams ace, his place on the roster is secure.
Beyond Key, JL Skinner, Tycen Anderson, Miles Scott, and Parker Robertson have been competing. What were two potential roster spots open at safety have now been trimmed to one with Rapp joining the club.
Skinner, Anderson, Scott, and Robertson have all had a moment or two in the preseason, but have mostly left much to be desired on defense. If the Broncos keep five safeties out of camp, as they have the past few years under Payton, it will be interesting to see which of these four players gets the nod.
Skinner is a former sixth-round pick and was part of Payton's first draft class as Broncos head coach. Scott is a seventh-round rookie still finding his way, while Robertson went undrafted this past spring, and has been working to overcome the odds.
Anderson was Denver's only outside free-agent signing in March. A young veteran, he didn't bring much experience on defense to the table, but like Skinner, Anderson is an accomplished contributor in the third phase.
Time will tell how the competition ultimately shakes out, but the Broncos saw an opportunity to upgrade the safety position, regardless of the team's exact motivations. Payton likes what Rapp brings to the table, especially his between-the-ears attributes.
"We've had experience playing against him," Payton said of Rapp. "He's got real good football instincts and awareness that serves you well at that position. So I think it was more availability than necessity, if that makes sense."
Rapp was a Los Angeles Rams second-round draft pick in 2019. He helped the Rams win a Super Bowl before departing to Upstate New York, where he's spent the past three seasons playing for the Buffalo Bills.
A knee injury cut Rapp's 2025 season short, which was a big reason the Bills released him this past offseason. The Broncos must have been comfortable with his recovery after working him out about a week before signing him .
Rapp brings a wealth of experience to the table, having appeared in 93 games, with 72 starts. He started on the Rams' Super Bowl LVI-champion team and has a lot of live-bullet experience playing in big-moment games.
Rapp has 12 career interceptions and has exceeded the 80-tackle mark four times in his career, including his rookie year, when he notched 100 tackles. The 6-foot, 208-pound safety played his college ball at the University of Washington, where he produced a decorated career.
Maybe Broncos fans will get to see Rapp on Friday against the Vikings, but it wouldn't surprise me if the team waits until the regular-season opener on September 14 to debut him. The Broncos will take on the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1 at Arrowhead Stadium on Monday Night Football .

title: Calvin Throckmorton Takes Five Stitches—and Keeps Delivering for Broncos
full_text:
The second-to-last day of Denver Broncos training camp was lit.
Last Tuesday — Day 13 of Broncos camp — the offense and defense went at each other with gusto. Tempers flared. Emotions ran hot.
Bo Nix was taken to the ground for the second time in camp, further inflaming the situation. There were multiple fights that broke out among teammates, and the final one was a melee of sorts that culminated in a big dogpile.
At the bottom of that pile was veteran offensive lineman Calvin Throckmorton, who got to his feet bleeding from his forehead. He was escorted to the locker room by Broncos trainers, but the next day, he was back at his post playing center with the first-team offense, with a big bandage above his left eye.
We learned from The Denver Gazette 's Chris Tomasson that the gash to Throckmorton's forehead actually required five stitches.
“It was the usual scrum with bodies flying in there,’’ Throckmorton said via Tomasson . “I knew pretty quickly I was going to need some stitches. Obviously, I wish it didn’t happen but sometimes football is football and those things happen.”
No worse for the wear, Throckmorton went on to start at center on Friday night against the Green Bay Packers in the Broncos' second preseason game of the season. For an exhibition game, it was a big moment because of Bo Nix's return to the field for the first time since fracturing his ankle in the playoffs.
Throckmorton was the man trusted to snap the ball and help protect Nix as the offensive line's pivot. Just as he'd done in camp and the first preseason game, Throckmorton acquitted himself well against Green Bay, showcasing his veteran competence and versatility.
Throckmorton has been with the Broncos since 2024, but he's lived the life of a bubble player, bouncing back and forth between the practice squad and the active roster. This summer, though, the Broncos faced a crisis in training camp when all three of their top centers went down with injuries over the course of a week.
Luke Wattenberg was injured on Day 3 of camp , which also happened to be the first padded practice. Only a few days later, his backup, Alex Forsyth, went down . And about a week after Wattenberg's injury, third-team center Michael Deiter suffered a season-ending quad injury .
This forced the Broncos to make some snap decisions, no pun intended. They asked Throckmorton to play center, and he obliged. He began with the second-team offense, but when Deiter went down, Throckmorton was vaulted to the first team.
Neither Wattenberg nor Forsyth have returned to full practice since their respective injuries, missing both preseason games, which has given Throckmorton an extended audition playing with the starters. It's one thing to accept the challenge and answer the bell in the team's hour of need, but he has played very, very well.
“It’s been fun,’’ Throckmorton said via Tomasson. “It’s been great to have the opportunity to show my flexibility to continue to improve and develop at that position as well as guard. I’ve been trying to take it in stride and try to get better every day.”
Throckmorton, 6-foot-5 and 311 pounds, went undrafted out of Oregon in 2020. He signed with the New Orleans Saints as a college free agent, whose head coach was still Sean Payton at the time.
After three years with the Saints, Throckmorton bounced between the Carolina Panthers and Tennessee Titans. But after playing his one year with the Titans, Throckmorton reunited with Payton in Denver.
As a pro, Throckmorton has appeared in 58 games with 27 starts. As a Bronco, he's appeared in 12 games but is yet to start, which is symbolic of Denver's remarkable good fortune when it comes to the offensive line staying healthy, with only a couple of exceptions over that span.
Entering his seventh season, the 30-year-old Throckmorton finds himself still in a depth role, but it's possible that the worm could be turning. The Broncos expect Wattenberg back well in time for the regular-season opener, but Forsyth's outlook is a bit more clouded.
A former sixth-round pick, Forsyth's place with the Broncos could be in jeopardy given how well Throckmorton has played at center. When it comes to the roster math, Throckmorton may not have a draft pedigree, but he can play multiple positions on the interior offensive line, whereas Forsyth is a center-only player.
With commitments to Alex Palczewski and rookie fourth-rounder Kage Casey, it's hard to see the Broncos keeping another swing guard on the 53-man roster out of camp, but if the team wants to kill two birds with one stone and keep a player who could offer center and guard depth, Throckmorton would be that guy.
I hope it works out for Throckmorton. And the Broncos had better think long and hard before August 30's roster deadline, because if they waive him in hopes of re-signing him to the practice squad, I seriously doubt he'd go unclaimed this time.
The NFL is always offensive line-needy, and Throckmorton has put together some impressive tape this summer running a unit that features two All-Pros up front.

title: Where Broncos Should—and Shouldn't—Go Heavy on the 53-Man Roster
full_text:
As we approach the third and final preseason game, the Denver Broncos will have to determine which positions to prioritize as they shape the final roster.
An important part of those determinations is identifying the positions where the Broncos need to keep more players on the 53-man roster , rather than cutting or exposing them to waivers.
While one can make a case for keeping more players at one position, doing so comes at the expense of another position. Thus, the Broncos — like any other team — must make trade-offs when it comes to determining how many players to keep at each position.
In some cases, it's not hard to figure out where the Broncos will go, but in other cases, things may not be as simple.
Let's examine the positions that could complicate the Broncos' roster math and trigger the most conversation behind closed doors at Dove Valley. We'll weigh the pros and cons, then try to get a feel for the decisions the Broncos might make.
Pro : Having the third quarterback on the 53-man roster means that a team can't sign him from the practice squad. This is particularly important when you look at teams that have lost quarterbacks to injury and need a new backup.
Con : The No. 3 quarterback is never active on game days, and that spot could be better utilized for more depth at another position, particularly when it comes to special teams. If one loses to a No. 3 quarterback to another team, it's not hard to find a new one.
Sam Ehlinger won't likely garner a lot of interest from other teams, so the Broncos can safely sign him to the practice squad.
Pro : Injuries tend to happen often to running backs, and J.K. Dobbins has missed time with injuries in most of his NFL seasons. Keeping a fourth running back ensures the Broncos have an injury replacement available without worries of losing him to another team.
Con : The Broncos are likely to keep a fullback on the 53-man roster, and he can be utilized as the fourth running back. Meanwhile, if a fourth back is kept, he'll be a game-day inactive barring injuries ahead of him on the depth chart.
Since it appears likely that the Broncos will keep fullback Adam Prentice on the 53-man roster, a fourth running back is a luxury the team can't afford.
Pro : There are a couple of wide receivers who have shown they can help in the return game. Having them available in that capacity could be useful.
Con : The Broncos appear likely to keep four tight ends, and they can be utilized in the receiving game. None of the wide receivers beyond the top five have stood out.
This is a close call. It likely comes down to roster math and which players the Broncos value more at which positions.
Pro : The Broncos don't want to expose Justin Joly to waivers, even if he hasn't stood out in the preseason. Also, Nate Adkins has proven useful to a degree because of his blocking ability.
Con : For most teams, a fourth tight end is a luxury. It doesn't always make sense to keep one at the expense of other positions. Also, the fourth tight end is likely to be a game-day inactive every week.
Between the Broncos' likely reluctance to expose Joty to waivers and Adkins' familiarity with the system, it appears likely they'll keep four tight ends.
Pro : The Broncos have typically kept seven defensive linemen on the roster. That allows them to maximize possible rotations on defense and have a couple available for special teams as needed.
Con : Keeping seven defensive linemen means a lot of roster spots devoted to that position. Once you get past the top six, there isn't a player who other teams are likely to covet, and it shouldn't be an issue to expose them to waivers.
This likely depends on what the Broncos want to do at other positions. The third preseason game is almost certain to determine what the Broncos do here.
Pro : Having cornerback depth is important. Furthermore, there are a couple of cornerbacks who have played well on special teams and might even factor into the return game if necessary.
Con : The Broncos typically carry five safeties, and a sixth corner might come at the expense of the fifth safety.
Again, the third preseason game will most likely dictate what the Broncos do here.
Pro : The Broncos have typically kept five safeties and utilize two of them on special teams. The addition of Taylor Rapp means that if the Broncos keep just four, a couple of players who can help on special teams would be cut or waived.
Con : Keeping a fifth safety means the Broncos won't keep a sixth cornerback. That position is more useful to defense, and there are cornerbacks on the depth chart who have done well on special teams.
Once again, the final preseason game should determine what the Broncos do here. With corners and safeties, the two positions will most likely go hand in hand.

title: Broncos Stock Report: 5 Risers, 5 Fallers After Packers Loss
full_text:
Entering the Denver Broncos' matchup with the Green Bay Packers in preseason Game 2, I highlighted 10 players to watch .
With the Broncos falling to the Packers 30-13, let's examine how each performed and whether they showed what they needed to.
Due to an injury to starter Luke Wattenberg and his backup, Alex Forsyth, Throckmorton was the first-team center, and he was one of the few depth players on the offensive line to put together a strong showing. He has taken to playing center, showcasing some versatility beyond just playing guard, and it's paying off.
Casey played mostly on the right side of the line, something he hasn't done before, and he had some clear issues. The few snaps he had working on the left side looked really good, so he may be one of those side-specific players who can't flip to the other side.
Miller was the third or fourth right tackle in the game, and he looked solid. He is a toolsy undrafted rookie with a lot of development still to come, but he showed good progress from just a week ago.
Jones was the sixth defensive lineman to take the field, but it came on an obvious passing down; then he was pulled and had to wait a little longer before seeing the field again. It wasn’t a good game for him, as he got bullied in the run game and struggled to create an impact as a pass rusher.
The rookie was quiet against the Atlanta Falcons, but he bounced back with a good game against the Packers . On one of Green Bay's touchdown drives, Onyedim blew up multiple plays in the backfield but wasn’t able to finish before finally stuffing a run.
There wasn’t much as a pass rusher, but he flashed his run defense throughout his time.
Schrader is the lowest back on the depth chart, but he once again outperformed Tyler Badie and Jaleel McLaughlin. It would be great to see Schrader get some touches earlier in the game, not in the fourth quarter when teams are going to their third- and fourth-stringers, to see if he can still outperform Badie and McLaughlin.
After an impressive game against the Falcons, Manjack wasn’t noticeable against the Packers. With his lack of special teams ability, he could be behind the mark, even when competing for a practice squad spot.
Murdock was the fourth linebacker against the Falcons, but was the fifth against the Packers, and he didn’t have the same big splash plays as he did a week ago. Jordan Turner took Murdock's spot as the fourth linebacker, returning from an injury, and he performed well.
What landed Fresch as a player to watch was his performance against the Falcons, and while he had a decent punt return against the Packers, he didn’t have any splash plays. However, for a cornerback, a lack of splash plays is fine when paired with the absence of negatives, and Fresch didn’t have any major negatives either.
Now, speaking of splash plays and negative plays, Taylor had a big splash as a run defender, but he had a bunch of negative plays in coverage. He was really struggling to stick with his assignment and gave up multiple big completions, not just in yards but in allowing first downs to be converted.

title: One Concern That Hasn't Been Solved Yet (And How Broncos Can Fix It)
full_text:
With two of three preseason games in the books, the Denver Broncos appear to have a problem.
Denver's special teams have been concerningly rough this summer, and it hasn't shown any progress in the two preseason games. From bad long-snapping to botched field-goal attempts to poor punt and kick coverage, and even a kickoff out of bounds, the Broncos' third phase has left much to be desired in the preseason.
The Broncos allowed 28.8 yards per kick return to the Atlanta Falcons in preseason Game 1 and 39.7 per return to the Green Bay Packers in Game 2. Denver's punt coverage has been much better, but the kickoff coverage has been shockingly bad.
“Obviously that wasn’t good enough," head coach Sean Payton said after Friday night's loss to the Packers. "There weren’t a lot of things... I said this after the game—just pick a topic. Pick penalties, we lose there, kickoff, kickoff return, we lose that battle; rushing numbers, we lose that... You can’t not pay attention to these games, these scrimmages, these important steps towards the start of the regular season.”
It's worth noting that many of the players covering these kick and punt returns in the preseason won't be on the Broncos' roster come September. Still, third-phase mavens like Devon Key and JL Skinner have been involved in many of these returns, so it's a troubling trend regardless.
Special teams coordinator Darren Rizzi enters his second year with the club after spending the preceding six seasons with the New Orleans Saints. Before Rizzi arrived, the Broncos' special teams were in pretty good shape under Payton, beginning in 2023 with the hiring of Mike Westhoff as a third-phase expert and Ben Kotwica as the coordinator.
No special teams unit is going to be perfect. There were some gaffes under the Westhoff/Kotwica regime, the most noteworthy being Leo Chenal's blocked field-goal attempt in Kansas City during Bo Nix's rookie season, which saw the Broncos snatch defeat from the jaws of victory.
Shortly after that ignominious moment, Westhoff stepped down , citing his advancing age and health, while Kotwica marched ahead. The coaching tandem achieved some great things together, though, including Marvin Mims Jr. earning Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors in 2023 and 2024 as a returner.
Following the 2024 season, Payton fired Kotwica . It was a shocking move at the time, but it seemed to be preemptive so that the Broncos' head coach could make room on the staff for Rizzi, who was about to become a free agent, so to speak.
Payton hired Rizzi shortly after, and one of his first moves as coordinator was the scouting and drafting of punter Jeremy Crawshaw. The Broncos invested a sixth-round pick in the Australian-born punter, which was their way of ensuring they landed Crawshaw, rather than taking their chances competing with other teams for his services as a potential undrafted free agent.
Crawshaw started off a bit rocky as a rookie, but he eventually found his footing, and is poised to take a big leap forward in Year 2. Also notable in Rizzi's first year as special teams coordinator was Mims's failure to earn any returner accolades for the first time in his young career, despite averaging a healthy 15.6 yards per punt return, including a touchdown, and 26.3 yards per kick return.
However, it must be noted that kicker Wil Lutz really flourished after being reunited with Rizzi in Denver. Lutz was excellent in the clutch, kicking one game-winning field goal after another throughout the 2025 season. He was a big reason for Denver's 11-game winning streak last year.
Under Rizzi's purview, Mims may not have earned a Pro Bowl or an All-Pro selection for the first time in his career, but Key set a new franchise record for special teams tackles and was named first-team All-Pro as a third-phase ace. So, with Rizzi, there have been concerning special teams developments, but also plenty of success stories for Payton to hang his hat on.
Honestly, I don't expect the Broncos' coverage units to show much improvement during the preseason. And there's only one more game to go.
If the coverage units look this bad in Kansas City on Monday Night Football come September 14, then my concern will morph into true alarm.
For now, though, the Broncos will continue to play inexperienced guys like Miles Scott, Parker Robertson, Tycen Anderson, Brent Austin, Sean Fresch Jr., Dallen Bentley, Taurean York, and others in the preseason finale because the team has to evaluate its depth players to make the best decisions come roster cut-down day.
That day rapidly approaches, though. The Broncos' preseason finale vs. the Minnesota Vikings is on Friday, and two days later — August 30 — is the NFL's deadline to trim rosters down to the final 53 players .
I do hope the players I mentioned above, and many others, are able to capitalize on their opportunity against the Vikings, especially after the Broncos' depth looked so collectively lost in last week's 30-13 loss to the Packers.
As for Rizzi, I'm still waiting for that big aha moment that makes it clear why Payton dumped Kotwica for him. One thing I know for sure, though, is that Payton trusts Rizzi, and that goes a long way.

title: Projecting the Broncos' Week 1 Starting Lineup Right Now
full_text:
The Denver Broncos now have two preseason games in the books.
We've learned a lot about the state of the 2026 Broncos since training camp started in late July. With only one final preseason game left to go, the early returns on the Broncos are exciting.
Sean Payton doesn't like the term "picking up where they left off," but it sure looks like that's exactly what the Broncos are poised to do, after winning 14 games, the AFC West, and pushing all the way to the conference title game before a shockingly untimely injury torpedoed the team's Super Bowl ambitions.
The Broncos will host the Minnesota Vikings on Friday to close out the preseason. Two days later is the NFL deadline for trimming rosters down to the final 53 players.
Based on what we've seen this summer, here's how the Broncos' 2026 starting lineups are shaping up.
Running Back : J.K. Dobbins
Wide Receiver : Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Pat Bryant
Tight End : 1a. Evan Engram, 1b. Adam Trautman
Left Tackle : Garett Bolles
Right Guard : Quinn Meinerz
Right Tackle : Mike McGlinchey
Prentice seems poised to make the 53-man roster out of camp. He's likely to get a few starts this season, depending on the opponent and game plan.
The only real developments on offense are the emergence of Bryant as the No. 3 receiver, and how the Broncos are using the tight ends. Bryant was the star of Broncos camp this summer, and while it hasn't translated to the field in the preseason, he's played a very limited number of snaps because the team wants to preserve him for the season.
Last year, the Broncos started Trautman at tight end more often than not because the offense tends to run the ball early on the first drive, and he's a better blocker than Engram. However, Engram has been asked to stay in to block a lot more this summer, which may have something to do with Davis Webb taking over as the offensive coordinator, and we're seeing the Broncos run a lot of two-tight-end sets.
Frankly, it wouldn't surprise me if the Broncos opened up in 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends) as often as 13 (one running back, three receivers). In 12 personnel, Engram and Trautman will be on the field. Even if I'm wrong about the two-tight-end tendencies Webb has shown this summer, the Broncos seem determined to rely on Engram more as a blocker in order to keep him on the field more.
Going with heavy tight end sets will help the Broncos' run game, which then opens up the possibility for some deadly play-action passing. It'll be interesting to see how it all takes shape.
A quick note: Wattenberg has been hurt since Day 3 of training camp, but the Broncos have remained publicly confident he'll be good to go by the season-opener in mid-September.
Defensive End : Zach Allen
Defensive End : Eyioma Uwazurike
Outside Linebacker : Jonathon Cooper
Inside Linebacker : Alex Singleton
Inside Linebacker : Justin Strnad
Outside Linebacker : Nik Bonitto
Cornerback : Patrick Surtain II
Nickel Cornerback : Ja’Quan McMillian
Depending on the opponent, you can expect the Broncos to start many games in their nickel sub-package, which would take one linebacker off the field, to be replaced by McMillian. Consider him a starter.
This opening-day starting defense looks much the same as last year's, with one exception. Uwazurike will start at defensive end in place of John Franklin-Myers, who departed in free agency.
Like Engram and Trautman above, this defensive end spot could be a 1a. and 1b. situation split between Uwazurike and Malcolm Roach. However, in both preseason games, Uwazurike has gotten the start, with Roach rotating in regularly.
That could change come September, but I doubt it. About a week-and-a-half into training camp, Jones theorized publicly that Roach would win the Franklin-Myers job and " run with it ," but Uwazurike hasn't allowed that to happen.
In the final analysis, these two trenchmen will likely end up getting even snaps, but this article is about projecting the starting lineup, and Uwazurike seems to have the edge.
Long Snapper : Mitchell Fraboni
Punt Returner : Marvin Mims Jr.
Kick Returner : Marvin Mims Jr.
Kick Returner : Jonah Coleman
The Broncos gave it the ol' college try this summer by signing undrafted rookie long snapper Luke Basso to compete with Fraboni, but the proof is in the pudding. If the Broncos want reliability, Fraboni is the guy; Basso had a bad long snap in preseason Game 1, leading to a botched field-goal attempt.
Again, this unit looks the same as last year's with the exception of the second kick returner. In a perfect world, the Broncos would rather not use Coleman back there, but he did get some returner action during camp, including in the planned scrimmage about halfway through.
The Broncos have been utilizing undrafted rookie receivers Kolbe Katsis and Cameron Ross as the kick returners in the preseason. At punt returner, it's been Katsis and undrafted rookie cornerback Sean Fresch Jr., who has looked great on defense and explosive on special teams.
Mims has not played in the preseason yet due to a soft-tissue injury suffered about a week into camp, but even if he were healthy, I doubt the Broncos would have done anything differently because they know what he can do; they want to see what Katsis, Ross, and Fresch can bring to the table.
Alas, though, unless the Broncos intend to keep six receivers or six cornerbacks on the 53-man roster, the likely outcome for Katsis, Ross, or Fresch is the practice squad. The Broncos could still utilize them on game day by elevating them, but it would be curious to elevate one player strictly to return kicks alongside Mims for, say, two to five plays per game.
Then again, the Broncos have mainly used their practice squad elevations on linebackers, cornerbacks, safeties, and receivers who can contribute on special teams kick and coverage units, and each game usually offers only a handful of such plays.
Still, I'm doubtful that Katsis, Ross, or Fresch make the 53-man roster , and given that the Broncos have one of the NFL's elite returners in Mims, I'm rolling with Coleman as the second kick returner, despite how good this undrafted trio has looked this summer.
It could be a running back other than Coleman, like Jaleel McLaughlin, Tyler Badie, or Cody Schrader, but that's only if the Broncos opt to keep four running backs on the 53-man roster. That's what Denver has done over the past few years under Payton, but it feels like only three true running backs will be kept along with the fullback.

title: Broncos May Have Three Players Worth Trading Instead of Cutting
full_text:
As the Denver Broncos decide which players are most likely to make the 53-man roster, they have to be prepared to expose some players to the waiver wire. Any player who hasn't accrued at least four seasons is subject to waivers and, thus, could be claimed by other teams.
Waiver claims don't happen as often as fans think, but they are frequent enough to make people realize that the wire carries the risk of another team claiming a player who might otherwise be a good practice squad addition. Remember, practice squad players can be elevated on game day, and a team can always promote them to the 53-man roster at any point.
When waiver claims happen, though, they tend to be for players with a larger sample size of NFL snaps, whether from the regular seasons or past preseasons. When it comes to recently undrafted rookies, teams are more likely to focus on keeping their own for a practice squad, unless they have a desperate need for help at a particular position.
Because players with NFL experience to some degree could be coveted, teams with lower waiver priority might be willing to trade for them. The Broncos have a couple of players who have seen plenty of NFL snaps and might return something in a trade from a team that's lower in the waiver priority and wants to ensure they get that player.
Let's look at three such Broncos other teams might be willing to trade for the right price.
Franklin became a bigger part of the Broncos' offense last year, and while he was solid, he didn't make a big impact. He now finds himself buried on the depth chart with the arrival of Jaylen Waddle and the improvement shown by Pat Bryant this summer.
If the Broncos decide to keep just five wide receivers and opt to keep somebody other than Franklin as the fifth wideout, he would likely fetch considerable draft pick compensation because, while he's not an impact player, he could be good for a team that needs pass-catching help.
However, it remains to be seen whether the Broncos take a route that means exposing Franklin to waivers. They could cut Lil'Jordan Humphrey and sign him to the practice squad, and will likely be able to expose other players to waivers, then get them to the practice squad without worrying about another team claiming them.
To be clear, I'm not suggesting that Franklin is absolutely going to be cut; such a move would raise some eyebrows. However, his role has diminished and the Broncos may want to prioritize a more versatile skill set when it comes to the fifth receiver they keep on the roster, and Franklin can't block or play special teams.
The Broncos don't appear to be prepared to keep four running backs on the 53-man roster . That would mean McLaughlin would get exposed to waivers because he's only accrued three NFL seasons, and the top three running backs are set.
McLaughlin has done some good things but is buried behind J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and Jonah Coleman, all of whom have more to offer to the team for one reason or another. But McLaughlin could be a good fit with other NFL teams.
McLaughlin won't command significant trade compensation, but even if it were just a seventh-round pick, it would be better than nothing, and not a bad return on a former undrafted player.
Skinner has stuck around with the Broncos for the past three seasons because of his special teams play. However, the former sixth-round pick hasn't shown much on defense, particularly when it comes to the Broncos' need for the third safety on the depth chart.
The recent signing of Taylor Rapp indicates the Broncos aren't happy with their depth at safety. Add in the fact that the All-Pro Devon Key is the Broncos' best special teams player, and the roster math may not work out for Skinner to stick around.
In this case, it might be a long shot, but a team with a great need for special teams help might be willing to do a Day 3 draft pick swap to acquire Skinner.
Franklin has the most trade value of these players, but that doesn't mean the Broncos will move him. However, if a team made an offer too good to refuse, the Broncos would likely take it.
McLaughlin and Skinner are less likely to be traded because they aren't as valuable, but such trades can't be ruled out. One team that's low in waiver priority could be prepared to make a trade to ensure they get that player.
Other players I considered are unlikely to get traded for one reason or another. Case in point is linebacker Drew Sanders, who may have netted a draft pick if he had stayed healthy this summer, but his most recent injury means teams aren't going to be interested, especially given his history.
