title: A Lot on the Line During Final Week of Packers Training Camp (Pun Intended)
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – This will be a hugely important week for the Green Bay Packers to solidify an offensive line that’s more wet cement than firm concrete.
The Packers will kick off their final week of training camp on Monday. The final practice of camp, a joint practice against the Cardinals, will be held on Wednesday. The preseason will conclude on Friday at Lambeau Field against Arizona. On Sunday, general manager Brian Gutekunst will handle the long, tortuous task of cutting the 91-man roster to the 53-player limit.
The line is filled with questions, with the coaches and standout former Packers lineman Mike Wahle providing answers.
Jordan Morgan has had a quietly good training camp. That, of course, is exactly the type of training camp you want from any offensive lineman. He’s just done his job and kept Jordan Love out of harm’s way.
“He’s done a nice job,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said of Morgan on Saturday, one day after the preseason win at Denver. “He’s just quietly gone in here and anchored down the left side. He’s been good. There’s not a whole lot to talk about because he’s gone in there, done his job and stepped up. I’m happy with him right now, for sure.”
Last year, standout Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat rushed from the defense’s right side and against the offensive left tackle about half the time. He hasn’t practiced during training camp due to chronic knee issues. If he comes off PUP, it would be a great test for Morgan if Sweat, who is coming off a season of a career-high 12 sacks, would be on the field for the joint practice.
“He's very athletic,” Wahle, who helps NFL linemen through his Process2Perform, said of Morgan. “He moves well off the line of scrimmage. I think his first step is really explosive. Obviously, can get into space really well.”
Wahle hopes more of Morgan’s power emerges through experience.
“I don't know if it's the way they're being taught, but they don't necessarily play with the power that is in that body from an athletic standpoint – like the hip pop, the snap extension with your hands. So, there's things like that that you can continue to improve on, both in the run and the pass game, but really good athlete.
“The thing that both those guys do well, talking about Zach (Bako-Bewele) and Jordan in particular, is they get into these spots where they are able to anchor down pretty well despite not maybe winning with their hands or being in a really upright position They're kind of catching those players and they're almost doing it by design.
“Guys like Terron Armstead made a career of doing this, where you're kind of by design catching a guy but you have the ability to sit down on it. For me, it's not the ideal way to play football, but Mark Tauscher made a career out of it and was pretty damn good.”
Because of a knee injury, the Packers’ $77 million man practiced sporadically for the first couple weeks of training camp before finally getting some 11-on-11 reps at practice last week. He has not played in the preseason. The starters probably won’t play in Friday’s game, so Banks will need the joint practice to show that he’s ready for the season.
Arizona’s defense features 2024 first-round pick Darius Robinson at defensive tackle.
“At some point, we’re going to need him to go out there and put it all together for a string of time,” Stenavich said. “Otherwise, you won’t know if you can rely on him as the season goes. I think that’s going to be a big thing for me over these next two weeks is just getting out there on a regular basis, getting through practices and performing at a high level.”
It’s rather incredible to consider that Sean Rhyan, who has made eight career starts (including playoffs) at center, is perhaps the sure thing on the line.
“I like Sean Rhyan's want to finish,” Wahle said. “I don't know if he's ever going to be the most powerful guy in the world, but there's a guy that really is maximizing his athleticism because of his footwork and body position into contact.”
Jacob Monk has gone from battling for a roster spot to perhaps being the Week 1 starter at right guard. He replaced returning starter Anthony Belton before Family Night and hasn’t looked back. With rookie Jager Burton set to focus on center this week, the deck has been cleared.
“Monk, love his play style,” Stenavich said. “He’s a nasty dude. So, watching him play has been really fun.”
Monk has the play style that offensive line coach Luke Butkus prefers.
“I think Jacob Monk was born with a chip on his shoulder. He showed that at Duke and that’s one of the reasons we were attracted to him,” Butkus said. “He is a physical and violent human being when he steps on that football field. I don’t know if you guys have noticed, but when he gets on that field, he flips that switch. Love it, and that’s the play style we talk about.”
Wahle, who talked to Packers On SI before the Denver game, liked what he saw from Monk against the Steelers.
“I've always kind of liked that body type,” Wahle said. “He's a little bit shorter, but I like that as you get to play with great leverage. Looks like he's put some weight on – some good weight. I think he moves really well.
“The thing that stood out in the Pittsburgh game was the lateral run game; he really excelled at it. Obviously, he's got a quick burst out of his stance. He takes good footwork, has that leverage. He was really able to extend that backside hand, particularly on some of those outside-zone-to-the-left plays. You just like the ability to kind of get into those bigger opponents.”
The problem with being a shorter lineman is having shorter arms; Monk needs to avoid lunging out and overextending, which is why he was beaten by Broncos star Zach Allen on Jordan Love’s touchdown pass.
“That’s a huge learning thing for him at guard,” Stenavich said. “You go against really good players, you have to play with great fundamentals. Otherwise, you’ll get exposed.”
The team’s best lineman suffered a knee injury at Denver last season and missed the rest of the season. The Packers are easing him back into things but “he’ll be ready to roll Week 1,” Butkus said.
With Aaron Banks’ on-again, off-again status, rookie Jager Burton has been Plan B at left guard throughout training camp, which has limited his ability to compete at right guard. This week, Stenavich said, Burton will focus more on center, which could make him the universal backup at all three interior spots.
Wahle has been impressed. Burton needs to play with better patience but is advanced in other facets.
“The guy does a really nice job of some real basic parts of playing offensive line and not just for a rookie,” he said. “Really good initial footwork. He's gaining leverage towards his opponent on every play. He comes in with a really great body profile. He stays square to the line of scrimmage in pass pro, for the most part.
“Again, nothing's perfect – it's not going to be as a rookie. My eye goes immediately to how good you are at the precontact basics of the sport, and he's really, really good at them. He's advanced for this group.”
Anthony Belton opened training camp as the presumptive starting right guard after stepping into the lineup for the stretch run of last season. Having lost the job early in training camp, he’s been filling in behind Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle. Since being replaced, he’s barely played any left tackle and he hasn’t played any right guard.
“There were enough positive traits last year that I certainly thought, OK, this guy should be expected to make a jump at right guard or at least be able to compete for the spot right now,” Wahle said.
“I think Jacob Monk could be a good player in the league. It’s Year 3 for him, so it’s kind of that time where you got to prove it. Maybe they've just seen so much that they like. You know, we never know what's going on in the background, but it is really surprising that he wouldn't get reps at right guard. He didn't do anything last year to dissuade me from thinking he…

title: Predicting the Packers’ 53-Man Roster With Cuts Looming Next Week
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have made it through the first two preseason games and are heading toward a meaningful final week of training camp with a joint practice and game against the Arizona Cardinals.
There are plenty of battles to be won as the depth of the roster has made for some interesting decisions and even given the Packers some potential trade chips if they choose to go that route.
Other spots are easy to project, and some jobs have been solidified with big-time performances in the preseason from kicker Trey Smack and defensive back Kamal Hadden.
Here is our second crack at a 53-man projection with a big week looming.
On the 53: Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor.
Not much to see here. Jordan Love is the starter. Tyrod Taylor will be the backup.
Kyle McCord has been excellent in the preseason, and the Packers may have to weigh whether a team would scoop him up if they release him on cutdown day. If he’s released and clears waivers, the Packers would likely be thrilled to have him back on the practice squad.
On the 53: Josh Jacobs, Marshawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks.
MarShawn Lloyd is healthy and proving why the Packers were willing to wait for him to work through his injuries through the first two seasons of his career. Chris Brooks is the team’s best blocking back and a core special-teamer.
One thing that could be interesting is what the Packers do with Pierre Strong Jr. He’s shown an ability to get downhill in the run game and return kickoffs. Strong returned a kickoff 68 yards to set up a Trey Smack field goal in the game Friday against the Denver Broncos. With legal questions surrounding Josh Jacobs, could the Packers look to keep an insurance policy?
On the 53: Christian Watson, Matthew Golden, Jayden Reed, Skyy Moore, Bo Melton, Savion Williams.
There are some intriguing practice-squad candidates with Isaiah Neyor, J. Michael Sturdivant and Will Sheppard proving their worth at different points in the preseason and training camp.
As far as the roster goes? There’s just not that much drama here. In order to keep one of the aforementioned players, they’d either have to keep seven receivers or release Bo Melton.
Seven receivers feels like a waste of a roster spot with all of the needs in other places on the roster. The likelihood is the Packers could get some, if not all of the aforementioned receivers, back on the practice squad.
Releasing Melton would be the shock of the century. The organization loves him. He might be the team’s best special teams player, and has made plays for them as a receiver. On Saturday, special teams coordinator Cam Achord said they are working 18 players at gunner but pointed only to Melton. Then, passing-game coordinator Jason Vrable said Melton is one of the receivers’ top blockers.
On the 53: Tucker Kraft, Josh Whyle, Drake Dabney.
The first two choices on this list are easy. Tucker Kraft is back, but they’re going to have to hold him back early in the season while he fully recovers from his torn ACL.
Josh Whyle is firmly entrenched as the backup tight end. After that, Drake Dabney’s name could read Dabney Drake and it may not make a difference. Dabney is making the roster at this point by default, but tight end feels like a position where the Packers are going to have to add someone from the outside.
Jonnu Smith is one possibility as he has played under coach Matt La Fleur. Zach Ertz is a veteran with some big-game chops, but the Packers are likely to lean toward a younger player who could potentially make an impact on special teams.
On the 53: Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Sean Rhyan, Anthony Belton, Zach Bako-Bewele, Darian Kinnard, Jager Burton, John Williams, Jacob Monk.
There may not be a player who has helped himself more in training camp than Jacob Monk. At the beginning of camp, it appeared he would be on the roster bubble. Now, he appears to be the overwhelming favorite to start at right guard against Minnesota in Week 1.
The back end of the offensive line room is starting to take shape. Jager Burton is the plug-and-play guy at all three interior spots if he’s not starting in favor of Aaron Banks. Anthony Belton is the swing tackle. John Williams is a potential super-sub with reps at left tackle, left guard and center during camp.
Darian Kinnard played well for the Packers a season ago if he can get off the injury report. Not only could he provide depth at right guard and right tackle but he played 66 snaps at tight end last season.
On the 53: Javon Hargrave, Devonte Wyatt, Chris McClellan, Karl Brooks, Jonathan Ford, Warren Brinson.
Jonathan Ford is one of the top performers in training camp and may start at nose tackle if the season were to begin tomorrow. He replaces Nazir Stackhouse, who made the cut in our initial projection.
One question that could upset the apple cart here is whether the Packers want to keep training camp stalwart Anthony Campbell. He’s been all over the field during practices and games, including his first sack against the Broncos on Friday. If the Packers don’t want to risk losing Campbell to waivers, they’d either have to keep him in favor of Ford, trade Karl Brooks, who is entering the final year of his deal, or keep seven.
That’s something worth monitoring as the preseason comes to a close.
On the 53: Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox, Dani Dennis-Sutton, Collin Oliver.
This group has had an up-and-down camp and is facing a big week with their joint practice session against the Cardinals. The pass rush was solid against the Steelers in the first week of the preseason, with Lukas Van Ness and Brenton Cox recording sacks.
Friday night against the Broncos, they were dormant against one of the better offensive lines in football. Nobody has really separated themselves in game situations, and that could make for one giant Micah Parsons-sized question mark as the season kicks off in three weeks.
On the 53: Zaire Franklin, Edgerrin Cooper, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty'Ron Hopper, Nick Niemann.
This is another pretty easy group to forecast. The Packers likely hope to sneak local product Kristian Welch onto the practice squad for the depth he provides at linebacker along with his special-teams ability.
Otherwise, Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper are the starters. The primary backups are Ty’Ron Hopper and Isaiah McDuffie, with Nick Niemann playing the role of special teams ace.
On the 53: Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, Brandon Cisse, Benjamin St-Juste, Domani Jackson, Kamal Hadden.
There has been a lot of drama at this position, but right now it’s hard to forecast any major changes coming. Carrington Valentine and Keisean Nixon could be trade candidates at the end of camp, but can the Packers really afford to sacrifice any depth at the position? As things stand, Brandon Cisse is likely to start Week 1. with Nixon, Valentine and Benjamin St-Juste battling it out for roles as the season goes on.
Kamal Hadden has popped since returning to action and could provide positional versatility as a boundary cornerback and slot. Domani Jackson has missed a good chunk of camp, but is back on the field, and the Packers liked him enough to draft him. He’ll get one of the final spots on the roster.
On the 53: Evan Williams, Xavier McKinney, Javon Bullard, Kitan Oladapo, Mark Perry.
The first three help form what is likely the best safety trio in all of football. Javon Bullard should return to action soon after missing time with a foot injury that has hampered him during training camp. Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams might form the best starting safety tandem in the NFL.
The big addition here is Mark Perry, who popped onto the screen in Friday’s win over the Broncos with an interception that led to a field goal late in the first half. Playmaking and his ability on special teams should give him the nod for one of the final spots on the roster.
On the 53: Daniel Whelan, Trey Smack, Matt Orzech.
Could there be a controversy here? It does not sound like it, according to the coaching staff. Incumbent snapper…

title: Updating Brandon Cisse and Key Injuries From Packers’ Preseason Win at Denver
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers cornerback Brandon Cisse missed most of Friday night’s preseason game at the Denver Broncos with a knee injury that is not considered serious.
After the game, Cisse told Packers sideline reporter Karley Marotta that he was “fine.” He probably was only going to play one more series with the rest of the starters, so the coaches pulled him prematurely for precautionary reasons.
Cisse just said “I’m good. I’m fine.” https://t.co/WgoztlmkSR
“I just got beat up a little bit,” Cisse said after game . “Nothing serious at all. I was trying to go back in. Just being precautionary. I’m fine. Nothing to worry about. I wanted to go back in.”
Cisse played six defensive snaps. He was targeted once but had great coverage on Courtland Sutton, so Bo Nix’s pass sailed over their heads.
Here are some more injury updates from the day after the game.
WR Savion Williams: Williams was coming off an impressive week of practice but wound up playing only two snaps against the Broncos due to an ankle injury.
“I think he's caught the ball really well this training camp,” passing game coordinator Jason Vrable said on Saturday. “Caught the ball with great hands, body control, staying on his feet. I think that was a big thing coming out of college. I just kept talking about it, just being more comfortable with the catch point. I think he's taken big strides there.
“And then, ultimately, I think it's been the playbook for him. Just from coming to college to our system, I'd say a little bit raw in some of the regards of maybe the routes we're asking him to run and what we're asking him to do down the field. A little bit newer to him compared to his role in college, but he's done a really good job with the playbook. And then I think when you know the plays and you're confident at the catch point, just building trust with Jordan (Love). I think, as you see, Jordan's giving him some opps in those practices and he did a great job.”
WR Jayden Reed: The only eyebrow-raising player on the preseason version of the inactives list was Reed, who practiced all week but was held out of the game. He wasn’t hurt, though. He was attending his grandmother’s funeral.
Without two of the top receivers, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden played 11 snaps apiece. Watson caught two passes for 19 yards and Golden caught one pass for 19 yards.
WR J. Michael Sturdivant: Sturdivant played in nine snaps and caught one pass but was woozy after a helmet-to-helmet hit late in the first half and taken out of the game to be evaluated for a concussion.
Because of the injuries, Isaiah Neyor (34 snaps), Will Sheppard (34), Kisean Johnson (25) and Bo Melton (24) got added opportunities.
DT Warren Brinson: Brinson was not on the list of players who wouldn’t play, but he was kept on the sideline after tweaking a calf during pregame warmups. Brinson has taken a big second-year jump and should have a big role on the defense, even at a crowded position group.
DT Devonte Wyatt: Wyatt was on the initial list of players who would not play. Instead, with Brinson a surprise scratch, he started and played four snaps.
Edge Collin Oliver: Oliver, who had a key block on Pierre Strong’s long kickoff return, was limited to only six snaps on defense because of a calf injury.
Two starters, left guard Aaron Banks and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, have been practicing but didn’t play against the Broncos. This week’s joint practice against Arizona will be big for both players to get them ready for Week 1 at the Vikings.
Bako-Bewele’s season ended last year with a knee injury sustained at Denver. He’s been splitting the first-team reps at right tackle with Anthony Belton as the coaches bring him along slowly.
“I think he’ll be ready to roll Week 1,” offensive line coach Luke Butkus said on Saturday. “He’s put some really good reps on film the last week and a half of practice, and that’s continued to grow. So again, we expect that this week, as well.”
Banks, who had practiced sporadically for most of camp, returned to 11-on-11 work last week. Jager Burton, however, got the start against Denver.
“He put some really good reps out there,” Butkus said of Banks. “Now, we just need to keep stacking them. Everybody can do it one or two times, but we need to build the stamina and the consistency to do it over and over.”
Burton, by the way, will focus on center this week as the coaches appear to be getting him ready to be the universal interior backup behind Banks, center Sean Rhyan and right guard Jacob Monk.
“Monk, love his play style. He’s a nasty dude,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “So, watching him play has been really fun. He can play guard, he can play center. Obviously, Jager played center in college. We haven’t gotten him as much center reps as I would like to have. We’re going to try to focus on that this week to try and just keep him working in there in case that has to come up later on in the year.”

title: Updated Packers Roster Projection, With Focus on Bubble (And Two Trades)
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers are deep. That much is clear as the team barrels full speed ahead toward the critical final week of training camp, which will be punctuated by a joint practice and preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals.
With tough decisions looming at a handful of positions, here’s our third roster projection. This emphasizes the players on the roster bubble and what changed since last week .
Today’s roster: Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor, Kyle McCord.
Week 1 projection: Love and Taylor.
Roster bubble: Nobody. McCord is having a good preseason and is worthy of a long look on the practice squad to determine whether he can be a legitimate backup. But his preseason hasn’t been so good that he’d be likely to be claimed off waivers.
Today’s roster: Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks, Pierre Strong, Jaden Nixon, Damien Martinez.
Week 1 projection: Jacobs, Lloyd, Brooks.
Roster bubble: With his vision and speed, Strong has had a productive training camp. He, of course, displayed those traits with his long kickoff return against the Broncos. Four running backs is a lot, though, and Brooks’ value as a pass protector is more important than Strong’s ability with the ball in his hands, since the ball needs to be in the hands of Jacobs and Lloyd.
Plus, there’s some roster-building thought to this, as well. Strong showed what he could do with the Patriots and Browns in 2022 through 2024 but spent all of last season on Green Bay’s practice squad. No team wanted to sign Strong to its 53 last year. Really, nothing has changed from a skill-set perspective.
Today’s roster: Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Savion Williams, Bo Melton, Skyy Moore, Will Sheppard, Isaiah Neyor, J. Michael Sturdivant, Kisean Johnson, Kaden Prather, Chris Hilton.
Week 1 projection: Watson, Reed, Golden, Williams, Melton and Moore.
Roster bubble: Neyor had a productive game at Pittsburgh. Sturdivant had a productive practice week. Sheppard had the big night on Friday by catching all six targets, including a highlight-reel touchdown.
All three players are capable of being legit contributors. However, seven receivers is a lot and most teams have someone like Neyor, Sheppard or Sturdivant making plays on the bottom of the roster, so there should be no fear of losing all the young depth to waivers.
Today’s roster: Tucker Kraft, Josh Whyle, Luke Musgrave (PUP), Drake Dabney, Messiah Swinson, McCallan Castles, Thomas Yassmin (international).
Week 1 projection: Kraft, Whyle, Dabney, TBA.
What changed?: Going from three tight ends to four.
Roster bubble: This could be a case where Dabney makes the 53-man roster next Sunday and general manager Brian Gutekunst reassesses the situation when he sees who’s available on Monday. Dabney has had a solid camp, but can the Packers do better? For now, we’ll go with Dabney and TBA rather than Dabney or TBA. After all, if a tight end is added, he’ll need to learn the offense. Dabney is good enough to contribute.
Today’s roster: LT Jordan Morgan, LG Aaron Banks, C Sean Rhyan, RG Jacob Monk, RT Zach Bako-Bewele, T/G Anthony Belton, T/G Darian Kinnard, C/G Jager Burton, T/G/C John Williams, T/G Travis Glover, G/C Donovan Jennings, T Brant Banks, T Dalton Cooper, G Dillon Wade, G Josh Gesky, G/C Dylan Barrett.
Week 1 projection: Morgan, Aaron Banks, Rhyan, Monk, Bako-Bewele, Belton, Burton, Kinnard, Williams.
Roster bubble: There are some tough decisions to be made at the end of the roster. The first seven players are the obvious locks. Kinnard was a solid backup last season who received a $1 million signing bonus. He can play guard and tackle on the line and played a lot of snaps as an extra tight end last year.
For the ninth spot, Williams has shown he can play multiple positions – a huge asset that’s worthy of being groomed after he missed his rookie season with a back injury. Jennings is a physical blocker who can play all three interior spots. Glover, who can play right tackle but has spent most of camp at right guard, and Wade, who has been locked in at left guard, played well against Denver.
This one could go down to the wire. For now, we’ll stick with the player who can play left tackle.
Today’s roster: Micah Parsons (PUP), Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox, Dani Dennis Sutton, Collin Oliver, Arron Mosby, Nyjalik Kelly, Arden Walker.
Week 1 projection: Van Ness, Sorrell, Cox, Dennis-Sutton, Oliver.
Roster bubble: Oliver, as a fifth-round draft pick with some potential pass-rushing juice, is the obvious front-runner for a fifth spot, but Mosby is a weapon on special teams and Kelly is coming on strong. He had one sack, one forced fumble and, according to PFF, three quarterback pressures.
I thought long and hard about sticking with three tight ends and keeping Kelly. Most times, the fear of losing a player on waivers is completely overblown. Kelly, though, could be an exception.
Today’s roster: Devonte Wyatt, Javon Hargrave, Karl Brooks, Jonathan Ford, Chris McClellan, Warren Brinson, Nazir Stackhouse, Anthony Campbell, Jaden Crumedy, Jordon Riley (PUP).
Week 1 projection: Wyatt, Hargrave, Ford, Brinson, McClellan, Campbell.
What changed?: Trading Brooks and keeping Campbell.
Roster bubble: The Packers, unexpectedly, are dealing from a position of strength. They have more players capable of contributing than spots on the roster. So, perhaps there’s a deal to be made.
Brooks would be the obvious man on the move. He is having a strong camp, had productive seasons in 2023 and 2024, and is entering his final season under contract. The Packers could move him to improve a position of weakness, such as tight end, or add another draft pick to their 2027 war chest.
Campbell, Stackhouse and Crumedy have all had good training camps. Campbell had a punishing sack and a team-high four pressures against the Broncos. Crumedy had a big-time pressure on a fourth-down incompletion. Stackhouse would add more beef at nose tackle. They’re all worthy of being on a 53-man roster.
The alternative is keeping seven. The Packers kept six in the old 4-3 scheme, which placed two defensive tackles on the field. In the 3-4, they’ll use three sometimes, so maybe that will sway the numbers.
Today’s roster: Edgerrin Cooper, Zaire Franklin, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper, Nick Niemann, Kristian Welch, TJ Quinn.
Week 1 projection: Cooper, Franklin, McDuffie, Hopper, Niemann.
Roster bubble: Really nobody, though Welch against Denver showed once again why he’s a professional special-teams player. He had two tackles and the key block on Pierre Strong’s long kickoff return.
Today’s roster: Brandon Cisse, Keisean Nixon, Benjamin St-Juste, Carrington Valentine, Kamal Hadden, Jaylin Simpson, Domani Jackson, Shemar Bartholomew, MJ Devonshire.
Week 1 projection: Cisse, Nixon, St-Juste, Hadden, Jackson.
What changed?: The subject of the trade, with Nixon staying (and starting) and Valentine going. With 30 starts in three seasons, Valentine should be able to help a cornerback-needy team while giving the Packers an asset in return. Plus, Simpson winds up being one of the last players cut as we go from six corners to five.
Roster bubble: The decision to release Simpson had nothing to do with Simpson and everything to do with Hadden, who was really good against Denver, and the developmental upside of Jackson, a sixth-round pick.
The Packers know Hadden can play cornerback; now, they know he can contribute in the slot, where the Packers need a backup with better coverage skills than big, physical Kitan Oladapo. title: Six Winners and One Key Loser From Packers’ Victory Over Broncos
full_text:
Preseason performance does not matter. A team could win or lose by 70 points and it would not affect it in any capacity once the regular season begins.
That being said, the last time the Green Bay Packers were in Denver for a preseason game, it was one of the worst performances they’ve had under coach Matt LaFleur. The Packers were bludgeoned 27-2 by the Broncos in August 2024.
Friday night’s performance was a little different. The Packers scored more than two points, as Jordan Love’s only series of the night yielded a touchdown on an impressive 12-play drive that came against one of the league’s best defenses.
The Packers would score 26 more points, with another big night from one of their biggest stars in the preseason.
With just one game left on the exhibition slate, here are our winners and losers from Green Bay’s 33-13 win.
When the Packers drafted Trey Smack, Brian Gutekunst was asked how to scout a kicker. Gutekunst raised his arms in the air as if to make the “good” sign.
Gutekunst was joking, but he’s right.
So far, that’s the only signal that Smack knows in games as an NFL kicker.
They don’t hand out MVP awards in the preseason but, if they did, it would be hard to argue against anyone other than Green Bay’s rookie kicker winning the award.
Smack was impressive in his debut in Pittsburgh, but the more good performances he can put together, the more confident he can become before the opener against Minnesota.
Smack was a perfect 7-for-7 against Denver with four field goals and three extra points. The highlight came on a 59-yard bomb that had plenty of room to spare. It’s early, and he has yet to kick in a game of consequence, but the Packers have to be thrilled with the progress of their rookie kicker in the summer.
Apart from Trey Smack, there may not be a player who needed a good training camp more than third-year running back MarShawn Lloyd.
Lloyd has always had the talent, but has needed to prove he could stay healthy.
Lloyd has made it through two games and showcased the talent that the Packers have been excited about through his injury-riddled career. The highlight of Lloyd’s night came as the capper of Green Bay’s opening drive on offense. Jordan Love found Lloyd on a Texas route in the middle of the field for an easy touchdown. It was his first touchdown in more than 1,000 days .
THINGS YOU LOVE TO SEE! 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/9mk7y1ry1o
“Honestly, trust my training,” he told reporters after the game. “It’s a choice route, so you could either break in or break out. Because of his leverage, I was able to break in. He gave everything off the inside, and once I got through the inside, I was able to get to the end zone from there.”
That is the type of impact that Lloyd can make in the passing game, and if the Packers can get him through one more preseason game healthy, he’ll be able to showcase it in a regular-season game for the first time since Week 2 of the 2024 season.
With roster cuts looming, the Packers needed someone to separate themselves from the bottom of the safety depth chart. Late in the first half, safety Mark Perry threw his hat into the ring, jumping a route as Denver’s backup quarterback, Jarrett Stidham, was trying to lead a 2-minute drive.
Perry jumped in front of Lucas Krull to grab his first interception of the preseason. His big play gave the Packers the ball back with a chance to put more points on the board, and it led to one of Trey Smack’s biggest plays of the night.
Mark Perry came out of nowhere 😳 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/I7Jsn4Fi9u
With Evan Williams, Xavier McKinney and Javon Bullard all set in stone on the roster, the Packers are trying to find some depth at that position. There’s room to make a run at a roster spot here, and Perry gave himself something to build on going into the final week of the preseason.
“It was a big confidence booster for me,” Perry said . “Every day in practice, trying to make the plays that come to you and not chase plays. … I think that was big for me and, obviously, it juiced the team right before the half (and) was able to score some points."
Who would play in the slot if Javon Bullard is injured? That’s a question the Packers hope they never have to answer when the regular season comes around, but they have to for the time being as Bullard is sidelined with a foot injury.
One of the candidates is Kamal Hadden, who returned to the field for the first time since suffering a horrific ankle injury in last year’s blowout loss to the Ravens.
Hadden is proving to be quite the versatile piece in the defense. He was drafted by the Chiefs in 2024 as a boundary corner. For the Packers at training camp this week, he started working in the slot, and he played well at his new position on Friday by making five tackles, including two for losses.
The more you can do, the easier it is for the general manager to decide to keep you on cutdown day. Right now, Hadden is trying to prove he can do just about anything on the field.
Remember when Aaron Rodgers smiled for the NBC broadcast following their season-opening 10-3 win over the Bears in 2019 and said, “We’ve got a defense.”
Perhaps the Packers are feeling that way after Friday’s game about their special teams, in general, and return game, in particular.
Through two games, Trey Smack has yet to miss a kick. On Friday, Pierre Strong had a 68-yard kickoff return and Skyy Moore had a 30-yard kickoff return and 16-yard punt return.
Strong’s return was set up by good vision and excellent blocking from those in front of him, including Kristian Welch and Collin Oliver. This likely goes without saying, but it would have been the longest for the Packers last season.
Pierre Strong Jr. with a 68-yard kick return 🔥 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QpchpKwmr0
Achord has been a breath of fresh air with the youthful energy and exuberance he has brought to a special teams that has been largely dormant during Matt LaFleur’s tenure as the head coach.
The job is not finished, as Achord has yet to coach in a real game for the Packers, but the early returns are encouraging.
Who is the young player who is going to make a run at the back end of the roster? Perhaps that could be Anthony Campbell.
Campbell has been swatting away passes during training camp like he’s Dikembe Mutumbo, but gave a glimpse that perhaps he could do a little more in Friday’s game. Campbell had one of the team’s two sacks and joined Chris McClellan on a tackle for loss. PFF credited him with a team-high four pressures.
Green Bay’s defensive line has been a surprising strength during the summer. Devonte Wyatt, Javon Hargrave, Karl Brooks, Warren Brinson and Chris McClellan are all very likely to make the team. Jonathan Ford has had a strong summer, and Nazir Stackhouse is someone the Packers liked enough to keep around all year a season ago.
Campbell is trying to state his case to force the Packers to make him their sixth defensive lineman, or perhaps roll with an extra guy in the early portion of the season.
If nothing else, Campbell has continued to make plays that should have him on the radar, whether in Green Bay or elsewhere.
On a night when there were not a ton of negatives for the Packers, one big one reared its ugly head early that could be a cause for concern when the regular season begins.
Green Bay’s pass rush has more than a few question marks surrounding it as Micah Parsons will not be ready for the start of the season. The quartet of Brenton Cox, Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell and Dani Dennis-Sutton have all had nice moments during training camp.
The three who played were silent during the cameo Green Bay’s starting defense made Friday night. Of the combined 21 pass-rushing opportunities for Van Ness, Sorrel and Cox, they contributed only one pressure (Cox). Including Collin Oliver’s five chances, they went 1-for-26.
Sure, the Broncos have one of the best offensive lines in football, but they’re going to…

title: Five Packers Who Helped Themselves vs. Broncos, Including Three on Bubble
full_text:
Life comes at you fast. In the NFL, it comes at a young player in the equivalent of a 4.4-second time in the 40.
So, a player like Green Bay Packers quarterback Kyle McCord can’t afford to look too far down the road. He’s got goals, though, and his performance at the Denver Broncos in Friday’s preseason game will help make them possible.
He’s one of five young players who really helped themselves in the 33-13 victory.
Kyle McCord is not going to make the 53-man roster. He could have thrown for 300 yards and five touchdowns against the Broncos and it probably wouldn’t have changed that reality.
Nonetheless, his second consecutive solid performance has all but ensured he will be the team’s No. 3 quarterback this season. That means a spot on the practice squad.
However, this year’s No. 2 quarterback, Tyrod Taylor, is 37 years old and on a one-year contract. It’s quite possible that being the No. 3 quarterback this season will jump McCord to the front of the line to be the No. 2 quarterback next season.
“Yeah, I would say that’s definitely the long-term goal,” McCord said this week. “But, at the same time, I feel like it’s so easy to get caught up in those long-term, down-the-line type of goals. I think the most important thing is being where your feet are and making the most out of every preseason game, every practice, every rep you get.”
This pass was perfectly placed 🤌 (Via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/ceKVjyprb7
McCord did that against the Broncos. He was 12-of-19 passing for 118 yards. Two of the seven incompletions were drops. Another came when it appeared the intended receiver missed the hot read as the Broncos sent an all-out blitz.
McCord played the final 32 minutes. The name of the game as a quarterback is to lead the offense to points. In five possessions, he led the Packers to three field goals and one touchdown.
Will Sheppard spent his final collegiate season at Colorado, making this game a homecoming of sorts.
He was the king of the receivers, catching all six targets for 47 yards and one touchdown. The touchdown was elite-level stuff as he got both feet down before being pushed out of bounds.
The catch. The toe tap. INSANE TD by Will Sheppard 🙌 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/a4Qprlj3uN
“At the catch point, it was kind of like slow motion almost,” he said. “I felt myself drag the toe, but I didn’t know exactly where I was on the field until the replay.”
The Packers’ top six receivers seem pretty well established. Could the Packers keep seven? Sheppard isn’t as flashy as Isaiah Neyor or J. Michael Sturdivant, but he’s been more consistently productive during camp.
Against Denver, Neyor was guilty of two penalties and one drop and Sturdivant didn’t return after a helmet-to-helmet tackle.
Pierre Strong has played well enough on the practice field to merit a spot on the roster, but the depth chart has made that an uphill climb . Josh Jacobs is the established starter, MarShawn Lloyd is healthy and ready to be the backup and Chris Brooks handles the intangibles such as pass protection and special teams.
Strong, however, had a 68-yard kickoff return and added eight carries for 37 yards.
YOOOOOOOOO 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/ytx4vBIY8m
“Not everybody can do special teams,” Strong said. “Some coaches say, ‘You have to be special players to be special teams.’ Just doing whatever coach asks me to do and get on special teams because not everybody’s good at special teams.”
Strong was a fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022. He boasted a 5.0-yard average during his first three seasons but was released by the Browns at the end of training camp last year. He spent all of last season on Green Bay’s practice squad without getting in a game.
With excellent vision and speed, Strong has produced several explosive cutback runs at practice. Now, with a strong game, he’s built some momentum headed into the final week of camp.
“I’m just doing my job, just bringing my best, being the best that I can be every single day,” he said. “So, you call it momentum, but I just call it consistency.”
The battle for the fifth spot at safety has been a spirited one between a pair of undrafted players, Mark Perry and Murvin Kenion.
To win the job, someone had to make a play .
Late in the first half, Perry read veteran quarterback Jarrett Stidham, made an explosive break on the ball and grabbed an interception.
OUR BALL 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/zYe9WKxDIW
“Yeah, it was a coverage we repped in practice,” Perry explained. “I had my eyes on the quarterback, and seeing the release of the tight end, I knew he was running that seam [route] because the release he had. Once I saw the quarterback let it go, it was just a matter of contorting my body to get inside, trying to get the ball. I knew it was coming and was able to come up with that play.”
Perry went undrafted in 2024. The Packers are his sixth team; he’s never been on a 53-man roster or played in a game. Before training camp, he said this opportunity “feels a little different” than the past couple seasons.
It was his first interception since the 2021 season, when he was a redshirt sophomore at Colorado.
For rookie kicker Trey Smack, it’s all about consistency.
After kicking inconsistently in OTAs, minicamp and the start of training camp, Smack made all four field-goal attempts at Pittsburgh. Critically, he did it again against Denver .
Officially, Smack is 7-of-7 on field goals during the preseason. Unofficially, he is 8-of-8 with four makes beyond 50 yards.
“I don’t know if there’s certainly a message that I can give to them,” he said of the Packers. “I’m just kind of trying to do my job, trying to live up to the expectation that they want me to. I’m very grateful that I’m here. I’m very grateful that I’m a Green Bay Packer. That never wants to change for me. I always want to be a Green Bay Packer, so whatever I can do – I’m not sure what that is – just make my kicks and honor that.”
That the Packers beat the Broncos is irrelevant. These are the three things that did matter. ⬇️ https://t.co/ugNFs94gvg

title: What Dylan Horton’s Season-Ending Injury Means for Texans
full_text:
The Houston Texans will be down a player on their defensive line for the 2026 season following Monday's training camp practice.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , Texans defensive end Dylan Horton is feared to have suffered a season-ending Achilles injury.
Horton was set to enter his fourth season with the Texans in 2026 and had been fighting to make it onto Houston's 53-man roster as a depth piece within their defensive end room.
However, in a practice before the Texans' third preseason game of the year against the Carolina Panthers, Horton would go down with a torn Achilles, thus ending his 2026 campaign and changing the outlook on Houston's defensive line along with it.
After three seasons in Houston, Horton was shaping up to have a bit of an increased role for the Texans' defense in 2026.
While he was battling to be the fourth defensive end on the depth chart after Houston signed Jadeveon Clowney earlier in training camp , Horton was only active in 25% of in his games played in 2025.
If he won out to be DE4, he had a chance to see that number, and his individual stats would take a step forward––which comes even more important in a contract year.
Last season with the Texans, Horton played in 16 games to log 26 total tackles and 0.5 sacks.
Now, the 2023 fourth-round pick will have to wait until 2027 to take his next snap, which may or may not be with the Texans, and take on the long road of recovering from a torn Achilles.
With Horton now out of the picture, the Texans' defensive line depth now looks a bit more interesting than it did this time last week. And this has been a group that's already seen a fair share of questions throughout training camp.
Besides Will Anderson, Danielle Hunter, and Jadeveon Clowney at the top, Houston is now down to free agent signings Dominique Robinson––who is currently hurt heading into game three of the preseason, Salomon Byrd, Ali Gaye, and Sebastian Harsh.
It's a group that has some promise, but not a ton of proven production. All four of them have a combined 4.5 sacks throughout their careers, with 3.5 of those coming from Robinson during his four years with the Chicago Bears.
As to who will be the best bet to take that DE4 role from Horton, Robinson feels like the most likely to do so . However, his recent injury could add even more uncertainty to the position creeping closer to the regular season, and perhaps more importantly, this weekend's 53-man cutdown.
With the look of Houston's defensive line depth, it feels likely for the front office to approach the position with an addition via free agency, or a trade if they're very interested in adding another defensive end.
The Texans have proven multiple times leading up to this season that, if they have a certain need on the roster, and there's talent ready to be acquired on the market, they're going to make the move to do just that.
Houston needs another edge rusher? Jadeveon Clowney is signed to a one-year deal. They need another receiver after Jayden Higgins suffers a season-ending injury? The front office goes out to trade for Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots .
The Texans have been continuously proactive in patching up their necessary holes, and doing whatever it takes to best position this roster to be a Super Bowl-caliber group by the time the season ends.

title: Instant Grade: Texans Land WR Kayshon Boutte in Trade With Patriots
full_text:
The Houston Texans are adding a new pass catcher to their wide receiver room.
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero of NFL Network , the Texans are acquiring wide receiver Kayshon Boutte in a trade from the New England Patriots.
Trade! The Patriots are sending WR Kayshon Boutte to the Texans for safety Jaylen Reed and a draft pick, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . pic.twitter.com/NZXCdOX4RT
The Texans are reportedly sending over second-year safety Jayden Reed and future seventh-round pick from the New Orleans Saints to the Patriots in exchange for Boutte.
It was a much-needed, and even partly an expected move for the Texans to make after the recent events that have taken place at their wide receiver position. 2025 second-round pick Jayden Higgins went down with a torn ACL earlier last week during practice , and will be sidelined for the entire 2026 season because of it.
And now, the Texans have acted quickly by bringing in Boutte as the latest name to their wide receiver room.
Let's break down the Texans' latest deal for what it means moving forward, along with an instant grade for how Houston fared.
Boutte has been circled as an easy trade target for teams–– and narely, the Texans–– across the league in recent days to weeks.
Boutte's in the final year of his contract, and on a Patriots team that acquired two other targets in A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs earlier this offseason, that makes it far less likely that he's in for a new deal with New England in 2027.
And for the Texans, they made sense as a perfect target . They had a clear need in their wide receiver room, and especially for someone that can effectively line up on the outside of Houston's offense as a starting-caliber pass-catcher opposite of Nico Collins.
Kayshon Boutte fits that mold quite well. He's a little smaller at 5-foot-11, but he's coming off of two quality seasons in New England, where he was a consistent, reliable target for Drake Maye.
In 2025, Boutte put together 33 receptions, 551 yards, and six touchdowns, the second straight year where he had over 30 catches and 500 yards. He was second in the Patriots' offense for total receiving touchdowns, and fifth in total receiving yards.
As a big-play, downfield threat, Boutte can be a noteworthy contributor. And pretty immediately, he could be in for some significant targets in the Texans' wide receiver room as the WR2 or WR3 behind Collins, and maybe Xavier Hutchinson.
As it relates to the Texans' deal to bring in Boutte and how well they fared, you can't imagine a much better outcome. The draft capital they sent out was minimal, and the player they shipped out was at a position they had a nice chunk of depth at anyways.
Jaylen Reed is a nice safety with solid potential to be a starting-level defender, but the Texans already have a lot to work with at the position with Calen Bullock, Reed Blankenship, Jalen Pitre, and fifth-round rookie Kamari Ramsey. Shedding a depth piece from that group and investing in their wide receiver group is a stellar way to manage those assets.
Now, the Texans can take a deep breath for what lies ahead in their receiver room, and have a solid group of weapons behind Collins to rely on to, at the very least, stay afloat without Higgins' presence for this season.
The only reason this move isn't an A+? Because of the uncertainty that lies ahead for Boutte in Houston past this season.
He's on an expiring contract, and in a wide receiver room that also faces pending free agents for Xavier Hutchinson and Tank Dell, there are no guarantees that this will be a multi-year pairing between the Texans and Boutte.
But for now, the move to bring in a trustworthy receiver like Boutte was necessary and took minimal cost to make happen. With that in mind, an A feels like the right grade.

title: Three Texans WRs Poised for More Targets Without Jayden Higgins
full_text:
The Houston Texans' wide receiver room is set to look a bit different than initially expected this season without second-year wideout Jayden Higgins in the lineup— who will be out for the 2026 campaign due to a torn ACL suffered in practice last week.
Without Higgins, who was overwhelmingly expected to be the Texans' No. 2 wide receiver in the offense, how this position could pan out for the offense this season could change drastically.
Guys are going to trend up the depth chart, get more targets and opportunities on their hands because of it, and might have some of their best seasons ever on the horizon.
Not having Higgins certainly hurts this Texans passing offense as a whole. But for these three wideouts on Houston's roster, they'll be in store for a lot more work without him.
The receiver who feels immediately due to claim the snaps left up for grabs from Higgins is none other than Xavier Hutchinson: someone who's healthy, fits the physical mold the Texans would want lining up as their Z receiver, and comes off a career-best season in 2025 entering a contract year.
The makings of an even better season are there for Hutchinson , who had over 30 receptions and 400 yards in 2025. Last season, he was fourth in the Texans' wide receiver room for target share at a little more than 10%. But now, two of the names that were above him in Higgins and Christian Kirk are no longer in the way for 2026.
Seeing Hutchinson log over 600 receiving yards this season and take that target share jump up to around 13% or higher certainly wouldn't be the most shocking outcome. And it could be what leads him to a nice payday once this next offseason arrives.
Second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel got a slow start to training camp due to the minor finger and hamstring injury he suffered at the end of July.
But now, he's trending back to full health heading into the final week of preseason. And with a smooth recovery, he could be due for an even bigger jump in opportunities from how things were shaking up in Houston's offseason program in the summer.
Compared to last season, Noel has another year of experience under his belt, won't have to compete for targets with either Kirk and Higgins, and feels like the most likely candidate to claim a majority of the snaps as the Texans' slot receiver throughout the course of the season. That role alone means Noel is due for a big jump in numbers.
Noel had a tiny 6% target share in the Texans' offense last season. If that number weren't in double digits by the time this season ends, it'd be a pretty big surprise.
Some may argue Tank Dell is in store for a significant jump in targets after Higgins' injury. But he hasn't even participated in a preseason game since recovering from his injury. And until he's back to a true 100%, his absence puts a star like Nico Collins in position for even more work than he was already expected to get.
Collins is about as trusted and proven a wide receiver that the Texans could have in their unit. He's already coming off of three straight 1,000-yard seasons, but less depth without Higgins, and maybe Dell to start the season, means those targets get further consolidated into top options like Houston’s WR1.
As long as the Texans don't make any major changes to the position , and Collins remains healthy throughout the year, seeing him post a career-best season might not be out of the range of realistic possibilities for 2026.

title: Texans’ Biggest Surprise Standouts From Preseason So Far
full_text:
Despite the Houston Texans losing both of their preseason games played thus far, there have been a handful of standouts worth nothing around the roster who have boosted their stock in one way or another leading up to the regular season.
Especially for the Texans' rookie class, who have gotten significant reps through Houston's showings against the Los Angeles Chargers and Las Vegas Raiders, things have looked notably positive for a select few.
And with one preseason game––along with a joint practice––to go against the Carolina Panthers, the hope is those who have shined can keep that momentum up and put themselves in position for an ideal start to Week 1, kicking off in less than three weeks.
Let's take a look at five players around the Texans' roster who have emerged as surprise standouts through two weeks of preseason.
The Texans’ wide receiver room has been due for someone down the depth chart to stand out following the injury to Jayden Higgins, and third-year wideout Jared Wayne has stepped up to the occasion to do just that.
In game one of the Texans' preseason action, he hauled in Houston's only touchdown score of the day on an impressive red-zone catch on a ball from Davis Mills. He's totaled five receptions for 30 yards through two games, and is the only receiver on the roster to log multiple receptions in both games.
Jared Wayne and the Texans get out to an early lead Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/WYMFNSLKtj
There's a lot of uncertainty as to what the Texans' receiver room will look like come Week 1 . But Wayne's recent performance could be creating an extremely compelling case that makes him the final name at the position to make it onto the roster past cutdown day.
Klein really needed a big preseason to showcase why the Texans invested in him so highly in April's draft with a second-round pick. And so far, he's done just that.
In Klein's first game, he had a game-high 31-yard reception that really put him on the map. In game two against the Raiders, Klein had an equally strong day with three catches on four targets for 31 yards.
OKAY MARLIN‼️ 📺: @abc13houston pic.twitter.com/tJ7JZBbIZt
Klein had a slow start to the Texans' offseason program earlier this summer, but his recent emergence could shoot him much further up the depth chart entering Week 1 from what anyone initially expected.
Woodaz seems likely to miss some time moving forward, as the rookie linebacker suffered a broken thumb in the Texans' second preseason game against the Raiders. But the sample size he's shown thus far is really promising for what his future will look like in this Houston defense.
Game one resulted in Woodaz putting together a quiet two tackles, but his second game against the Raiders is where he really shined: two total tackles, a pass defended, and an interception returned 80 yards for a touchdown on this year's No. 1 overall pick, Fernando Mendoza.
OPEN UP A CAN OF WOODAZZZZZZ 🤯 📺: @nflonespn pic.twitter.com/Ke0lrYupPs
Time will tell how long it'll be until Woodaz is back in the fold, and whether or not he starts the season on injured reserve. But when he is back, there's a pretty solid chance he finds his way to that LB3 role on the depth chart that's been wide open since E.J. Speed's been out with a torn quad.
The Texans selected two linebackers in April's draft. And so far, both of them have been exceeding expectations when factoring in how well seventh-round pick Aiden Fisher has been producing through two showings .
Game one against the Chargers saw Fisher log a game-high seven combined tackles and one tackle for loss. Game two saw him collect a similarly impressive six combined tackles, which tied for second-highest on the Texans' defense in tackles behind Brandon Codrington.
Combining the recent injuries in the room with the performances of Fisher might be the perfect storm for Fisher to be someone who sneaks onto a 53-man roster spot, so long as he keeps the momentum going into this week's game against Carolina.
Fifth-round rookie Kamari Ramsey deserves a shoutout for his interception on Trey Lance against the Chargers in week one of the preseason. But another safety in the room who's also performed well through two games is second-year talent Jaylen Reed, who's done nothing but produce strong numbers.
He has a combined 11 tackles with a pass defended in two games. He's one of three players with double-digit tackles through both games alongside Aiden Fisher and cornerback Stephen Hall.
Reed's chances to make the Week 1 roster were already pretty solidified entering training camp, but production like this certainly does lock that status in even further for what appears to be a deep and versatile safety room.

title: How Wade Woodaz's Latest Injury Changes Texans' LB Room
full_text:
The Houston Texans' linebacker room has been hit with another injury: fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz .
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , Woodaz is expected to undergo surgery following the broken thumb injury he sustained in the Texans' preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders.
His timeline for return reportedly remains undetermined, but placing Woodaz on injured reserve before the season remains a possibility.
It's one of multiple injuries the Texans have seen in their linebacker unit before Week 1 of the regular season.
Woodaz joins both E.J. Speed (quad) and Jake Hansen (ankle) as candidates who could end up missing the start of the year, and thus makes the position group even thinner from what they were working with.
Let's break down what the injury to Woodaz means for the Texans' linebacker room moving forward:
After the Texans' training camp work and two games of preseason, it felt like Woodaz was the primary candidate in the lead to claim Houston's LB3 role before the season .
It's been a spot that's been open on Houston's defense since E.J. Speed first suffered his quad injury earlier this summer, but felt increasingly settled in Woodaz's hands, especially after his 80-yard pick-six on Fernando Mendoza against the Raiders that really made a statement on top of what he had already done through training camp.
But now, the Texans could have that LB3 job back up for grabs, at least to begin the 2026 season while Woodaz is off to the side. Perhaps that comes via someone already on the roster, or maybe Houston goes out to acquire someone via trade to really fill the position.
The two names who stick out with the most likely odds to get work in Houston's linebacker room are veteran Marte Mapu and seventh-round rookie Aiden Fisher .
Both have performed well throughout the past few weeks that the Texans have been back in the building, and will now have even more opportunity on their hands––especially if Woodaz is going to be placed on injured reserve to start the year.
Two other names to keep an eye on: fourth-year linebacker Jamal Hill and offseason free agent signing Jake Hummel. Each might be more geared towards being primarily a special teamer, but as the room continues to get slimmer, they'll have a better chance to lock themselves into a 53-man roster spot, but also into a bigger role defensively.
The Texans have already acted by adding extra depth within their linebacker room since Woodaz's injury, reportedly signing veteran Caleb Johnson. who's entering his sixth season in the NFL.
#Texans set to sign veteran linebacker Caleb Johnson after successful workout, per a league source. Johnson, the first @HouChristianU #NFL player in school history, Has 40 career tackles, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, previously #Bears #Jaguars #Falcons #Dolphins … https://t.co/aqb3QREnEi pic.twitter.com/2OcqJXTAQv
The undrafted product out of Houston Christian has been mostly a special teamer throughout his five years in the pros, having played for the Chicago Bears, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Miami Dolphins. He has 40 career tackles and one forced fumble throughout his career.
Johnson has over 1,100 snaps on special teams throughout his time in the league. With the Dolphins last season, he played just two games and just 22 snaps, suffered a shoulder injury, and saw his 2025 campaign shortened because of it.
He may not have an inside track for the Texans roster with a week to go until cutdown day, but he will be someone to watch getting snaps in preseason later this week, as Houston travels to face the Carolina Panthers for their final preliminary showing on Friday, August 28th.

title: Derek Barnett's New Deal Proves Texans Got a Steal on Jadeveon Clowney
full_text:
A former piece of the Houston Texans' defense found a new home over the weekend.
According to a report from NFL insider Jeremy Fowler of ESPN , the Cleveland Browns have agreed to sign free agent defensive end Derek Barnett to a one-year, $5.5 million deal.
Defensive end Derek Barnett is signing with the Cleveland Browns on a one-year deal up to $5.5M, per source. The former first-round pick is back for Year 10, spent previous three years in Houston. pic.twitter.com/zyJT0hKM8q
The move for the Browns comes after their starting defensive end, Alex Wright, would be ruled out for the 2026 season with a ruptured Achilles, thus requiring Cleveland to go out to plug up their depth on the defensive line.
Barnett, still on the free agent market less than a month away from the regular season kicking off, made sense to fill that hole, as he now makes Cleveland his next stop after spending the past three years with the Texans.
Before Barnett had found his new home in Cleveland, there had been chatter leading up to training camp linking him to a potential reunion with the Texans this season.
Houston was in need of edge depth. Barnett had been familiar with their defense for three seasons, and he was a veteran on the market still looking to find somewhere to play for 2026.
Barnett had played 39 games with the Texans through the past three seasons, had over 60 tackles and 12 sacks, finishing his 2025 campaign with five sacks and 20 games.
Texans general manager Nick Caserio even made mention during training camp that the front office had conversations with Barnett on a new deal earlier this offseason. So Houston still clearly had its eyes on Barnett as a potential signing deep into the summer.
But the Texans went in another direction for that depth on their defensive line. They went out to sign former No. 1 overall pick Jadeveon Clowney, who, by most accounts, is an upgrade over what Barnett brings to the table.
Last season with the Dallas Cowboys, Clowney was more productive as a pass rusher and in defending the run than Barnett while playing fewer games. He had over 40 tackles and eight sacks through 13 games.
And now entering the 2026 season, the Texans brought in Clowney at virtually the same price as Barnett just went for in Cleveland. And they did so two weeks after Barnett signed.
While Barnett will be netting $5.5 million on his contract for the 2026 season, Clowney will be due a maximum of $8 million with incentives , a $5.5 million base value, and $4.5 million guaranteed.
So the Texans upgraded their defensive line by adding a presence like Clowney , but did so at essentially the same price that Barnett just went for.
It's a credit to not only the great business the Texans did with their acquisition of Clowney, but also to Clowney himself for being willing to take a pay cut in order to join a situation like Houston's.
Clowney noted at his opening press conference with the Texans that he could've gotten more money to join another team and likely get more snaps in the process. But his priority was to win games.
And in Houston, with the talent they have on their defense, he's got ample opportunities to do just that––albeit on a bit of a pay cut.
As a result, the Texans' defensive line will be looking deeper, stronger, and even more potent from how they finished their 2025 campaign, where this pass-rush may have already had the best one-two punch at the position with Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter.

title: DeMeco Ryans Explains Texans’ Zay Jones, Sterling Shepard Signings
full_text:
Earlier this week, the Houston Texans went out to add a couple of new veteran wide receivers to their 90-man roster: Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones .
It's no secret as to why the move was done. The Texans, after they saw second-year wide receiver Jayden Higgins go down with a season-ending ACL tear earlier in the week, felt the need to go out and add more depth at the position.
Shepard and Jones were brought in for a workout. Houston liked what they saw. And now, both guys will be competing for a spot on the 53-man roster.
But after the Texans' latest training camp practice, head coach DeMeco Ryans was able to open up on his thoughts about his two newest wide receivers in the building.
In Ryans' mind, he sees a ton of veteran experience within the two guys they signed on in Sterling and Jones. And after the loss of Higgins, their presence could end up being pretty valuable.
"We signed two veteran guys, and we’ll see what they can provide," Ryans said after the Shepard and Jones signings. "When it comes to adding depth in our receiver room, it’s no secret that we lost a very significant piece in our receiver room in Jayden Higgins.”
"We’re still trying to find a way to help out in our receiver room, and that’s what those two guys provide: veteran experience, guys who have done it before, done it at a high level, played in a lot of different systems, and we will see what they can bring to us.”
When it comes to receivers who were on the free agent market, not many are left up for grabs who offer that necessary edge of experience, while still potentially being a productive piece on the field.
Sterling and Jones, though, who each are over 30 years old with over eight years of NFL experience, seem to have enough upside to bank on to bring into the building and essentially try out for their 53-man roster.
Sterling is fresh off another 300-yard campaign with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He's played 10 years in the NFL with 4,800 career receiving yards and 25 touchdowns.
He'll be entering his age-33 season here in Houston, but he's remained a consistent depth piece in the receiver room both in Tampa Bay and the New York Giants, that makes him a worthwhile dart throw to bring onto the roster.
As for Jones, he's only a few years removed from his 800-yard campaign with the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2022, but also has a ton of experience in multiple receiver rooms that could end up being beneficial for this Texans group.
In nine years pro, he's played for the Jaguars, Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and the Buffalo Bills, and has collected over 300 receptions, 3,200 receiving yards and 18 touchdowns.
Will either Shepard or Jones showcase enough to warrant the Texans bringing them onto the 53-man roster? That depends on how they show up in practice and in their final preseason game of the year vs. the Carolina Panthers before cutdown day hits next weekend.
But based on the current state of the Texans' wide receiver room after Higgins' injury , nothing can be ruled out for how the front office opts to approach the position ahead of Week 1. So keep a close eye on both Sterling and Jones and their chances to make the roster in the days ahead.

title: Texans' QB3 Spot Looks Less Certain After Raiders Preseason Game
full_text:
The Houston Texans' QB3 spot was shaken up significantly earlier last week when second-year signal-caller Graham Mertz went down with a torn ACL , effectively ending his 2026 campaign.
In the days following, the Texans went on to sign veteran quarterback Brett Rypien , an experienced name at the position who became an easy favorite to fill into that QB3 spot for the season and play the next couple of preseason games to prove that he's worth it.
But with week two of the preseason down against the Las Vegas Raiders , there's a chance that the Texans' QB3 outlook now looks a little more complicated than expectations were shaping up after the Rypien signing.
In Rypien's Texans debut, his performance wasn't exactly exemplary. He played the entire second half of the game and entered as Houston was up 20-3, and proceeded not to score another point.
In all, Rypien completed six of his 10 passes for 44 yards, was sacked twice, threw an interception on the last drive of the game, and lost one of his two total fumbles on the night. Houston would be outscored 19-0 in the second half and drop their second preseason game in a row.
For a performance in which the quarterback is battling for staying power and a roster spot for Week 1, it's not exactly the most ideal outing. C.J. Stroud had a strong performance, Mills played well in his first quarter reps, but Rypien fell short of expectations.
Of course, it's one preseason outing, and Rypien probably isn't going to get many snaps for Houston this season anyways. There are certainly other pressing matters to address around the roster.
But for the Texans, at the very least, Rypien's lackluster day might just open up the question of whether or not they should add another name to the position for their third and final preseason game to add some more competition under center.
The Texans have three routes they could take for their QB3 position: they roll with Rypien, they bring in another name off the free agent market or via trade, or they simply carry two quarterbacks into Week 1 with C.J. Stroud and Davis Mills.
All three have a real possibility of being the end result. The outcome that can't be ruled out is the Texans bringing in just two quarterbacks for Week 1 if they can't find a strong enough QB3 in the time between now and cutdown day.
However, it's certainly a bit more complicated of a situation compared to what Houston entered their second preseason game with.
When it comes to the Texans' first and second quarterbacks on the depth chart, there are no doubts about who will be the two filling things out. But that third spot––whether it ends up being Rypien, someone else, or nobody else––will remain one of the bigger question marks in the days ahead of cutdown day at the end of August.

title: Predicting Texans' WR Depth Chart After Shepard, Jones Signings
full_text:
The Houston Texans' wide receiver room has taken a bit of a different shape from where things stood this time last week.
Jayden Higgins is out for the season with a torn ACL. Guys like Tank Dell and Jaylin Noel are still slowly recovering from their respective injuries . And just recently, the Texans added two new veteran wide receivers onto their 90-man roster: Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones.
The #Texans are signing veteran WRs Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones, sources tell me and @RapSheet . Both impressed in a workout today and join the mix in Houston after the loss of Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL. pic.twitter.com/oYlmSVJ4BT
So now feels like about as good a time as any to break down how the Texans' wide receiver room is expected to shake out, how the depth chart could be ordered, and who might be in (or out) of the 53-man roster picture once cuts arrive at the end of the month.
Let's sort through everyone on the Texans' roster at wide receiver and see where they stand less than 10 days out from cutdown day:
With or without Jayden Higgins on the field, Nico Collins was always going to be bound for the most snaps as the Texans' X wide receiver, and the most targets in the offense as a whole. But without Higgins there to complement him as his No. 2, there's a chance that Collins could be en route to the best season of his career.
Last season, Collins had over 1,100 yards and 71 receptions with six touchdowns in 15 games. There's a good chance he surpasses all three of those marks in 2026, so long as he's able to remain healthy.
This is right where you'd expect to see Higgins in the Texans' depth chart. Now, the offense has to pivot, and the wideout with the best chance to fill the void that he leaves is fourth-year veteran Xavier Hutchinson.
Hutchinson is coming off a career season in 2025 with over 400 receiving yards, has been with C.J. Stroud in Houston every year since he arrived in 2023, and has the ideal skillset to complement Collins on the opposite side of him in the offense––even if not as athletically gifted or as explosive as Higgins is.
Jaylin Noel is slowly returning to the Texans' lineup after suffering a hamstring and a finger injury at the start of training camp . And as long as he's good to go for Week 1 of the regular season, he's the clear favorite within this wide receiver room to take the most reps in the slot.
The second-year wideout could have a case to be one of the Texans' biggest breakout candidates since Higgins' injury. He's a young pass-catcher who's due for a huge jump in snaps offensively, had a similarly productive offseason to Higgins, and Houston invested a good bit into him last year as a third-round pick. He'll be someone to keep an eye on in the weeks ahead.
Once cutdown day hits, the Texans' wide receiver room could come down to six to seven names. Four of those––Collins, Hutchinson, Noel, and Dell––are virtual locks. So the final two to three are widely up for grabs.
I think of the two newest signings, Sterling Shepard has a better chance to make it to Week 1 . He's been more productive than Zay Jones in recent seasons, even if Jones fits a better physical profile to what the Texans need. Lewis Bond has been a camp star worthy of a 53-man spot, and a veteran like Justin Watson might now be more valuable to have with Higgins out.
Zay Jones could still make it to the 53-man roster, but he needs to prove that he can still remain on the field consistently at 31 years old, while also being a productive pass-catcher at this point in his career. Since 2023, he's played in 208 games and averaged less than two catches and 25 yards per game.
Jared Wayne is also someone to keep a close eye on . He's been someone making noise throughout camp and in preseason, and as a 6-foot-3, 210-pound wideout, maybe the Texans could value him as a bigger target to have in the room, who's also been around the building since 2024.
These five wide receivers are still listed on the Texans' 90-man roster, but don't exactly have an inside track to make it past cutdown day at the end of the month.
Perhaps a practice squad nod is in store for one or multiple of them. Daniel Sobkowicz has been someone many have liked when he was picked up as a UDFA in April , so maybe he finds his way in there. But when compared to the nine players clearly sitting ahead of them in the pecking order, it doesn't feel like anything more is within reach for anyone in this tier.

title: Texans Announce Release Date for New Rivalries Uniforms
full_text:
The Houston Texans have announced the release date for their newest Rivalries uniforms for the 2026 NFL season .
And it looks like the release of those new uniforms for Houston sits right around the corner.
The Texans put out a promotional video for their upcoming uniform release, where players around the roster reacted to the new threads for the first time.
And in that video, the Texans revealed that those uniforms will be officially unveiled to the public on Tuesday, August 25th .
No peekingggg 👀 pic.twitter.com/oC1xmJDmy6
The reviews from some of the players were clearly positive, which could be a sign of things to come for next week’s reveal.
"That s---- gas," said Tank Dell.
"Oh, that's tough," was what Reed Blankenship said.
"I can get jiggy with that," came from Kamari Lassiter.
And along with the release date and the reaction video from the players, the Texans also released a new teaser for the new uniforms on the horizon––where the uniform was described as a set that'll seek innovation, being different, and "the most Houston thing that you've ever seen on the gridiron."
Houston, this one’s for you 🤘 pic.twitter.com/LmCAaELDCv
With the Texans set to receive their Rivalries uniforms for next season, it'll be one of five uniforms that Houston will be able to wear throughout the year: their typical home and away jerseys, their all-red alternates, and their dark-blue "Space City" themed uniforms, and now, another set of alternates.
On most weeks, the Texans will be wearing their typical home and away uniforms as they typically do. But for three weeks throughout the season, Houston will bring out those alternates.
For their Rivalries set, that'll come during their Week 11 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts , a game that'll take place on Thursday Night Football at Houston in Reliant Stadium for one of the Texans' more exciting games throughout the regular season altogether.
The NFL first kicked off Rivalries uniforms across the league for the 2025 season, where the league and Nike released eight new uniforms for the AFC East and the NFC West to wear one time throughout the year for three seasons in a highlighted divisional matchup.
And the theme of those uniforms was designed to put together a more unique, modern look for each team that wore them. Nike describes the Rivalries uniforms from last season as ones that "celebrate storied local traditions and unite fan communities with designs unique to select cities and teams."
After the first two divisions got their uniforms last year, the AFC South and the NFC North would be next up on the list to receive their Rivalries uniforms in 2026. In 2027, the AFC West and NFC East will get their own.
But following a long and anticipated wait , the release of those uniforms for the 2026 slate is right around the corner for the Texans and every other team in this wave of announcements.
Expect the reveal for the Texans' Rivalries uniforms to come at 9 a.m. CT on Tuesday morning, along with the other seven teams in the mix who are in for their own.
