title: Everything I Saw at Day 17 of Jaguars Training Camp: OL Gets Some Answers
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are entering the last week of training camp, and Day 17 offered us perhaps our best answers yet as to what Week 1 may look like.
So, what did we see during Sunday's practice at the Miller Electric Center following Friday's preseason game against the Panthers? We break it all down below.
It sure seems like we are starting to get answers on what the Jaguars' Week 1 starting offensive line will be. Joint practices against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Tuesday and Wednesday will be the true telling sign of who the Jaguars plan to trot out against the Cleveland Browns in Week 1, but Sunday's unit sure felt like what we are going to (mostly) see, depending on the health of Cole Van Lanen.
The Jaguars' starting line had Anton Harrison at left tackle, Emmanuel Pregnon at left guard, Robert Hainsey at center, Ezra Cleveland at right guard, and Walker Little at right tackle. The only question here really seems to be whether Van Lanen will be available for Week 1; if he is, he can slot into right tackle. If not, Little can start.
If the Jaguars' plan was to start Cleveland at left guard and go with a different option at right guard and tackle, logic would suggest they would implement that now. But the fact that this was the starting unit today said a lot to me. Also of interest: the backup offensive line was, from left to right, Ricky Lee, Daniele Faalele, Jonah Monheim, Wyatt Milum, and Chuma Edoga.
It sure looks like the Jaguars have made their Week 1 plans for Travis Hunter clear. While Hunter is still expected to play a role on offense, he spent the vast majority of last week's practices, including the joint practice with the Carolina Panthers, at cornerback. The Jaguars once again leaned heavily toward the defensive side of the ball on Sunday, with Hunter getting zero 11-on-11 reps on the offensive side of the ball on Day 17.
This is not to say the Jaguars are completely going away from Hunter's role on offense, but as we have long expected, the Jaguars clearly think the priority for him is at cornerback. The Jaguars want Hunter ready to take a large load at cornerback right off the bat, and it is becoming more and more clear that is he will be deployed the most against the Browns.
I think Nate Boerkircher had his best practice of training camp on Sunday. The Jaguars' rookie tight end got a lot of work with Trevor Lawrence in 7-on-7 drills in the red-zone, and he made the most of his oppurtunities in a big way. Boerkircher had some solid reps as a route-runner and was consistently getting open for Lawrence, and he made his best practice of camp on an in-breaking target with Antonio Johnson draped over his back.
Despite the contact, Boerkircher secured the pass and clearly frustrated Johnson considering how close he was to breaking up the pass. Boerkircher looked like a reliable safety blanket with some upside on Sunday, and he took his most significant step yet in training camp -- at least from a pass-catching perspective.
Jaguars wide receiver Jakobi Meyers got banged-up in last week's joint practice on Wednesday, leading to him wearing medical equipment on his right hand while on the sidelines during Friday's preseason game. Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Friday that, "We will have to see. He kind of jammed it. We will have to see where it is at when we get to Tuesday and just kinda see. I don’t want to push it too much." As a result, it was not surprising to see Meyers not on the practice field Sunday.
What was interesting, however, was how the Jaguars looked to replace Meyers on the practice field. It felt like both Josh Cameron and CJ Williams got significant run with the first-team offense and Lawrence on Sunday, with the Jaguars clearly throwing the rookie duo into the fire to see which one might be the most prepared to take over for Meyers in the short-term this week.
Jaguars defensive tackle Matt Dickerson didn't just have the play of the day -- he arguably had the play of training camp. With the Jaguars attempting a screen pass, Dickerson was able to read Trevor Lawrence's eyes, diagnose the play, and then find the ball in the air before making the interception and returning it for a touchdown. It was an incredibly athletic play by the backup defensive tackle, who continues to simply make it evident that he will be on the 53-man roster.

title: 4 Things We Learned From Jaguars' Loss to Panthers: Joey Aguilar's Impression
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With another preseason performance turned in by the Jacksonville Jaguars against the Carolina Panthers on Friday night, there is another four quarters of lessons on Liam Coen's squad.
So, what did we learn from the Jaguars' 34-17 loss to the Panthers? We break it all down below.
Joey Aguilar has not been able to get a ton of reps over the course of training camp, but he has certainly made the most of his chances in the preseason. His lone pass last week was a 40+ yard bomb to set the Jaguars up to win the game, while he averaged 13 yards per attempt on Friday night and threw as many touchdowns as incompletions (1).
Aguilar is too young and inexperienced to push for the QB2 job, but he could be the Jaguars' best option at QB3. He showed off some exciting developmental traits that the Jaguars have not really had with the practice squad quarterback spot in recent seasons.
It was pretty clear watching Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile on the sidelines last night that he was not ... thrilled with the defensive performance. A few key backups played, but only one true starter (either Ventrell Miller or Branson Combs) was on the field for Campanile's unit, but that doesn't take away from what the depth chart put on the field on Friday.
They did have a solid opening drive against Bryce Young and the Panthers' starting offense, but things fell off after that. The Panthers scored on four of their next five drives, while the Jaguars recorded zero sacks, turnovers, or even pass breakups. The fact that so few plays were made by key pieces of the defensive depth chart is not ideal.
After a tough go at it against the New Orleans Saints, Nick Mullens certainly came out of Friday with some positive momentum. Mullens went against parts of the Panthers' first-team defense but largely looked in complete command of the offense, going 6-of-7 and leading a 70+ yard field goal drive that would have ended in a touchdown if not for an Ameer Abdullah drop.
Mullens looked as good on Friday as he has in any preseason performance since signing with the Jaguars last March. The offensive line blocked better this time around, which likely played a factor, but Mullens certainly did enough in his own right to quiet any external questions on whether he was the right QB2 behind Trevor Lawrence.
The Jaguars have plenty of reason to be optimistic about their starting cornerbacks, even if the joint practices have been a bit up-and-down for the secondary this summer. But after Travis Hunter, Montaric Brown, Jourdan Lewis, and Jarrian Jones there is still a need for someone to step up to take the top depth spot. After Friday's game vs.the Panthers, it remains to be seen if that player is on the roster.
The two best candidates are veteran cornerback Christian Braswell and second-year cornerback Jabbar Muhammad. Neither had a great outing against the Panthers' passing attack on Friday, though, and the Jaguars look like a team that might be in the market for a cornerback once the first waiver wire is put together.

title: Grading the Jaguars: Nick Mullens Leads QB Room in Passing Performance vs. Panthers
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With the Jacksonville Jaguars' 34-17 preseason loss to the Carolina Panthers now in the rearview mirror, it is time to take stock and review which position groups stood out the most.
So, which units get passing grades after the high points of Friday's game against the Panthers? We break it all down below.
Nick Mullens had maybe his best week as a Jaguar over the last seven days. After a tough outing against the New Orleans Saints last week that had more to do with the offensive line than anything else, Mullens bounced back and had a solid week of practice. He was then 6-of-7 on Friday and would have been 7-for-7 with a touchdown pass were it not for a drop by Ameer Abdullah in the end-zone.
Carter Bradley's lackluster outing does bring the grade down a bit, but the Jaguars also saw Joey Aguilar have a terrific performance with 9-of-10 passing for 130 yards and a touchdown as he took over the second-half. Between Mullens and Aguilar, the Jaguars got some good football from their backups on Friday.
"It felt good. I was out there trying to be super calm and smooth. I still had a lot of mental errors I want to fix and clean up to operate better, but I felt like it was a good experience," Aguilar said after the game. "It was a great time going out there. I appreciate the O-line for finding that edge and grinding it out. So shout out to those guys for coming out the second half, still grinding."
As for why this grade is not an A, only two plays come to mind: a fumble from DeeJay Dallas and a dropped touchdown pass from Ameer Abdullah. Otherwise, the performance of Abdullah alone would have been enough for the Jaguars to get a great grade from the backfield. Abdullah was the only one of the three running backs who really produced, but he sent a big message while doing so.
"I thought he showed up tonight and it’s what we’ve seen in practice. You talk about a pro’s pro, a guy who does everything right," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game. "He’s one of the first guys in the building, along with Parker (Washington). He takes care of himself, treats himself right in terms of his body and getting his mind right for practice every day.  And he was able to show up tonight and look a little better than everyone else."
The Jaguars' wide receiver room was really, really sharp on Friday. Josh Cameron made a big grab downfield, CJ Williams caught every single one of his targets and looked as reliable as ever, and the Jaguars also got big plays out of undrafted rookie receivers like Michael Wortham and Trebor Peña. It was a less productive night for Austin Trammell, who caught one of five passes for five yards, but it was overall an exciting showing from the Jaguars' young wideouts.
For the second week in a row, it felt like a very forgetable night for the tight end room. Nate Boerkircher did not play, while Tanner Koziol only played 13 snaps before being sat for the night. Through two games, the Jaguars' tight end room has combined for two catches for seven yards. It has just been that quiet for them to this point.
It felt like the Jaguars' offensive line had a much better outing on Friday compared to the first week of the preseason against the New Orleans Saints. The Jaguars allowed one sack and three quarterback hits but Liam Coen said after the game that he was happy with the way the protection held up, especially considering the unit that played the whole game was made up of the Jaguars' third-team offensive line. The lack of running lanes for DeeJay Dallas and J'Mari Taylor does impact the grade, however.
I thought that the Jaguars got some good reps out of the early group of B.J. Green, Danny Striggow, and Ruke Orhorhoro. After that, it felt like the Jaguars' pass-rush just didn't have time to get to the quarterback at the speed that the Panthers got the ball out of their hands. The biggest knock to the grade here is the fact that the Panthers averaged 5.3 yards a carry and were able to get some chunk gains on the ground.
I thought it was mostly a solid showing for the Jaguars' linebackers. The backups made a few plays against the run and as blitzers, while Ventrell Miller had a strong showing in limited snaps to start the game. There were just a few miscues, such as a Yasir Abdullah missed tackle and a run rep by Branson Combs, but Combs also had some positive flashes as well. Consider Dennis Gardeck and Foyesade Oluokun didn't play, this was a good night for the linebackers.
I do not think the Panthers threw the ball all over the yard against the Jaguars; the Panthers' three quarterbacks completed 24-of-35 passes (68.6%), but a lot of it was dinking and dunking. With that said, there just wasn't a big play made from the secondary as the Panthers went with a soft passing game. The second-team secondary couldn't really run with Tetairoa McMillan, but that was always to be expected -- especially after his performance in joint practice earlier in the week.
Cam Little has been very reliable for the Jaguars, while Ross Matiscik nearly forced a big fumble on coverage teams. With that said, it does feel like the Jaguars have been a bit quiet so far in the kick return game. The Jaguars averaged 23.8 yards per kick return compared to 30.5 averaged kick return yards from the Panthers. As we saw from the Saints game, that is one area the depth of the roster has to be better.

title: Chiefs Rookie Mansoor Delane Details How Shoulder Injury Prepared Him for NFL Debut
full_text:
A month after trading star cornerback Trent McDuffie to the Rams, the Kansas City Chiefs drafted LSU standout Mansoor Delane with the No. 6 overall pick in this year's draft. He is expected to eventually develop into the CB1 for Steve Spagnuolo's defense.
While he entered the spring with lofty expectations, Delane suffered a shoulder blade injury during OTAs that sidelined him for the beginning of training camp. He finally shed his non-contact jersey last week and was cleared for contact ahead of the Chiefs' preseason matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. For a large portion of camp, Delane was essentially playing one-handed against opposing wide receivers to avoid aggravating his shoulder. He admits that it was a frustrating experience given his competitive nature, but he was able to grow from the experience.
"I was definitely just eager to get back healthy, but I think it was a sign. I think it was meant to be," Delane said. "It's always hard not to be on the field, it's what you love to do. But like I said, I think it allowed me to step back and see from different perspectives... I took that time and valued every second of it."
Since he didn't play in the preseason opener, Delane made his NFL debut this past Saturday and was solid across 11 defensive snaps. Although fans didn't get an extended look at his coverage skills, he feels good about his performance and wants to continue building from it. "Obviously, it wasn't too many reps, but just getting my feet wet," Delane said about his NFL debut. "Getting that experience, I think that was the biggest thing for me."
"My big thing is, if you're going to do something wrong, do it at full speed," he later continued. "That's how I play the game, playing fast. My first game out there, I'm not timid, I'm not scared, I'm going to do everything 100%. So, I just want to put that on display."
Delane says his confidence grew throughout the rehab process because he knew what he'd be capable of once he returned to full health. He feels he has held his own against his teammates during practice, but there is still a significant difference between college and the NFL that he's adjusting to.
The Maryland native praised quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs' wide receivers for giving him little room for error. Going against that level of competition has forced him to correct mistakes quickly that he wouldn't have otherwise noticed at LSU.
Delane may still be limited in how many preseason snaps he receives, but the rookie is ready to contribute in whatever role the Chiefs need him to play. He doesn't feel the need to be overly cautious anymore and is ready to let his talent speak for itself. "I'm just leaving that up to [Athletic Trainer] Rick [Burkholder] and the training staff to let that all process out, but I'm ready to go," Delane confirmed.

title: Chiefs Injury Report: Trey Smith Returns to Practice, Andy Reid Provides Update on Patrick Mahomes' Timeline
full_text:
After being sidelined due to a hip injury since August 7, Kansas City Chiefs right guard Trey Smith is returning to practice.
In the midst of training camp in St. Joseph, Missouri, Smith briefly left the team to meet with a specialist about a hip ailment. Smith never returned to on-field participation in St. Joe and did not appear in either of the team's first two preseason games.
On Monday, however, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid confirmed that Smith would return to the field for the first time in more than two weeks.
"Well, we'll see how he does today, ease him back in, but he wants to get out there and get going," Reid said. "It's been killing him not to be out there, so he's kind of wired that way."
While Smith's absence was evident during his time on the sidelines, Reid said it was worthwhile in order to prepare Smith for the regular season.
"Trey loves to play, but it was important that he let that thing heal up like he did, and I think it'll pay off for him down the road."
The Chiefs' most high-profile recovery of the preseason belongs to quarterback Patrick Mahomes. While Kansas City's signal-caller was cleared for participation throughout camp, Mahomes has not appeared in either of the team's first two preseason games, though he has suited up and gone through pregame warmups in both instances.
Asked if there was any update regarding Mahomes' status for Week 1 of the regular season, Reid made it clear that he wouldn't be guaranteeing anything today.
"Listen, he's doing great," Reid said. "We'll just see. I'm literally taking it day-by-day; no predictions here on anything. If the doctors and trainers and everybody that [is] involved in this give him an OK, then, most of all, if he feels like he can, then we'll address that when we get there."
Noting that Mahomes has spoken about generally wanting to be on the field, Reid was asked if Mahomes was being held back as a coaching decision or if he is still waiting for another degree of medical clearance.
"Yeah, you know, probably not cleared enough," Reid said with a smirk.
The Chiefs are still without a long list of players on Monday, including safety Alohi Gilman, who was ruled out with back spasms during pregame warmups on Saturday , and defensive end Tyreke Smith, who suffered a hamstring strain in Tampa Bay.
Left tackle Josh Simmons, safety Chamarri Conner, defensive end Ashton Gillotte , linebacker Jack Cochrane, quarterback Chris Oladokun, guard CJ Hanson, and wide receivers Jeff Caldwell and Jimmy Holliday were all sidelined for Monday's practice. Reid noted that Oladokun is in the concussion protocol after experiencing symptoms following Saturday's game.
Later Monday afternoon, the Chiefs announced that they waived Caldwell with an injury designation and signed free agent defensive end Niles King. King played for San Diego State in 2025 and signed with the Los Angeles Chargers before being waived by LA in May .

title: Why Chiefs Offensive Tackle Situation Is More Concerning Than It Seems
full_text:
Kahlil Benson had become one of the hottest stories in Chiefs training camp , earning first-team reps at right tackle since the second day of the summer and quickly drawing praise from the coaching staff. However, those good vibes halted on Saturday when he made his first start at right tackle in a preseason matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .
The undrafted rookie out of Indiana was alarmingly inadequate, getting beaten badly on multiple reps by rookie Rueben Bain Jr. that went viral on social media. Granted, Bain was a first-round draft selection and is one of the best pass rushers in this year's class, but Benson will have to deal with more talented edge rushers in the AFC West if he opens the season with the starting five linemen. Benson's poor showing simply means the Chiefs will slot veteran Jaylon Moore back into the right side as expected, right? Well, that's not necessarily the end-all solution for Kansas City.
The team's three tackles finished the loss with the worst Pro Football Focus (PFF) grades among any linemen on the roster. Benson had the lowest score on the field at 33.4, but Moore (40.7) and Esa Pole (41.4) didn't fare much better.
With second-year standout Josh Simmons sidelined by lingering back stiffness, Moore took over at left tackle, where he's played the majority of his snaps in the NFL. Meanwhile, Benson made his first start on the opposite side.
Despite his large contract, Chiefs fans already knew heading into training camp that Moore was far from a sure thing. He was Trent Williams' backup in San Francisco and performed well in a swing tackle role when needed, but he has not proven he can be a consistent 17-game starter in the NFL. Then, there's a case to be made that Kansas City is relying too heavily on Simmons. The 23-year-old is in tremendous physical shape and was impressive during the games he did play as a rookie, but he still remains a bit of a wild card.
Simmons missed nine contests due to personal issues and a broken wrist in 2025. So, is it really smart for the Chiefs to lean on him to miraculously solve an otherwise dire offensive tackle situation?
Kansas City is only one more injury to Simmons away from its offensive line blowing up and the team scrambling for a midseason trade. Benson is extremely strong and possesses plenty of positive physical traits, but if he's not ready to serve as the team's swing man in Year 1, Andy Reid has a significant problem on his hands.

title: Chiefs Balancing Flexibility but 'Open for Business' With Roster Cuts Looming
full_text:
With the preseason winding down, the Kansas City Chiefs' roster and depth charts are beginning to take shape. The team still has one more outing left to make last-minute evaluations, then the real work begins before 5 p.m. CT on Sunday, August 30.
At that point, each team must have its 53-man group finalized. Some players will return on the practice squad or once procedural moves are made elsewhere, but others could hit the waiver wire and never return to Kansas City. Somewhere in between, might there be an addition or two made?
With limited financial wiggle room and a roster that's mostly set, there's an easy case to be made for that answer being no. The Chiefs aren't shutting the door, however, as evidenced by assistant general manager Mike Bradway's comments to the media prior to last weekend's game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers .
“Once we get that final preseason game and we have all the information from teams, guys that might be available and what it might take to get them," Bradway said. "I think you balance out, is it worth giving up a future pick for a guy? You have to be sure that that guy is going to come in and have a role so you aren’t just wasting assets.
"There's got to be buy-in from the personnel side and, obviously, the coaches. Are they going to use them whether it’s offense, defense or special teams? There could be an opportunity for a player-for-player type of move. We are certainly open for business, open for anything.”
There is some proof of concept here for Bradway and the rest of general manager Brett Veach's staff. In 2024, for instance, the club moved a seventh-round pick in the ensuing year's NFL Draft in exchange for defensive end Cameron Thomas. In the same sweep of transactions, tight end Peyton Hendershot was also acquired for a conditional pick in this year's draft.
Finding the requisite late-round draft capital to land a player isn't much of an issue for the Chiefs, nor is being patient or lucky with breaks on waivers. Finances, as mentioned, are another story. Per the NFLPA's public salary cap report , Kansas City has just $3.5 million in available funding to work with.
Is there a path to more fluid cash? Assistant general manager Chris Shea, citing past instances of being surprised by opposing teams' cutdown-week decisions, believes that valve is also far from shut off.
“Sure, well, having done this for a long time, I think more than you'd think," Shea said of how often he raises his eyebrows at other front offices. "Retaining flexibility to be able to entertain the unforeseen is an important aspect of how we try to structure our cap management philosophy. We really want to present coach (Andy Reid) and Brett with the flexibility to entertain smart roster moves that are independent of cap constraints that we may have.
"We certainly have some of them, but we don't have a perfect crystal ball, none of us in the front office. Opportunities present themselves that are unforeseen so, yeah, we plan to be flexible. There are limits to that given that we have a lot of good players under contract, but we try to present Brett and coach with opportunities through our cap management.”
Aside from scouring the free agent market, the next week could be the Chiefs' only avenue to improving on the fringes. There are several teams in better positions to land intriguing talents, sure, but there are also less active front offices (and less savvy ones, too).
With Veach and company assessing the league landscape, don't be surprised if there's a new face wearing red and white once the month of August comes to a close.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From Chiefs' Preseason Week 2 Loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers
full_text:
The Chiefs dropped their eighth straight preseason game Saturday night in Tampa Bay, which of course means absolutely nothing. They did not capture a win in either of the previous two preseason years. One of those years they went to the Super Bowl. The other, they went 6-11. Take the record for what it is worth.
What does matter is what the individual performances told us, and there was plenty to digest.
Before getting into the biggest winners and losers, it is worth noting that safety Jaden Hicks, defensive tackle Marcus Harris, and running back Emmett Johnson all played well enough to be in the winners column.
Harrison Butker was a mixed bag, drilling an incredible 69-yarder and starting the preseason going 7-for-7, which also included two 59-yard field goals, before missing two kicks. One would have made the score a 16-16 game by the end of it, and the other a 43-yard kick with just over three minutes to go, missing a likely game-winner.
Let’s dive into the three biggest winners and losers of this 16-15 loss to the Bucs.
As a fifth-round pick from just a year ago, wide receiver Jalen Royals may have solidified his place on this team Saturday night. That is not usually a concern for second-year draftees, but Royals had shown very little up until this point.
That changed in Tampa Bay.
He was targeted six times and hauled in all six, showcasing the yards-after-the-catch ability that made him an attractive pick out of Utah State. His six catches between Justin Fields and Garrett Nussmeier netted 51 yards, and he was the Chiefs' highest-graded receiver on the night, according to PFF.
For a player whose roster spot has been quietly in question, Saturday was a statement.
Saturday night may have been the best we have seen from defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah in a Chiefs uniform. In 16 pass -rush snaps, the four-year veteran supplied four pressures and delivered the biggest highlight of the night, flattening Buccaneers backup quarterback Jake Browning for his first sack of the preseason.
His 26.7 pass-rush win rate led all Chiefs defensive linemen. For a former first-round pick whose career has been defined by injuries and unfulfilled potential, this was the kind of performance that could propel the former Kansas State Wildcat into the starting lineup.
Defensive end R Mason Thomas did not light up the box score, but this is in recognition of his continued showing from a week ago. In 10 true pass sets, the rookie again supplied pressure, collecting a hurry and a quarterback hit.
For an undersized pass rush specialist at 6-foot-2 and 249 pounds, that kind of consistency is exactly what the Chiefs were hoping to see, especially on third downs. Having someone who can generate quick pressure and allow Chris Jones and George Karlaftis to clean up is something this team has been missing for years.
Both Thomas and Anudike-Uzomah stepping up simultaneously is a particularly welcome sight given that Ashton Gillotte's injury timetable remains uncertain. With both stepping up last night, Chiefs OnSI’s Jordan Foote noted that Gillotte’s absence may not be the doomsday scenario we all thought.
Right tackle Kahlil Benson drew the start at right tackle, which is something he had been building toward all training camp. How the depth chart looks when the Chiefs return to practice Monday will be worth monitoring, because Saturday was not a good showing.
He essentially whiffed on two pass sets, with one resulting in a strip sack and the other forcing an incomplete pass, with Justin Fields needing to get rid of the ball quicker than anticipated. He graded out as the worst pass blocker on the field according to PFF with a 33.4, allowing two pressures in 11 true pass sets.
The one silver lining, if you can call it that: Jaylon Moore graded out second-worst on the team with a PFF pass blocking grade of 40.7, so neither tackle distinguished himself Saturday night.
It is somewhat unclear how realistic it is for cornerback Melvin Smith to make the 53-man roster when cutdown day arrives a week from now. He seems like a prime candidate to slip through waivers and onto the practice squad.
That said, he was treated as more of a contributor than veteran Kristian Fulton last week, which made Saturday's performance more consequential. He graded out worse than any other defensive back, allowing four catches for 38 yards on four targets.
The names doing the damage, Ko Kieft, Kameron Johnson, Dean Patterson, and Eric Rivers, are not exactly household names. That is an uneasy sign when the opening regular season assignment would be Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton. A four-phase special teamer was his likely role anyway, but he did not look remotely ready for a defensive role.
Tight end Jared Wiley was technically third on the team with two catches and 15 receiving yards, but he was targeted four times and had a drop. He looks smooth catching passes in open space, but Travis Kelce and Noah Gray already fill that role.
What the Chiefs need from a third tight end is someone willing to do the dirty work, and Wiley has not shown that.
For the second straight week, second-year undrafted free agent Jake Briningstool collected three catches for 28 or more yards and has shown solid open-field blocking as well. Briningstool is not a road grader either, but he is contributing more to the offense.
Wiley's roster spot will depend heavily on how the Chiefs construct the rest of the 53. If they keep four running backs or push toward seven wide receivers, given how Royals, Nikko Remigio, and Andrew Armstrong have shown specific skill sets, four tight ends may be off the table.

title: Too Good to Hide: Garrett Nussmeier's Promising Preseason Could Force the Chiefs' Hand
full_text:
Take a look around the NFL at any given moment, and you'll quickly be confronted with a universal truth: there just aren't enough good quarterbacks.
A large swath of the league permanently resides in quarterback purgatory, while even the lucky few teams with franchise signal-callers have to find capable backups for when injuries inevitably arrive.
At age 41, Joe Flacco is on a one-year, $6 million deal to back up Joe Burrow in Cincinnati. The Los Angeles Rams, with reigning MVP Matthew Stafford, spent a first-round pick on Ty Simpson in hopes of avoiding the QB carousel in a post-Stafford world. The Cleveland Browns have sunk remarkable draft capital and absurd amounts of cash into their current quarterback room, resulting in nothing but disasters at every turn.
You may already understand what this has to do with rookie Chiefs quarterback Garrett Nussmeier.
Through two preseason games, Nussmeier has looked like an NFL quarterback. Not a Week 1 starter—not even like a player who is about to jump current backup Justin Fields on KC's depth chart—but like a quarterback who has a place on a professional football field, with potential to grow from there.
When the Chiefs selected Nussmeier in the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft, his spot on the 53-man roster was far from guaranteed. He was the ninth-to-last pick of the draft (No. 249 of 257), but it was a noteworthy swing at the time.
With Patrick Mahomes as the team's superstar and Fields as the clear backup for 2026, Nussmeier may have chosen to go elsewhere if he would have been an undrafted free agent. Instead, the Chiefs used their last pick to ensure that he'd join their quarterback room, at least for offseason activities, training camp, and the preseason.
A draft pick spent on a quarterback is always a cause for some intrigue, but Nussmeier's pedigree made Kansas City's selection even more alluring.
In an October 2024 mock draft that projected how the 2025 NFL Draft would play out, Chris Trapasso of CBS Sports mocked Nussmeier at No. 12 overall .
"Right this very instant, if there's one quarterback I had to choose to ascend boards over the next four months, it'd be Nussmeier, who plays with such effortless arm talent, accuracy, and toughness within the pocket," Trapasso wrote nearly two years ago.
Instead of leaving as a potential first-round pick after the 2024 season, Nussmeier stayed at LSU , ultimately hurting his draft stock as he battled through injuries in a disappointing year for the Tigers.
Still, Nussmeier earned a third-round grade in the KCSN Draft Guide , which slotted him in as the No. 3 quarterback in the class. When the Chiefs took Nussmeier in the seventh round, he was the 10th quarterback to be selected.
Again, none of that guaranteed anything for Nussmeier, but it's important context to remember when trying to project what his career could become.
In two preseason games, Nussmeier has seemed comfortable running the Chiefs' offense , looking less like a seventh-round pick and more like a player with more than 1,000 pass attempts at an SEC powerhouse.
This has all come in a very small sample size, and it's far from an assurance that he'll become the long-term answer as Mahomes' multi-year backup, but it's also how the rest of the league will be looking at Nussmeier if the Chiefs decide that they don't have room for three quarterbacks on their 53-man roster .
Nussmeier has made the cut in our Chiefs On SI roster projections, but the Chiefs have preferred to carry only two quarterbacks in recent years, allowing that extra roster spot to go to another position group.
Personally, I've seen enough from Nussmeier to make the call. He's worth protecting on the 53-man roster this season, with hopes that his development in Kansas City could lead him to a career that far exceeds his seventh-round draft selection.
If the Chiefs don't agree, there are plenty of quarterback-poor teams that would be wise to give him a longer look.

title: Chiefs Snap Count Analysis: Reading Between the Lines After Game vs. Buccaneers
full_text:
All 32 NFL teams are still learning about their respective rosters at this stage, and the Kansas City Chiefs are no different. The club's second preseason outing against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers featured plenty of tweaks from the week prior, which showed up primarily in how snaps were divvied up.
In the opener against the Los Angeles Rams, it was the first taste of somewhat real football since Kansas City's season ended in early January. With that came overreactions galore, but this most recent bout at Raymond James Stadium brought a few of those questions into clearer focus. The division of labor from Andy Reid and his staff might've tipped how the coaches feel about a select handful of players.
Now that snap counts have been released, what jumped off the page? Let's take a look at three noteworthy takeaways from another week of Chiefs football.
With Xavier Worthy and Rashee Rice attempting to ensure that they're 100% healthy for Week 1 of the regular season, the Chiefs have given supporting pieces of the wide receiver room opportunities to showcase their talents this preseason. Prospects Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen, Day 3 NFL Draft pickups from the 2025 and 2026 NFL Drafts , naturally draw the most attention of those remaining on the list.
Allen's star didn't shine nearly as bright in his second unofficial game as a pro, but Royals made the most of yet another heavy workload.
For the second weekend in a row, the former fourth-round selection played a whopping 36 snaps on offense. Sure, that can oftentimes be a reflection of someone who isn't part of a team's plans, but Royals' context makes it feel like a different scenario. He needs the reps to flash any sort of improvement in his sophomore year, which he did on Saturday. Playing with multiple quarterbacks, he led the Kansas City offense in targets and receptions (six), as well as yards with 51.
In a downright critical year for Royals' development, he was a slow burner at camp but made more plays over time. That trend has been replicated in preseason play.
The Chiefs knew coming into the preseason that first-round rookie Mansoor Delane would step into a starting role on the boundary as long as his shoulder injury healed up in time . That wound up being the case, with the No. 6 overall pick playing on Saturday and earning 11 snaps alongside projected starter Nohl Williams . The real uncertainty revolved around the slot position, especially with  each contender for the job coming with some baggage.
Free agent signing Kader Kohou is coming off a torn ACL and didn't play against LA due to injury. L'Jarius Sneed hasn't been active at all this preseason. Jadon Canady, for all the promise he brings, is a Day 3 rookie . Chris Roland Wallace is more of a safety-nickel hybrid than a true every-down player. Did defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo accidentally tip his hand with how he utilized Kohou down in Tampa?
The former Miami Dolphins standout had one special teams snap on kickoff coverage and played only seven reps on defense, in the same ballpark as high-profile starters. Each of those snaps saw him line up in the slot, via Pro Football Focus . This could've been merely an instance of load management and Spagnuolo wanting to get Kohou's feet wet a bit, although it also could've been an unwritten message that the 27-year-old is still slated to fill the void most expected when he signed.
Yes, I'm cheating here and weaving two positions into one takeaway. Rules, even self-imposed ones, are meant to be broken.
A week ago, Emari Demercado's usage seemed to throw a fork in the blueprint those in Chiefs circles anticipated for the running back room. He didn't play until the second half versus the Rams and was also utilized equally as much on special teams as on offense.
The Buccaneers game depicted someone who will get work during the regular season, however, as the offseason acquisition had 21 offensive snaps. Rookie Emmett Johnson (25) and 2025 seventh-rounder Brashard Smith (14) also saw the field plenty, but it's now increasingly evident that Demercado doesn't appear to be on the outside looking in.
At the tackle position, both Jaylon Moore and Kahlil Benson looked bad against the Tampa Bay pass rush. Benson stayed in the game far longer than his elder counterpart, though, playing 35 snaps to Moore's 12. The latter mark aligned with the first-team protectors, signaling Moore being the clear leader for the right tackle job once Josh Simmons returns healthy on the left.
Benson's story remains awesome, and he likely isn't going anywhere once it's time for roster cutdowns, but a healthy version of the Chiefs' offensive line figures to have Moore in it and not him.

title: Andy Reid Won’t Ignore Chiefs’ Preseason Struggles After Another Blown Lead
full_text:
Had yesterday's preseason loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers been a regular season game, it would have been one of the more heartbreaking defeats the Chiefs have suffered in recent years. They snatched defeat from the jaws of victory in the second half, largely due to an erratic performance from veteran kicker Harrison Butker .
Most NFL fans agree that winning preseason games doesn't determine how teams perform when the actual season comes around. However, fans might be surprised to learn that the Chiefs now haven't won a preseason game in 1,093 days.
The last time K.C. came out on top in an exhibition was in August 2023, when they defeated the Cleveland Browns 33-32 in a thriller at Arrowhead Stadium. Since then, the Chiefs have appeared in two Super Bowls and won one, but haven't been on the winning end of a preseason matchup. To some, this is a quirky stat that means nothing in the long run. But to Chiefs head coach Andy Reid, there is a tiny level of concern knowing that the team hasn't been able to get it done in eight consecutive tries, even if it's mostly the second and third teams getting the majority of the reps.
"Listen, it's America. You want to win everything you do," Reid said about preseason games. "That's how it goes. So, to say you don't want to win, these guys want to do that. We just got to eliminate some of these mistakes, but again, you're doing that and trying to evaluate everybody at the same time."
There is a level of attention to detail that NFL players must have, regardless of whether they're playing with the starters or backups. Reid's frustration is not surprising given the unusual string of losses K.C. has suffered in the preseason.
In each of Kansas City's two preseason games this year, the Chiefs led going into the fourth quarter yet were unable to hold off the opposing team's offense. Everyone will probably forget about this stat going into the Week 1 opener against the Broncos, and there's still an opportunity for them to break the streak next Saturday against the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks.
One thing is for certain is that the Chiefs' coaches will be ripping their players a new one following yesterday's effort that caused them to blow the lead.

title: Despite Rough Output, Chiefs' QBs Supported for Performance vs. Buccaneers
full_text:
Sometimes, it simply isn't your day. That was made clear at multiple spots for the Kansas City Chiefs against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday, as everything ranging from scoring points to executing situational football or avoiding getting in their own way seemed to be an uphill battle all night long.
There were some bright spots, namely wide receiver Jalen Royals on the offensive side of the ball and safeties Jaden Hicks and DeShon Singleton on defense. Despite what the box score says, head coach Andy Reid believes his quarterback trio also belongs in that group.
The collective of Justin Fields, Garrett Nussmeier and Chris Oladokun posted a combined stat line of completing 23 of 35 passes for just 155 yards, no touchdowns and in interception. It was an ugly showing by about every measurement available, yet Reid still gleans something positive.
Taking the podium shortly after the conclusion of Saturday's Chiefs preseason game , Reid kicked his quarterback-related thoughts off by complimenting his rookie for making some tough throws.
"I'll go back and look at it a little closer, but if you're asking specifically about Nuss, I thought he had some nice throws in there," Reid said. "There were a couple where they were tight throws — I've got to look at the route to see if we should've maybe been a little more aggressive coming back to the ball in those tight situations, but it looked like he handled things well. He's getting more comfortable."
He then continued by addressing Fields making the most of his mobility and shielding Oladokun from some of the blame regarding his late-game turnover.
"Justin, I thought, had some good plays in there," Reid said. "A couple of nice throws on the move. And then Chris, you know, Chris had a big third-down play that got tipped and dropped and intercepted. That really gave them a big advantage. Listen, those things happen. You've got to go through them, learn from them and move forward."
Based on sheer efficiency, Fields was the most productive Kansas City signal-caller on Saturday. He completed nine of his 12 passes for 64 yards, also carrying the ball once for a 15-yard gain on third-and-10. Oladokun, whose pass to tight end Tre Watson was imperfect but entirely catchable, had that go down as his lone incompletion but averaged all of 2.8 yards per pass.
Nussmeier was somewhere in the middle, both statistically and via the eye test. In all, he completed just over half of his 17 throws and mustered 74 yards on them. He offered both pluses and minuses with his play once again, whether it be climbing in the pocket to deliver a 17-yard strike to wideout Jalen Royals or making back-to-back passes that were poorly timed and could've been picked off by a better defensive back.
As is frequently the case in the preseason, some of the raw numbers were out of the quarterback's control or didn't show up in a traditional sense. For example, TruMedia reveals that Fields' aforementioned run brought the second-most EPA (expected points added) on offense at 2.5. Nussmeier's deep-ball heave to receiver Andrew Armstrong, which ended in a defensive pass interference call, took the cake at 3.2.
On the flip side, Oladokun's partial-fault interception slotted into the other end of the spectrum (-4.6). Fields also had some lackluster pocket navigation this weekend, worsened by poor tackle play. A 20-yard sack in the first half immediately comes to mind as an example of teach tape in both realms.
Ups and downs are a natural part of the quarterback position, which Reid has always been consistent about. As the Chiefs work to figure out how many field generals they'll carry on the eventual 53-man roster, the legendary head coach is going beyond the data on this one.

title: Andy Reid Backs Harrison Butker After Chiefs Kicker’s Up-And-Down Showing
full_text:
Longtime Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker was on his way to becoming the hero against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers tonight — until he was the exact opposite.
The three-time Super Bowl winner accounted for all nine of Kansas City's points in the first half, connecting on field goals from 45 and 58 yards before drilling an incredible 69-yarder as time expired. Although the NFL doesn't count preseason statistics toward the record books, this would have been the NFL's longest-made field goal had it been tracked. The kick sailed through the uprights with several yards of room to spare, giving K.C. a two-possession lead heading into halftime.
But Butker's strong night took a turn after the break, missing an important extra point following Emmett Johnson's touchdown run before pushing a 43-yard field goal wide right with just over three minutes remaining. The attempt came from the right hash and never hooked back toward the middle. Had he made it, the kick would have put the Chiefs up by two and potentially won them their first preseason game since August 2023.
Ironically, Butker's two misses came on his shortest attempts of the night, emphasizing the inconsistency that has crept into his game . Still, head coach Andy Reid made it clear after the contest that he has the utmost confidence in his kicker.
"I trust him. That happens," Reid said. "He'll learn from it and move on. He's made enough of the big ones for us. He's just got to make it. He'll make an adjustment there."
Reid has plenty of reason to feel that way, as Butker has delivered countless big kicks for the Chiefs. He sent them to the Super Bowl in 2023 with a game-winning field goal against the Bengals and forced overtimes in the 2022 divisional round against the Bills and the 2024 Super Bowl against the 49ers. His list of clutch moments in the red and gold goes on and on. Butker is one of the league's more reliable legs, finishing 33-of-38 on field goals last season. However, that was the third-lowest conversion rate of his career, and he also missed four extra points and posted the worst PAT% of his career.
The leg strength is obviously still there for Butker to remain among the NFL's elite kickers, even if his accuracy has dipped somewhat from his peak. At 31 years old, he has plenty of his prime ahead of him, and Reid and the Chiefs clearly haven't lost faith in him despite tonight's up-and-down showing.

title: 1 Bold Comment by Chargers’ Mike McDaniel Creates More Questions Than Answers
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers appear to have a serious breakout on their hands with Jacob Spomer . For an offensive line littered with problems, it’s the same story with the quick rise of Branson Taylor .
Which…makes recent comments by Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel all the more confusing.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, McDaniel suggested that the starting left guard job is Kayode Awosika’s to lose.
"I think the No. 74 [Awosika] might stick, he's been fortunately been coming along, but realistically the battle wasn't complete and guys have to solidify their spots," McDaniel said. “…I would just say Kayode has kind of taken the lead in terms of it's almost his job to lose because of his growth in the last two weeks.”
That’s a bit of an odd turn of events as the Chargers still sort out a starting spot this close to the regular season.
The Chargers offensive line situation was a mess before the devastating Tyler Biadasz injury.
Jake Slaughter, previously in the lead for that left guard spot, or so it seemed, will now start at center. Awosika, Taylor, Trey Pipkins and a few others were in the fight at the left guard spot.
Monday, at the same time McDaniel was talking up Awosika, it was Pipkins getting first-team reps during a training camp practice.
One has to wonder, then, if things are really as cut and dry as McDaniel says.
There are more questions, too:
Either way, the fact the Chargers are still trying to figure out this job and making these sorts of comments isn’t a good sign this close to the regular season.
All of this happened on the same day unquestioned and unchallenged starting right guard Cole Strange was beating himself up publicly for his recent preseason performance:
Cole Strange on last week’s game: “Not happy with how I played. I’d like to play better.” Said he was out of position, but felt that it’ll be simple to fix pic.twitter.com/lTdykOgzkb
So…not a great look for the Chargers as a whole.
As we’ve said a few times now, no matter what the Week 1 lineup ends up being, the discussion around the Chargers might just be whether or not this current group can field a better line than what was out there last year.

title: Akheem Mesidor's Breakout Proving Chargers Right About Odafe Oweh Decision
full_text:
Maybe the Los Angeles Chargers got it right with the Odafe Oweh and Akheem Mesidor decision after all.
That decision was a mildly controversial one this offseason. Despite trading for and getting solid production from Oweh in the middle of last season, Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz and the front office didn't want to pay up to keep him in free agency.
The Chargers then turned around and attempted to counterbalance that decision by drafting Mesidor in the first round . Good prospect, questionable age: Mesidor might be more pro-ready than most because of his age, but he’ll also be looking at fifth-year option discussions at the age of about 30.
Luckily for the Chargers…Mesidor is starting to break out majorly this preseason.
Mesidor has had some solid showings when on the field, be it practices or preseason.
Solid is sort of underselling it, too.
As ESPN’s Kris Rhim pointed out after the Chargers’ latest practice, Mesidor won his limited one-on-one chances and had roughly four pressures and sacks: “On one, he nearly pushed Joe Alt into Justin Herbert before stopping because of the practice tempo. Another came on a quick spin move that shook Josh Kaltenberger.”
The Chargers have some serious problems on their offensive line right now. But as Pro Football Focus pointed out…Mesidor isn’t just doing this in practice, but live preseason reps:
Top graded defensive rookies this preseason, among first round picks Rueben Bain Jr           88.8 Arvell Reese                88.2 Akheem Mesidor       81.6 pic.twitter.com/5uB8UA4StN
Maybe this wasn’t hard to see coming. Back in early August, Joe Alt was one of the guys who hinted at big things for Mesidor.
“I think it's work ethic,” Alt said at the time, according to Rhim . “There hasn't been a day yet where I'm like, ‘He took that play off or he didn't go hard on that play.’ Every single play, he is trying to better himself and be the best person, the best player you can be. And you can see that and it tests everybody.“
So far, it’s a huge win on a small risk by the Chargers. If Mesidor can come in and provide that third rotational presence with capable pressures alongside Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu, the Chargers stand a much better chance of surviving the loss of defensive coordinator Jesse Minter.
At every important checkpoint along the way, Mesidor has looked the part and helped prove the Chargers right. The next step is Week 1.

title: Every Surprise Los Angeles Chargers Standout From Preseason
full_text:
Preseason is where unexpected names start to make some noise. For the Los Angeles Chargers , this year was no different. While the spotlight usually lands on the suspected stars or highly anticipated rookies, several players have turned heads . Making it a point to show the coaching staff that they belong on the roster.
From first year athletes, to guys still trying to make their name known, here is every surprise standout from the Chargers preseason .
Branson Taylor has quietly turned himself into one of the more intriguing stories of Chargers training camp. After barely making an impact as a rookie, the second-year offensive lineman has looked like a completely different player this offseason, earning first-team reps at both left guard and left tackle and consistently putting himself in the middle of the competition.
This type of camp is not going unnoticed either, as the coaching staff has complimented his game several times. Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh stated "It's been an incredible offseason...It's carried into training camp," via Chargers.com . This is the best endorsement you can get as a young guy trying to create some buzz.
The second-year quarterback was not supposed to make this competition for the backup spot so close. Uiagalelei has been solid throughout camp and continues to be consistent. He has had some ups and downs for sure, but has lots of upside.
Entering the offseason, Uiagalelei was a quiet name. With a touchdown in each game, DJ has been able to command the field well. The improvement compared to last is clear, so with more positive performances he should keep making noise. The battle is very close, and only time will tell who will ultimately win.
Former Clemson QB DJ Uiagalelei tossed a touchdown last night. pic.twitter.com/k24541iIQ7
Avery Smith has been one of the biggest surprises of Chargers training camp. The undrafted rookie cornerback has consistently made plays throughout camp, including two pass breakups on Day 4 before becoming one of the defensive standouts again on Day 5
For an undrafted player competing for one of the final spots in a crowded secondary, Smith has done exactly what he needed to do: make it increasingly difficult for the coaching staff to overlook him
This one should make most fans happy, as the former third-round pick is finally living up to his potential. While having 2 seasons of bad circumstances, Colson has emerged as a legit linebacker who could potentially land a meaningful roster spot. The room is full of talent, yet he has plenty of opportunity to make something great happen.
Junior Colson notably flashed against the 49ers, where he recorded the Chargers' first touchdown with a pick-six. It was a splash play that gave the team some momentum. Colson had vision and the athleticism that I have not yet seen from him. The preseason has gone very well for him, and should continue in the right direction
❕Junior Colson pick six ❕ NFL Preseason on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/NTgEKDp4Sg
Travis Burke has quietly turned himself into one of the more impressive young players in Chargers training camp. The fourth-round rookie has shown that his massive 6-foot-9 frame is more than just a physical trait, consistently competing in the trenches and making his presence felt against the Chargers’ defensive front. On Day 14, the Chargers reported that Burke won all four of his one-on-one reps, via Chargers.com.
What makes Burke’s development even more encouraging is that he’s already earning opportunities against NFL-caliber competition. The Chargers previously highlighted him as one of the standouts when the team first put the offensive linemen through full-padded practice.
This one is fascinating as many saw him as an immediate successor to some of the veterans on the defensive line, but it did not go the way they expected. Some players need more development than others.
Kyle Kennard is one of those guys, flashing in the 2026 camp . He has been a frequent name on every camp recap, making countless plays when needed. As the defensive front continues to change, Kennard could possibly have a role if he keeps up the great preseason.
Recent circumstances have created real chances for this young center. Being underdrafted is already an uphill battle and does not get easier as time goes on. Jacob Spomer has created real buzz though, especially with Tyler Biadasz officially on injured reserve.
Spomer displayed pretty good pass blocking for both quarterbacks in last week's matchup with San Francisco The need for a backup center has suddenly become a topic that needs to be addressed, but it might be solved quicker than anticipated.
OL Jacob Spomer (#60) has been impressive all summer. Spomer allowed zero QB pressures on 34 opportunities. He also consistently reached the second level quickly. title: From Unknown UDFA to PFF’s Top-Graded Center: Jacob Spomer Is Stealing Chargers Camp
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have a strong history of finding good undrafted free agents to come in and fit the team. This year, there are several undrafted free agents who have a shot at making the roster.
Undrafted free agents often have to have play undeniable football and circumstances have to align for them to make an NFL roster. According to Pro Football Focus, the Los Angeles Chargers have the highest-graded center in the NFL through two preseason games and that player is undrafted Fresno State Bulldog Jacob Spomer.
Following the draft, the Chargers released their initial list of undrafted free agent signings. The list included 18 players, many of whom I was familiar with from the pre-draft process and had studied film on them. There were a handful of others on the list I knew nothing about, Jacob Spomer was one of them.
I was relieved when NFL analyst and draft expert Daniel Jeremiah gave a shoutout to Spomer on the Rich Eisen Show but also admitted to having no idea who he was coming in. In Dane Brugler's annual bible of NFL draft prospects, Spomer is ranked as the 25th center and has no notes attached to him.
Spomer's history easily explains how he flew so under the radar as a draft prospect. His true freshman season was delayed by a year after graduating high school in 2020 right into the height of the early covid pandemic days. He spent one season at Diablo Valley College in the Bay Area where he played offensive tackle, his high school position.
After one season at Diablo Valley College, he received offers from Texas State, Missouri State, Sam Houston and Fresno State. He opted to stay closer to home with a coaching staff that he trusted at Fresno State. At Fresno State, he continued to play left tackle. He suffered a season ending injury late in the 2023 season that caused him to miss all but four games and their bowl bowl in the 2024 season.
In the offseason before the 2025 season, Fresno State convinced him to move to center. He is a smaller offensive lineman in general at 6'3 290lbs, he was a very small offensive tackle so the move made sense, especially if he had aspirations of playing professionally. His athleticism and speed made him a perfect center.
The athletic traits immediately popped on film and it is what drew me to him thinking he would be a perfect scheme fit for the new Mike McDaniel offense, especially after the recent success of Aaron Brewer in Miami. He entered the Chargers organization with a long shot to make the roster.
Jacob Spomer walked into the Bolt as the presumed fourth center on the depth chart behind veteran free agent arrival Tyler Biadasz, rookie center/guard Jake Slaughter, and second-year player Josh Kaltenberger.
Spomer must have impressed offensive line coach Butch Barry during OTAs. When the Chargers opened training camp, Spomer was the third center and Kaltenberger had moved to guard.
Spomer caught the attention of a wider audience after he played the majority of snaps in the Chargers first preseason game against the Houston Texans after Jake Slaughter started the game and quickly exited. Spomer was the third-highest-PFF-graded blocker on the Chargers against the Texans and gave up zero pressures.
He followed up that performance operating with the second team and playing most of the game again against the San Francisco 49ers following the injury to Tyler Biadasz earlier that week. Against the 49ers, Spomer was the highest PFF-graded blocker on the field for the Chargers.
Two preseason games and 102 offensive snaps later, Jacob Spomer is now the highest graded center in the NFL, not just amongst rookies, and has yielded zero pressures.
The late start to his college career paired with a redshirt season makes Spomer an older rookie at 25 years old. His resume as an undrafted free agent is not his pedigree but his film. The level of play in which Spomer is putting on film for two weeks now is entering into the undeniable category.
Jacob Spomer is currently the Chargers backup center. Having two rookie centers is a risk but how can Spomer be denied a spot on the initial 53-man roster with his level of play. The Chargers may not have to hit the panic button on the center position with the news of Tyler Biadasz being placed on season-ending injured reserve.
The Chargers front office may choose to add a veteran to the room after roster cutdown day, potentially just to have on the practice squad. But, after two preseason games with one to go and a week before roster cutdown day, the former unknown Fresno State Bulldog Jacob Spomer has certainly earned a roster spot.

title: Chargers Offense Misfiring, Injury Updates, Tyler Biadasz Move, Sunday Practice News
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers took the field for another practice on Sunday morning, their second since their preseason loss to the San Francisco 49ers. The Chargers were hoping to bounce back from their poor showing on Thursday and get back work at practice, Saturday did not go very well , at least for the offense and unfortunately, Sunday was not much better.
The good news is that the Chargers defense seems to be stringing together positive practice days and the starting unit that took the field against the 49ers was missing several key players and still held San Francisco's offense in check. Based on the unsettled offensive line and the need to establish continuity following the loss of Tyler Biadasz, the defense may have to carry the Chargers offense in the early parts of the season.
Let's dive into the news of the day and important notes from practice. The Chargers are gearing up to take on the Rams in their final preseason matchup on Thursday night with roster cutdown day Sunday August 30th.
The Chargers officially placed Tyler Biadasz on injured reserve today all but ending any speculation that he will have any chance at returning this year. There is a minor procedural move that the Chargers could make by designating him for return during roster cutdowns, otherwise and the most likely scenario is that he will miss the entire 2026 season.
Chargers place C Tyler Biadasz (knee) on season-ending IR. pic.twitter.com/Civ71sBPRj
Biadasz' injury has been an odd mystery. There has been no public release of what he is actually dealing with, if and when he will have surgery
Rashawn Slater maintained his ramp up protocol for the second straight day of practice and is essentially on a pitch count from the team and medical staff as he works his way back into the fold. While Slater has exited practice, for the second straight day Trey Pipkins and rookie Travis Burke have been taking his place on the offensive line.
Defensive tackle Jamaree Caldwell, despite leaving practice on Saturday early with trainers, was back in the action on Sunday.
Wide receiver Brenen Thompson was also back on the field wearing a gold jersey.
The following Chargers players did not participate in practice on Sunday: Tight end Scott Matlock Edge rusher Kyle Kennard Offensive lineman Branson Taylor Running back Keaton Mitchell Wide receiver Sincere Brown Cornerback Eric Rogers
For the second day in a row, the Chargers offense had a rough go against the defense. There were some glimmers of hope and energy provided throughout but for the most part, the defense won the day handily.
Is the hangover from losing of Tyler Biadasz haunting their performance? There is reason to still hold out hope after watching the 49ers game. It appears Mike McDaniel put forth a very vanilla version of the offense but the concerning aspect of that thought is that there were still multiple pre-snap penalties.
Heading into the season the line and quarterback Justin Hebert have a few weeks to gain continuity, depending on how long it takes to name a starting left guard. McDaniel and the offensive staff will be able to scheme much more opponent specific gameplans to hopefully give the group stronger footing to stand on.
The starting left guard is still not settled with Trey Pipkins getting the first run with the first team two days in a row. This may simply be giving Pipkins a chance to prove himself after spending the past few weeks at left tackler with Slater sidelined. Head coach Jim Harbaugh did say before Saturday's practice that Kayode Awosika was in the lead for the job but they were not ready to declare as starter.
On the back end of the roster, current injuries may have an outsized impact on those tough battles and narrow decisions. Kyle Kennard, Branson Taylor and Eric Rogers were all battling for roles and even roster spots. With them being on the sidelines, it may make some roster decisions tougher than others. The next few days will be worth keeping an eye to see which of them gets back into practice and prepares for the Rams on Thursday night.

title: 4 Options After Chargers Reveal Final Tyler Biadasz Injury News
full_text:
It’s officially over for Tyler Biadasz and the Los Angeles Chargers in 2026.
The Chargers were trying to hold out hope that Biadasz might be able to return later in the 2026 season after recovering from a serious knee injury.
In the wake of the Chargers’ second preseason game, though, the team put an end to that with the reveal that Biadasz will move to injured reserve.
The crusher: According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport , Biadasz “exhausted all options before the move was made. Likely meaning, no return is possible.
So, where do the Chargers go from here?
The Chargers drafted Slaughter to play guard, despite being a college center. He’s back at center now and will stay there. Barring a shocker, he’s the unquestioned starter. But his reps in preseason Week 2 were up-and-down, as expected.
More concerning, at least for now, is just who might actually emerge at left guard, where at least three names still appear to have a chance at starting there.
Now 32 years old, Daniel Brunskill spent last year with Miami. That wasn’t his only connection to Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, either, given his years in San Francisco from 2019-2022. Right now, he’s currently with Washington, but it’s an option worth exploring as a backup if he doesn’t make it through final cuts or winds up on the trade block.
Graham Glasgow and James Daniels are two veterans with the ability to play multiple spots on the interior of an offensive line.
Glasgow is 34 years old and spent the last few years in Detroit. He’d need to be willing to accept a backup and mentor-type role behind Slaughter, though.
Similar story for Daniels, who happened to spend last year in Miami, but saw his three-year deal become just one after an injury derailed things. He’s still 28 years old, but would need to accept a spot behind Slaughter.
Because of the absolute mess that is left guard, this is an extremely uncomfortable place for the Chargers to be right now. Finding a backup center isn’t that big of a deal. Neither is starting a rookie center, provided the veterans around him are reliable.
But left guard is a question mark, right guard always felt a little unaddressed with Cole Strange and Rashawn Slater has already had a minor injury setback at a tackle spot. Instead of the best-ever line with a flashy new coordinator, the conversation shifts to whether the line can even be better than last year’s unit.

title: Chargers Training Camp Problem Might be Going From Bad to Worse
full_text:
Roughly one week into the preseason, perhaps the biggest problem the Los Angeles Chargers faced was just who might end up at one of the starting guard spots in front of Justin Herbert.
Fast forward to now, it’s almost a red-button emergency situation.
The fallout from the Tyler Biadasz injury is immense. Rookie Jake Slaughter now has to kick back to center, leaving a mess of things for the Chargers to figure out at left guard.
Making matters even worse, the backup offensive line spots don’t seem so hot , either. Keep in mind that’s with the Chargers adding free agents for Mike McDaniel and spending four of their eight draft picks on linemen.
Time is running out for the Chargers to show signs of life in that area.
With Biadasz down, Slaughter, the rookie center drafted to play guard, has kicked back to center. The four or so names still involved in the left guard battle aren’t exactly standing out one way or another.
Just look at updates from ESPN’s Kris Rhim , who said the first practice after the preseason beatdown at the hands of the San Francisco 49ers “was one of the worst days for the offense.”
Rhim noted that Justin Herbert threw one interception and multiple turnover-worthy passes beyond that. Slaughter struggled against the likes of Jamaree Caldwell and that overall it was a bad day for the line.
All that while shuffling things around in a big way. Rashawn Slater briefly returned to practice after his apparent setback. Otherwise, Travis Burke and Trey Pipkins rotated at left tackle. But Pipkins started the day at left guard before giving way to Kayode Awosika.
There’s really just…nobody emerging at guard. The fact Pipkins, the primary backup swing tackle, keeps getting first-team reps there, probably isn’t a good sign. Awosika is a mid-tier free-agent add who isn’t establishing himself there.
Keep in mind that Branson Taylor, a former practice squad member last year, has been one of the biggest “breakouts” of training camp. His rise has been surprising and it could very well end up being him as the starter in Week 1. But with how things have been going, one has to wonder if perhaps his rise is, at least in part, a result of so much uncertainty and middling competition at guard.
None of this is to say anything about Cole Strange, who most agreed was a pretty questionable, non-challengeable signing as a starter at right guard by McDaniel. He’s been up-and-down at times and will now need to line up next to a rookie center.
It would be one thing if the Chargers were simply seeing a rookie center go through growing pains. But the fact there’s still a left guard competition next to him right before the third preseason game and no reliable way to get a good player in the door in a lineman-starved NFL is a panic-worthy thing.

title: Injury Updates, Offensive Line Sparks Concerns, Chargers Try to Recover at Practice
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers returned to practice on Saturday while still licking their wound from an embarrassing night of football on Thursday night against the 49ers. The team seemed to have taken the loss of Tyler Biadasz due to a major knee injury as a punch to the gut that they have yet to recover from.
Practices are no longer open to the public and therefore news and highlights will be limited but there is still plenty to go over from Saturday's return to the Bolt. Let's dive into news and questions about the Chargers from Saturday's practice.
The Chargers had several starters return to practice in some capacity on Saturday. Left tackle Rashawn Slater, wide receivers Tre' Harris and Quentin Johnston, cornerbacks Tarheeb Still and Donte Jackson all were on the field on Saturday
The following players were sidelined due to injuries: Tight End Scott Matlock (who was wearing a walking boot on the sidelines during the loss to the 49ers) Edge rusher Bud Dupree Edge rusher Kyle Kennard Offensive lineman Branson Taylor Wide receiver Brenen Thompson Cornerback Eric Rogers
The status of center Tyler Biadasz still has yet to be labeled or updated in regards to whether he will be put on injured reserve and miss the entire 2026 season or if there is a chance at a last season comeback.
Defensive tackle Jamaree Caldwell left practice early and was working with trainers off to the side.
Rashawn Slater's return to practice included individual drills and one session of 11-on-11 team period. Head coach Jim Harbaugh made it clear at his pre-practice press conference that Slater would be ramping back up to full practice. Slater exited practice following the first team period and watched from the sideline.
Jim Harbaugh said it himself, "The film did not lie. I mean, we got beat and beat ourselves as a team in all three phases." The most concerning part of the Chargers offense from joint practice, through the game and even Saturday's practice, is rooted in the offensive line. The interior of the offensive line, when the starters were in, got routinely beat whether is pass protection or run blocking.
The offensive line woes could be directly tied to the lack of continuity between Jake Slaughter and the guards next to him after he was thrust into the starting role. Slaughter's move to center, his natural position, removes him from the left guard competition. Branson Taylor was sidelined today and instead of Kayode Awosika getting valuable reps next to Slaughter, Trey Pipkins was the first left guard in team period with Rashawn Slater's return.
Roster cutdown day is a week away and the Chargers are still not settled on their starting offensive line. They have three weeks to gel and work together but Harbaugh has indicated they are not close to naming a starter. For a team that gave up historic levels of pressure up the middle in 2025, fans' frustration with the process and the current results is understandable.
It remains to be seen if the front office smashes the panic button and makes a trade for a depth piece with starting potential. ESPN's Kris Rhim covers the Chargers and his practice notes may have been clearly indicative over the levels of concern facing the Chargers. His first note of the day said "It was one of the worst days for the offense. Interior offensive line struggled, and the passing offense wasn't great."

title: The Chargers Rookie Nobody Expected to be Talking About
full_text:
The NFL preseason is full of players trying to turn a few weeks of football into an opportunity that can change their careers instantly. Many players come and go during training camp. However for a undrafted rookie in Los Angeles, an opportunity on the 53-man roster has started to look very real.
Jacob Spomer entered Los Angeles Chargers training camp without the same spotlight that followed some of the team’s draft picks. He wasn’t selected during the 2026 NFL draft, and there was no guarantee he would make enough of an impression to stick around.
But so far, he’s giving the Chargers plenty to think about. With the offensive line dealing with multiple injuries, Spomer could be a legit depth piece for the Bolts. Based off recent seasons and the offensive line woes, this addition is more important than ever.
Throughout training camp, Jacob Spomer has continued to receive opportunities at center and has looked comfortable handling the responsibility . He has been able to work with different combinations along the offensive line, giving the coaching staff a closer look at what he can provide. As of right now, he looks to be a very promising player. For an undrafted player, those reps are important. Every practice gives him another chance to show that he belongs.
Spomer's training camp has been solid, being reliable and improving every day. He seems to be beating expectations at a rapid speed. The biggest positive came from last Thursday's game, where he performed very well.
The center posted a 82.6 percent pass blocking rate , with zero sacks or pressures, according to Pro Football Focus. That statistic shows how steady he is in pass protection. We all know what happened last year when Herbert thew the ball. Spomer could be a perfect piece for the line in the future.
The Tyler Biadasz injury was heartbreaking to hear, and was a punch in the gut for the Chargers. This makes the timing of Spomer's recent breakout especially important. The need for a serviceable center depth-wise, has become a sudden topic of discussion. Spomer's ability to step in when needed, protect the quarterback, and handle pressure can give Los Angeles another option. His recent success does not mean much, as many things are up in the air. However, it should make you feel better about the future of the offense.
