title: Raiders Training Camp Report 25: Jeanty Injured, Pressure Mounts
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—One week from today, Las Vegas Raiders GM John Spytek will turn in his original 53-man roster for the Silver and Black for the 2026 season.
The pressure is mounting for many of the men on this roster, as the team, clearly in the midst of a Raiders rebuild best characterized as a youth movement, has to make some very difficult decisions.
Today marked the first of the final three days of practice. With the pressure on and the intensity at an all-time high for the year, gone are the collegial atmosphere of OTAs, the business-casual approach to mandatory minicamp, and the business-meeting environment of camp. These three days are more like the frenzy of Wall Street moments before the closing bell on a high day of trading.
Borderline players fiercely try to put one last piece of tape on for the coaches and John Spytek to see. Secure players can breathe as they turn their attention to the long season, while others not on the bubble fight for a chance at the practice squad.
Roughly two-thirds of the way through practice, Ashton Jeanty was on a pass route and dove for a ball thrown by Kirk Cousins. He was being covered by Darien Porter, but from my vantage point, it did not appear that there was any collision.
Jeanty did not put any pressure on the right leg while being assisted off the field. While there has been no official statement from the team, Jeanty's teammates, upon noticing the injury, quickly took a knee and were seen visibly praying for the Silver and Black burgeoning star.
While the injury occurred on the right leg, it would be purely speculative at this point to try to assess the exact part of the leg. What has to hurt for Kubiak is that the team was holding a walk-through. They weren't even in pads.
On Sunday night, I reached out to a member of the Raiders' organization and was told, “Nothing to report here as rock solid, but I would say preliminary thoughts are that it isn’t disastrous as thought, and considering of how bad it could have been, it appears as good as could hope. Would expect more tests tomorrow to confirm, so I don't think anything is definitive.”
Since Klint Kubiak arrived, he has preached competition. Normally at this time in training camp, teams tend to stay in pads with multiple roster spots up for grabs, or lean toward no pads if the battles are mostly settled.
Today, the Raiders were not in pads as mentioned above, but OC Andrew Janocko said there are plenty of spots on his offense to be won when I asked him about it.
“We're always competing. We're trying to find the best player at every position, and I don't think from the top on down, I think we're always evaluating to get the best player on the field. So, I don't think there's anybody that should get comfortable."
"Ourselves, as a coaching staff, we're constantly trying to get better ourselves, and we're evaluating ourselves all the time. And then we look around, and that's the same in every position. So, I think Klint [Kubiak] said it best: we don't want anybody to get comfortable."
There is no doubt that this position is the weak link of the Raiders' offense. Klint Kubiak wasted no punches calling them out, and Janocko discussed that unit.
"From the receiver position specifically, what we're looking for is guys to get off the ball at the right tempo, guys to get their precise depths, guys to make sure that their break points are correct, and then guys that make moment of truth plays. That's anything. That's specific to that room, but it's what we're asking every position."
This team has multiple sayings that all point to the same premise: football is a business; take care of your business. Or as Bill Belichick says, “Do your job.” Klint Kubiak demands that his wide receivers block with the ferocity and commitment of the offensive line. Tre Tucker shared one of those colloquialisms with us today.
“I think as a whole unit, we've got to be better in the run game. I mean, that's where it starts. We can't eat if the run game's not eating, and as you guys know, that's been something that we've been trying to get better and trying to work on. Like, Coach Z [Zach Azzanni] just sent me something the other day – no block, no rock.”
Another colloquialism is the constant preaching for the defense to get the ball back to the offense. It is a culture; it is a mantra that this defense has to get turnovers. Eric Stokes broke it down.
"Man, I still want to steal the ball. That's the biggest thing that we got to do. Especially on defense, you take the ball away, you give Kirk [Cousins], you get everybody more opportunities to go score, all that stuff. So, the biggest thing for us has just been taking the ball away. Let's go ahead and take the ball away. Let's go ahead and get off the field.”
There is plenty of speculation as roster spots get tighter around AOC. He has had some very high and some low moments with the Raiders, but the consensus around the NFL is that he is very intriguing. Janocko is thrilled to have him on the roster, as projections indicate the Raiders will keep all three QBs.
"I think Aidan [O’Connell], like all of those guys, to play quarterback in this league, you have to be very intelligent, and you have to be functionally intelligent. The things that Aidan sees, based off of his experience, and things he's seen, whether he's played the game or some of the other quarterbacks he's been around, he just brings a wealth of knowledge to the position that's really beneficial to everybody else and myself especially."
"He sees things in a manner where he can see it from playing the game, and he can see it from a perspective of how a receiver may see it or how a running back may see it, how the overall offense sees it. So, I think his just overall awareness of game and position is really valuable to us."
The Raiders are placing enormous value on special teams. More than any team I have personally covered. Olubi is a special teams standout, and for the first time all year, I now think he will make the 53-man roster, and the Silver and Black will carry five ILBs. Remember, that is where he is listed, but he is nearly exclusively a special teams player.
The biggest battle on this team coming into camp continues today with this RG battle. It continues today with JPJ back at practice and both men back in some rotation. Janocko addressed the battle.
"I see a group that really pays attention to the details. It's a group of guys that comes to work every day. It's not a group that you have to pump up. They're ready to go every single day. Whether it's the guard position, the center position, those are guys that really love their job. Their approach is something that's exciting and something that allows you to, as a coach, coach them hard and be on them all the time for every little detail because that's what they're asking for."
Tre Tucker’s entire career has been essentially the same story. His speed gets him open, and he has to stop and wait for the ball, usually underthrown. I asked him today about having a QB room that can get him the ball anywhere on the field, so he can go full speed and trust it to be there. His smile told the story as much as his words.
“Yeah, it's exciting. I'm just very blessed to be able to play with Kirk [Cousins], Fernando [Mendoza] and Aidan [O’Connell] because those guys just play with anticipation. Like, it's so cool to see. I'll go and watch the quarterback copy of a play, and the quarterback will start on one side and as soon as he flips his hips, the ball's out."
"It's not like I got to see what he's doing, it's just a trust factor. So, that plays a long way. It puts more pressure on us to get open and do our job. But the ball's where it needs to be and that's where a lot of good things happen.”
MWJ has had an outstanding camp, long before Jeanty suffered his injury today. While we wait for word on the former Boise State star, there was already plenty of attention on MWJ, as the young Razorback has been turning heads all camp,…

title: Best-Case, Worst-Case for Raiders After Ashton Jeanty Injury
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders took to the practice field again Sunday morning, aiming to take the next step in their development. Las Vegas will play its final preseason game on Thursday night against the San Francisco 49ers. That will be their last matchup against another team until Week 1.
Until Thursday, Las Vegas plans to do all they can to improve on every level. After playing some of their starters in their first preseason game and resting all of their starters in their second , how Las Vegas approaches Thursday night will directly impact the results of the first game of the season.
Yet the Raiders now have other concerns that may impact much more than just their season opener against the Miami Dolphins. Sunday's practice witnessed Las Vegas improve even more, but it also witnessed what appeared to be a significant injury to running back Ashton Jeanty.
During practice, Jeanty landed awkwardly while trying to catch a pass. He stayed down for some time before being helped off the field by trainers, having trouble putting any weight on one leg. As of now, it remains unclear how serious the injury is, but based on his teammates' reaction, it was not good.
Jeanty's injury would make this the third consecutive season the Raiders have suffered a significant early-season injury to a player they depend on. Brock Bowers suffered an injury in Week 1 last season. The season before that, Malcolm Koonce suffered a serious injury days before Week 1.
Until more information is released, there is only so much that can be figured out.
The Raiders' ground game was undoubtedly going to be based around Jeanty moving forward. It is too early to panic, as nothing has been confirmed about the injury. However, if Jeanty misses significant time, it is hard to overstate how massive a blow that would be for Las Vegas.
It would be a significant short-term loss and would be a significant injury to the knee of a running back they drafted with the sixth overall pick just one offseason ago. Las Vegas has worked to add depth to the unit, but it's nearly impossible to replace Jeanty, let alone this close to the season.
Things could certainly work out for the best, and Jeanty's injury could turn out not to be as bad as it looked, but it was the first time I can recall Jeanty not getting up after going to the ground. It seems that regardless of how bad it was, Jeanty is likely to miss time.
The weeks between now and Week 1 may or may not be enough time for him to bounce back. Time will tell. Everything depends on how bad the injury turns out to be. The Raiders will now turn to rookie running back Mike Washington, who has had a solid training camp and preseason.
"I think Mike [Washington Jr.] comes to work. He works very hard every day. Mike comes and he studies very hard. He asks great questions. He's on his craft all the time, and it's something that you see translate into the practice field. It's something that we keep pushing him every single day,” Andrew Janocko said Sunday morning before practice.
“It's something that's always going to be a point of emphasis for him that he comes out every single day, he's prepared to the best of his ability, and then you see it translate onto the grass. So, that's something that we are always going to constantly be on him."
Sunday's practice was productive. The work the Raiders have been putting in was apparent. They are not the same team that took the field at the start of camp, and they are certainly not the team that last took the field in 2025. They have improved from the coaching staff to the last player on the roster.
Still, it is hard to think about much else concerning the Raiders after watching Jeanty go down the way he did. After an offseason filled with positives and progress, Jeanty's injury is a reminder of how fleeting success and expectations can be in the National Football League. Best-case scenario, the injury is minor.

title: More Moves: Dolphins Ahead of 2019 Pace with Roster Shuffling
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are now six days away from having to trim their roster by 38 players, but that doesn't mean they're not willing to take a look at new players before then.
There has been a whole lot of roster churning going on already in 2026, and it continued Monday with four more moves.
The Dolphins announced Monday they had signed linebacker Jehaim Thomas and tight end Ethan Conner, making room for them on the roster by waiving center Jim Bonifas and cornerback Ahmari Harvey.
Thomas (6-2, 232) joined the Dolphins out of the UFL, where he was a member of the league champion Louisville Kings. He finished his college career at Wisconsin in 2024, but went undrafted last year and didn't sign as an undrafted free agent with any team.
Conner (6-4, 245) spent time with the Jacksonville Jaguars this summer after going undrafted out of Troy.
Their signing will leave them precious little time to make an impression on the Dolphins before the roster cuts to 53, a dilemma head coach Jeff Hafley addressed in a Zoom media session Sunday related to players who signed with the team late last week.
"Certainly it's going to be just by the nature of it, it's going to be a little bit harder because they're going to have limited reps, in practice this week, but then they're going to get another shot Friday night to play a lot," Hafley said. "So we'll give them a fair chance. Watch the tape. See if we see the talent in the individual, the make-up of the player. So we're going to have to dig in as coaches and they're going to have to give us everything they have. It's just going to be a much smaller sample size. But at the end of the day if we feel those players can make us better then we got to really think hard about that. I mean, harder, but they'll have a chance."
By our calculations, Thomas and Conner became the 21st and 22nd new players signed by the Dolphins since they put together their undrafted free agent class. That number surpasses the total of 20 for the Dolphins before the roster cuts to 53 in 2019 when they also were undergoing a massive rebuilding project.
The Dolphins' total this year includes 16 players signed as free agents, four players claimed on waivers, and two players acquired via trade.
The Dolphins, based on comments from GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and Hafley, aren't done shuffling the back end of the roster and who knows what that number of player acquisitions will look like by the time the 2026 comes to a close.
One area to watch is waiver claims.
Again using 2019 as a gauge, the Dolphins picked up a whopping 20 players off waivers, even if they only had two before the cuts to 53. That Miami team landed five players off waivers the morning after the cuts, and it should surprise no one if the Dolphins match or top that number this year.
And it also should surprise no one if the Dolphins made even more roster moves before Sunday at 4 p.m. ET.
They clearly have shown no hesitation to look for any way possible to improve the roster.

title: Dolphins Evaluating Another Former First-Round Pick on the Rebound (And Who Could Be Next)
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' roster additions and auditions have focused almost exclusively on young players looking to establish themselves in the NFL, but they also have brought in two failed former first-round picks looking to rebound and revive their career.
And now they're ready to take a look at another one of those players, with a report Monday morning they'll be having a workout for 2020 Los Angeles Chargers first-round pick Kenneth Murray.
Murray went unsigned this year as an unrestricted free agent after playing last season with the Dallas Cowboys following one year with the Tennessee Titans and his first four in the NFL with the Chargers.
A former standout at Oklahoma, Murray has a lot of starting experience in the NFL with 83 starts, including five seasons with 14 or more, but his performance has been uneven at best, unsatisfactory at worst.
Pro Football Focus has ranked Murray 73rd or worse among qualifying linebackers (a number always in the 80s) in five of his six seasons and Pro Football Reference has him with a career 109.0 opponent passer rating when targeted.
Murray made $7.5 million with the Cowboys in 2025, but right now he's looking at not drawing a paycheck this year, so perhaps he'd be willing to settle for a one-year, prove-it contract, the kind of deal the Dolphins have been giving their newcomers (not named Malik Willis) this year.
The Dolphins already have signed two former first-round picks this year, bringing in former Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Jalen Reagor and former Las Vegas Raiders defensive end/edge Clelin Ferrell.
The Dolphins also gave a workout earlier this summer to former Kansas City Chiefs running back Clyde Edwards-Helaire but didn't wind up signing that other former first-round pick.
Reagor and Ferrell shouldn't be considered locks to be on the 53-man roster and project as backups if they do wind up making the team.
Murray's workout coincides with a rash of injuries at linebacker, with Jordyn Brooks, Tyrel Dodson, Trey Moore and Ronnie Harrison Jr. all missing practice Monday.
With Murray only 27 years old, this would be a good gamble for the Dolphins if they can get him at the right price because maybe he could shine enough to earn a second contract with Miami.
And the reality is there are other current players available who fit the same mold.
By all calculations, there are 21 other former first-round picks currently without a team and still active — unlike former Dolphins backup QB Teddy Bridgewater, who recently announced his retirement.
Because of where they are as an organization, we think focusing on those under 30 makes sense, which would eliminate a good bunch of them, including former Miami first-round pick Christian Wilkins, who will turn 31 in December and is a special case regardless because he's not out of work for performance reasons.
But there are four current free agents who are former first-round picks and younger than 30, including former Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold, who already has agreed to terms with the Seattle Seahawks but must navigage some legal issues.
That leaves three and those three are: former Cincinnati Bengals tackle Jonah Williams, former New York Jets tackle Mekhi Becton, and former Lions cornerback Jeff Okudah.
Interestingly, Okudah and Becton both were selection in the first round in 2020 when the Dolphins had three picks. Okudah went third overall, two spots before Miami selected quarterback Tua Tagovailoa; Becton went 10th, eight spots before Miami drafted USC tackle Austin Jackson.
Becton certainly is interesting. He has started 59 of his 61 NFL games, but he had a rough 2025 season with the L.A. Chargers. His PFF grade was 37.1, which ranked 77 out of 79 qualifying NFL guards, ahead only of Cincinnati's Jalen Rivers and the Dolphins' Jonah Savaiinaea.
Becton had signed a two-year contract worth up to $20 million with Chargers last offseason after enjoying a breakout year with the Eagles in 2024, but was released after just one season.
Okudah, meanwhile, played for a different team each of the last four years and didn't start a game for either the Houston Texans in 2024 or Minnesota Vikings last year.
Williams has started all 74 games he has played in his NFL career, but injuries limited him to 15 combined starts over his two seasons with the Arizona Cardinals.
The Dolphins certainly could use depth on the offensive line and at cornerback — shoot, they could use depth everywhere on the roster — so maybe they should consider at least bringing any or all three of those players in for a visit or a workout.

title: Miami Dolphins Training Camp Practice 14 Observations: Big Bell, Ewers News (But With a Caveat), Johnson Shines
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins were back at practice Monday for a short session that featured some half-speed work, but more notably the return of a couple of notable players.
Quarterback Quinn Ewers was back at practice for the first time since the preseason opener against the Washington Commanders when he sustained what was reported as a groin injury.
Rookie wide receiver Chris Bell practiced without a red jersey for the first time since being activated from the Non-Football Injury list, and cornerback JuJu Brents took part in team periods for the first time in a couple of weeks.
Before we declare any of those players fully back, though, just based on their participation Monday, we should point out the team reps not involving the first-team offense and defense were done at half speed.
Head coach Jeff Hafley said before practice that would be the plan and was a byproduct of the projected starters not playing in the preseason game against the New York Giants on Saturday and the backups getting a lot of snaps in that 26-3 loss.
Bell did get a couple of full-speed reps, but he didn't make a catch, dropping a Malik Willis floater in the middle of the field after the pass barely cleared linebacker Jacob Rodriguez.
The practice, which came in under 90 minutes, was conducted most of the way in the rain, at first light but increasing in intensity after a bit.
The Dolphins still practice without several key veterans and the tight end room is getting thinner.
Defensive tackle Zach Sieler, linebacker Jordyn Brooks, edge Clelin Ferrell, linebacker Ronnie Harrison Jr. and defensive tackle Kenneth Grant again missed practice but were in attendance.
Rookie linebacker Trey Moore, edge Cameron Goode and cornerback Ahmari Harvey were the three players who didn't practice and were not spotted.
At tight end, rookie draft picks Will Kacmarek and Seydou Traore joined Ben Sims on the sidelines.
-- The first-team defense had the better of the offense, with Malik Willis completing 7 of 16 passes in team periods without necessarily having a bad day. He did have his share of passes broken up, often because of tight coverage, though once on a pass thrown a bit behind the receiver.
-- Rookie first-round pick Chris Johnson was the standout player on traffic with some outstanding coverage once again. His highlight play came early in practice when he blanketed Caleb Douglas on what looked like a go route, to the point where Douglas gave up and Johnson became the closest player to the deep pass that Willis threw. This wasn't the first time that Johnson has shut down Douglas, as he continues to look better and better.
-- On the flip side, Douglas continues to be awfully quiet following all the national praise that came his way with his circus catch in the Washington preseason game. He was held without a catch for a second time in three practices.
-- Rookie free agent D.J. Herman continues to make his case for a spot on the 53-man roster. He came up with a couple of nice lead blocks on running plays.
-- Guard Jonah Savaiinaea also appeared to have a nice opening block on a De'Von Achane run where he found some daylight up the middle.
-- There were no officials at the Baptist Health Training Complex, which might have been good news for left tackle Patrick Paul, who was kinda sorta holding on a couple of pass-protection reps against Chop Robinson and Josh Uche.
-- Linebacker Willie Gay Jr. had a would-be sack when he came in free on a blitz.
-- Tight end Greg Dulcich had a nice high catch over the middle on a Willis pass thrown a bit behind him.
-- Jalen Tolbert had a nice touchdown catch in a red zone period when he went up in the back of the end zone to beat safety Michael Taaffe.
-- Ewers also had a touchdown pass in the red zone to running back Carlos Washington Jr., but again that was at half-speed.
-- Tight end Jeremiah Franklin had a touchdown catch from third quarterback Cam Miller.
-- With Ewers back, Mark Gronowski didn't take snaps in team reps and his time on the roster obviously is short.

title: Dolphins 2026 53-Man Roster Projection 4.0: How Things Stand One Week Before Cuts
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are now a week away from having to slash their roster to the NFL-mandated limit of 53 players, with three days of practice and the preseason finale against the Atlanta Falcons representing the remaining opportunities to make a final case.
At this point, though, head coach Jeff Hafley and his staff have a pretty good idea what group they'll be taking to Allegiant Stadium on September 13 for their regular season opener against the Las Vegas Raiders.
Through 12 intrasquad practices, two joint practices and two preseason games, there has been some movement in the pecking order of the Dolphins roster, and injuries also have and will play a factor in the final composition of that roster.
With that in mind, here is Miami Dolphins On SI Publisher Alain Poupart's fourth 53-man roster projection of 2026:
On the 53: Malik Willis, Quinn Ewers
Off: Cam Miller, Mark Gronowski (R)
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: While it's entirely possible the Dolphins' No. 2 quarterback currently is on another team's roster, we'll have to go right now with the status quo and the only question continuing to be whether Cam Miller has done enough — look beyond the stats because he's not getting any help — to be kept as a third QB on the 53.
On the 53: De'Von Achane, Jaylen Wright, Ollie Gordon II
Off: Donovan Edwards, Carlos Washington Jr.
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: There's no reason to think anything has changed the top three spots here and the only question as it's been all along is whether the Dolphins would consider keeping four, and if that happens, then Washington would be that fourth guy.
On the 53: Jalen Tolbert, Chris Bell (R), Caleb Douglas (R), Kevin Coleman Jr. (R), Malik Washington, Jalen Reagor
Off: Tahj Washington, A.J. Henning, Terrace Marshall Jr., Donaven McCulley (R), Tutu Atwell, Theo Wease Jr.
Changes from projection 3.0: Reagor in, Wease out
Analysis: Chris Bell remains a wild card here because he still hasn't practiced at full speed and it's not inconceivable he could begin the season on IR (with a designation to return). if he's not, then the reality is there's a free-for-all behind the three rookie draft picks and Washington.
On the 53: Greg Dulcich, Will Kacmarek (R), D.J. Herman (R), Ben Sims
Off: Cole Turner, FB Jeremiah Franklin (R), Seydou Traore (R)
Changes from projection 3 .0: Herman in, Traore out
Analysis: While we feel pretty confident about four being the target number here, what's unclear is the injury status of Ben Sims, who hasn't practiced in a few weeks, as well as whether the Dolphins actually would go ahead and cut their rookie fifth-round pick. Based on what we've seen, Herman has earned his spot as a rookie free agent.
On the 53: Patrick Paul, Austin Jackson, Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, Kadyn Proctor (R), Charlie Heck, Andrew Meyer, Caedan Wallace, Josh Priebe
Off: Marques Cox, Kevin Cline (R), DJ Campbell (R), Jim Bonitas (R), Gottlieb Ayedze, Jamaree Salyer (IR)
Changes from projection 3 .0: Wallace and Priebe in, Salyer and Campbell out
Analysis: Teams more often than not keep eight offensive linemen, but we've been consistent in thinking the Dolphins will go with the extra player for more versatility. We've got a second rookie draft pick cut here because Priebe simply has been ahead of Campbell all summer.
On the 53: Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Clelin Ferrell, Robert Beal Jr., Max Llewellyn (R)
Off: David Ojabo, Rodney McGraw (R),  Cameron Goode, Seth Coleman-Lyles, Trey Moore
Changes from projection 2.0: Beal and Llewelly in, Ojabo and Moore out
Analysis: The name that stands out here obviously is Moore, who we would predict at this time will start the season on IR, hopefully with a designation to return. But Jeff Hafley's words Sunday morning suggest he won't be available for at least the first month of the season, hence putting him on IR. Then we're going under the assumption that Ferrell and Beal, who have been nursing injuries, will be ready for the start of the regular season. Lastly, we had Llewellyn off the 53 up to now, but he's picked up his game. The one player tough to keep out was Goode, and it would not surprise us to see him on the 53.
On the 53: Zach Sieler, Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers, Matthew Butler
Off: Alex Huntley, Keith Cooper Jr., Fatorma Mulbah, Cam Rice (R)
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: Cooper and Mulbah have had their moments recently, but it's just really difficult to envision the Dolphins not wanting a little bit of veteran presence here with Sieler and Butler.
On the 53: Jordyn Brooks, Tyrel Dodson, Jacob Rodriguez (R), Ronnie Harrison Jr., Kyle Louis (R), Jackson Woodard
Off: Willie Gay Jr., Stephen Dix Jr., Cam Riley
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: We've been consistent with this group, but injuries could become a factor. The tough call here obviously is moving on from Gay, and we absolutely could see a scenario where either he or Dodson get traded to a team in need of a veteran linebacker.
On the 53: JuJu Brents, Chris Johnson (R), Jason Marshall Jr., Ethan Bonner, Alex Austin, A.J. Green III
Off: Miles Battle, Darrell Baker Jr., Ahmari Harvey (R), Storm Duck, Marco Wilson, Jai'Onte' McMillan (R)
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: The first four remains pretty solid and it remains a free-for-all for the final two spots, though it's clearer than ever is that Duck and Baker likely will start the regular season on Reserve/PUP and will be out for at least the first four games. The battle for the final two spots remains as wide open as when camp started, and we could see a scenario where Wilson makes the 53.
On the 53: Dante Trader Jr., Michael Taaffe (R), Zayne Anderson, Lonnie Johnson Jr.
Off: Louis Moore (R), Major Burns
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: This position also involves some kind of need for a veteran presence, which is why Johnson gets the nod over Burns and Moore. But we absolutely could see a scenario where either of the last two sneak onto the 53.
On the 53: K Riley Patterson, P Bradley Pinion, LS Tucker Addington
Changes from projection 3.0: None
Analysis: Once Zane Gonzalez was placed on IR (and subsequently released with an injury settlement), it makes things pretty simple here.

title: Report Card: Grades from Dolphins' Forgettable Day Against the New York Giants
full_text:
If the preseason opener for the Miami Dolphins was one step forward, this week was a sobering reminder of what it can be like to take two steps back.
During both the joint practice session and the game Saturday against the New York Giants, it was clear what team is on the cusp of making a run out of their rebuild and into the postseason.
The Dolphins were not that team. They were outclassed in almost every possible measure in the game Saturday. The Giants piled up 41 minutes of possession, and ran 79 plays to the Dolphins’ 36.
If there was something the Dolphins did well Saturday, it was get out of the game.
The good news is, it’s still the offseason. Malik Willis and several other key contributors did not suit up, but the grades for this week’s performance are certainly going to reflect a team that did not look ready for battle when the ball was kicked.
With Malik Willis in street clothes for the game Saturday, it was Cam Miller who got the nod to start. Quinn Ewers was out of the lineup as he’s nursing an injury, and Willis got his work done during the joint practice session earlier in the week.
Miller completed 6 of his 10 pass attempts for 60 yards and was sacked twice. He added 18 more yards with his legs before giving way to Mark Gronowski who only attempted five passes of his own.
The Dolphins’ passing offense looked mostly inept with nearly half of their yardage coming on one completion to Kevin Coleman.
If Willis were to miss time during the season, the Dolphins are going to be in trouble. They’re in even bigger trouble if Ewers goes down.
Miami’s top two rushers were their quarterbacks. That tells you all that you need to know.
Jaylen Wright had six carries for 9 yards. Ollie Gordon had four carries for eight yards. Overall, the Dolphins carried the ball 18 times for 50 yards, and Jaylen Wright lost a fumble, one of the four fumbles the Dolphins had on the day.
Again, some key players did not play, but that’s an unacceptable effort that does not inspire much confidence. The Dolphins are back to the drawing board in their run game.
Kevin Coleman made the biggest play of the Dolphins when he hauled in a 30-yard reception. Coleman was the only player who played Saturday to catch more than one pass. Of the six receivers who caught a pass Saturday, only three recorded more than 10 yards. The passing game was as anemic as the run game against A Giants team who proved to be significantly ahead of the Dolphins this week.
Tutu Atwell had a drop and failed to come up with another catchable ball and Jalen Tolbert was called for holding on a running play.
Without much room to move in the run game, the tight ends are an extension of that. Will Kacmarek has a chance to become a focal point in the run game, and was credited as an above average blocker in 11 potential snaps. Kacmarek and Seydou Traore combined for two catches for 6 yards. That fit in with the rest of the offense.  Jeremiah Franklin was officially targeted once, but did not catch a pass.
While this won't factor in to the offensive grades, it is worth monitoring that Traore and Kacmarek both played multiple special teams snaps. Traore had nine, while Kacmarek had seven. Cole Turner added nine snaps on special teams while Franklin only had one. Oftentimes, that can be the tiebreaker between making the roster versus not. That could be where a job is won during the final week of the preseason.
There were no holes to run through in the run game. Cam Miller was sacked twice, and the passing game was inept.
The identity of this Dolphins team revolves around its offensive line. The only offensive line starter who played was rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor, but he was done after three plays. That does not account for the inability to move the ball at all. No, it’s not as if the quarterback was getting drilled on every play. It’s also true that there was nothing going for Miami’s offense Saturday. It’s hard to give any portion of the offense a grade higher than a D.
Miami’s offense was bad in the game Saturday. Its defense was almost as putrid, allowing the Giants to pile up 41 minutes of time of possession. It’s not as if the Giants had a dominant phase of their game, they just were able to execute a death by thousand paper cuts offense.
New York’s run game was led by Devin Singletary, who averaged 5 yards per carry. The Giants as a whole only averaged 3.7 yards per carry on the ground.
What was alarming, was the lack of big plays. In more than 70 plays the Dolphins had just one sack and four TFLs. That’s not enough plays even if the starters were kept out.
The linebacker corps helped keep the Dolphins marks in the run game respectable. As previously mentioned, the Giants did not pile up a ton of yards on the ground, and averaged less than 4 yards per carry. Willie Gay Jr. had five solo tackles and one TFL during his time on the field.
The biggest storyline this group is an unfortunate one as ascending linebacker Trey Moore left the game with an injury. He was unable to put any weight on his leg before leaving the field on a cart. The ramifications of that injury could be devastating in the coming weeks.
Jackson Woodard had one of the highlights of the day, recovering a fumble from Tyrone Tracy to secure the Dolphins’ only takeaway of the day.
There might be nothing that Jameis Winston wants more than to put the ball in harm’s way. Winston has proven himself to be a capable backup in the NFL, but does have a propensity to turn the ball over.
Against Miami’s defensive backs? Winston was comfortable as he sliced through Miami’s defense for 150 yards on 21 pass attempts. He did not take a sack, and a good portion of his completions were not contested.
Brandon Allen and Jake Haener finished 16-for-21 during their time in relief of Winston. The Giants played without their top receivers outside of Darius Slayton and the current version of Odell Beckham Jr. In 42 pass attempts, the Dolphins were credited with just two PBUs, and did not take the ball away. There just was a lot to be desired in the secondary in the game Saturday.
If one of the best players on the field during a game is a punter, chances are the game did not go very well. The game Saturday was no exception. Bradley Pinion was busy early and often, kicking the ball away seven times. He averaged 45.4 yards-per-punt with two that were downed inside the 20. That included a long of 57 yards to help flip the field. Those are small things that might matter in a game that was closer. Unfortunately, it was just a positive footnote in an otherwise forgettable day for the Dolphins.
In addition to Pinion, Riley Patterson drilled a 53-yard field goal for the Dolphins’ lone points of the day. That gives the special teams far and away the highest mark of the day. However, Pinion even had some tough moments as he shanked a 15-yard punt late in the second quarter that gave the Giants prime field position leading to a field goal. ,
The punt team also gave up two punt returns of more than 10 yards, and Tahj Washington muffed a punt on the final play of significance in the game. Hey, when nothing is going right, nothing is going to go completely right, right?

title: Dolphins Snap Count Observations for Giants Game: Rookies Get a Taste
full_text:
Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley was satisfied with the work his front-line players got in the joint practice against the New York Giants, but he still wanted his rookies to experience the feel of a game.
It's why all of the 13 draft picks, except for third-round wide receiver Chris Bell, saw action in the 26-3 loss at Hard Rock Stadim on Sunday, though they were cameos for a lot of players.
And even Bell was in uniform for pregame warmups, even though Hafley said there never was a thought that he would play in the game considering he has yet to be cleared for full contact.
"I thought it was really good for him," Hafley said. "The whole routine is different in this league, and I wanted him to feel it, go through it, so if he doesn’t get to play in a preseason game, when he does play in a real game, it's not the first time. But he was not going to play today. Just like our guys who played a lot of snaps on Thursday, we weren't going to play them today."
For early picks like Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez and Caleb Douglas, it also looked like an issue of giving them the home game experience, however briefly, because none of them reached 10 snaps. Fourth-round pick Trey Moore played only two snaps, but that's because he went down with an ankle injury.
The list of players who sat out, according to the official NFL gamebook, was quite larger than that in the preseason opener against Washington and consisted of QB Malik Willis, WR Malik Washington, CB JuJu Brents, EDGE Josh Uche, QB Quinn Ewers, Bell, LB Jordyn Brooks, CB Darrell Baker Jr., LB Tyrel Dodson, RB De'Von Achane, CB Storm Duck, EDGE Chop Robinson, EDGE Robert Beal Jr., T Patrick Paul, C Aaron Brewer, C Jim Bonifas, G Jonah Savaiinaea, T Austin Jackson, DT Kenneth Grant, T Kevin Cline, TE Ben Sims, DT Zach Sieler, DT Zeek Biggers, DT Jordan Phillips, and EDGE Clelin Ferrell.
The biggest takeaways from the snap counts in a game where non-rookie starters and front-line players are kept out usually involves the veterans with a lot of snaps or very few.
Here's what caught our eye from that standpoint:
-- This has to start with veteran wide receivers Tutu Atwell and Jalen Tolbert, the two free agent acquisitions. Both of them played about half the offensive snaps, which clearly indicates their spot on the 53-man roster is far from secure. On the contrary, it's clear both are in danger, if not outright on their way out.
-- On the flip side, it's not a good sign (barring an injury issue during the game) for Theo Wease Jr. or rookie free agent Donaven McCulley that each got only three snaps on offense. McCulley did play 10 snaps on special teams, but it's still probably not very encouraging for him.
-- While they took part in the joint practice, we can only assume some kind of medical issue with both Kevin Cline and Jim Bonifas for them not playing because they clearly aren't roster locks, so the Dolphins should have wanted at least a little look at them. As it was, tackle Caedan Wallace and Josh Priebe played every snap on the offensive line against the Giants, with Priebe sliding over to center to replace Andrew Meyer for the final six snaps.
-- Tackles Gottlieb Ayedze and Marques Cox each played only snaps, which doesn't bode well for them considering Charlie Heck played 30 snaps at tackle.
-- It remains questionable how many running backs the Dolphins will keep, but Carlos Washington Jr. clearly has the edge over Donovan Edwards considering Washington got 10 offensive snaps and Edwards was the only non-specialists whose only snaps came on special teams.
-- We also should watch the tight end situation, where fifth-round pick Seydou Traore got only four snaps on offense but nine on special teams. Even recent waiver pick-up Jeremiah Franklin got more offensive snaps with six.
-- On defense, what has to stand out is linebacker Stephen Dix Jr. playing 34 snaps in the second half after not even joining the team until Friday. Steve came in, met him, and he started the whole second half where we had to tell him the call, he had to give the call, then we had to tell him what to do on every single play," Hafley explained. "So we were able to play only like two calls in the second half, which has never happened to me in my life. So I just give him credit for going out and fighting. That's what the preseason is all about, to find out who those guys are.
-- Safety Dante Trader Jr. got a long look in this game, with 36 defensive snaps plus 10 special teams, but this wasn't about a job audition so much as getting him into the flow after he sat out the Washington game with an injury.
-- With a much longer injury list on defense than offense, more familiar names were forced to play significant snaps in this game, but it still was interesting to see EDGE David Ojabo and LB Willie Gay Jr. get 36 and 37 defensive snaps, respectively.
-- Major Burns (34) getting more snaps than Louis Moore (26) in a case where both young safeties still are in prove-it and earn-it mode would suggest Burns is ahead of the rookie free agent from Indiana at this point.
-- We did find it interesting that cornerback Jason Marshall Jr. played, albieit only for a while, despite having been a starter all summer and not being a rookie. It's not like the Dolphins were short on cornerbacks for this game, so perhaps there was something Hafley and his staff wanted to see.

title: Four Winners And Four Losers in the Miami Dolphins Preseason Loss Against the New York Giants
full_text:
Now that the second game of the preseason is in the books for the Miami Dolphins, it's time to look at those who left a decent impression and those who are running out of time to prove that they belong here.
With most of the big-name starters out for this game, it opened the door for Miami's reserves to get the spotlight. The opportunity presented itself, but a 26-3 loss to the New York Giants only reinforced the constant criticism of the Dolphins' depth.
Again, it's wise to never overreact to what you witness in the preseason. In this instance, however, it would be nice to have something to overreact to. And the defense isn't safe, either. At the very least, some names on both sides of the ball walked away from this with something to be proud of.
Let's address the elephant in the room: There's no clear-cut winner to come from this offense. To say Coleman is a major winner is a stretch, but from the limited sample size we saw, at least there was some good.
Two catches for 32 yards off five targets isn't amazing, but his 30-yard one-handed grab while being interfered with might have been the only offensive bright spot of the game. It brings a similar vibe to the reception that Caleb Douglas pulled off against Washington a week ago.
The fifth-round pick out of Missouri appears to be keeping up the new tradition of rookie receivers making spectacular catches in the preseason. For Miami's sake, they could use even more of these young receivers taking advantage of the opportunities given to them.
With De'Von Achane not playing in this game and Ollie Gordon II exiting early with an injury, this was Wright's moment to prove that he should be considered the main backup runner.
That did not happen. Even before Gordon got injured, the running game looked off. Wright did not fix the issue, recording 9 yards on six carries. More egregious than that, however, was his fumble, having the ball stripped away on first contact and adding to his consistent problems with ball security.
On special teams, Wright looked decent with a couple of kick returns. But the depth of the running back position has taken a massive hit. If Gordon is seriously hurt, Wright did not do himself any favors in making people believe he can be the main backup.
Woodard had a sneaky good performance in this game with an exceptional play that has done great PR - a fumble recovery in the red zone that killed a drive that began on Miami's 39-yard line. Similar to Coleman's catch, it might have been the biggest highlight on defense the whole night.
Woodard didn't see a ton of action in this game, but he was fast and physical when he was near the ball. He racked up five total tackles, four of them being on his own. He was one of the few defenders who stood up to New York's ground game. On special teams, he made a pair of tackles on punt coverage, though one of them was negated by a holding penalty.
He came into this summer trying to earn a spot on the practice squad, and that's where he'll most likely end up. But he led the team in total tackles last week and kept up the momentum against the Giants. If he can pop off one more time in the preseason against Atlanta, he might just sneak into the 53-man roster.
It almost seems unfair to note either quarterback as one of the biggest losers of this game because of weapons like Tutu Atwell struggling from the jump. This has been a brutal summer for Atwell, who ended the day with no yards on no receptions — straight cardio.
The story of the night for Atwell was his inability to reel in targets. He had two drops against the Giants — one was contested, while the other was a straight miss on third down, which would have been helpful considering Bradley Pinion had to punt from inside the end zone to close out that drive.
Miami almost needs to be grateful for what they've gotten out of the rookie receivers so far in the preseason, because a lot of the veteran pass-catchers they've brought in haven't lived up to expectations. Atwell is, unfortunately, high on that list.
The quarterback room needed someone to give it hope in case something were to happen to Malik Willis. Quinn Ewers is still dealing with a groin injury, so the Dolphins turned to Miller once again and got clear improvement from a week ago.
Miller's performance was miles better than what he and Ewers put on last week, especially considering the shortcomings of just about everyone around him. He recorded 60 yards off six completions with no interceptions. Both of his sacks were nearly impossible to avoid, and he can't control the drops his receivers managed.
He threw some accurate passes and wasn't afraid to get out of the pocket, leading the team on the ground with 18 rushing yards. That said, his decision-making is still under question, with some completions just so happening in double coverage.
Yet another week where the backup offensive linemen didn't impress, and they got significantly more time to do so against the Giants. Heck struggled to contain the Giants' pass rush, and even when Gordon managed a gritty run before he got hurt, Heck wiped it off the board with a holding penalty.
Since Heck was signed back in March as an unrestricted free agent, he's been an experiment that has struggled all camp. There have been little to no flashes of progress in either preseason game, though you can say the same thing for a good chunk of the reserve linemen Miami has to offer.
Yep, we're at this point as far as winners go. Miami only scored three points today, and they were off the foot of Patterson on a 53-yard field goal attempt.
Patterson was certainly an accurate kicker in 2025, converting 27 of 29 field goals. The sample size is small, with just this field goal and an extra point last week against Washington. However, it looks like he's continuing to be a reliable answer on special teams, exactly what Miami wants at the position long-term after releasing injured veteran Zane Gonzalez back on August 19.
As a wide receiver, Washington made the most of his single target, a contested catch for 12 yards. But this placement is solely for his work as a returner, muffing a punt in the final two minutes to close out the game - a fitting end to Miami's performance as a whole against the Giants.
This muffed punt made no real impact on the game. But all in all, Washington is running out of time to prove that he can be a reliable weapon to the coaching staff. Miami is clearly impressed with what they've seen from Coleman, Douglas, and even Chris Bell now that he's off the non-football injury list.
Instead, this is the second straight week that Washington is featured on one of these lists, and that's not a good thing.

title: Dolphins Preseason Game 2 Instant Takeaways: Miller, Coleman, Injuries, and More
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins' shaky preseason showing continued at Hard Rock Stadium on Saturday when they faced the New York Giants in a battle featuring a whole lot of backups.
The 26-3 loss once again illustrated the Dolphins' well-chronicled but still alarming lack of depth, which wasn't helped by a couple of first-half injuries.
Unlike the preseason opener, the Dolphins didn't have a brilliant first drive on which to build because this one was rough from start to finish.
-- Zero issues from here about the idea of sitting starters for this second preseason other than the rookies — Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez included. They're young players and could benefit from the experience of a home game, even in the preseason.
-- Of course, this backfired with rookie fourth-round pick Trey Moore when he sustained an apparent ankle injury while hitting QB Jameis Winston on a pass rush. It would be easy to second-guess here and suggest the Dolphins should have sat their rookie starters as well, but that's playing the results. We'll be doing enough second-guessing the rest of 2026 that we don't know to overdo it here.
-- While Cam Miller looked better in practice the past week or so, this game showed the Dolphins have a major backup QB issue if Quinn Ewers doesn't get his game back on track. Period. As we've said with Ewers, though, it's unfair to put all the blame on Miller because it's not like he got a ton of help.
-- For one thing, the running game was brutal. And that was before Ollie Gordon II left the game with what appeared to be an oblique injury (teams aren't required to announce injuries during the preseason).
-- Jaylen Wright has had ball security issues in his time with the Dolphins, and his fumble before contact was  not ideal — to say the least.
-- Miller also wasn't helped by his receivers, most notably Tutu Atwell, whose rough summer continued. It remains very difficult to see how the former Miami high school star will make the 53-man roster.
-- The Dolphins have been churning the roster over the past couple of weeks, and maybe what we've seen with their depth in the preseason is an indication there's still work to do there. The Dolphins backups again didn't match up against the Giants backups, and that's in every facet of the game.
-- Backups or not, it's pretty depressing that the Dolphins didn't even have 100 yards of total offense in the first three quarters.
-- And on defense nobody emerged as a potential playmaker despite the Giants basically having the ball the whole game. This is why the Dolphins will keep looking for more players, like they did when they claimed a Colts cornerback on the day of the game.
-- Not sure what to make of Willie Gay Jr. getting so many snaps beyond the team being short at linebacker, but him not being able to make more of an impact perhaps what was most telling.
-- But, hey, Riley Patterson did nail that 53-yard field goal attempt in the first half.
-- So there was something positive, right?
-- And guess we should mention new linebacker Cam Riley's tackle for a 5-yard loss on a running play early in the fourth quarter too. But on the very next play Riley missed a tackle to allow an extra 6-7 yards on a 14-yard reception.
-- A muffed punt by Tahj Washington just inside the two-minute warning was a pretty fitting way to end things for the Dolphins before the Giants mercifully just kneeled to end this game — actually this mismatch.
-- This game was Exhibit A for those who want to reduce the number of preseason games because it was a tough watch. And that's being very kind.
-- The best news of all is there's only one of these left before the real games start on the second weekend of September.
-- The Dolphins, though, need to use all the time they have to upgrade their roster. This game against the Giants was just another example the non-starters just aren't good enough.

title: 10 Players to Watch in Second Dolphins Preseason Game
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will be back in action when they take on the New York Giants at Hard Rock Stadium on Saturday afternoon, and it will provide another opportunity to evaluate those players fighting for roster spots.
At this stage of the summer, GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach Jeff Hafley probably have a good idea what the bulk of the Dolphins' 53-man roster will look like, but they certainly could be swayed by strong individual performances here and there.
After the front-line players got a lot of work during the joint practice Thursday, we'd expect backups and younger players will be at the forefront for the second of the preseason games, along with some veterans who maybe have yet to cement their roster spot.
With that in mind, here is our list of 10 players to watch in this second preseason game, which kicks off at 4 p.m. ET.
Is it possible that Miller could play his way onto the 53-man roster? That remains to be determined, but the fact remains that he has looked much better in the last several days than earlier in camp, and Quinn Ewers' struggles and current groin injury maybe have opened the door for him. This is a huge game for him.
Tolbert and Tutu Atwell were the two veteran wide receivers of note the Dolphins added in the offseason, but neither has distinguished himself this summer to the point where their roster spot should be considered secure.
All rookie draft picks, regardless of what coaches might say, get a bit more leeway than other players during training camp and at roster cut time, but it doesn't mean their spot is guaranteed. And the reality is that Traore has dropped a few passes this summer and shouldn't be considered a lock to make the roster. A strong performance against the Giants could change that.
Likewise, Campbell needs to string together some good performance to make the roster as a sixth-round pick and he should get an elevated role after fellow guard James Ester was waived-injured Thursday.
Herman is a rookie like Traore and Campbell, but he was undrafted, which shouldn't get him the benefit of the doubt. Yet Herman has played himself into a position where the Dolphins coaches are going to be thinking hard about whether they should keep him as the lone fullback on the roster (instead of going the H-back route when they want to use two backs in the backfield).
Mulbah hasn't been around very long, but he's certainly looked the part, both in the preseason game against Washington and in practice. There sure does appear to be something to work with when it comes to the former Jets player.
The seventh-round pick from Iowa really has come on of late and he has played himself clearly into the picture at the fairly thin edge position. Another solid outing against the Giants could help put him over the top.
The former UFL interception leader is trying to make his way in a safety room that's lacking proven commodities and now also might include rookie fourth-round pick Kyle Louis after he got work at that position all week.
See Burns. The same comments would apply, except that Moore led major college football in interceptions last year, not the UFL. But his situation is almost identical to that of Burns.
It's going to be awfully difficult for any young defensive tackle to make the Dolphins 53-man roster when the team already has three second-year players who all were draft picks — Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phililps, Zeek Biggers — particularly considering Matthew Butler's strong training camp showing. But Cooper at the very least deserves a spot on the practice squad based on what he's shown so far and maybe he won't be cuttable if he shines against the Giants.

title: Dolphins Saturday Mailbag: Bubble, Bell, J-Rod, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of a Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag ahead of the preseason game against the New York Giants:
Who wins at the same point in the year the 2019 Dolphins or 2026 Dolphins?
Hey Adam, I’m pretty sure the 2026 Dolphins win, and I think rather decisively. Now, if we’re talking late in the season, maybe it’s a different story. But this Dolphins team looks so much better prepared to compete at the start of the regular season than the 2019 group.
From Jorge Francisco boyd:
Hi Alain, what have you seen from the safeties and the CB and who could probably have starter material among them?
Hey Jorge, what I’ve seen from the secondary is a young group that’s made some plays here and there, but also will need a lot of help from the pass rush. It’s a group that’s clearly a question mark heading into the regular season. As for players who could be starter material, you have Chris Johnson, JuJu Brents (if he can stay healthy) and maybe Dante Trader Jr. at safety. It’s definitely a group that could use some reinforcements.
Longtime admirer of your work. Which undrafted free agents do you see making the 53-man roster?
First off, thanks very much. Second, the better question might be “will any undrafted free agents make the 53-man roster?” Because right now I’m just not sure I see any of them making it. It’s funny because back in May this was touted as one of the best rookie free agent classes in the entire NFL. But right now I’d say safety Louis Moore and edge Rodney McGraw have a shot, but I don’t know that it’s a very good shot.
What’s the bar for Malik to be considered the starter for next year vs targeting a QB in the first round of next year’s draft? My thought is unless they did the unthinkable and shock the world to actually make the playoffs, then you have to target QB in round 1 next year.
I will respectfully disagree with you because I do think that the Dolphins could miss the playoffs and still not need to draft a quarterback. Making that the bar for Willis is unrealistic because this is flat out not a playoff-caliber roster and there’s only so much he can do. As I’ve said before, for me it’s not about won-loss record or stats but rather the eye test — and not my eye test, but that of Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley. They’ll know whether Willis should be their guy in 2027 or beyond regardless of stats or record.
Which vets are on the bubble and need to step up their game to make the season-opening 53?
Hey Ed, you can get that kind of info in my story on the roster tiers heading into the Giants preseason game, but names that immediately come to mind would include Jalen Tolbert, Tutu Atwell, Cameron Goode and maybe Willie Gay Jr.
Who is RB2? Is that competition something to keep an eye on?
It’s definitely a competition to watch, and it wouldn’t surprise me if it ended up that the Dolphins use Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon II almost equally. For right now, I would give Wright the slightest of edges.
How does this Giants joint practice compare with the infamous Detroit Lions one where it was universally agreed we got bullied? It feels the Giants practice was more a case of skill level discrepancy vs. not being tough enough.
Hey Kevin, the one joint practice where the Dolphins were “bullied,” if you want to use that word, was the one at Chicago and a big part of the reason was that the Bears were ridiculously physical for a joint practice. Against Detroit, the first of two joint practices was just a matter of the Dolphins being outclassed by a better team, not necessarily bullied. And, yes, the Giants didn’t “bully” the Dolphins as much as they outperformed them (at least their defense versus the Miami offense).
Hi Alain, is it time to worry about Grant and our depth in the secondary? Also am I the only one worried about Bell getting time on the field early considering his ACL injury and this season not being a contender; why the rush?
Hey Colin, it’s time to worry — actually past time — to worry about depth at just about every position. Running back and linebacker might be the only two exceptions there. As for Grant, how I would say this is that he needs to show some clear improvement in his second season and there were no clear indications it was happening before he was sidelined with his current injury. Lastly, I don’t know if “worried” is the term I’d use with Bell, but rather understanding the long term is what matters here and the Dolphins need to slow-roll him as opposed to trying to get a lot out of him early in the season. If this means the Dolphins putting him on IR at the start of the season with a designation to return, so be it. Again, the Dolphins need to play the long game here.
Hopefully I’m not too late. Mr. Poupart. I got a bone to pick with you. Na jk, but I am inquisitive to your reasoning on your JRod critiques of the Giants team practice. JRod had an athletic INT with a long return, possibly a ff and some tackles at the line of scrimmage. From what I read. I was not there. I know he was targeted early and often matched up against a TE in coverage and the Giants had some success throwing in his direction. I’ll be honest, there aren’t many Linebackers in this league who are going to look good in coverage against a pass catching TE. On the Dolphins Collective, you and Omar seemed to have an overall negative review of Mr Rodriguez but from where I sit a player who averages an INT and FF per game would not only be headed to the HOF but would be considered the greatest defensive player of all time. My question is can you gives us a more detailed critique of Jrod’s practice performance to add nuance to why you weren’t thrilled with his performance?
Hey Dana, as I disclosed on both the All Dolphins Podcast and the Dolphins Collective, my focus during the joint practice was  on the Dolphins offense and, if you’ve ever watched a joint practice you’d understand it’s impossble to see everything. In my written recap on this website, I wrote that Rodriguez had a pick but also his hands full trying to cover Likely, and that was based on what the folks watching the defense were saying and sharing. So I can’t provide you with many details about J-Rod’s practice performance other than to defer to Omar, and you can ask on the next Collective. I did see a video clip of his interception, and he caught it while falling down after tipping the ball up in the middle of the field, so I’d question the idea of a long return there.

title: Jacob Thomas’s Outlook Is Skyrocketing as Vikings Prepare for Preseason Finale
full_text:
MINNEAPOLIS, MN — Ask any regular attendee of the 2026 Vikings camp who stood out most, and you’ll find a variance in answers.
Rookie cornerback Chuck Demmings stole the show early with his physical pass-breakups and confident persona. Second-year wideout Tai Felton had explosive plays in the passing game on a near-daily basis. Rusher Demond Claiborne flashed blazing speed in the running game. Talent and storylines were easy to find wherever you looked.
But one name largely stayed under the radar while piecing together an incredibly consistent camp: Jacob Thomas.
The undrafted safety out of James Madison did the little things daily to make positive impacts and impress coaches, and with a season ending in injury to Jamal Adams , those stacked days started to carry more weight. Despite picking up the loss, Saturday’s game against the Ravens was no different.
After an impressive first preseason game against the Giants that included an interception, Thomas put together another strong showing this past weekend against the Ravens. He tied LB Jacob Roberts for the team lead in tackles with six, posted an 84.6 Pro Football Focus grade (h/t thorku), a pass break-up and almost brought in another interception. He also proved to be an absolute missile on the field (h/t VikingsFanPage).
Jacob Thomas laid the BOOM. pic.twitter.com/YoQx5dmYta
Thomas's impressive performances in the team’s two preseason games are rightfully turning heads, but they’re simply a carryover from what he’s been putting together daily in practice.
The odds are stacked against any undrafted rookie entering training camp; there’s a reason, after all, that we celebrate those who end up having successful careers. Thomas is no different, entering camp with a massive challenge ahead of him, but after three weeks of camp, he found himself taking first-team reps against Lamar Jackson in joint practice against the Ravens. Quite the NFL welcome for the 22-year-old.
The best part? He held his own and carried that over into the game on Saturday against the Ravens’ backups.  Defensive coordinator Brian Flores clearly sees something special in the young defensive back.
The Vikings need Thomas and others in the room to step up in a major way.
The safety position is one of the bigger question marks heading into 2026 as Harrison Smith’s plans and whereabouts seem to be a total mystery. The addition of Adams to the room after he initially signed as a linebacker signaled optimism that the team would be okay if the "Hitman" decided to hang it up, but his devastating quad injury against the Giants raised further doubt.
Thomas’s ability to immediately step up and naturally fit in with the first-team defense may come as a surprise to some, but this isn’t the first time he’s had the odds stacked against him after walking on at JMU before becoming a key staple of their defense.
Thomas will likely have the chance to prove himself further this Friday against the Broncos , and if he continues to play at a high level, he could see the field often on Sept. 13 against the Packers.

title: Vikings' Still Have One Glaring Unsolved Issue Heading Into Last Week of Preseason
full_text:
Now that the Vikings have played their second game of the preseason, only one more exhibition contest remains before the start of the 2026 NFL regular season. By then, head coach Kevin O'Connell should have the team ready for action.
Most of the starters sat out Saturday's 3-13 loss to the Ravens, but there was still plenty to learn from Minnesota's second preseason game. Although fans' main focus over the weekend was watching the quarterback play, that became difficult to do.
Abysmal play from the offensive line forced Minnesota's backup quarterbacks to rush throws and feel pressure more often than not, making it even more obvious that depth and talent on the offensive line are a huge issue.
Four of the starters on the Vikings' offensive line should be fine. Christian Darrisaw, Donovan Jackson, Will Fries and Brian O'Neill are returning from last season and should be ready to go for Week 1 of the regular season.
However, starting center Blake Brandel is about to embark on his first season as the full-time starter at center. He did a decent job filling in last season when Ryan Kelly was sidelined due to concussions. Now that Kelly has retired from football, it is up to Brandel to step up to fill the role this season.
Sadly, Brandel has been inconsistent during training camp and practices . He has struggled in multiple practices where he failed to get the ball to the quarterback in shotgun formation, which is an error Minnesota can't afford during the regular season.
Brandel is a question mark at the moment, but the depth behind him is even scarier.
Michael Jurgens struggled mightily against the Ravens and the Giants this preseason. He owns an uninspiring 50.4 overall grade on Pro Football Focus after allowing two pressures across 73 offensive snaps so far this preseason.
Clearly, is no safety net in case Brandel continues to struggle to get the ball to Kyler Murray.
Past Jurgens on the depth chart is rookie Gavin Gerhardt. Minnesota took Gerhardt in the seventh round of the 2026 NFL Draft, but he hasn't made much of an impression at all during training camp or the preseason, which isn't a good thing.
Minnesota is so desperate for help at center that they put guard Joe Huber in that role during training camp, when Brandel wasn't there to see how he would perform. That isn't a glowing endorsement for the backups at the position.
It wouldn't be surprising if the Vikings worked out a trade for a quality center before the start of the season. Sports Illustrated 's Trevor Ripley floated the idea over the weekend that Minnesota should trade for offensive lineman Olu Oluwatimi, who's fallen out of favor in Seattle.
The Vikings can also pick up a center who is released by another team when trimming down to the 53-man roster, as the deadline is approaching on Sunday at 5 p.m. CT.
The center plays such an important role in the NFL that the Vikings can't afford to gamble on someone they aren't completely comfortable with. Time is running out for Minnesota to solidify its offensive line this season, and there aren't many clear options at the moment.

title: Saturday’s Loss Told Vikings All They Need to Know About J.J. McCarthy and the QB2 Spot
full_text:
MINNEAPOLIS, MN — Flashback to April 25, 2024, as Vikings fans flooded into U.S. Bank Stadium for the team’s annual draft party. The franchise had recently let longtime quarterback Kirk Cousins walk to Atlanta in free agency and seemed destined to draft a new QB after acquiring a second first-round pick from Houston a few weeks before.
After four signal-callers were selected in the first nine picks, Minnesota traded up one spot with the Jets to select Michigan QB J.J. McCarthy, making him the highest-drafted QB in team history. Fans in attendance erupted in excitement, hopeful they had their homegrown franchise QB to pair with offensive guru and head coach Kevin O’Connell and an elite set of weapons. It seemed destined to work.
Then 849 days later, McCarthy took the field in that same stadium , fighting for his future with the franchise. The results? Seemingly a breaking point for even some of his most optimistic supporters. After losing the starting job to Kyler Murray, McCarthy now appears too unreliable to even be the team's backup, opening the door for journeyman Carson Wentz to jump up the depth chart.
McCarthy was simply all over the place on Saturday, missing throws that any level of QB should easily complete. His bright spots came in a truly impressive throw down the right sideline to wide receiver Tai Felton, where he navigated the pocket and stepped up through pressure to let it fly downfield for a 50-yard completion. He also had an impressive throw to wideout Myles Price towards the left sideline while getting hit that Price couldn’t bring in, which ended McCarthy’s day.
. @jjmccarthy09 steps up and slings it to @taifelton . 📺: @Fox9 | @NFL + pic.twitter.com/MHUiiqmX7V
But man, those misses. After the great throw to Price, the team failed to score in the red zone as McCarthy missed multiple throws, including an inexcusable overthrow to a wide-open Price. Another bad miss came on a throw to Jeshaun Jones over the middle.
McCarthy can’t connect with Jeshaun Jones. pic.twitter.com/w9bUVjXUsF
McCarthy would end the day 5-for-10 for 81 yards, but that stat line provides a generous telling of his performance.
This isn’t just about one game, though, as Saturday may have been the perfect encapsulation of McCarthy’s tenure in Minnesota, as one or two impressive plays sprinkled their way in amongst some absolutely brutal quarterbacking.
Just look at his one year as the team’s starter. The exciting fourth quarter in Chicago, after three rough quarters in his pro debut; a solid performance in Detroit in his return from a high ankle sprain; and showing out in Dallas after already being eliminated from playoff contention seem to be the highlights so far.
Outside of those brief moments, it’s been a lot of missed games and even more missed throws.
McCarthy’s single preseason appearance in 2024 had the fanbase incredibly excited before the team announced a few days later that he would undergo season-ending surgery for a torn meniscus. Since then, he has never recaptured the touch and accuracy he showcased in his one appearance as a rookie, and people are starting to notice.
If Kyler Murray were to miss time due to injury, can the team truly afford to take such a risk with the consistency of their backup QB? Probably not, and that's where ole reliable comes in : Carson Wentz.
I’m aware that referring to Wentz as a reliable QB seems to be quite the statement, but compared to McCarthy and Max Brosmer, he’s as steady as they come, and the Vikings are likely thankful he returned this past spring.  Wentz certainly has his flaws, and his ball placement and accuracy left much to be desired at points on Saturday. But he knows how to operate the offense while, for the most part, avoiding total disaster.
Wentz ended his day 9-for-11 for 92 yards and a 101.5 passer rating, but the value Wentz brings isn’t quantifiable by stats alone. After being at nearly every practice of training camp, the difference in processing speed and confidence between McCarthy and Wentz is vast. The game simply moves at different speeds.
While Wentz will have occasional interceptions or rough moments, his baseline level of performance is much more reliable than McCarthy's, even if he never quite reaches the same rare highs.
Carson Wentz is like the mini-van your wife convinced you to buy: safe, smart, not exciting in anyway, gets the job done. J.J. McCarthy is the hot-rod your uncle built in his garage: most fun you’ve ever had for the 30 seconds it works before it goes completely out of control…
I was very high on McCarthy when he joined the Vikings. But outside of brief glimpses of what could be, I’ve been wrong to this point.  It can be hard to admit that, especially when you’re this wrong, but we can only ignore what's in front of us for so long. The same can be said for O’Connell and the Vikings.
I’m torn on where I see things going, especially with McCarthy still only 23 years old and 10 NFL starts under his belt. But the reality is, this is becoming unsalvageable.
If the Vikings aren’t comfortable with McCarthy at QB2, would the likely day-3 trade value be worth shipping him off? Or would the team stash him as QB3 with hopes he can develop behind the scenes? The reality is, no answer is ideal, and the team will likely deal with the repercussions of this apparently failed marriage for years.
In the meantime, the franchise must do what's best for providing stability in 2026, and right now, that means naming Wentz as Murray’s backup.

title: Every Viking Who Hurt Their 53-Man Roster Odds in Loss vs. Ravens (Including Ivan Pace Jr.)
full_text:
With NFL teams mandated to trim their rosters to 53 men in less than a week's time, players are quickly running out of time to show they belong. Unfortunately, for several players, their poor showing in the Vikings' 13-3 loss to Baltimore has put their roster dreams in jeopardy .
The Vikings will once again have playoff aspirations in 2026, and every roster spot counts.  With that in mind, here are three players who may be playing themselves off the team if they can't turn things around going into the final stretch of the preseason.
Throughout the offseason, Ivan Pace Jr. has been brought up as a potential cut or trade candidate, especially after the Vikings extended Eric Wilson and added Jake Golday in the second round of the NFL Draft. Once an undrafted free-agent darling, Pace has seen his playing time drop dramatically over the past two seasons.
Despite being healthy all season, he played just 30% of the defensive snaps in 2025. And with just five tackles this preseason, he hasn't shown much to deserve more in 2026.
What complicates his situation further is the emergence of Jacob Roberts, who has consistently made plays throughout the preseason , nabbing an interception and making plays in the backfield for several stops. While Pace remains a strong special teams player, the Vikings could opt to keep just four off-ball backers in Wilson, Golday, Roberts and veteran Blake Cashman, leaving the former starter Pace looking for work elsewhere.
What a day to forget for Henry Byrd. Giving up several pressures and getting called for a critical hold on third down left the backup lineman needing a big performance next week. Byrd has been riding the bubble all summer, but Saturday might have been the nail in his coffin. Despite miraculously receiving a respectable 67.9 Pro Football Focus grade , Byrd's name was called far too much against the Ravens' second team.
While third-round rookie tackle Caleb Tiernan hasn't looked especially great either, his draft stock will be his saving grace to make the final 53. Byrd doesn't enjoy that same luxury and really needs a standout showing in the final preseason game against Denver to show he belongs.
There was always a world where the Vikings would cut bait with J.J. McCarthy and move on to Max Brosmer up to the third-string quarterback spot. But with McCarthy struggling and subsequently plummeting his trade value, it's more likely he sticks around —at least for 2026. For Brosmer, who hasn't been any better this preseason, he'll almost certainly revert to the practice squad after failing to capitalize on an extended look against Baltimore.
Minnesota's strange infatuation with the 25-year-old Brosmer has continued into 2026. After one of the worst displays of professional football against the Seattle Seahawks last year, the Vikings opted against putting him in jail for life and instead brought him back for another year in purple. Against Baltimore, Brosmer went 11-for-17 for 98 yards and a pick, and brought the Vikings' so-called quarterback depth further into question .
