title: 3 Things to Watch When Saints Face Rams in Preseason Week 2
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face the Los Angeles Rams in their second preseason game at 3 p.m. Saturday at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
New Orleans is coming off a 24-20 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in its preseason opener, while the Rams won their first preseason game 20-12 over the Kansas City Chiefs.
Key storylines for the Saints include the ongoing backup quarterback competition and the emergence of potential roster locks. Saturday's matchup offers a critical look at the following three areas as training camp continues.
That is question No. 1 for a lot of people, and for good reason.
Spencer Rattler was the backup quarterback to Tyler Shough heading into the first preseason game against the Jacksonville Jaguars . However, Zach Wilson outplayed Rattler in that game, which ultimately led to a change in the rotation, with Wilson taking the first snaps with the second-team offense.
After that, Wilson took the first reps with the combined second- and third-team offense. Is that a sign that a rotation has taken place? Well, Wilson may be expected to go on the field first, but he still has to outplay Rattler if he wants to win the backup quarterback job and make the final 53-man roster.
In a crowded receiving corps, standing out by any means necessary is essential — a challenge wide receiver Bub Means is actively meeting.
During last week's preseason matchup against the Jaguars, Means paced the offense with four receptions for a team-leading 77 yards. His performance featured a 28-yard reception that initially appeared to be a touchdown before being overturned on video replay.
Pro Football Focus (PFF) named Means the Saints’ highest-graded wide receiver against Jacksonville last Saturday, with an 81.0 grade. Beyond his receiving numbers, he impressed the coaching staff with the finer details of his game. He also earned a standout 84.7 run-blocking score from PFF, trailing only left tackle Asim Richards .
Last week, Means and Wilson were the breakout stars offensively, as their connection in the passing game drew extra attention to them for the rest of training camp.
Defensive end Michael Heldman has been a training camp darling, but his two sacks against the Jaguars last week have made some predict him as a lock for the 53-man roster.
Linebacker Jaylan Ford and defensive back Jayden Price also locked in their place among the second team.
With the injuries in the running back room, could Kendre Miller and Devin Neal remind people they are still here? Can Ty Chandler show the Saints that the 86-yard kickoff return to open the game last week was no fluke?
Could we have a breakout performance from wide receivers Kevin Austin or Trey Palmer ?
We will find out on Saturday.

title: Saints Stock Watch: 3 Saints Players Who Are Trending in the Wrong Direction
full_text:
During the NFL preseason, players must perform well or risk being cut from the roster, unless they hold a guaranteed starting role.
Several New Orleans Saints players excelled Saturday, with some delivering surprise performances while others continued a steady positive trend.
The following players saw their stock fall after last week’s action.
Spencer Rattler was the backup quarterback to Tyler Shough heading into the first preseason game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. However, Zach Wilson outplayed Rattler in that game , which ultimately led to a change in the rotation, with Wilson taking the first snaps with the second-team offense in the joint practice against the Rams on Thursday.
Rattler was 8-for-11, but for only 42 yards as most of Rattler’s completions were conservative throws. He also fumbled the ball away giving it right back to the Jaguars on a strip sack deep into Saints territory in New Orleans’ 24-20 loss to Jacksonville Jaguars last Saturday.
Second-year center/guard Torricelli Simpkins III had been steadily climbing the depth chart during the first two weeks of training camp, but his momentum stalled during the preseason opener against the Jaguars.
His struggles began with a shotgun snap that nearly went to the running back instead of his quarterback. Later, he was beaten cleanly by a swim move up the middle, resulting in a sack of Wilson.
Although Charlie Smyth served as the New Orleans Saints kicker during the second half of the season where he made 12 of his 16 kicks, he faces a difficult path to the 53-man roster.
The kicking competition remained tight throughout training camp, with Tanner Brown holding a marginal lead. However, Saturday’s preseason game against the Jaguars provided the first clear separation between the two candidates.
Smyth converted two extra points but missed a 52-yard field goal attempt. Brown, conversely, was successful on both of his attempts from 29 and 49 yards.
Following Smyth’s miss, the statistical advantage has shifted toward Brown as he has made 35 of his 40 kicks, a rate of 87.5%. Smyth, on the other hand, has converted 35 of 44 kicks, or 79.5%.
That’s a small margin, sure. But the more you miss, the more a kicker will likely be cut.

title: Giants Aren't Done Exploring Making Trades
full_text:
A week after trading offensive lineman Daniel Faalele to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a sixth-round pick, the New York Giants might not be done yet trying to make deals.
“Yeah, I mean, if we could, we'd do it as much as we possibly could,” head coach John Harbaugh said on Monday. “We'd like to take advantage of the opportunities, if they'll come up, as much as we can.”
The Faalele deal came as a surprise to many, largely because he was trending toward not making the roster to begin with, plus the Giants were able to get a concrete sixth-round pick with zero conditions attached.
The additional pick gives the Giants six in next year’s draft, with the team, again, looking to add more picks wherever they can.
“We do have some guys,” Harbaugh said of the possibility without going into specifics. “We're kind of deep in a few positions, and maybe that'll happen. It doesn't happen that often, but maybe it will.”
That the Giants are in a position to make a deal speaks to the job Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen did in assembling the training camp roster.
“You know, it's not too often you can trade a player for a sixth-round pick in the middle of training camp,” Harbaugh said. “But sometimes teams have needs.
“Any time you can add picks, it's a valuable thing. It's a future thing. Doesn't seem like much now, but it'll matter on Day 3 of the draft. It'll be something that we'll be happy we've got.”
Among the leading possibilities for a trade are kicker Ben Sauls, one of receiver Darius Slayton or Darnell Mooney, and perhaps an offensive lineman like center/guard Jake Kubas and inside linebacker Darius Muasau.
But for a trade to happen, the Giants will obviously need to find a team that isn’t willing to be patient and wait out the waiver-wire game.
As for the Giants, if they can swing another deal or two and land a compensatory pick, Big Blue could put itself in position to have a full hand of seven picks—and then some.
They're also in position to acquire a fourth-round pick if former offensive lineman Austin Schlottmann, now with the Tennessee Titans, wins and holds the starting center job there.
“The draft is a little bit of a numbers game,” Harbaugh said. “The more swings you can take, the more chances you have to hit on guys. So, having more picks over time, I hope that's something that we're able to accumulate and have a lot of picks year to year.”

title: Malik Nabers Sheds the Red Jersey, but Harbaugh Won't Guarantee Receiver's Status for Week 1
full_text:
One gets the feeling that the New York Giants know it’s going to happen: that receiver Malik Nabers will indeed be ready for Week 1 of the regular season, especially after the receiver took the next step in his return by shedding the red “no-contact” jersey after wearing it last week and participating in 11-on-11 and 7-on-7 drills.
Malik Nabers with the white jersey at practice today pic.twitter.com/2GRssvh3Vk
But head coach John Harbaugh stopped short of declaring Nabers’s readiness for the start of the regular season, which will be here in a little under four weeks.
“I don’t want to make any kind of statements like that,” Harbaugh said when asked if Nabers was trending toward being ready for Week 1 of the season, barring any setbacks.
“I think it’s reasonable to assume that. Those are all things to assume based on watching him practice. The only thing I know more than you guys do is what the trainers and doctors tell me about his rehab, and he’s doing really well with it. He’s strong, in a good place. How he gets through practice and how ready he is to play and protect himself is really based on practice.”
Nabers will obviously need to take some hits during practice as the next step in his return, which he didn’t do during Monday’s shorts and shells practice.
Come Tuesday, when the Giants are next scheduled to be in pads, it’s anticipated he’ll get to experience live contact (although not tackling to the ground) for the first time in a practice.
"It'll be a protect each other kind of deal, but that'll be true for everybody right now,” he said. “We'll be in this mode this week; we'll be a little more, as far as the contact part of it, probably a little more in-season-ish in terms of taking care of one another.”
Despite Harbaugh’s reluctance to make a definitive statement about Nabers, it’s not hard to get excited about the increasing likelihood of the third-year receiver being ready for Sunday Night Football against the Cowboys.
“I thought he looked good,” Harbaugh said. “He was moving well–probably moving the best we've seen him look. It was a good practice for him today. Got the red shirt off. That was a good step.”
The players have apparently voted on the Giants' new leadership council, and eight guys were identified as part of that group : quarterbacks Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston, outside linebacker Brian Burns, safety Jevon Holland, inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, left tackle Andrew Thomas, tight end Chris Manhertz, and punter Jordan Stout.
The group was spotted speaking with Harbaugh about what the coach described as logistical matters after the team concluded practice. It’s unclear, though, if those eight players are also viewed as the team captains.
“We've been doing it for a long time,” Harbaugh said of having a leadership group. “I do try to emphasize to the team that everybody's a leader and everybody has every opportunity to speak their mind. Talk to anybody in the organization about anything they need to, any suggestions they have.”
Besides the team leadership being defined, what’s also noteworthy about this development is that Manhertz, who some may have thought was in danger of losing his roster spot, appears to be safe for the coming season; otherwise, he wouldn’t have been part of the discussion.
Receiver Jalin Hyatt (ankle/leg), offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu (leg), tight end Tanner Conner (unknown), receiver Braxton Berrios (soft tissue), guard Francis Mauigoa (stinger), right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (unknown), defensive lineman Shelby Harris (unknown), and linebacker Jack Kelly (unknown) did not practice.
Harbaugh said that Eluemunor will be fine and “should be back tomorrow (Tuesday),” as should Mauigoa.
Cornerback Colton Hood (quad) returned to practice.
Tight end Theo Johnson collided with outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux during practice and appeared shaken up. “I think he's okay,” Harbaugh said. “Didn't get a report back that it was serious, but they'll look at it. I haven't talked to him since, so I'll go in and find out here when we get done.”

title: John Harbaugh Opens Up on the Hardest Part of Cutdown Week: 'Very Challenging'
full_text:
And just like that, the dog days of training camp for the New York Giants are behind them as they enter the final week of the preseason, a critical week for head coach John Harbaugh, the coaching staff, and the players.
There are roster decisions to be made, regular-season routines to get used to, and, through it all, improvements still rule the daily agenda.
It’s a critical point for Harbaugh, who, in recognizing the human element of what’s to come, knows that in a matter of a week, he’ll have to be the bearer of bad news to almost half of his rostered players who have given the team everything they have, only to eventually learn that it wasn’t enough to continue on their journey with Big Blue.
John Harbaugh spoke at length when asked roster cuts looming "Everybody's pulling for everybody. Guys that are competing for the same position - they're rooting for each other. You see so many of the best things about human mature come out on a football team" pic.twitter.com/HJ1kQMltF6
“We tell them your best dream is not too big; in fact, it might not even be big enough,” Harbaugh, in response to a question posed by New York Giants On SI, said in a lengthy answer.
“If they're not laughing at your dream, then it's not big enough either, so say it, speak it, and go for it. These guys have really done that. I feel like they've really put that out there and they've talked to each other; they've committed to helping one another achieve each other's dreams. Everybody's pulling for everybody.”
The supportive structure Harbaugh described is precisely the type of culture he sought to build when hired by the Giants to lead the franchise out of its modern-day Wilderness Years.
The bond the team has built has been evident. There’s been nary a training camp scuffle, and there's also been more and more cross-training, to the point where offensive and defensive players have come together to share feedback and tips to help each other improve, while even players in direct competition share feedback between plays.
“You see it on the sideline, you see it between guys who are competing for the same position,” he said. “They're rooting for each other and helping each other along. I mean, you see so many of the best things about human nature come out on a football team, believe it or not.
“And maybe people that aren't a part of the sport would have a tough time believing that, but I think those of us who've been around the sport understand that this is how it works and it's a cool thing.”
Harbaugh, now in his 19th year as head coach, undoubtedly finds having to tell guys who have given everything they have that it wasn’t good enough one of the most gut-wrenching aspects of the job.
There is no easy way to do that, after all, but the veteran head coach, in his message to those who don’t make the initial 53-man roster, wants to leave those players with hope for the future.
“This week, to your point, is a very challenging week because there will be guys that won't be here after this week. Now, maybe they'll come back–we brought (defensive lineman) Ben (Barten) back, the defensive lineman who just got released by the Jets and came back to us again here this week,” Harbaugh said.
And if they don’t, Harbaugh said he hopes the young men who do receive a visit from “The Turk” understand that it’s not so much about what they didn’t accomplish as about how far they’ve come.
“How many of us who played football wouldn't have loved to have had an opportunity to be in a football camp in the National Football League? To be invited, to get a tryout even? All the not-so-good players like me would have loved that,” he said.
“I tell these guys, ‘You are the very best. Every single player here in this room is a great football player.’ You talk about the top .0001 percent of football players, even athletes, in the world that are going to be in a football camp.
“But then there are levels to that too, just like there are levels to anything else. I would say everybody, every one of our guys, whether they're here the next week or they're not, will look back and say they did their very best, they put their best foot forward, and it's something that they can look back on really for the rest of their life proudly.”

title: Tyler Nubin Tabbed as Giants' Breakout Candidate by PFF Amid Safety Competition
full_text:
After a disappointing second season, New York Giants safety Tyler Nubin is in a battle for his starting job .
Offseason additions Ar'Darius Washington and Jason Pinnock have been making strong cases to overtake Nubin , earning attention from head coach John Harbaugh in recent weeks.
Pro Football Focus writer Gordon McGuinness isn't concerned about the mounting pressure on Nubin, having named Nubin as the Giants' top breakout candidate for 2026, citing the safety’s slight improvement in his PFF coverage grade from 58.1 in his rookie season to 60.0 in his second year.
“Entering his third NFL season, don’t be surprised if Nubin generates more buzz, particularly if he can recapture the level of run defense he showed as a rookie," McGuinness concluded.
With 98 tackles and a forced fumble in just 13 games in his rookie season, Nubin looked like a long-term starter for the Giants. Big Blue tried to cover up his coverage deficiencies by using him as a box defender on nearly half of his snaps.
Those strengths were much less apparent in his second season. Nubin missed 16.9% of his tackles (up from 9.4% as a rookie) and made 78 tackles despite playing more snaps. He was part of the problem in the Giants' run defense, which ranked near the bottom of the league .
Nubin will have to adjust his game to thrive in new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson's system . The safety was much stronger in man coverage than in zone coverage last season. He earned a PFF grade of 64.5 in man and a grade of 54.1 in zone.
Wilson is anticipated to use zone coverage at a significantly higher rate than previous coordinator Shane Bowen did. Last season, his Tennessee Titans ran zone coverage on 75% of their snaps , while the Giants were down at 63.6%, near the bottom of the league.
Wilson has been encouraged by Nubin's progress this offseason.
"Tyler Nubin is getting better,” he said recently. “His biggest challenge right now is just looking at the right things. When he consistently looks at the right things, he makes plays. So, that's been his focus, but he's flashed.”
Before naming Nubin for a breakout campaign, he needs to secure the Giants' starting strong safety role. If he can make the adjustments that Wilson's system requires, he'll be set up for the breakout that McGuinness projects.
If not, his time as a starter may be limited.

title: Giants Waive Wide Receiver Ryan Miller, Clearing Room on Crowded Depth Chart
full_text:
The New York Giants have thinned out their crowded wide receiver room by waiving wide receiver Ryan Miller, the team announced.
Miller, an undrafted free agent out of Furhman who signed with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2023, joined the Giants' practice squad after being waived by the Bucs. He did not contribute to the Giants' offense, however, as he sat on the practice squad for the duration of that season.
He re-signed with the Giants on a reserve/futures deal this past offseason, but with the team having a crowded receiver room, Miller was stuck near the bottom of the depth chart.
In two games this summer, he caught one of his two targets (both of which came in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings) for 14 yards.
His other pass target was intercepted by the Vikings, Miller having failed to attempt to swat the ball away.
Overall, Miller appeared in 41 snaps on offense, 32 of which came in this past weekend’s preseason game against the Miami Dolphins.
Miller also appeared in 10 snaps on special teams for the Giants this summer, with his main contributions coming on the punt return unit, where he had 7 of those snaps.
With one more week to go in the preseason before setting the initial 53-man roster, Miller, who was listed as the last receiver on the team's unofficial depth chart, wasn’t going to make it given the crowd in the receivers room.
Despite his hard work, he  he never rose from the third-string offense, so unless there was an injury involved in this transaction, Miller now gets a chance to catch on elsewhere.
Miller, who was initially added more so for special teams, also didn’t do anything to distinguish himself in that area this summer.
The Giants appear to have several other candidates who can be devoted to special teams. They also still have a crowded receiver room, the lineup of which is starting to crystalize.
Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields, Darius Slayton, and Calvin Austin III appear to be the locks at the receiver position. That would leave the Giants with two or three more slots to fill from a group that includes Odell Beckham Jr., Braxton Berrios, Darnell Mooney, and Dalen Cambre.
The Giants now have an opening on their 90-man training camp roster. We will update this entry once we learn who filled the spot.

title: John Harbaugh is Not Ready to Give Up on Tyrone Tracy Jr. Despite Costly Mistakes
full_text:
When it comes to New York Giants running back Tyrone Tracy Jr., who has had a rough couple of weeks, head coach John Harbaugh isn’t ready to throw the baby out with the bathwater.
Tracy, for those who missed it, committed two significant gaffes in the team’s first two preseason games that usually lead to a running back being benched.
Against the Vikings in the preseason opener, Tracy whiffed on a blitz pickup against Vikings safety Jay Ward, the hit rocking quarterback Jaxson Dart and sending him to the blue medical tent for the sixth time in his NFL career.
Then last week against the Dolphins, Tracy lost the handle on a wet football inside of the Dolphins’ 10-yard line; Miami recovered the ball to snuff out a Giants scoring drive.
“I don't think you say, hey, a bad play or even two bad plays nullifies a whole career body of work, so to speak,” Harbaugh said Sunday.
“And even in the game, he played well. He had numerous good runs, catches—pass protection pickups were good, but he had the one play that's the one thing you don't want to have as a running back. And in the last two games, he's had two things you don't want to have. So, nobody feels worse about it than he does.”
Tracy, who is seeking his third straight season with 1,000+ yards from scrimmage, is very much aware of his mistakes and is one to attack his weaknesses with vigor, which Harbaugh said he appreciates.
But there is still the balancing act that Harbaugh, who said that a football team can’t have those missteps, must strike.
It’s often easier said than done, however.
“First of all, you can't let your emotions get involved, and you've got to try to take everything in perspective. Perspective of the player, the perspective of the big picture of the room, what you need in the room, and what's best for the team,” he said.
“There's just a lot of variables that go into that, so as best as you can.”
Yet at the same time, it’s perfectly understandable if the head coach’s trust in the running back is shaken just a bit to the point where Tracy, the team’s fifth-round pick in the 2024 draft, potentially slides down the running back depth chart.
This is especially the case given Najee Harris's arrival and Devin Singletary's strong showing in the win over Miami.
If Harbaugh's faith in Tracy is shaken to where he’s considering a change in the pecking order, the head coach wasn’t ready to admit as much.
“It's ongoing right now. It's still to be determined over the course of the next week to see exactly where it shakes out, and we'll keep working at it,” he said.

title: Giants Defense Grades: Deonte Banks Shows New Physicality in Dolphins Win
full_text:
The New York Giants defense wasn’t on the field very much against the Miami Dolphins–just 36 times. So the sample size for grading isn’t very large, though some stood out and others didn’t.
Having earned the start this week, Murphy rewarded the coaches’ confidence in him by delivering a team-leading four tackles.
Though we haven’t been thrilled with Murphy’s pass rush game to date, his playing instincts and nose for the football are hard to ignore.
He also has the physicality the coaches are looking for in their outside linebacker room.
We suspect if the Giants keep four at this position, it will come down to Murphy or Khalid Kareem. If it were up to us, we’d go with Murphy, whose mobility and low power are more intriguing qualities.
The other starting outside linebacker this week, Kareem has provided good, consistently physical edge play in both preseason games and has a chance to augment the lean athleticism with his big body and physicality.
We think Caleb Murphy is a little bit better at finding the ball, but Kareem’s physicality can certainly play a role.
This active but undersized outside linebacker continues to flash, attacking gaps and edges with consistent aggressiveness that is hard not to like.
Though he only got credit for one tackle, we thought Ford’s penetration on the edges, even his pass coverage against tight ends, were flash plays.
We will always appreciate his defensive temperament and his attack mentality, even if he lacks the length to be a consistent contributor.
Getting a starting assignment but only playing two series, the ball never found the first-round rookie as he played mostly pass coverage.  He still was able to assist on the game’s opening tackle.
McFadden recorded the defense’s lone turnover when he jumped on a first-half fumble.
McFadden only played a couple of series and left with this only dent on the stat sheet.
Kelly received 20 snaps at inside linebacker and had a mostly positive showing. His lone glitch came when he badly overran his gap on one cutback run that went for 15 yards, a play that was fortunately called back by a holding penalty.
Kelly filled several gaps with his long reach and recorded his lone tackle in space.   That aforementioned bad read was simply a rookie mistake, and hopefully one he’ll learn from.
One of the defense’s biggest plays of the game was Barnes reading a screen near the Miami end zone, making the solo tackle in space, and never nearly recording a safety.
It was Barnes’ lone tackle of the day, but with that said, we have little doubt that Barnes is making this team not just for his contributions on defense but more so for his special teams ability.
Though his name came up empty on the defensive stat sheet, we swear we saw Muasau get in on several late-game tackles. That said, Muasau’s ticket to a roster spot is on special teams, where he had a mostly quiet, yet solid showing.
This long-shot summer signing barely got on the field, playing just three snaps, and did not flash.
Back from his hamstring strain, Adebo started the game and responded with two tight press coverages and one tight tackle as a result of tight zone coverage.  Adebo only played two series before leaving the game for good, but they were a positive showing.
Also back from injury—Newsome had been sidelined with a knee sprain—Newsome came out fast with an instinctive run tackle, a coverage knockaway, then another edge leverage run stop for little gain, as you draw it up on the blackboard.
We loved Newsome’s fiery aggressiveness, something this room could use a whole lot more of. Newsome did little to hurt his chances of locking down one of the starting cornerback jobs on this team.
Banks knocked away two balls with tight trail coverages, then jumped into the fray with two run game tackles. Banks has been playing like a much different player this year, one who is not only full of confidence but also more physical than ever.
Banks has always had the physical goods to back up a physical style of play, but has lacked the want-to. So far this summer, he’s showing both, and we’ll take that every day.
Banks finished with the two tackles and the two knockaways before leaving after several impressive series on the field.
Another cornerback who returned from injury (knee), Phillips looked bad early on when he couldn’t find the ball while covering a go route, and then he grabbed the receiver to draw a flag. To make things worse, the receiver caught the ball for a 30-yard gain.
Coverage being a struggle at times, Phillips then showed greater effectiveness in attacking the line of scrimmage.
He blew up a slip screen out of the slot all by himself, making the tackle for no gain.  Then he run-blitzed off an edge, knifed in, and attacked the ball carrier, who seemed surprised by the ferocity of Phillips’ hit and lost the ball, which turned into the Giants’ lone defensive turnover.
We’re not sure what can be done about Phillips’ problems in coverage, but when it comes to everything else on the field, he is all-football and as physical pound-for-pound as anyone on this team.
He sees things fast, and he attacks them hard, but only if it happens around the line of scrimmage.  Trap him in space, and he becomes almost a different player. Phillips finished with three tackles in six snaps.
Getting 10 snaps at corner with the two’s and three’s, Green held up to the physical demands as always, but he wasn’t challenged in coverage at all.
Similar in style to Dru Phillips, Jones’s instinctive reactions to plays at or around the line of scrimmage are something to like about his game.
Jones isn’t as vicious a hitter as Phillips, but he is better in coverage.  He drew a hold on a wide run and made another short-gain tackle out of the slot.
Jones finished with two total tackles in limited snaps.
We’re not sure Jones has a place on this defense, but we really respect how well he sees the play and the angles he takes to limit those plays.
Getting just 13 snaps this week on defense, Black made more of an impact on special teams.
Getting three boundary snaps late in the game, we remain impressed by Woods’ size but are unsure of his ability to keep up with NFL receivers.
He’s a safety by nature, so this move to corner is in its infancy.
Continuing to be the most active of the safeties fighting for a starting job, Pinnock made one play in deep coverage.
But it was his discipline, shown in his contain against the run during the scrimmage, that was really impressive. Pinnock had one tackle on the day, but he was around the ball more often than not.
Pinnock’s competition for that starting safety job that’s up for grabs, Nubin flashed early on a deep middle throw and knocked it away.  He also had a good close against a tight end’s catch that went for little gain.
However, we did not like how slow Nubin looked attempting to close on that deep 30-yard completion that most starting safeties would have been able to knock away or intercept.
Nubin was so deliberate on his turn-and-go that it’s obvious why he’s been a target in the league for two years now, and we can see why there might be some question as to whether he’s starting material in this league.
Washington made one early run blitz from the edge and closed down the play from pursuit for the tackle.
If there’s one way to help out a floundering run defense, it’s to provide occasional edge blitzes to help out.  It’s not something to do regularly, or you could get burned, but early on it can be an effective deterrent.
Washington’s too small to plug in as a starting safety, but he’s got that Swiss Army knife element to his game that, combined with his aggressiveness, gets him near the action an awful lot of the time.
This veteran safety was once again spotted playing some press corner on the boundary. Though the ball never came his way, he looked competent enough.
Owning cornerback size, Campbell plays with a safety’s demeanor, which makes for an intriguing combination.
He’s also a good special teamer.  We…

title: Malik Nabers Could Shed No-Contact Jersey This Week, Harbaugh Says
full_text:
It’s been a long road back for New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers from his ACL injury suffered last season in Week 4. Still, the third-year receiver could be on the verge of taking yet another significant step forward toward a Week 1 return.
Head coach John Harbaugh told reporters that there was a “possibility” that Nabers, who over the last week-plus has been practicing wearing the red “no contact” jersey, could shed that garment from his locker this week.
"That's a possibility," Harbaugh said. "We'll just have to see where that's at. I don't think it's a necessity this week. We're still three weeks out from the game, the first game and then after that. We'll see where he's at this week. We'll see how he feels tomorrow."
Nabers, who is not expected to play in the preseason finale Friday night against the Jets, has been shielded from having contact in team drills.
Harbaugh has declined to mention a firm date for Nabers to take the next step, but he did say that he didn’t think the receiver would spend the rest of the summer in the red jersey.
“He'll be out of a red jersey before he plays in a game,” Harbaugh said last week. “He's going to have to get bumped around. You just have to feel that and know how to deal with it to protect yourself.”
“There are certain formulas that we use that kind of tell us what the risk factors are in practice,” he added.
“That's part of it with him. It's also to your eye. It's also how he feels, and then ultimately with the doctors. So, I think you do it slowly, and you just keep building to the point where it's not like all of a sudden he's doing something, and now he's doing everything. You work your way towards that.”
Harbaugh said that offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu was kicked in the back of the leg in the team’s 26-3 preseason win over Miami, an injury that forced him out of the game preamturely.
The good news is that the injury is not beleived to be serious and that the young offensive lineman, who has been snake-bit throughout his entire NFL career, would be day-to-day.
Harbaugh also said he anticipated having offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa, who suffered a stinger in the joint practice with the Dolphins, and cornerback Colton Hood, who was sidelined most of last week with an undisclosed ailment, back at practice this week.
Otherwise overall the Giants came out of Saturday's preseason game clean injury-wise.

title: Giants Preseason Snap Counts: Who Played the Most and What Did We Learn?
full_text:
The New York Giants are celebrating after a 26-3 win against the Miami Dolphins inside Hard Rock Stadium in the second week of the preseason.
The Giants mostly played their second string on both sides of the ball, but they were still able to dominate the Dolphins, who have one of the worst rosters in the league going into the 2026 season.
Regardless, the Giants get a massive boost with the win, as the confidence should trickle down the depth chart following a win like this.
Here's a look at the snap counts for each side of the ball, according to the NFL gamebook, and what to take away from the coaching staff's decisions about who to play:
The Giants didn't invest a lot of playing time with many starters, but they started sixth-round rookie J.C. Davis in the game, and he went the distance.
The offense was dominant throughout the game, playing 81 snaps compared to 36 for the Dolphins. Davis played extremely well, and his high level of visibility against the Dolphins likely secures his spot on the 53-man roster.
From the quarterbacks, Jameis Winston was the player most active with 38 offensive snaps. He drew the start for the Dolphins and immediately set the tone for the contest, which gave the Giants the green light to impose their will on Miami.
“Absolutely. You expect Jameis to play just like that. Jameis was in control. He ran the show. He's poised in the pocket,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said.
“He was very accurate with his passing. He played at a high level just like you'd expect him to. That's a great thing to have a quarterback like that as your number two. Jameis has been a starting quarterback in this league for a long time. He's started a lot of games. I thought he played exactly the way we’d expect him to.”
The Giants opted to keep most of their defensive starters on the sidelines for the game. The Giants only had 36 total defensive snaps, and nobody on defense played more than 24.
The starters who saw the field and are worth noting are outside linebacker Caleb Murphy, who led the way for the Giants, defensive tackle Darius Alexander, who appeared 21 times, cornerback Paulson Adebo , who was there for 20 snaps and safety Tyler Nubin, who logged 17.
Players on the defensive roster bubble made their moments count against the Giants, and it's clear that there is a lot of competition to try and make the final 53-man roster. The urgency shown against the Dolphins shows exactly where the team is, which should please Harbaugh and the coaching staff.
"Well, I mean, our guys, our younger guys, we played our backups so to speak. But there's a lot of guys fighting for jobs on this team. And I thought they came out and they made a point to try to make their case. And they did a good job of it," Harbaugh said.
Preseason snap counts don't mean a ton in the grand scheme of everything because there still has to be production during practices and training camp. The Giants treated the joint practice and the preseason as two separate practices, which is why many of the starters didn't participate in the game.
In a dominant win, the Giants had the snap counts. That may give clues as to who has an edge in the final couple of roster spots, but there is still a lot of work that needs to be done between now and the 30-roster-cut deadline this next week. That should be the true determining factor in who makes the roster and who's heading to the practice squad.

title: Giants O-Line, D-Line Preseason Week 2 Grades: Depth on Display Against Dolphins
full_text:
If, at the start of the preseason, we had told you that the New York Giants ' offensive line depth was as deep as it has been in years, would you have believed us?
Neither would we, and yet that was the case for the Giants' offensive line backups, which were no match for the Dolphins' backups. Overall, the offensive linemen gave up just four of the team’s five quarterback pressures and got good movement against Miami’s backups.
“I thought they did well,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game. “The protection was good. We ran the ball well. All that was good.”
The defensive line? Mixed results, including some carryover from last week that is becoming more of a concern. With that said, let’s get into the grades.
Getting the start at right tackle, Mbow played the entire first half and really shined with his pass-blocking.
There were a handful of running game misses that he’d like to have back, but it’s obvious Mbow is a lock for the swing tackle spot.
Though he didn’t get the start at right guard—the role went to Aaron Stinnie—Ezeudu eventually stepped right in at the position on the game’s second possession and, to be frank, he looked most comfortable there.
There were some easy power run-blocking snaps inside out of Ezeudu, who moved very well as a guard.
He also got some snaps at right tackle in the second half and looked solid enough, though there was another mental mix-up in the protection Ezeudu was involved in that led to a sack.
Also, late in the game, Ezeudu had to leave with a lower-body injury, which seems like a weekly occurrence with this snake-bit athlete.
Based on talent and skill alone, Ezeudu should make the final 53, but there has to be a trust issue with this player when it comes to his availability.
Getting the start at left tackle and going the distance, Davis played it very well throughout.
We didn’t spot a single pass-blocking loss in Davis’ game.  His run blocking had enough plus plays to earn him a passing grade there, too.
Davis has a good feel for angles and dealing with the unexpected.  It’s called football instinct, and we think Davis has plenty of it.
He’s also got the size, arm length, and balance you would want at the position, as well as the mental game—not a single flinch or tug in two games so far.
For years, this organization has struggled to find quality offensive tackles. Still, suddenly, the Giants have five legit offensive tackles on their roster, plus a longshot UDFA (Ryan Schernecke) who should end up on the practice squad as a developmental guy.
Davis, a sixth-round draft pick with legit starting potential, has obviously made this team.
Of course, there’s the matter of stepping up in class somewhere down the road that must be addressed, but against second- and third-teamers, he has been dominant.
If there’s a choice to be made at the cutdown date between Davis and Ezeudu, the choice is clear in our eyes: it’s got to be Davis.
Schernecke got some third-quarter snaps and all the fourth-quarter snaps at right tackle.  Suffice it to say that he is far from ready, but that’s to be expected given he comes from the small school program at Kutztown.
We still like how quick Schernecke is off the ball, his feistiness, his size, and his mental game, but we haven’t yet seen the mobility, balance, or athleticism required to compete at this level.
Some of his movement snaps have been hard to watch.  This kid lacks experience and strength, and there is a lot to work on here. That said, technique has gotten many a blue-collar blocker a place in this league.
Through two games, Schernecke has not allowed a sack or committed a penalty, though there have been times when he’s been living on the edge.  The practice squad beckons.
One of two starting offensive linemen to get a start this week—John Michael Schmitz was the other—Runyan, in one series, lost his first run-blocking assignment but bounced back with a bunch of smooth pass-blocking snaps, the strength of his game as always.
Where Runyan continues to struggle is in run blocking, with his 52.3 PFF grade this week the worst among the offensive linemen. Runyan has always been more of a finesse technician who excels in zone blocking rather than a mauler with heavy hands to win at the point of attack.
The Giants can get by with him at left guard if they need to, but the more we see him play, the more we are convinced that he doesn’t fit the offensive line profile that John Harbaugh has favored in the past.
Getting the start today at right guard thanks to Francis Mauigoa nursing a stinger suffered in the joint practice, Stinnie was solid in every aspect of the position.
He resembles a bowling ball out there, banging into walls and crashing into pins without ever giving an inch.
He also received some snaps at left guard in the second half and acquitted himself there well, too. If he doesn’t make this team, we’d be stunned.
Getting all of his 43 snaps at left guard, we spotted three Kubas pass-blocking losses that led to hurries and hits on his quarterback; this against Miami’s third stringers, mind you.
Though he had plenty of snaps where he mixed things up pretty well, especially on running downs, the pass-blocking misses in space were hard to ignore.
Kubas can give the team snaps at guard and center, but he still needs some additional development, which is why he might be better suited for another run on the practice squad.
Getting all of his second-half snaps today at right guard, Neal did nothing to solidify his spot on the roster.
His size and power and high first-round draft pedigree will always persuade some team to give him a shot.
Still, the lack of movement skills and the fact that he may just be too tall to play inside—his struggles with keeping his pad level low are a big problem—don’t bode well for his long-term future with this team.
Returning from a concussion he suffered early in the penultimate practice in West Virginia, the team’s de facto starter at center started and only played the first two series, leaving the game late in the first quarter.
Schmitz’ game was reliable and economical; he always seems to get his man while rarely hitting him.  The grades are there, but the physicality we suspect the coaches want is not.
Also returning from an injury-related absence that caused him to miss the preseason opener, Patrick got all the second-team snaps at center, and it was obvious to see what this veteran brings to the table.
His experience showed in his play, with zero hesitation; his reliable mental game is his greatest asset at this point in his career.  This 33-year-old, nine-year vet knows how to play the position and run an offense.
He’s not the niftiest player out there, but he’s got enough size to hold up to power and the smarts to know where to be on every snap.
A knee issue needed to be managed early in camp, making Patrick’s chances at landing the backup center role shaky. But if the trainers have that under control so it won’t be an issue moving forward, that bodes well for Patrick’s chances of a roster spot.
Shunted back to the third team with the return of Schmitz and Patrick to the field, Hudson played the majority of the second half over the ball.
We were disappointed that Hudson did not get any snaps at guard for versatility’s sake, but the young interior offensive lineman did well again in his opportunities.
He once again played his simple, clean type of game snap-to-snap with a preference for mixing things up in the pit, with just enough mobility to make the occasional block in space.  Hudson still looks like starting material to these eyes.
This veteran signed for depth purposes when Schmitz and Patrick went down, got today’s final possession and did not embarrass himself.  He ran the offense smoothly and kept everything in front of him.
Getting a start to salvage his sinking chances of making the team, Fotu worked his way into two tackles with some positive movement plays.
However, he wasn’t much of a factor in the pit, as his instinct…

title: 3 Studs & 3 Duds from Jets' Training Camp Practice (8/24): Geno Smith Builds Off Preseason Debut
full_text:
Another week, another start to New York Jets training camp. By this time next week, the organization will be down to 53 players, highlighting the job ahead for general manager Darren Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn.
However, until that time, the Jets can focus their efforts on the final few practices of training camp ahead of the preseason finale against the New York Giants. As is always the case, there are plenty of studs and duds from the day of practice.
Let's get to the list now.
New York has seen a different Geno Smith over the last week. Coming off a dominant preseason performance in which he didn't throw a single incomplete pass and led a touchdown drive, Smith was back on the field and looked quite strong in New York's move-the-ball period and in the red zone.
As always, it's important to remember that Smith can have weeks with excellent play and poor performances.
The highlight of the day was a touchdown pass from Smith to rookie Omar Cooper Jr., which displayed the former Indiana prospect's improved play. Over the last several days, though, Smith has come on. And provided Jets fans with further hope for the 2026 season.
After the first couple of weeks of spirited competition, the Jets' kicking battle has devolved into a concerning conundrum. Cade York made 3-of-5 kicks, with misses from 38 and 43 yards. Not to be outdone, Jason Sanders went just 2-of-5 with three misses all around the 40-yard mark.
While 40-yard kicks are never a guarantee, the Jets need better from this kicker battle. The longer these struggles go on, the more likely it is that New York's Week 1 kicker isn't actually on the roster.
After missing the first few weeks of camp, Ossai has been a welcome addition to the Jets' defense . Not only has he been able to generate pressure, but he's also been very good at stopping the run, an underrated reason why he was added to the organization in the offseason.
Pairing Ossai with a young edge rusher like David Bailey seems like the most obvious course of action for the Jets in Week 1. So long as Ossai continues to play well, the group should feel much better about their defensive line moving forward.
There is serious concern about the offensive line depth, especially if one of New York's most important players along the line goes down with an injury. Anez Cooper is still a developmental player, but it isn't good that Cade Klubnik was consistently pressured at practice.
Again, it might not be an issue should the Jets have to replace one player, but the group's depth remains a big question after Friday's contest against the Steelers, and it's only getting worse.
There are legitimate questions surrounding the Jets' safety room. Most pressing among them is whether the organization is prepared to play Minkah Fitzpatrick as a center-field type safety, as opposed to the box to placate Belton's skill set.
Yes, it feels like a foregone conclusion that Belton has won the starting safety job opposite Fitzpatrick thanks to his physicality and improved coverage skills. He made numerous plays in practice, particularly against the run. While Andre Cisco is a quality third safety , especially in coverage, the Jets will need to be creative with how they break down the reps for this room.
There is some good news on this score. Breece Hall was seen working out on the side field, and Nahshon Wright returned to practice. Both players will be depended on heavily throughout the 2026 season, so seeing them return to the field either in a rehab capacity or full-time is a great thing.
There is still concern, though. D'Angelo Ponds has yet to participate in training camp, and Kenyon Sadiq was seen working on the side field. Both players are still in line for Week 1, but it's hard to see any legitimate role for the rookies without getting legitimate practice time.

title: 4 Jets on Thin Ice Heading Into Preseason Finale: Cade York, Braiden McGregor Fighting to Make 53-Man Roster
full_text:
Wins and losses in August don’t reflect how good or bad a team is. Still, it’s hard not to feel excited when your team wins—especially in dominating fashion.
That’s exactly what the New York Jets did Friday night, shutting out the Pittsburgh Steelers, 17-0, at Heinz Field. Several players stood out and strengthened their roster odds in the victory, like Jason Sanders and Jelani Woods. For the others, however, the night did more harm than good.
That said, here are the four Jets who are on thin ice heading into the preseason finale against the New York Giants.
York was one of several kickers the Jets brought in after Nick Folk’s departure and is a finalist for the starting kicking job alongside Sanders. Entering the first preseason game, York appeared to have the edge in the competition given his play in recent practices.
Despite making both of his field goal attempts against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, his 38-yard field goal attempt appeared to sail wide right. Meanwhile, Sanders converted his lone 47-yard try.
Since then, York has lost all momentum , and Sanders now has the advantage. In last Monday’s practice, Sanders outdueled York , making 7-of-8 field goal attempts, while the former LSU Tiger went 5-of-8, missing from 48, 51, and 54 yards.
York’s fall continued Friday night against the Steelers, missing a 59-yard field goal, while Sanders converted a 39-yard attempt.
Although there is still time for York to turn things around with a strong showing in this week’s slate of practices, he’ll need to prove himself in the preseason finale to make a strong impression with the coaching staff.
If it feels like McGregor has received several opportunities to earn a rotational role in the Jets’ defense, it’s because he has. In his two-year tenure with Gang Green, McGregor hasn’t proved himself useful on either defense or special teams, which is especially concerning given last year’s horrendous team.
The former Michigan Wolverine had chances to solidify his roster spot in the preseason but hasn’t been much of a factor. In 58 defensive snaps, he’s recorded just two pressures and two total tackles, per Pro Football Focus .
Meanwhile, Nate Lynn, who wasn’t even on the team at the beginning of the week, has outperformed McGregor despite playing in 31 fewer snaps, posting four total tackles and two sacks. Even though McGregor’s stock has fallen, he still has a legitimate path to making the 53-man roster.
The Jets could opt to keep five edge rushers, giving McGregor another opportunity to stick around. However, he’ll need to make a noticeable impact in the preseason finale to earn that spot. Otherwise, the Jets could look elsewhere for the final spot.
Zappe appeared to be the frontrunner for the QB2 role after OTAs, but he’s since fallen on the depth chart. Poor showings in minicamp and training camp have led to Zappe being surpassed by rookie Cade Klubnik, who has firmly established himself as the backup to Geno Smith.
His underwhelming play carried over into the preseason opener against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where he threw two interceptions. Although Zappe played better against the Steelers, completing 6-of-8 of his passes for 68 yards, Brady Cook got the better of him, capping off the game with a 31-yard touchdown pass.
Despite this, Zappe remains the favorite over Cook, as he continues to receive more reps than him. However, this doesn’t guarantee the veteran will make the 53-man roster. The Jets could look to bolster their quarterback depth through the trade market, with Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy and Eagles quarterback Andy Dalton potentially available if their respective teams decide to move on from them.
A strong performance in the preseason finale could help Zappe solidify his standing, but another underwhelming showing gives New York reason to explore its options elsewhere.
Trayanum has had a golden opportunity to earn a roster spot over these last few weeks. However, the former Toledo Rocket has failed to take advantage of increased reps with Isaiah Davis and Breece Hall sidelined with injuries.
Across two preseason games (31 offensive snaps), Trayanum has been inefficient running the ball, rushing for just 24 yards on nine attempts. Trayanum has arguably been worse in protection, allowing two pressures in five pass-blocking snaps, per PFF.
He’s also struggled to make an impact on special teams, missing a tackle and picking up a holding call on a kick return. Not only has his roster chances taken a massive hit, but Trayanum isn’t guaranteed to make New York's practice squad anymore.
If Trayanum is to remain in New York, he’ll need a strong showing against the Giants to keep his practice squad hopes alive. If not, the Jets could look elsewhere to find an RB to stash on the taxi squad.

title: 2 Reasons Why Geno Smith Can Succeed with Jets Despite Any Lingering Concerns
full_text:
The Jets have seen both the good and the bad side of veteran quarterback Geno Smith's game through the first month of training camp and the first two weeks of free agency.
When he's good, Smith is a productive thrower of the football, using his strong arm and years of experience to move the ball down the field with an assortment of weaponry by his side. However, when things aren't going well, Smith's gunslinger mentality has led to interceptions and stalled offensive production.
At 36 years old, it would be hard to find anyone who feels Smith can become a top-10 quarterback in the league. You simply can't teach an old dog new tricks, especially when that dog has thrown more interceptions than anyone in the last two years combined.
But if Friday night's 17-0 preseason win over the Steelers showed anything, it's that the Jets were not only right to bring Smith in for the 2026 season, but that he should be successful in his second stint with New York.
And there's two key reasons why.
Look at last year's offensive depth chart for the Raiders around Smith. Now look at the group playing with Smith this year in Florham Park. Most objective analysts and fans can agree that the Jets have the more impressive supporting cast than the Raiders.
While the Silver and Black have an excellent tight end in Brock Bowers, there really isn't a position last year where they had a better player than the current Jets roster does right now.
That's a fundamental difference that will aid Smith this season.
In his final year in Seattle, an organization one year away from a Super Bowl title, Smith won 10 games. He finished with 15 interceptions and at times looked like he held the team back, but still, 10 wins is nothing to scoff at.
That highlights one key part: if he has the right supporting cast, an NFL organization can win with Smith along for the ride. New York understands this reality, simply because they aren't paying him an  extreme amount of money to start for them in 2026. There is also no long-term guarantee he'll be around beyond the upcoming season.
But if the Jets' key players on offense —wide receiver Garrett Wilson, running back Breece Hall, and the stalwart tackles in Armand Membou and Olu Fashanu—all stay healthy, then Smith will have a cast that can allow him to distribute the ball evenly and on time.
Against Pittsburgh, the Jets saw that firsthand. New York's offense was unstoppable on its lone drive of the game that resulted in a touchdown. Much of that came down to Smith. But in a deeper sense, it had to do with the supporting cast as well.
That brings us to the second point too.
Smith went 7-for-7 for 65 yards and his lone touchdown pass. New York's offense converted several third downs, and four different receivers caught passes on the opening drive. That balanced distribution—coupled with a perfect passer rating—means Smith's day was efficient.
not a bad start 😮‍💨 📺: #NYJvsPIT on @NFLonCBS , @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/Ias9l0WIsu
If the Jets are going to find success in 2026, they'll need that word to be a central theme for the offense with Smith leading the way.
"Very efficient," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said of Smith's performance on Friday. "I think he had two 3rd down completions. Within that, he threw to five different receivers within that drive. He looked very comfortable, did exactly what we were looking for."
Smith's completion percentage shows of an efficient player. He has completed more than 64% of his passes in each of the last four seasons as a starter. With the Raiders, he completed 67% of his passes. It shows he wasn't the key problem for Las Vegas's offense last year.
If the Jets can get that kind of accuracy and efficiency from Smith, their offense will be significantly better than the last-place group from last season. Expectations aren't exactly too high to clear in 2026, but Gang Green should feel confident that Smith will be up to the task.
If anything, the unit showed on Friday they'll be a far better watch compared to last year.
And that might make all the distance for Jets fans.

title: Every Jet Who Helped Their 53-Man Roster Odds in the Win vs. Steelers (Including Jason Sanders)
full_text:
After falling to the Buccaneers to open the preseason, the Jets got their first exhibition win Friday night , shutting out the Steelers, 17-0.
We learned plenty from Gang Green’s victory . Geno Smith and the offense looked great in the opening drive, where he engineered a 10-play drive, going 7-for-7 for 65 yards and throwing a touchdown to Jelani Woods. At the same time, David Bailey recorded his first of (hopefully) many sacks.
The star players weren’t the only ones who shined. Several players on the bubble strengthened their chances of earning a spot on the 53-man roster with their performance. That being said, here are the five players who increased their chances of making the final roster.
Since joining the Jets in early June, Jason Sanders and Cade York have been in a back-and-forth competition for the starting kick job. While both players have made a compelling case over the last few months why they deserve the job, neither kicker had separated themselves until last week.
Sanders has emerged as the leader in the last few practices, particularly on Monday, when he converted 7-of-8 of his field goal attempts, while York made 5-of-8. The former All-Pro kicker strengthened his lead Friday night, nailing both his lone field goal and extra point attempt, while York missed his 59-yard attempt.
Although the battle is still far from being over, Sanders can establish himself as New York’s starting kicker with another solid week and by converting on all his field goal attempts.
With Kenyon Sadiq, Mason Taylor and Jeremy Ruckert at the top of the Jets’ tight end depth chart, Jelani Woods was considered an afterthought for a roster spot. Teams rarely carry four tight ends on their active roster, and the former 2022 third-round pick has played in just four games over the last three seasons combined.
For Woods to give himself any chance to earn a spot, he needed to capitalize on every opportunity. So far, he’s done just that. With Sadiq sidelined due to a setback from his hernia surgery, Woods has put together a string of solid performances in practice and has made a strong case for the final 53-man roster.
He bolstered his chances against the Steelers, capping off the opening drive with a touchdown. Woods has also made an impact as a blocker in the two preseason games, earning a 70.2 and 67.4 pass-blocking grade , respectively, per Pro Football Focus.
Another strong showing in the team’s preseason finale against the New York Giants could secure his roster spot.
Another player who was widely considered an unlikely candidate for a roster spot was Samuel Womack. With New York crowded at cornerback, the former 2022 fifth-round pick faced a challenging path to making the final roster
But with multiple injuries to the cornerback room, Womack has taken advantage of every opportunity and has been one of the standout players in the Jets' training camp. His play in coverage stood out in the victory against the Steelers, where he recorded an interception, allowed no receptions across 20 coverage snaps, and earned an 89.9 coverage grade per PFF .
Womack’s play so far has been encouraging and has put him on the right path to securing a spot on the 53-man roster. However, he’ll need to prove that he can be a reliable contributor on special teams to solidify a spot with New York.
Kiko Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball, and Mykal Walker have been competing for the Jets’ top backup role for the last few months. While each has had some solid moments in practice, none has firmly established themselves as a legitimate candidate.
This, along with New York not upgrading at the position, allowed Chase Wilson to make his case for a roster spot. The undrafted free agent out of West Virginia played a critical role in the team’s shutout win, leading the team in tackles alongside Jordan Clark with six while also recording two pressures and a sack.
Wilson also played well in coverage, being targeted once across 24 coverage snaps. While Wilson still faces an uphill battle to make the roster, his performance against Pittsburgh showed that he deserves to be in the conversation. He’ll need to continue making plays in the preseason finale to give himself a chance.
Talk about making a strong impression, Nate Lynn played a significant role in the Jets' win. Having just signed three days earlier, Lynn had the game of his life, recording four tackles, four pressures, and two sacks in 27 defensive snaps, earning an 85.9 pass-rush grade , per PFF .
Lynn remains a long shot to make the final roster given New York’s depth at edge rusher. However, his play against the Steelers has put him on the radar for the preseason finale. His previous experience with head coach Aaron Glenn in Detroit could also give him an advantage as he competes for a spot.
s/o Nate Lynn "it was a no brainer to get him here" pic.twitter.com/bcLcKqn5Ey
Still, the practice squad remains the likely outcome for Lynn. If he can replicate another strong showing against the Giants, though, New York may have a much tougher decision to make.

title: Major Concern No More: Jets' Defense Is Clearly Turning a Corner in Key Area
full_text:
History was made last year with the Jets, and not the kind of history teams want to make .
Much has been made about the Jets' failure to record an interception last year. No team in NFL history had failed to record one for an entire season up until that point. But New York took steps along the offseason to make sure that dubious distinction.
All-Pros like Minkah Fitzpatrick were added to the secondary. New York even drafted David Bailey to improve the pass rush as a way to force quarterbacks into more mistakes .
Through two preseason games, the investments seem to be paying off early. The Jets intercepted not one, but two Steeler passes in Friday's 17-0 win in the Steel City.
Andre Cisco in the right place at the right time 😌 NYJvsPIT on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/eLGuXJYqMB
While four-time NFL MVP Aaron Rodgers didn't throw either errant pass, it did highlight the Jets' improved mindset in forcing turnovers.
Even if there's still room to grow.
Former Pro Bowl cornerback Nahshon Wright was the first player to acknowledge the team's lack of interceptions last year. Instead of harping on the record, though, New York has focused more on improving the process they run that leads to forcing turnovers.
"I honestly don't think it's been brought up at all in meetings," Wright said. "I think 2025 was 2025, and I think we're trying to turn over a new leaf, so we haven't spoken about it at all."
Their improved mindset has already paid off. Andre Cisco got the party started with an interception in the first half. Samuel Womack III responded some time later with an interception of his own. Fitzpatrick and Wright did not record any interceptions. Nor did the combination of Brandon Stephens and AZ Thomas.
But one thing the Jets and head coach Aaron Glenn should be pleased with is their thought process, leading to an improvement in forcing turnovers.
Part of the reason why the Jets were so poor at creating turnovers last year was that they were also bad at getting to the quarterback. New York was among the worst teams in the league in both pressure rate and sacks. If quarterbacks have all day to throw, they won't make so many mistakes. It's why Glenn also addressed the trenches throughout the offseason .
He understands that if the team is to end its interception drought, it won't only come from players in the secondary, but also from getting after the quarterback.
If the Jets can get both sides of the ball to work together, they could bump their interception numbers considerably from last year.
It's also important to note that while the two-INT game on Friday will have fans celebrating, it mirrors last year's preseason. New York's last recorded pick in any game setting was in the preseason finale last year. That highlights a clear part of this whole problem as well.
Getting pressure on a quarterback and recording interceptions in practice and the preseason is one thing. Doing it when the games actually matter will be the next step in improving the current Jets defense.

title: 'Ferociousness:' How David Bailey Is Turning Heads During Jets' In-Game Setting
full_text:
Friday night could not have gone better for the New York Jets. They not only came away with a nice 17-0 victory over the Steelers, but the Jets players who needed to step up when it mattered most did .
Starting quarterback Geno Smith threw a touchdown pass, the defense recorded two interceptions, and there even appears to be a clear winner in the kicking battle so far.
Arguably the best part of the victory, though, came from the team's second overall pick. Rookie pass rusher David Bailey recorded a sack on a power rush move early in the contest. He also added a tackle for loss in the run game.
first of many for the No. 2 pick 📺: #NYJvsPIT on @NFLonCBS , @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/P6yF0fjJZ5
Bailey's total showing would excite every Jets fan. But for head coach Aaron Glenn, it wasn't anything he hadn't already seen.
"We know what (David) can do as far as a pass rusher, but obviously in my head there were a couple things that he has to improve on that showed up in the game, and he will," Glenn said. "He's there early every day working on his body and things like that. I know for a fact that he's going to improve on some of those mistakes that he had."
The Jets' coaching staff wants more from their top pick. The players around Bailey, though, know that he brings something new to the organization that they haven't had.
The first thing that stood out about Bailey over the course of training camp wasn't his pass-rushing ability. It was his never-ending motor that seemed to make him a "pain in the (EXPLETIVE)" to even the best offensive linemen on the team.
There's another word to describe Bailey's motor, though. And it comes from one of Bailey's top edge-rushing teammates , Joseph Ossai.
Expectations are as high as ever for Bailey after his latest preseason game. Not only did he make several plays against the run, but his pass rushing skill set gives the Jets something they simply haven't had in years: an edge rusher who seems to be just scratching the surface of what he can do.
As the organization prepares for its opening day contest against the Titans , the ferociousness that Bailey's teammates are using to describe him will be needed more than ever for himself and the Jets.
It might be the difference between Gang Green struggling in 2026 and finally laying the building blocks needed to show that the roster is improving after all.

title: How Aaron Glenn Is Already Succeeding as Jets' Defensive Play-Caller Before 2026 Season Begins
full_text:
It's head coach Aaron Glenn's superpower. For better or worse, it will drive the Jets through the 2026 season as well.
When Glenn announced at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine that he would call plays for the Jets' defense this year, the decision was met with some skepticism. Sure, he succeeded as a play-caller in Detroit, but the current head coach seemed to struggle with his wide range of duties last year.
Would he get better at the job while adding another key responsibility?
Through two preseason games, it's too early to tell whether the Jets will be successful as a play-caller. What is clear, though, is that the juggling act that Glenn appears to be on is working. From the player and coach perspective, things are on the up and up.
Early returns from Glenn's play-calling specifics proved beneficial to key starters along the unit. While every play-caller has tendencies, New York's head coach wants to make sure his players understand where he's coming from with each call.
Veterans like defensive lineman Harrison Phillips have commended Glenn for his openness in the line of communication.
"I really appreciate (that Glenn) comes into our defensive meeting and he'll explain his mindset going into certain situations," Phillips said. "The preseason game, we're not showing every play we have. But the way we're doing these little meetings—it's been some of the most fun meetings I've ever been a part of."
Through two preseason games, the Jets have liked what they have seen from their starting defense. In Friday's shutout victory over Pittsburgh , New York forced two turnovers and recovered a fumble. More importantly, the unit also racked up four sacks in the victory, as well as 17 pressures , according to Pro Football Focus .
While Gang Green's starters were going against backups, and that should be expected from the main group, the mistakes committed across the 2025 campaign at least show that improvement has been made from each level of the unit.
Especially from Glenn's basic scheme.
"This is the second week in a row where I thought our defense played fairly well," Glenn said after the win on Friday. "They were stout. But again, there are some things as far as our coverage that we've got to get better at, and I don't want to get too much into that, but I know for a fact that we've got to get better at some of those things. That's what training camp is for."
New York fans will get a better glimpse of Glenn's "superpower" early during the 2026 season.
The process the team is operating, though, is extremely important. In many ways, that process has worked well. Gang Green's run fits are far better than anything they showed last season, and an improvement at safety lets the team operate in unique ways to address their pass-defense concerns.
The 2026 Jets will hinge greatly on Glenn. If the head coach can call plays competently and improve his in-game management, the organization will be far better than it was last year and could challenge for an AFC playoff berth.
Through two preseason games, the Jets appear on that track, leaving it to time to tell if that trend will continue into the preseason finale against the Giants on Friday night.

title: What I'm Seeing in Jets' Position Battles Heading Into Final Week of Training Camp (Including Who's Leading)
full_text:
We're through two weeks of NFL preseason action, and the Jets are getting closer to knowing which position battles are at an end and which ones seem to just be getting started.
When camp first began, New York had clear battles going on at safety, receiver, kicker, and cornerback. While there is still a preseason game left to play and a few camp practices left, the Jets should approve of where each battle is.
Let's get to some of those updates now as the Jets head into the last week of the NFL preseason .
This contest hasn't been so much a position battle as it has been a domination by one player . Dane Belton was signed in free agency after a breakout performance the previous year with the Giants. New York wanted him to compete for the starting job opposite Minkah Fitzpatrick with Andre Cisco.
Through two preseason games and weeks of camp, Belton is firmly in command of winning the job. His physicality, tackling ability, and improved coverage skills have caught New York's eye. Cisco did come through with an interception during the Jets' preseason win on Friday, but his role seems to be best served as the third safety in the defense. Not as an every-down starter.
This battle may not be over . But if there's a current standing of who is in the lead, Jason Sanders would be my pick. The former Miami Dolphin All-Pro made his lone kick on Friday and has been consistent over the last week of practice.
The same cannot be said for Cade York. While he missed a very difficult 59-yard kick, a miss like that in Friday's game puts him behind in a position battle. He has also gone through his fair share of misses over the last few practices.
Things can, and probably will, change over the next few weeks, but it seems more likely now that Sanders will win the job.
Nahshon Wright has been dealing with an injury over the last few weeks, and that has opened the door to AZ Thomas putting the finishing touches on the position battle at cornerback opposite Brandon Stephens.
Has Thomas done enough, though?
That remains to be seen. While his size and physical nature are both seamless fits in the scheme head coach Aaron Glenn wants to run, the lack of speed and an over-aggressive nature all tend to be hindrances to Thomas' game.
As of now, I would say Thomas has won this position battle. But I would argue it has more to do with Wright's injury, more than Thomas's play, that has gotten us to this conclusion.
Plenty of Jets fans were put into a panic last week when Isaiah Williams, New York's special teams ace, was seen in snaps with the first team ahead of the team's first-round rookie. That panic lasted all of around five days.
Omar Cooper Jr. was seen running with the first-team offense in Friday's game, a clear indication that his prior standing was to allow the game to slow down for him. It was never an indication of the Jets seemingly not being pleased with his work.
I would expect Williams to still get plenty of reps with the starting offense, but as for who will be the third receiver option for the offense, my bet is still with Cooper.

title: 3 Jet Dark Horses Who Could Make the 53-Man Roster as Cuts Near
full_text:
As the New York Jets get closer to their Week 1 showdown against the Tennessee Titans , the organization must make final decisions on the 53-man roster. Cutdown day is still over a week away, but Gang Green should have a pretty good idea on who they want to keep.
That being said, while the Jets' 53-man roster appears to be all but set, there are three dark horses that are making a late case to get by the last round of cuts.
And after the team's victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday night in a road preseason contest, New York should be giving those dark horses more of a thought. Let's go through the list now.
No one has been more surprising or impressive as a dark horse than former San Francisco 49ers corner Samuel Womack. The former fifth-round pick has been excellent throughout training camp. He's competed hard and showed he deserves an opportunity to make plays.
On Friday against Pittsburgh, he showed what he could do. Womack picked off an errant throw in the second quarter in New York's win, and continued to lock players down throughout the first half. He won't be getting any starter reps, but has been more than deserving of a spot on the 53-man roster.
If camp and preseason production is any indication, Womack has been one of the biggest winners.
New York's starting linebacker duo is set. Jamien Sherwood and Demario Davis aren't going anywhere. But what happens behind them remains something of a question mark. Kiko Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball and Mykal Walker are all competing for a spot on the roster.
Now there's a newcomer that his making his presence felt.
Wilson was given a tryout at Jets minicamp and has made the most of his chance. On Friday, he led the team in tackles while recording a sack and tackle for loss. Impressively, he did this while also being a plus man in coverage. Pittsburgh did very little in the second half offensively and Wilson was one of the players why.
It will be a longshot for him to make the 53, but it's clear Wilson won't go down quietly. If anything, he's an underrated player that's making a name for himself at the end of camp.
It was once thought of as ludicrous that an NFL team would keep four tight ends on their 53-man roster. There are simply other spots that are needed with more attention.
The New York Jets are going to be going against the grain when they do that this year, but it will be for a very good reason. Jelani Woods has bounced around practice squads over the last few years, but he has more than deserved a role on the 53-man roster this season.
In the team's preseason win over Pittsburgh Friday, Woods caught the lone touchdown of the game and was stingy as a blocker. He won't be playing over the likes of Mason Taylor or Kenyon Sadiq, but Woods has deserved his standing.
